The system is internally coherent insofar as faculty distinction, cognitive cooperation, and logical purification perform different functions rather than mutually cancelling one another.
The reconstruction remains underdetermined concerning how conceptions are connected to intuitions in a cognition of determinate objects.
The structure is strongest where it separates the normative validity of pure logic from empirical descriptions of human cognitive performance.
The structure depends on an asserted asymmetry between formal laws of thought and psychological laws of mental occurrence without yet demonstrating that asymmetry.

The designation of applied logic as merely cathartic creates a tension because it treats empirically conditioned thought as indispensable for human use while denying it the status of proper logical science.
General logic abstracts from the content of cognition and from cognition’s relation to objects, retaining only the formal relations among cognitions.
The distinction between pure and empirical intuition entails a corresponding distinction between pure and empirical thought of objects.
A logic of pure thought cannot abstract from all content because it investigates the a priori relation of thought to objects while excluding empirical content.
Transcendental status belongs not to every a priori cognition but to cognition of the a priori possibility or use of representations in relation to objects.
The transcendental/empirical distinction therefore concerns the critique of cognition rather than a division among objects themselves.
A science determining the origin, extent, and objective validity of pure object-directed cognition is designated transcendental logic.
General logic abstracts from all content of cognition and from cognition’s relation to its object.
General logic examines only the formal laws governing the relations among cognitions.
General logic treats representations according to their logical use regardless of whether their source is pure a priori or empirical.
Pure and empirical intuition permit a corresponding distinction between pure and empirical thought of objects.
A logic of pure thought of objects cannot abstract from all content because it excludes cognitions containing empirical content while retaining a priori object-directed cognition.
A logic distinct from general logic must examine the origin of cognition insofar as that origin cannot be attributed to objects themselves.
Transcendental cognition concerns the a priori possibility or a priori use of representations in relation to objects.
The mere a priori character of a representation does not make that representation transcendental.
Space and a priori geometrical determinations are not themselves transcendental representations.
Knowledge that a representation is non-empirical and can relate to objects of experience a priori is transcendental.
Applying space to objects in general is transcendental, whereas restricting its application to objects of sense is empirical.
The transcendental/empirical distinction belongs to the critique of cognitions and does not classify objects themselves.
Pure concepts can function as acts of pure thought that are neither empirical nor aesthetic in origin.
A science of pure understanding must determine the origin, extent, and objective validity of pure object-directed cognitions.
Transcendental logic concerns the a priori relation of pure understanding and reason to objects, whereas general logic treats empirical and pure cognitions without distinction of this kind.
General logic is not an inquiry into the origin of cognitions.
General logic is not restricted to pure cognition or to pure thought of objects.
Transcendental cognition is not identical with cognition that merely happens to be a priori.
Space is not itself a transcendental representation.
An a priori geometrical determination is not itself transcendental.
The application of space to objects of sense is not transcendental but empirical.
Transcendentality is not a property assigned directly to objects.
Transcendental logic does not include empirical content as constitutive material.
Pure concepts are not derived from empirical or aesthetic sources.
Formal laws governing thought in general do not by themselves constitute a science of a priori object cognition.
Because general logic brackets both content and origin, it can apply its formal laws to representations from any source.
A priori origin is insufficient for transcendental status; the representation must also be considered according to its a priori applicability or possibility in relation to objects.
The same basic representation can receive transcendental or empirical status according to the scope of its application.
Transcendental inquiry must combine an account of origin with an account of possibility, use, extent, and objective validity.
Transcendental logic retains object-directed content at the level of a priori relation while excluding empirical content from the pure science.
The decisive difference between general and transcendental logic is not the presence of a priori cognition but the examination of its a priori relation to objects.
Formal logical validity cannot establish the objective validity of pure object-directed cognition without a separate transcendental inquiry.
Pure understanding can be investigated as a source of object-directed concepts without reducing those concepts to sensory intuition or empirical acquisition.
Transcendental logic occupies an intermediate structural position between source-indifferent formal logic and empirical cognition of particular objects.
The notion of content is internally divided: empirical material is excluded, while the a priori mode of object-directed cognition remains operative.
Transcendentality is relocated from the mere possession of representations to the conditions governing their a priori use and objective reach.
The system makes the scope of application an epistemic determinant: universal object-reference and sensible-object reference do not carry the same status.
The proposed science converts pure understanding from a presumed faculty into an object of inquiry whose origin, limits, and validity must be established.
The argument displaces the question of object cognition from formal consistency alone to the conditions under which pure thought can have objective validity.
Pure a priori origin cannot by itself ground transcendental status.
Empirical origin cannot serve as the explanatory ground of the pure object-directed cognition under investigation.
Empirical content cannot constitute the material of a science of pure understanding.
Formal logical form cannot by itself determine the objective validity of cognition.
Transcendental analysis cannot be reduced to an ontology of objects.
A representation cannot be identified with the conditions governing its use.
The distinction between transcendental and empirical cannot be settled by source alone; it requires analysis of object-directed applicability.
The system excludes both the reduction of cognition to empirical derivation and the reduction of transcendentality to bare a priori form.
No direct passage from pure thought to objectively valid cognition is admitted without an intervening inquiry into possibility, extent, and validity.
No object-independent formal logic exhausts the conditions of object cognition, yet no empirical object-content can ground the pure science.
The transcendental is not an ontological realm of objects but a critical status assigned to cognition’s a priori relation to objects.
The text forecloses any framework in which the distinction between transcendental and empirical is determined solely by the objects considered.
Cognition has content and object-relation → general logic abstracts from both → only formal relations among cognitions remain.
Pure and empirical intuition are distinguished → pure and empirical thought of objects become distinguishable → a non-general logic becomes necessary.
Pure thought of objects is isolated → empirical content is excluded → a priori object-directed content remains as the domain of inquiry.
A representation is a priori → its a priori applicability or possibility in relation to objects is examined → transcendental status is assigned only where that relation is established.
Application is universal or object-general → the application is transcendental; application is restricted to sensible objects → the application is empirical.
Origin, extent, and objective validity are made into explicit questions → a science of pure understanding and rational cognition is constituted → that science is named transcendental logic.

Abstraction of cognition’s content and object-relation → distinction between pure and empirical thought → retention of a priori object-directed content → criterion of transcendental use → separation of universal from sensible application → science of origin, extent, and objective validity → transcendental logic.
Transcendentality is reclassified from a feature of an isolated representation to a feature of its a priori possibility or use in relation to objects.
The boundary between general logic and transcendental logic is redrawn around object-directed a priori validity rather than around the simple presence or absence of formal thought.
The opposition between a priori and empirical is made scope-sensitive: one representation can receive different statuses according to the domain of its application.
The origin of cognition becomes philosophically relevant only when distinguished from derivation through objects.
Objective validity is transformed from an implicit assumption of pure thought into a problem that the proposed science must determine.
The object of logical inquiry expands from the form of thinking in general to the conditions under which pure thought can relate to objects.
Surface — The text distinguishes general logic from transcendental logic and pure thought from empirical thought.
Structural — The distinction is generated by different treatments of content, origin, object-relation, applicability, scope, and validity.
Metastrategic — The argument establishes a criterion for identifying which a priori cognitions belong to a critique of object-directed cognition rather than to formal logic in general.

Ontological/Temporal — The system treats objects as termini of cognition rather than as the direct determinants of transcendental status, and treats a priori priority as a condition of use rather than as sufficient proof of validity.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the distinction between general logic, pure thought, empirical thought, and transcendental logic.
The formal sequence preserves the argument’s movement from abstraction through differentiation to the proposal of a new science.
The extracted system leaves the specific contents of pure understanding and the detailed proof of their objective validity underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent provided transcendentality is treated as a critical status of cognition rather than as a property of representations or objects in isolation.
The system is strongest in distinguishing a priori givenness from transcendental use and in making application-scope epistemically decisive.
The principal unresolved tension is that transcendental logic must retain object-directed content while simultaneously excluding empirical content from its domain.
A second unresolved tension is that the science is defined by its task of determining objective validity before that validity has itself been demonstrated.

units.title: III. Of the Division of General Logic into Analytic and Dialectic.

items.text: The demand for a universal and secure criterion of truth is tested against the definition of truth as accordance between cognition and its object.
A criterion valid for all cognitions must abstract from their objects and therefore from the content upon which material truth depends.
The demand for a universal material criterion of truth is therefore self-contradictory.
General logic can supply only formal criteria that exclude self-contradiction, not criteria that establish agreement with objects.
Logic is consequently a negative canon for testing cognition, not an organon for producing objective knowledge.
Dialectic arises when formal logic is misused as an organon and is therefore recast as the critique of this illusion.
Truth consists in the accordance of cognition with its object.
The truth or falsity of a cognition depends on the particular object to which that cognition relates.
A universal criterion of truth must apply to cognitions without distinction of their objects.
A criterion that abstracts from all objects also abstracts from the content of cognition.
Material truth depends on the content of cognition and its relation to an object.
The universal laws of understanding provide criteria for the formal consistency of thought.
Contradiction with the universal laws of understanding is sufficient for formal falsity.
Formal consistency does not establish agreement between cognition and its object.
Objective judgment requires information about objects obtained independently of general logic.
General logic becomes dialectical when it is treated as an instrument for extending objective knowledge.
Dialectic, in its legitimate sense, is the critique of the illusion produced by the organonic misuse of general logic.
No universal criterion can establish the material truth of all cognitions.
Formal accordance with logical laws is not objective truth.
General logic is not a source of cognition about objects.
General logic is not an organon for the extension of knowledge.
Logical non-contradiction does not exclude material error.
Dialectic is not a positive method for generating objective assertions.
The universality of a truth-criterion can be retained only by restricting it to form, thereby abandoning any claim to certify material truth.
Logical laws function as necessary conditions of truth because every objectively valid cognition must at least avoid self-contradiction.
Analytic is the legitimate function of general logic because it resolves formal cognition into elements and tests those elements negatively.
Material investigation must follow logical testing because logic can invalidate incoherent cognition but cannot establish its objective content.
Any apparently objective assertion generated from formal logic alone possesses only the semblance of knowledge.
Dialectical illusion is structurally enabled by the fact that formal correctness can imitate the appearance of truth without supplying objective validity.
The very abstraction that makes logic universally applicable also prevents it from determining the truth of object-directed cognition.
The distinction between canon and organon separates the regulation of already given cognition from the production of cognition about objects.
Error divides into formal contradiction, which logic can detect, and material discordance with objects, which logic cannot detect by itself.
Critique becomes necessary not because logic is invalid, but because valid formal procedure can be illegitimately converted into apparent objective knowledge.
Objective reference cannot be generated from the universal form of thought alone.
The laws governing thought cannot, merely by governing thought, guarantee that thought reaches objects.
Truth is not reducible to consistency within cognition.
A universally valid procedure cannot supply universal material knowledge merely by being universally valid.
The absence of contradiction is not a positive ground of objectivity.
No direct transition from subjective logical form to objective truth is available within general logic.
The positive source of objectively valid content remains outside the resources of general logic.
The system forecloses the possibility that logic alone could be self-authorizing as knowledge of objects.
The discourse is organized around the unavailability of a universal positive mark of material truth.
Truth as cognition–object accordance → object-relative content becomes indispensable to material truth.
Demand for a universal criterion → abstraction from objects and content → incapacity to certify material truth.
Retention of formal laws → exclusion of contradiction → necessary but insufficient condition of truth.
Formal canon treated as objective organon → production of merely apparent knowledge → dialectical illusion.
Dialectical illusion identified → organonic pretension withdrawn → dialectic becomes critique.
Truth defined as object-relative accordance → universal truth-criterion demanded → content necessarily abstracted → material criterion shown impossible.
Material criterion denied → formal logical laws retained → contradiction excluded → logic established as negative test.
Negative test mistaken for productive knowledge → formal appearance mistaken for objectivity → dialectic identified as illusion → critique instituted.
Truth is divided into material truth concerning objects and formal truth concerning consistency of thought.
Logic is reclassified from a purported producer of knowledge into a restrictive test governing the permissible form of cognition.
Dialectic is reclassified from a technique of argument into a diagnostic category for the illusion of formal knowledge-production.
Error is redrawn as containing an irreducibly material dimension that cannot be resolved by formal analysis alone.
The apparent opposition between rigorous logic and empty sophistry is reorganized, since sophistry can borrow rigor’s formal appearance without its objective ground.
Surface — The text determines whether general logic can provide a universal criterion for the truth of cognition.
Structural — The text distinguishes formal laws of thought from the object-related content required for material truth.
Metastrategic — The text limits the legitimate use of logic by separating critical regulation from the production of objective claims.
Epistemic — The text presupposes that objective validity requires a relation to objects not supplied by universal formal laws.
Temporal-Methodological — The text orders inquiry so that formal testing precedes, but cannot replace, examination of the material validity of cognition.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the argument from the definition of truth through the impossibility of a universal material criterion to the critical delimitation of logic.
The system is internally coherent if material truth and formal consistency are maintained as distinct conditions of cognition.
The structure is strongest where it derives the impossibility of a universal material truth-criterion from the abstraction required by universality.
The system leaves underdetermined the source, status, and validation of the independently obtained information that objective judgment requires.
The system depends on the unargued persistence of the correspondence definition of truth while using that definition to restrict what logic can establish.
The decisive tension is that logic is universally necessary for judging cognition but structurally incapable of furnishing the objectivity that truth requires.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the negative function of logic is kept distinct from any positive theory of how cognition reaches objects.

identity.title: III. Of the Division of General Logic into Analytic and Dialectic.

units.title: IV. Of the Division of Transcendental Logic into Transcendental Analytic and Dialectic.

items.text: Transcendental logic isolates the understanding and examines cognition originating from it alone.
Pure understanding has objective validity only when its concepts are applied to objects given in intuition.
Transcendental analytic identifies the elements and principles required for any object to be thought and thereby functions as a logic of truth.
The understanding becomes dialectical when it treats its formal principles as materially valid beyond possible experience.
Transcendental dialectic critiques the illusion produced by this hyperphysical use of understanding and reason.
The proper role of transcendental logic is therefore to regulate empirical judgment and prevent sophistical overreach, not to generate unrestricted cognition.
Transcendental logic isolates the understanding from sensibility and examines its pure cognition.
The application of pure cognition requires objects to be given in intuition.
Cognition without intuition has no objects and is therefore void of content.
Transcendental analytic contains the elements and principles without which no object can be thought.
The principles of transcendental analytic constitute the conditions of objective validity and truth.
Experience is the source from which the matter or objects required by pure concepts is obtained.
Pure understanding is prone to extend its formal principles beyond the limits of possible experience.
The use of pure understanding beyond possible experience produces judgments about objects that are not given and may not be giveable.
Transcendental logic is properly a canon regulating the empirical use of understanding.
Transcendental dialectic critiques the hyperphysical use of understanding and reason and guards judgment against sophistical illusion.
Pure cognition is not self-sufficient apart from intuition.
Cognition without reference to an object is not genuine cognition.
Formal principles of understanding are not by themselves material knowledge of objects.
Transcendental logic is not an organon for the universal and unlimited exercise of understanding.
Pure understanding cannot legitimately determine objects in general without their being given.
Transcendental dialectic is not an art for producing metaphysical illusion.
Transcendental principles do not by themselves discover or enlarge cognition beyond experience.
A pure concept becomes objectively empty when no intuition supplies an object for its application.
The truth of a cognition depends not only on formal consistency but also on reference to an object.
Transcendental analytic can function as a logic of truth only within the conditions that make object-reference possible.
Extending the categories beyond possible experience converts a canon of judgment into an illegitimate organon of object-production.
Judgments concerning objects that cannot be given lack the material conditions required for objective determination.
Dialectical illusion arises when the understanding mistakes the formal conditions of thinking for sufficient grounds of knowledge.
Critique must assess the legitimacy of judgments made through pure principles rather than extend those principles into new domains.
The distinction between analytic and dialectic is generated by the difference between legitimate object-directed use and illegitimate object-independent use of pure principles.
The same formal structures that make objective cognition possible become sources of illusion when detached from the conditions of their application.
The boundary of possible experience is simultaneously the boundary between truth-producing cognition and empty metaphysical pretension.
Transcendental critique transforms the task of reason from expanding cognition by pure principles to policing the conditions and limits of their valid use.
The validity of a concept is not secured by its logical form alone.
The possibility of thinking an object does not entail the possibility of knowing or encountering that object.
A faculty’s possession of formal principles does not authorize unrestricted synthesis concerning objects.
The absence of intuition cannot be compensated for by increasing abstraction, formal rigor, or transcendental speculation.
The critique of metaphysics cannot itself operate as an alternative metaphysical organon.
Unconditioned cognition of objects through pure understanding alone is excluded.
A domain of objectivity independent of intuition and possible experience is excluded.
The self-authorizing expansion of cognition through transcendental principles is excluded.
The possibility that formal thought can generate its own objective matter is excluded.
The understanding is isolated as the source of pure cognition.
Pure cognition is subordinated to intuition as the condition of object-reference.
The principles securing object-thought are constituted as transcendental analytic and as a logic of truth.
The detachment of these principles from intuition and experience produces empty synthetic judgments and dialectical illusion.
Transcendental dialectic is instituted as the critique that exposes this detachment and restores the principles to their regulative, empirical function.
Isolation of pure understanding → dependence on intuition → constitution of analytic truth → misuse beyond experience → production of dialectical illusion → critical restriction of reason.
Formal condition of thought → required object-reference → boundary of possible experience → exposure of hyperphysical overreach → canon rather than organon.
The distinction between analytic and dialectic is relocated from two subjects of logic to two uses of pure cognitive principles.
Objectivity is reclassified as requiring both formal conditions of thought and intuitively given content.
Metaphysical error is reclassified from simple falsehood to the misuse of valid formal principles outside their domain.
Critique is reclassified from a generator of higher knowledge into a regulator of the legitimacy of cognition.
The boundary of experience becomes a functional boundary separating truth-bearing judgment from empty synthesis.
Surface — Pure understanding is distinguished from intuition, and transcendental logic is divided into analytic and dialectic.
Structural — Objective cognition requires the conjunction of formal principles with intuitively supplied matter.
Metastrategic — The proper critical strategy is to test the use of principles and block their conversion from canon into unlimited organon.
Ontological/Temporal — Objects are cognitively available only under conditions of possible intuition and experience; beyond those conditions, formal thought loses objective reference.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the division between transcendental analytic and transcendental dialectic.
The system is internally coherent insofar as objective validity requires both formal conditions and given intuition.
The central unresolved tension is that pure understanding supplies necessary conditions for object-thought while remaining unable to produce objects or their matter.
The relation between intuition, experience, and objects that may never be given is compressed rather than fully differentiated.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement from the conditions of truth to the critique of their hyperphysical misuse.

identity.title: IV. Of the Division of Transcendental Logic into Transcendental Analytic and Dialectic.

units.title: First Division. Transcendental Logic. Transcendental Analytic. § 1

items.text: Transcendental analytic seeks to dissect a priori cognition into the elementary constituents of pure understanding.
Its objects must be pure, intellectual, elementary, and exhaustive of the sphere of pure understanding.
Exhaustiveness cannot be established through an empirical aggregate of repeated observations or attempts.
Completeness requires an idea of the totality of a priori understanding and a systematic division determined by that idea.
Pure understanding is autonomous from both empirical cognition and sensibility.
The systematic completeness and articulation of pure understanding provide a criterion for testing the legitimacy of its components.
The system is organized into the concepts and principles of pure understanding.
Transcendental analytic concerns the elements of a priori cognition belonging to understanding.
The proper conceptions of transcendental analytic are pure rather than empirical.
The proper conceptions belong to thought and understanding rather than to intuition and sensibility.
The proper conceptions are elementary rather than deduced or compound.
The table of elementary conceptions must be complete across the whole sphere of pure understanding.
Empirical aggregation cannot establish the completeness of a science of pure understanding.
Completeness requires an idea of the totality of a priori cognition of the understanding.
The division of elementary conceptions must be determined through their connection within a system.
Pure understanding is self-subsistent and self-sufficient.
Pure understanding cannot be enlarged by additions from outside itself.
The cognition of pure understanding forms a system governed by an idea of totality.
Systematic completeness and articulation can test the correctness and genuineness of individual cognitions.
The system of transcendental analytic contains separate divisions for the conceptions and principles of pure understanding.
Pure understanding is not empirical.
The elementary conceptions are not derived from intuition or sensibility.
The elementary conceptions are not deduced or compound conceptions.
Completeness is not an empirical aggregate produced by repeated experiments and attempts.
Pure understanding is not dependent on additions from outside itself.
The table of pure concepts is not a partial or merely provisional inventory.
The system is not an unconnected collection of cognitions.
The legitimacy of a cognition is not secured independently of its systematic place.
The objects of transcendental analytic must be selected by their relation to pure understanding rather than by their occurrence in experience.
A conception qualifies as elementary only when it is neither composed from other conceptions nor obtained through derivation.
A complete table requires a principle capable of determining the entire domain to be tabulated.
The criterion of completeness is architectonic rather than inductive.
The relations among conceptions are constitutive of the table’s completeness, not merely explanatory after the table has been assembled.
The autonomy of pure understanding entails that its elements must be sought within a self-contained domain.
The systematic form of cognition allows the whole to function as a criterion for its parts.
The division between conceptions and principles is required by the internal organization of the system of pure understanding.
The system of pure understanding is generated deductively from an anticipated totality rather than reconstructed retrospectively from collected instances.
The validity of individual categories is inseparable from the completeness and articulation of the system that contains them.
Pure understanding is treated as a closed epistemic domain whose boundaries are established by its own form rather than by external material.
The argument converts classification into a test of legitimacy: a conception is authenticated through its necessary place within the complete system.
The subsequent architecture of transcendental logic is predetermined as a movement from elementary conceptions to the principles they organize.
The system cannot be grounded in an open-ended accumulation of observations.
The system cannot admit sensibility as a constitutive source of the pure concepts under investigation.
The system cannot treat its elementary units as arbitrary analytical subdivisions.
The system cannot recognize an external supplement capable of completing pure understanding.
The system cannot validate its parts through isolated inspection detached from totality.
The system cannot regard incompleteness as a neutral condition of the science.
The possibility that the domain of pure understanding is fundamentally unbounded is foreclosed.
The possibility that experience supplies the final standard for the classification of pure concepts is excluded.
The possibility of a legitimate pure cognition lacking systematic necessity is disallowed.
The argument presupposes that the totality of pure understanding can be conceptually determined before every element has been exhibited.
The system leaves no internal place for an unassimilated remainder within pure understanding.
A priori cognition of understanding → isolation of its elements → restriction to pure, intellectual, elementary conceptions.
Requirement of completeness → rejection of empirical aggregation → appeal to an idea of totality.
Idea of totality → systematic division of conceptions → determination of the complete table.
Systematic totality → reciprocal test of whole and parts → validation of the correctness and genuineness of cognitions.
Autonomous pure understanding → self-contained system → division into conceptions and principles.
Dissection of a priori understanding → specification of purity, intellectuality, elementarity, and completeness.
Demand for completeness → exclusion of empirical enumeration.
Exclusion of enumeration → positing of totality as the organizing idea.
Organizing totality → systematic division and interconnection of elementary conceptions.
Systematic interconnection → whole-to-part test of validity.
Self-sufficient understanding → twofold architecture of concepts and principles.
Completeness is relocated from the accumulation of content to the structure of a system.
The boundary between pure understanding and sensibility becomes a constitutive boundary of the science.
Classification is transformed from inventory-making into the determination of necessary relations within a totality.
Individual cognitions become assessable through their systematic position rather than through isolated examination.
Transcendental logic is mapped as an internally articulated domain with concepts as one level and principles as another.
Surface — The immediate task is the analysis of a priori cognition into elementary conceptions of pure understanding.
Structural — The possibility of a complete table depends on systematic totality, internal division, and reciprocal relation between whole and parts.
Metastrategic — The argument replaces empirical discovery with architectonic determination as the method for securing completeness.
Ontological/Temporal — Pure understanding is presupposed as an autonomous, self-sufficient unity whose totality can guide the determination of its elements prior to their complete exposition.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from transcendental analysis to systematic completeness.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between purity, intellectuality, elementarity, and completeness.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s central methodological opposition between systematic determination and empirical aggregation.
The exact contents of the elementary conceptions and principles remain underdetermined because the table itself is deferred.
The system is internally coherent insofar as autonomy, totality, systematic division, and whole-to-part validation mutually reinforce one another.
A structural tension remains between the claim that pure understanding is self-sufficient and the need for an idea of totality to determine its completeness.
A second tension remains between using systematic completeness to validate the parts and presupposing the totality required to construct that system.
Reconstruction preserves the real argumentative movement but cannot independently establish whether the promised table is actually complete.

identity.title: First Division. Transcendental Logic. Transcendental Analytic. § 1

items.text: The problem is to determine how conceptions à priori are possible.
The inquiry is reframed from analysing given conceptions to analysing the faculty of understanding that produces them.
The understanding is treated as the proper birthplace of pure conceptions.
Transcendental philosophy investigates the pure use of this faculty, while general philosophy retains the logical treatment of conceptions.
Pure conceptions are traced from their germs in understanding through their empirical occasions to their separation from empirical conditions and presentation in purity.
An analytic of conceptions is not primarily the dissection of the content of given conceptions.
The faculty of understanding can itself be analysed.
The possibility of conceptions à priori must be investigated through the understanding alone.
The understanding is the birthplace of pure conceptions.
Transcendental philosophy is concerned with the pure use of the understanding.
The logical treatment of conceptions belongs to philosophy in general rather than to the distinctive task of transcendental philosophy.
Pure conceptions possess germs and beginnings in the human understanding prior to their empirical development.
Experience provides occasions on which conceptions already rooted in understanding are developed.
The understanding can remove empirical conditions from conceptions developed through experience.
A conception can be distinguished from the empirical conditions through which it becomes manifest.
An analytic of conceptions is not the ordinary clarification of conceptions by dissecting their content.
The origin of conceptions à priori is not sought in experience.
Transcendental philosophy is not reducible to the logical treatment of conceptions.
Pure conceptions are not constituted by the empirical conditions under which they are first developed.
The inquiry does not begin with already presented conceptions as its ultimate objects.
The possibility of a priori cognition requires an inquiry into the producing faculty rather than only into the products of cognition.
The analysis of the understanding must be transcendental because it concerns the conditions under which conceptions can be possible prior to experience.
The purity of a conception is determined by the understanding’s capacity to distinguish its own contribution from empirical conditions.
Experience functions as an activating occasion for pure conceptual germs rather than as their sufficient origin.
The investigation must proceed genetically from the beginnings of conceptions in understanding to their developed and purified form.
The distinction between transcendental and general philosophy is established by separating the investigation of the faculty’s pure operation from the logical handling of its conceptions.
The text establishes a layered model of conception in which origin, activation, empirical contamination, and purification are distinct moments.
The understanding is simultaneously the source of a priori form, the agent of conceptual development, and the instrument of purification.
The text converts the relation between a priori and empirical cognition from a simple opposition into a sequence of germination, occasion, development, and abstraction.
The legitimacy of transcendental philosophy depends on preserving both the non-empirical origin of pure conceptions and their empirical occasions of manifestation.
The system excludes the claim that conceptual necessity can be established by analysing only the content of concepts already in use.
The system excludes an empiricist account in which experience generates the conceptual forms it merely occasions.
The system excludes a faculty-transcendent source of pure conceptions; the relevant source must be internal to understanding.
The system excludes a conception of purity as absolute isolation from experience; purity is achieved through the removal of empirical conditions from an empirically occasioned development.
The system excludes a static account of a priori conceptions by requiring their recovery through germs, development, and purification.
The argument cannot permit experience to be either the complete origin or an irrelevant background to pure conceptions.
The argument forecloses a separation between the understanding as source and the understanding as historically activated by experience.
The system leaves no legitimate account of conception in which empirical development alters the a priori ground itself; development must expose or elaborate what understanding already contains.
The text’s force depends on the unavailability of a neutral standpoint outside both the understanding and its empirical occasions.
Given conceptions are encountered → their content-based analysis is rejected as insufficient.
The object of inquiry shifts from conceptual products to the faculty that produces them.
The understanding is isolated as the birthplace of conceptions à priori.
The pure use of understanding is assigned to transcendental philosophy.
Pure conceptual germs are traced through occasions supplied by experience.
Empirical conditions are removed by the same understanding that developed the conceptions.
The resulting conceptions are presented as unalloyed and a priori.
Content-analysis of given conceptions → inadequacy of the ordinary analytic.
Inadequacy → analysis of the understanding itself.
Analysis of understanding → identification of its a priori conceptual germs.
A priori germs + empirical occasions → developmental account of conception.
Developmental account → separation of conceptual form from empirical conditions.
Separation → transcendental presentation of pure conceptions.
The object of analysis is reclassified from concepts as contents to understanding as a generative faculty.
Experience is reclassified from origin of a priori conceptions to occasion for their development.
Purity is reclassified from absence of experiential contact to abstraction from empirical conditions.
Transcendental philosophy is separated from general logical analysis by assigning each a distinct operative task.
The history of a conception is divided into its internal germ, empirical activation, and transcendental purification.
Surface — The text defines what is meant by an “Analytic of Conceptions.”
Structural — The argument distinguishes the understanding, experience, and the logical treatment of concepts as different functions within one conceptual process.
Metastrategic — The inquiry is redirected from analysing products to recovering the conditions and operations that generate them.
Ontological/Temporal — Conceptions are treated as possessing an a priori origin, an empirical developmental occasion, and a later purification into unalloyed form.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the shift from ordinary conceptual analysis to transcendental analysis.
The axioms preserve the distinction between a priori origin and empirical occasion.
The axioms preserve the distinction between transcendental philosophy and general logical treatment.
The system is internally coherent if empirical development is understood as activation rather than production of pure conceptual germs.
The principal unresolved tension lies between the claim that conceptions are found in understanding alone and the claim that they develop on occasions supplied by experience.
The reconstruction depends on treating purification as an operation performed by understanding rather than as the discovery of concepts untouched by experience.
The extracted structure preserves the argument’s movement from rejected content-analysis to faculty-analysis, genetic tracing, and purification.
The problem is that mechanically discovered conceptions do not yield a determinate or systematic totality.
Mere resemblance and graded complexity organize conceptions without establishing their necessary order.
Transcendental philosophy reframes the task as the principled discovery of conceptions arising purely from the understanding.
Because pure conceptions are treated as expressions of an absolute unity, their relations must be governed by a single ordering conception or idea.
The governing principle makes possible both the assignment of each conception to its proper place and the a priori determination of the system’s completeness.
The uncontrolled exercise of a cognitive faculty produces conceptions according to variable circumstances and degrees of investigative effort.
Mechanically discovered conceptions do not disclose in advance where their accumulation will end.
Conceptions discovered without a governing principle lack systematic order and unity.
Resemblance and increasing quantity of content can arrange conceptions into series without generating a systematic structure.
Transcendental philosophy must seek pure conceptions according to a principle.
Pure conceptions arise unmixed from the understanding as an absolute unity.
Conceptions arising from an absolute unity must be connected according to one conception or idea.
A governing connection supplies a rule for assigning each pure conception its proper place.
The same governing connection permits the a priori determination of the system’s completeness.
The discovery of conceptions is not sufficient merely because additional conceptions continue to manifest themselves.
A mechanically accumulated collection is not a determinate system.
Resemblance is not a sufficient principle of systematic connection.
A series from the simpler to the more complex is not thereby a systematic order.
The completeness of the system is not to depend on choice or chance.
Without a governing principle, the inventory of conceptions remains open-ended and its endpoint cannot be established.
Similarity can produce classificatory proximity without establishing the necessary relation among conceptions.
Systematic unity requires more than ordering conceptions by their amount or complexity of content.
If pure conceptions originate in one unity, their systematic articulation must be generated from that unity rather than assembled externally.
The principle that orders the conceptions also functions as a criterion for identifying what belongs to the system.
The passage converts the problem of discovering conceptions into the problem of deriving and locating them within a closed systematic order.
Systematicity is treated as a condition of epistemic legitimacy rather than as an optional improvement in presentation.
The same unity that grounds the conceptions supplies both their internal relations and the possibility of proving that none are missing.
A priori completeness becomes possible only when classification is subordinated to derivation from a common principle.
The system excludes the assumption that the totality of pure conceptions can be secured by indefinite empirical or psychological observation.
The system excludes the assumption that accumulation eventually reveals its own completeness.
The system excludes a pluralism of conceptions lacking a unifying ground.
The system excludes external or accidental relations as adequate grounds for the internal organization of pure conceptions.
The system excludes the separation of classification from the question of whether the inventory is complete.
The argument depends on the impossibility of treating the understanding as a merely additive source of independent conceptions.
It forecloses a conception of knowledge in which order is imposed only after discovery and has no grounding in the faculty itself.
It treats an unprovable boundary between the known and the still undiscovered as incompatible with a complete system of pure conceptions.
The argument’s force depends on denying that contingency can remain at the foundation of transcendental classification.
Variable cognitive exercise → contingent manifestation of conceptions → indeterminate accumulation.
Indeterminate accumulation → resemblance-based association and complexity-based sequencing → non-systematic collection.
Non-systematic collection → demand for a governing principle supplied by transcendental philosophy.
Pure origin in the understanding → presupposed absolute unity → connection through one conception or idea.
Governing connection → rule of proper placement → a priori criterion of completeness.
Mechanical discovery → open-ended accumulation → resemblance-based ordering → failure of systematic unity.
Failure of systematic unity → transcendental demand for a principle → derivation from absolute unity.
Derivation from absolute unity → rule for assigning proper places → a priori determination of completeness.
The object of inquiry shifts from collecting conceptions to determining the principle that generates and orders them.
Classification is reclassified as a test of systematic necessity rather than a convenient arrangement of similarities.
Completeness becomes an a priori structural question rather than an empirical result of continued investigation.
The understanding is mapped as an internally unified source whose conceptions are related by derivational order.
Surface — The passage contrasts the accidental discovery of conceptions with their principled ordering.
Structural — A system requires an internal rule that determines relations, placement, and boundaries among its elements.
Metastrategic — Transcendental philosophy claims authority by replacing contingent collection with principled derivation.

Ontological/Temporal — Pure conceptions are treated as originating in an absolute unity of the understanding, allowing systematic completeness to be determined a priori rather than through temporal accumulation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from uncontrolled discovery to principled systematicity.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between associative classification and necessary systematic connection.
The reconstruction preserves the coupled functions of the governing principle: proper placement and determination of completeness.
The central tension is that the passage asserts an absolute unity and a single ordering idea without yet specifying their content or derivation.
The system is internally coherent at the level of method, but its concrete completeness remains underdetermined until the governing principle is exhibited.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement: contingent manifestation → failure of accidental order → principled unity → a priori systematic completeness.

units.title: Section I. Of the Logical Use of the Understanding in General § 4

items.text: The problem is to determine the understanding independently of sensibility without treating it as an intuitive faculty.
The argument distinguishes intuition, conception, and judgment as successive modes of cognition.
Human cognition is reframed as discursive because the understanding cognizes through conceptions rather than intuitions.
Conceptions are grounded in spontaneous functions that unify diverse representations under common representations.
Because concepts relate to objects only mediately, the understanding operates through judgments.
The complete classification of judgment-functions is presented as the route to exhibiting all functions of the understanding.
The understanding is a non-sensuous faculty of cognition.
Independent of sensibility, the understanding cannot possess intuition.
Human cognition proceeds either through intuition or through conception, and cognition through conception is discursive.
Sensuous intuitions depend on receptivity to affections.
Conceptions depend on the spontaneity of thought.
A function is the unity of the act of arranging diverse representations under one common representation.
The understanding can use conceptions only by judging through them.
Only intuition relates immediately to an object; a conception relates to an object through another representation.
A judgment is the mediate cognition of an object and therefore represents a representation of that object.
Every judgment contains a conception that applies to multiple conceptions and includes a representation immediately connected with an object.
Judgments unify representations by subsuming multiple possible cognitions under a higher representation.
All acts of the understanding can be reduced to judgments.
A conception is a predicate of a possible judgment because other representations are contained under it.
The functions of the understanding can be discovered by completely exhibiting the functions of unity in judgments.
The understanding is not a sensuous faculty.
The understanding is not a faculty of intuition.
Human cognition through the understanding is not intuitive but discursive.
A conception does not relate immediately to an object.
A judgment is not immediate cognition of an object.
The understanding does not use conceptions apart from judgment.
A conception is not an isolated representation detached from relations of containment and predication.
The distinction between receptivity and spontaneity assigns intuition and conception to different sources of cognition.
Since conceptions depend on functions, conceptual cognition requires the unification of otherwise diverse representations.
Since the understanding can use conceptions only in judging, thought by the understanding is structurally judgmental.
Since concepts lack immediate object-relation, object-cognition by the understanding requires mediation through representations.
A judgment connects a higher-order conceptual unity with a representation that is directly related to an object.
The unity of a judgment permits many possible cognitions to be collected into one cognition.
The analysis of judgment is sufficient in principle for the analysis of the understanding.
A concept relates to an object only through the representations subsumed under it.
The understanding is constituted not by direct access to objects but by organized mediation among representations.
Judgment is the fundamental operational form through which spontaneity becomes determinate cognition.
The logical structure of judgments functions as the access-point for reconstructing the general structure of conceptual thought.
Object-directed cognition by the understanding is necessarily layered: object-related representation, conceptual subsumption, and judgmental unity.
Cognition by the understanding is not a self-sufficient intuition of objects.
Conceptual universality is not produced by immediate resemblance between concept and object but by the subsumption of representations.
The unity of cognition is not supplied by the object alone; it is enacted through the spontaneous activity of thought.
The understanding is not analyzed through its contents alone but through the functions by which it unifies representations.
Immediate intellectual intuition is structurally unavailable to the human understanding.
An object cannot enter conceptual cognition without passing through a representational order.
No account of the understanding can bypass the formal organization of judgment.
Sensible affection → receptive intuition → representation immediately related to an object.
Spontaneous thought → function of unification → conception under which diverse representations are arranged.
Conception → predication and subsumption → judgment as mediate cognition.
Judgmental unity → collection of multiple possible cognitions → systematic analysis of the understanding.
Complete exhibition of judgment-functions → complete exhibition of understanding-functions.

Negative definition of understanding → exclusion of intellectual intuition → distinction between receptivity and spontaneity → conception as function of unification → judgment as the only use of conception → mediate object-cognition → reduction of understanding to judgment → classification of judgment-functions.
The understanding is reclassified from a faculty that might receive objects directly into a faculty that organizes representations.
Judgment becomes the structural hinge between conceptual thought and object-directed cognition.
The analysis of cognition shifts from the relation of isolated concepts to the functions of unity operating in judgments.
The distinction between receptivity and spontaneity replaces a simple subject-object model with a two-source architecture of cognition.
Surface — The understanding is defined as a faculty that cognizes through conceptions and judges by means of them.
Structural — Cognition is organized through the relation among affection, intuition, representation, conception, and judgment.
Metastrategic — The route to the general structure of the understanding is shifted from introspective description to the systematic enumeration of judgment-functions.
Ontological/Temporal — Human cognition presupposes a non-immediate relation to objects in which object-directedness is constituted through ordered mediation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the negative definition of understanding to its reduction to judgment.
The system preserves the distinction between intuition as receptive and conception as spontaneous.
The derivational structure explains why judgment mediates between concept and object.
The final transition to the next section remains programmatic because the actual classification of judgment-functions is not included here.
The system is internally coherent insofar as every higher-order claim depends on the exclusion of immediate conceptual intuition.
The unresolved tension is that cognition is object-directed while the understanding never relates to the object immediately; this tension is retained as the constitutive condition of judgment.

identity.title: Section I. Of the Logical Use of the Understanding in General § 4

units.title: Section II. Of the Logical Function of the Understanding in Judgements § 5

items.text: Judgement is analysed by abstracting from its material content and isolating the intellectual functions through which thought orders a given cognition.
The complete logical function of judgement divides into quantity, quality, relation, and modality, each with three irreducible momenta.
General logic’s classifications are insufficient where they suppress distinctions required for evaluating cognition according to its transcendental significance.
Singular and infinite judgements acquire independent status when judgement is considered as cognition rather than merely as an instrument of syllogistic inference.
Relations of judgement organize predicates, consequences, and mutually delimiting divisions into determinate forms of conceptual connection.
Modality orders the status of a judgement for thought as possible, actual, or necessary without adding determinate material content.
The table establishes a complete set of elementary functions through which the understanding judges and through which pure cognition can subsequently be investigated.
The intellectual form of judgement can be considered independently of the content judged.
The functions of thought in judgement are exhaustively ordered under quantity, quality, relation, and modality.
Each fundamental function of judgement contains three distinct momenta.
The logical treatment of a judgement may differ from its transcendental treatment because general logic abstracts from cognitive content.
A singular judgement is formally usable as universal in syllogistic inference but is quantitatively distinct as cognition.
An infinite judgement affirms a negative predicate while providing only a limitative determination of cognition.
Categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive judgements respectively express subject-predicate connection, ground-consequence connection, and the reciprocal ordering of divided cognitions.
A hypothetical judgement asserts the connection of propositions without deciding the truth of its component propositions.
A disjunctive judgement combines mutual exclusion among alternatives with their collective completion of one cognitive sphere.
Modality concerns the validity of the copula in relation to thought rather than the content of the judgement.
Problematical, assertorical, and apodeictical judgements represent a proposition respectively as logically possible, logically actual, and logically necessary.
Logical necessity arises when an assertorical judgement is represented as determined by the laws of the understanding.
The table is not limited to the classifications needed for syllogistic use.
Singular judgement is not identical with universal judgement merely because both can function equivalently in inference.
Infinite judgement is not simply affirmative judgement despite its affirmative logical form.
The exclusion of a predicate-class is not a positive determination of the subject’s content.
Hypothetical relation is not an assertion that either antecedent or consequent is true.
Disjunction is not merely an aggregate of alternatives; it is a structured totality of reciprocal exclusions.
Problematical judgement is not objective possibility or objective assertion.
Modality is not an additional constituent of a judgement’s material content.
A complete transcendental table must preserve distinctions that formal logic may legitimately collapse for inferential purposes.
Singular judgement marks cognition as a unity rather than as an instance of general extension.
Infinite judgement narrows the field in which an object may be placed without positively specifying what the object is.
Hypothetical judgement permits conditional cognition to be used even when its component propositions remain undecided or false.
Disjunctive judgement determines a cognition by assigning it to one complementary sphere and thereby excluding the others.
Logical possibility functions as a provisional admissibility of a proposition within thought.
The progression from problematic to assertorical to apodeictical judgement represents increasing incorporation of a proposition into the understanding.
The table transforms logical forms from a taxonomy of propositions into functions that measure distinct ways cognition can be determined.
Negative determination is structurally indispensable because cognition can be delimited without being materially enriched.
The understanding can organize truth-directed inquiry through propositions that are not themselves asserted as true.
Completeness of cognition requires both positive connections and an articulated field of exclusions among possible determinations.
Necessity is represented as a relation to the understanding’s lawful activity rather than as an additional predicate belonging to the object.
Cognitive quantity cannot be reduced to the extension relevant to formal inference.
Logical affirmation cannot be equated with positive cognition of an object.
Conditional intelligibility does not require prior truth of every proposition employed in a relation of consequence.
Completeness is not obtained by eliminating alternatives but by preserving their reciprocal boundaries within a common sphere.
Necessity is not derived from repeated assertion but from lawful determination by the understanding.
No unmediated access to an object’s positive determination is available through infinite judgement, which only removes an excluded region.
No proposition is granted objective standing merely because the understanding can provisionally admit it as possible.
No complete logical architecture can rest on isolated propositions, because determination requires relations of consequence, exclusion, and totality.
No modal status is treated as a property added to objects independently of their relation to thought.
Abstraction from judged content → isolation of intellectual form → four fundamental functions of judgement.
Formal-logical equivalence → transcendental differentiation of cognitive worth → independent status of singular and infinite judgement.
Predicate relation / consequence relation / divisional reciprocity → categorical / hypothetical / disjunctive forms of connection.
Logical possibility → accepted logical actuality → law-determined logical necessity.
Mutual exclusion among alternatives → collective completion of a cognitive sphere → determinate assignment of cognition.
Limitation without positive enrichment → negative determination → transcendental relevance of infinite judgement.
Abstraction from content → classification of forms → fourfold table of judgement-functions.
Formal-logical simplification → recognition of cognitive distinctions → separation of singular from universal judgement.
Logical affirmation by negation → limitative cognitive value → separation of infinite from affirmative judgement.
Forms of relation → predicate, consequence, and reciprocal division → categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive judgement.
Copular validity for thought → possibility, actuality, necessity → modal sequence of judgement.
Complete functional table → groundwork for inquiry into pure a priori cognition.
The distinction between formal validity and transcendental cognitive significance redraws logic as more than an instrument of syllogistic classification.
Negative predicates become visible as operators of limitation rather than as sources of positive object-determination.
Disjunction becomes a structure of jointly exhaustive and mutually exclusive cognitive positions rather than a merely alternative syntax.
Modal terms become statuses of a proposition’s relation to thought rather than degrees of objective being.
Provisional propositions become legitimate components of truth-directed cognition without being mistaken for truths.
Surface — Judgements are classified by quantity, quality, relation, and modality, each containing three momenta.
Structural — The classification differentiates inferential form, cognitive quantity, limitative content, relational architecture, and modal validity.
Metastrategic — General logic is subordinated to a transcendental procedure that asks what each form contributes to possible a priori cognition.
Ontological/Temporal — Necessity is produced through the progressive integration of judgement into lawful understanding, while possibility remains a merely logical admission.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the fourfold table and the justification for its departures from ordinary logical classification.
The system depends centrally on the distinction between logical form and the transcendental worth of a judgement for cognition.
The treatment of singular and infinite judgement is coherent only if inferential equivalence is kept distinct from cognitive identity.
The account of relation is strongest where consequence and reciprocal exclusion are treated as different forms of conceptual connection.
The account of modality remains structurally tense because modality contributes nothing to content while still functions as a necessary moment of thought.
The transition from logical possibility to logical necessity relies on the unexplicated authority of the laws of understanding.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if negative limitation, provisional assumption, and disjunctive totalization remain distinct operations.

identity.title: Section II. Of the Logical Function of the Understanding in Judgements § 5

units.title: Section III. Of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding, or Categories § 6

items.text: The problem is to explain how pure concepts of the understanding can yield a priori cognition of objects rather than merely formal conceptual order.
The argument relocates the origin of cognition from analysis of given concepts to synthesis of a manifold supplied through pure sensibility.
Cognition requires a sequence in which intuition supplies diversity, imagination combines it, and understanding represents its necessary unity.
The unifying function exercised in judgment is identified with the function that unifies the manifold of intuition.
The logical forms of all possible judgments therefore determine the exact inventory of pure concepts applicable a priori to objects.
The category table is defended as a systematic and exhaustive derivation, then extended downward into deduced concepts while excluding illegitimate additions.
The argument moves from conditions of cognition to an architectonic program for rational science and a restriction on metaphysical predicate-making.
General logic abstracts from all content of cognition and can only analyse representations received from another source.
Transcendental logic requires the manifold of pure a priori sensibility as its content.
Representations must be given before they can be analysed, and analysis cannot generate the content of concepts.
Synthesis joins a manifold of representations into one cognition and is the first requisite of cognition.
Imagination performs the indispensable synthesis of the manifold without thereby producing cognition in the proper sense.
Pure synthesis requires an a priori synthetic unity in order to yield a pure concept of the understanding.
Understanding supplies concepts that represent the necessary synthetic unity required for cognition of an object.
The function that unifies representations in judgment also unifies the manifold in intuition.
There are exactly as many pure concepts of the understanding as there are logical functions in all possible judgments.
The category table is derived systematically from the faculty of judgment rather than assembled inductively from encountered concepts.
Original categories generate pure but deduced concepts through their combination with one another and with modes of pure sensibility.
The third category in each triad arises through combination of the first two while requiring a distinct and primitive act of understanding.
Mathematical categories concern objects of intuition, whereas dynamical categories concern existence and relations of objects to one another or to understanding.
Community represents reciprocal co-ordination among independently existing substances rather than a one-way causal sequence.
Unity, truth, and perfection are logical criteria of cognition derived from transformed categories of quantity, not additional categories or properties of things in themselves.
General logic is not a source of transcendental content or of pure concepts applicable a priori to objects.
Analysis is not the origin of conceptual content.
Mere receptivity to an intuitive manifold is not cognition of an object.
Imaginative synthesis alone is not cognition in the proper sense.
The category catalogue is not an empirical, rhapsodic, or Aristotelian-style inventory gathered without a guiding principle.
Modes of pure sensibility, empirical concepts, and deduced concepts are not original categories of the pure understanding.
Predicables are not primitive concepts even when they are pure and a priori.
Third categories are not merely derivative composites of the first and second categories.
Community is not unilateral determination of an effect by a cause.
Unity, truth, and perfection are not transcendental predicates that enlarge the category table.
Logical conditions of coherent cognition are not properties attributable to objects as things in themselves.
A complete vocabulary and definitions of categories are not required for the immediate critical task.
Analysis can operate only upon a manifold already synthesized into a provisional cognitive unity.
Cognition of an object requires the ordered cooperation of sensibility, imagination, and understanding.
Pure concepts acquire transcendental rather than merely logical significance by representing the necessary unity of intuitive synthesis.
The logical table of judgments becomes a complete source-table for categories because judgment and intuition are unified by the same function of understanding.
The category inventory can claim completeness only if the logical functions of judgment are themselves complete and exhaustive.
Deduced concepts can be generated systematically without expanding the inventory of original categories.
A category may be structurally composite while remaining primitive because the act of combination has irreducible cognitive content.
The distinction between mathematical and dynamical categories determines two different domains of a priori conceptual ordering.
Reciprocal interaction constitutes a whole of co-ordinated substances that cannot be reduced to a linear causal relation.
Scholastic transcendental predicates are reclassified as tests of the consistency and completeness of cognition rather than as ontological additions.
The objective applicability of categories is grounded in their role as conditions for synthesizing an intuitive manifold into object-cognition, not in empirical abstraction or independent ontology.
The system combines finite closure at the level of original categories with indefinite derivational expansion at the level of predicables.
The category table functions simultaneously as an inventory of primitive concepts, a rule for classifying derivative concepts, and a blueprint for rational science.
The triadic form of the table prevents higher conceptual unities from being reduced to an additive sum of simpler determinations.
The relation category of community makes simultaneous mutual determination intelligible without assimilating it to causal succession.
The completed table limits metaphysics by preventing logical norms of thought from being converted into predicates of things in themselves.
The intuitive manifold must not contain or generate its own necessary unity independently of synthesis.
Pure concepts must not receive cognitive content independently of sensibility.
Logical forms of judgment must not be merely subjective classificatory devices disconnected from the synthesis of intuition.
The category inventory must not exceed, fall short of, or remain independent from the complete table of logical functions.
A metaphysical predicate must not be validated merely because it expresses a formal condition of coherent cognition.
The faculties of cognition must be sufficiently determinate and finite for an architectonic enumeration of their primitive functions to be possible.
The system forecloses cognitive entitlement to characterize objects wholly independently of the syntheses through which they become objects of cognition.
The system forecloses an ontology whose primitive vocabulary is selected by inherited metaphysical usage, semantic convenience, or empirical accumulation.
The system forecloses a passage from pure logical form alone to determinate cognitive content.
The system forecloses an indefinitely revisable category list whose completeness cannot be grounded in a prior systematic principle.
A priori sensibility supplies a manifold of intuition that is given but not yet cognized as an object.
Imagination synthesizes the manifold into a connected representation without yet supplying objective cognition.
Understanding represents the necessary unity of synthesis through pure concepts and thereby makes object-cognition possible.
The unifying operation in judgment is identified with the unifying operation imposed upon intuition.
The complete table of logical judgment-functions determines the complete inventory of original categories.
Original categories generate subordinate predicables through regulated combinations with one another and with modes of pure sensibility.
Taxonomic exclusions remove empirical concepts, sensible modes, derived concepts, and merely logical criteria from the register of primitive categories.
The purified category table becomes an architectonic schema for the division, completion, and critique of a priori rational science.
General logic’s abstraction from content → pure sensible manifold → priority of synthesis over analysis.
Given manifold → imaginative connection → conceptual representation of necessary unity → cognition of an object.
Unity in judgment → unity in intuition → logical functions → original categories.
Original categories → derivable predicables → systematic conceptual genealogy.
Systematic table → exclusion of false categories and predicates → architectonic plan for metaphysics and rational science.
The origin of cognition is relocated from analytic decomposition to pre-analytic synthetic unification.
Categories are reclassified from a collection of high-order concepts into functions required for thinking an intuitive object.
The distinction between original categories and predicables permits conceptual expansion without inflation of the primitive inventory.
The distinction between mathematical and dynamical categories redraws the field between the constitution of objects of intuition and the ordering of existence and relation.
Unity, truth, and perfection are shifted from alleged ontological predicates to formal criteria governing cognition’s consistency with itself.
Community becomes visible as reciprocal co-ordination within a whole rather than as a variant of one-directional causality.
Surface — The text enumerates categories, distinguishes them from predicables, and organizes their classes, triads, and relations.
Structural — Cognition is produced through the ordered dependence of sensible manifold, imaginative synthesis, and conceptual unity.
Metastrategic — A systematic derivation from judgment replaces empirical cataloguing and regulates which concepts may enter transcendental philosophy.
Ontological/Epistemic — Objects are cognizable only under a priori conditions of synthesis, while logical conditions of cognition are denied direct status as properties of things in themselves.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central movement from sensible manifold through synthesis to categories and systematic conceptual architecture.
The derivation of categories depends on the asserted identity between unification in judgment and unification in intuition, but this identity is stated more than demonstrated here.
The claim of exhaustive completeness depends on the completeness of the logical table of judgments, which functions as a premise rather than a result of the argument.
The triadic doctrine creates a pressure point because third categories are described as generated through combination while also retained as primitive.

The distinction between categories, predicables, sensible modes, empirical concepts, and logical criteria is structurally necessary but depends on classificatory judgments not fully formalized in the passage.
The correspondence of community to disjunctive judgment is the explicitly difficult case and reveals the weakest point in the category-to-judgment mapping.
The restriction against treating logical criteria as properties of things in themselves coheres with the system only if applicability to objects is confined to objects as cognized under synthesis.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement, but detailed definitions of categories and the full derivation of their objective validity remain deliberately deferred.

identity.title: Section III. Of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding, or Categories § 6

units.title: Section I. Of the Principles of a Transcendental Deduction in general § 9

items.text: Pure concepts require a juridical justification of their objective employment, not merely an account of their factual acquisition.
Transcendental deduction is required because pure a priori concepts claim applicability to objects independently of experience.
Space and time can be justified through their role as forms under which objects are given in intuition.
Categories generate a distinct problem because they are conditions of thought rather than conditions under which objects are intuitively given.
The category of causality exposes the problem because necessary lawful connection cannot be derived from observed regularity.
Critical philosophy must either establish the objective validity and limits of pure concepts or abandon claims to cognition beyond possible experience.
The factual origin of a concept does not establish its right to apply to objects.
A deduction establishes the legitimate objective employment of a concept.
Pure a priori concepts claim application to objects without derivation from experience.
The legitimate a priori application of a pure concept requires a transcendental deduction.
An empirical genealogy explains the occasioned production of a concept but cannot justify its a priori validity.
