The unresolved tension lies between the independent origin of categories in understanding and their necessary applicability to material supplied by sensibility.

units.title: In Cognition, its Application to Objects of Experience is the only legitimate use of the Category § 18

items.text: The argument addresses how a pure concept can become cognition of an object rather than remain thought without an object.
Cognition requires both a conception through which an object is thought and an intuition through which the object is given.
Because human intuition is sensuous, categories acquire cognitive significance only through application to empirical intuition.
Pure intuition and mathematics yield cognition only of the formal structure of phenomena and do not establish the existence of corresponding things.
Categories extended beyond empirical intuition become empty forms because no available intuition can provide them with objective significance.
The transcendental argument moves from the conditions of cognition to the delimitation of legitimate categorical use and the exclusion of positive knowledge beyond experience.
Thinking an object and cognizing an object are distinct acts.
Cognition consists of a conception through which an object is thought and an intuition through which the object is given.
A conception without a corresponding intuition remains formally thinkable but yields cognition of no object.
All intuition available to human cognition is sensuous.
Sensuous intuition is either pure intuition of space and time or empirical intuition involving sensation.
Pure intuition yields a priori cognition only of the formal conditions under which objects appear as phenomena.
Pure mathematical conceptions become cognition only under the presupposition that objects can be represented according to the forms of pure sensibility.
Categories produce cognition only insofar as they can be applied to empirical intuition.
Categories render empirical cognition possible, and this category-enabled empirical cognition is experience.
The legitimate use of categories is restricted to objects of experience.
Pure concepts of the understanding can be extended formally to objects of any sensuous intuition, but extension beyond human intuition provides no cognitive advantage.
Empirical intuition alone gives categories significance and meaning for human cognition.
Merely specifying what a supposed object is not does not establish proper knowledge of that object.
No category can be validly applied to a supposed object whose intuition is non-sensuous.
Cognition is not identical with thinking.
A category without corresponding intuition is not cognition of an object.
Categories do not by themselves provide cognition of things.
Pure intuition alone does not establish that things corresponding to its formal conditions exist.
Mathematical conceptions are not cognition independently of their relation to representable objects.
Space and time have no validity as conditions of objects beyond sensuous experience.
Extending categories beyond available intuition does not reveal the possibility or impossibility of an object.
Negative predicates concerning a non-sensuous object do not constitute knowledge of that object.
A non-sensuous intuition cannot supply a legitimate field of categorical application.
Objective cognition requires the joint operation of conceptual determination and object-giving intuition.
Human cognition can acquire objects only through sensuous givenness, while conceptual determination organizes what is given.
Mathematical a priori cognition is restricted to the formal structure of possible phenomena.
Categories become objectively meaningful only when their synthesis can determine empirical intuition.
Experience is neither bare sensation nor pure conceptual form but their synthetically ordered combination.
The formal universality of categories does not entail their legitimate cognitive use beyond experience.
A non-sensuous object can be marked by exclusion of sensuous predicates without being positively determined as an object of cognition.
The category of substance has cognitive meaning only where empirical intuition supplies an occasion for its application.
Cognitive validity is produced by the relation between concept and intuition rather than possessed by the concept in isolation.
The distinction between sensibility and understanding establishes a dual limit: sensibility restricts what can be given, while understanding restricts how what is given can be determined.
The system permits formal thought beyond experience while denying that such thought can become cognition without corresponding intuition.
A priori form acquires objective force only through an empirical condition that it cannot generate by itself.
Mathematical necessity cannot independently establish the existence of objects corresponding to mathematical forms.
Discourse about non-sensuous objects is reduced to a boundary operation: it can negate sensuous determinations but cannot provide positive cognition.
The restriction of categorical use converts the question of metaphysical objecthood into a question of available conditions for cognition.
Human cognition has no intellectual intuition through which objects could be given independently of sensibility.
No object can become cognitively available through conceptual determination alone.
No category carries autonomous objective reference apart from a mode of intuition.
No formal consistency of a conception guarantees the existence of a corresponding object.
No transition from pure form to actual existence is available without empirical givenness.
No negative determination can be converted into positive content merely by multiplying exclusions.
No extension of categorical concepts can overcome the absence of an intuition capable of giving them meaning.
Positive cognition of objects beyond possible human experience is structurally unavailable.
An ontology that treats categories as self-sufficient determinations of things is inadmissible.
A non-sensuous object can function only as an indeterminate limit of thought, not as a cognized object.
A purely intellectual route from conception to object is foreclosed.
The existence of things corresponding to formal conditions cannot be secured by the forms of thought or intuition alone.
Distinguish formal thought from cognition of an object.
Require the conjunction of conceptual determination and object-giving intuition.
Restrict object-giving intuition, for human cognition, to sensibility.
Separate pure formal determination from empirical object-givenness.
Permit categories to generate cognition only through empirical synthesis.
Treat extension beyond empirical intuition as empty formal possibility rather than cognition.
Convert non-sensuous object-talk into negative boundary-marking without positive determination.
Conclude that the legitimate use of categories terminates at objects of experience.
The argument moves from the distinction between thinking and cognizing to the requirement of both conception and intuition.
It moves from the concept–intuition requirement to the restriction of human intuition to sensibility.
It moves from sensibility to the distinction between pure formal cognition and empirical object-givenness.
It moves from the category’s formal role to its empirical application as the condition of experience.
It moves from attempted extension beyond experience to empty conceptions, negative determinations, and the restriction of legitimate categorical use.
The category is reclassified from an independently object-producing concept into a condition of empirical cognition.
Experience is reclassified from immediate givenness into a synthesis of empirical intuition and categorical determination.
Mathematics is separated from unrestricted ontology and assigned a formal validity concerning phenomena.
The distinction between formal conceivability and objective cognition becomes structurally decisive.
Non-sensuous discourse is reclassified from possible positive knowledge into apophatic limitation.
The boundary of knowledge is redrawn according to conditions of application rather than according to the abstract scope of concepts.
Surface: The text distinguishes thinking an object from cognizing an object.
Structural: Cognition is organized as the synthesis of conceptual form and intuitive givenness, with empirical intuition supplying objective significance.
Metastrategic: The argument redirects metaphysical inquiry from unrestricted conceptual extension toward the conditions under which concepts can legitimately determine objects.
Ontological/Temporal: Space and time are treated as forms belonging to sensuous appearance, while objects beyond these forms remain unavailable to positive human cognition.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the central argument from the distinction between thought and cognition to the restriction of categorical use.
The reconstruction preserves the decisive sequence: concept and intuition, sensibility, empirical application, experience, and exclusion of cognition beyond experience.
The system is internally coherent if formal extension and legitimate cognitive use are treated as distinct levels.
Its strongest point is the dependence of objective cognition on the conjunction of conceptual determination and intuition.
The system leaves underdetermined the precise status of objects of non-sensuous intuition and the relation between categories and intuitions unlike those available to humans.
Its principal fault line is the coexistence of the categories’ formal extension to intuition in general with their cognitive restriction to empirical intuition.

The argument depends on the compressed transition from the absence of corresponding intuition to the emptiness of the concept and from negative characterization to the impossibility of positive knowledge.

Reconstruction preserves the real movement of the text because the final limitation is generated by the initial distinction between thinking and cognizing rather than appended as an external restriction.

identity.title: In Cognition, its Application to Objects of Experience is the only legitimate use of the Category § 18

units.title: Of the Application of the Categories to Objects of the Senses in general § 20

items.text: Pure categories require sensuous intuition to yield cognition of determinate objects.
The understanding secures objective application by determining sensibility through a transcendental synthesis of imagination.
Figurative synthesis mediates between the intellectual unity of apperception and the manifold given in sensuous intuition.
Internal sense is receptive and formally temporal, while understanding actively affects and synthetically determines it.
Self-consciousness as “I think” establishes existence only as thought, not as an intuition of the self as it is in itself.
The argument moves from the applicability of categories to phenomena toward the restriction of both outer and inner cognition to appearance.
Categories are pure forms of thought and cannot cognize a determinate object without intuition.
Intellectual synthesis unifies a manifold under apperception and grounds the possibility of a priori cognition.
Human intuition is sensuous and supplies its manifold only through receptivity.
Internal sense has the a priori form of time but contains no original synthetic conjunction of its manifold.
The understanding is spontaneous and can determine internal sense in conformity with the synthetic unity of apperception.
Imagination belongs to sensibility insofar as it provides intuition, but is spontaneous insofar as it synthesizes and determines sensibility.
The synthesis of imagination under the categories is the first application of understanding to possible objects of intuition.
The objective reality of the categories extends only to objects given as phenomena.
Productive imagination supplies a priori synthesis, whereas reproductive imagination follows empirical association.
Apperception is the source of synthetic unity and is distinct from internal sense.
Self-cognition requires not only the thought “I think” but also an intuition through which the self’s manifold can be determined.
Human self-intuition is sensuous and temporal rather than intellectual; therefore the self is cognized only as appearance.
Categories are not independently cognitive representations of determinate objects.
Intellectual synthesis is not identical with figurative synthesis.
Imagination is not merely receptive sensibility or merely understanding.
Productive imagination is not reproductive association governed by empirical psychology.
Internal sense is not identical with apperception.
The understanding does not discover a pre-given synthetic order within internal sense.
Inner intuition does not disclose the self as it is in itself.
The “I think” is not knowledge of a substantial, intuitively given self.
Human cognition is not intellectual intuition.
Motion as an empirical determination of an object is not a priori geometric cognition.
The categories acquire objective validity only through their application to sensuously given appearances.
A priori cognition requires a synthesis that is both intellectual in its rule and sensible in its presentation.
Figurative synthesis is the operative mediation by which categories determine the sensible manifold.
The temporal order of inner experience is produced through the understanding’s determination of internal sense.
Geometrical and temporal representation presuppose an active construction of intuition rather than passive reception of completed forms.
The self can be conscious of its synthetic spontaneity without possessing intuitive knowledge of itself as a spontaneous being.
The distinction between self as thinker and self as intuited does not divide the subject into two substances.
Objectivity is constituted neither by bare concepts nor by bare sensation, but by lawful synthesis whereby spontaneity orders receptivity.
The same structure that enables cognition of objects limits cognition to appearance, because the required intuition is sensuous.
Self-relation is structurally asymmetric: the subject determines its inner sense while receiving itself only as temporally affected.
Time is not a transparent medium of self-presence, because temporal self-givenness depends upon an act that cannot itself become intellectual self-intuition.
The transcendental account excludes psychology from explaining the conditions of a priori cognition, except where psychological processes are subordinated to transcendental synthesis.
Cognition cannot arise from a self-sufficient conceptual intellect that determines objects without receiving intuition.
The unity of consciousness cannot be explained by a passive inner faculty already containing synthesized representations.
Self-consciousness cannot yield metaphysical knowledge of the soul merely by reflecting on the “I think.”
The distinction between appearance and thing in itself cannot be cancelled by shifting inquiry from external objects to the inner self.
A priori necessity cannot be grounded in empirical association, repetition, or psychological habit.
Immediate self-possession is unavailable because the subject encounters itself only through a form of receptivity it actively determines but does not intellectually originate as intuition.
An absolute coincidence of thinker, intuited self, and known self is foreclosed for finite cognition.
Noumenal self-knowledge is structurally inadmissible because its possibility would require an intellectual intuition denied to human understanding.
The ultimate ground of the capacity by which spontaneity affects its own receptivity remains unobjectified within the account.
Category as empty thought-form → requirement of an intuitively given manifold.
Sensuous manifold under temporal form → insufficiency of receptivity for synthetic unity.
Spontaneous understanding → determination of internal sense according to apperceptive unity.
Productive imagination → figurative synthesis connecting categories to sensuous intuition.
Figurative synthesis → objective validity of categories for phenomena.
Reflexive application to the self → consciousness of existence without cognition of the self in itself.
Temporal self-intuition → self-knowledge restricted to phenomenal appearance.

Empty categories → necessity of sensuous intuition → transcendental imagination as mediator → understanding’s affection of internal sense → temporal constitution of self-experience → phenomenal restriction of object- and self-cognition.
Objectivity is relocated from correspondence between concepts and independently known things to the lawful synthesis of appearances.
Imagination is reclassified from an auxiliary image-making power into the constitutive mediator of understanding and sensibility.
Internal experience is reclassified from immediate self-disclosure into an affection-mediated phenomenal intuition.
The opposition between active understanding and passive sensibility is rendered non-simple, because spontaneity actively determines the receptive faculty.
The “I think” is separated from empirical or metaphysical self-knowledge, preserving existence-consciousness while denying determinate noumenal cognition.
Surface — Categories apply to sensible objects only when imagination synthesizes the manifold of intuition.
Structural — Apperception supplies synthetic unity, understanding determines internal sense, and time receives the resulting inner determinations.
Metastrategic — The apparent paradox of self-affection is resolved by distinguishing the determining intellect from the receptive mode in which its activity becomes intuitable.
Ontological/Temporal — Finite subjects exist and think spontaneously, yet can determine and know their existence only under temporal conditions of appearance.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from empty categories to their objective application to phenomena.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the mediating necessity of productive imagination and figurative synthesis.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the distinction between apperception, internal sense, and phenomenal self-cognition.
The system is coherent if spontaneity can determine receptivity without thereby converting human intuition into intellectual intuition.
The principal underdetermination concerns how one and the same subject can be both spontaneous determinant and receptively affected without an account of their ultimate common ground.
The system depends on the asserted distinction between thought of existence and intuitive determination of existence; without it, the restriction of self-knowledge to appearance fails.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the restriction on cognition is treated as generated by the very mechanism that makes objective cognition possible.

identity.title: Of the Application of the Categories to Objects of the Senses in general § 20

units.title: Transcendental Deduction of the universally possible employment in experience of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding § 22

items.text: The problem is to establish why categories, though originating a priori in understanding, necessarily govern every object that can appear in sensuous experience.
Perception is reframed as an achieved unity of apprehended sensible manifold rather than as immediately given awareness.
Space and time supply the sensible manifold and its a priori formal unity, but the conjunction that makes perception possible requires intellectual synthesis.
Because every empirical apprehension must conform to categorial synthesis, every possible perception is subject to categories.
Experience is cognition through conjoined perceptions; categories are therefore a priori conditions of possible experience.
Nature, as the lawful connection of phenomena, is possible only under categorial conditions, although its particular empirical laws cannot be derived from categories alone.
Categories are a priori forms of intellectual synthesis.
Perception is possible only through a synthesis of apprehension that combines the manifold of empirical intuition.
Every synthesis of apprehension must conform to the a priori forms of space and time.
Space and time, as formal intuitions, contain an a priori unity of the manifold they present.
The unity required for apprehending a manifold is the same primitive unity of consciousness expressed intellectually through categories.
The same spontaneity conjoins sensible manifold under the name of imagination and gives this conjunction intellectual unity under the name of understanding.
Experience is cognition produced through conjoined perceptions.
Whatever is a condition of possible perception is a condition of possible experience.
Phenomena exist only in relation to a subject possessing sensibility, and their lawful conjunction exists only in relation to a subject possessing understanding.
Categories prescribe a priori only the universal conditions of lawfulness required for nature in general.
Particular empirical laws require experience for their determination.
Things in themselves remain unknown with respect to what they are independently of their phenomenal representation.
Categories are not abstracted from nature or empirically regulated by nature as their model.
Perception is not a merely receptive registration of a sensibly given manifold.
Space and time are not merely empty forms lacking manifold or unity.
The formal unity of space and time is not reducible to sensibility understood as passive receptivity.
Laws of phenomenal conjunction do not subsist in phenomena independently of their relation to understanding.
Categories do not yield particular laws governing empirically specified phenomena.
Nature as appearance is not identical with things in themselves.
The validity of categories does not extend by this deduction to objects beyond possible experience.
Every possible perception is necessarily categorially structured because apprehension requires a synthesis whose unity is intellectual.
Categories are valid a priori for every object of possible experience because experience consists of conjoined perceptions.
The perception of spatial magnitude necessarily presupposes the category of quantity.
The perception of an event as temporally successive necessarily presupposes the category of causality.
Nature in the material sense, as the totality of phenomena, is subject to categories insofar as all phenomenal perception requires categorial conjunction.
Nature in the formal sense, as necessary lawfulness among phenomena, depends on categories as its a priori ground.
Empirical investigation is necessary for particular laws even though its objects must already conform to universal categorial lawfulness.
The deduction converts the necessity of natural law from a property inferred from independently given objects into a condition of objects as objects of possible experience.
The understanding legislates only the form of possible nature, while sensibility supplies the manifold to which that legislation applies.
Objective necessity within experience is generated through the cooperation of receptivity, apprehension, imagination, and understanding rather than secured by access to things in themselves.
The categories function as limits on possible empirical objectivity: they make experience possible while also restricting their own legitimate use to experience.
No independently knowable order of objects can ground the validity of categories, because the relevant objects are objects only as phenomena.
No empirical fact can establish the universal necessity of categories, because empirical cognition already presupposes categorially unified perception.
No purely sensible intuition can constitute perception as objective experience without a non-sensible act of synthesis.
No deduction of particular scientific laws from pure understanding is possible, because pure categories determine only the form of lawful nature.
No claim about the intrinsic constitution of things in themselves can be licensed by the demonstrated necessity of phenomenal lawfulness.
The system forecloses an unmediated encounter with an object before the subjective conditions of its apprehension, synthesis, and consciousness have operated.
The system forecloses a nature that is both empirically accessible and wholly independent of the forms through which experience is possible.
The system treats the ultimate ground of correspondence between phenomenal lawfulness and things in themselves as unavailable rather than demonstrable.
The system cannot admit a complete a priori science of materially determinate nature, because empirical specification remains irreducible.
Sensible manifold in space and time → synthesis of apprehension → perception.
Formal unity of space and time + primitive unity of consciousness → categorial determination of apprehension.
Categorially determined perception → conjoined perceptions → possible experience.
Possible experience → objects as phenomena → universal lawfulness of nature.
Universal categorial lawfulness → formal nature only; empirical determination → particular laws through experience.
A priori origin of categories → demand for their universal experiential validity → analysis of perception as synthesis.
Synthesis of apprehension → dependence on spatial-temporal formal unity → identification of this unity with categorial synthesis.
Categorial synthesis of perception → experience as connected perception → a priori validity of categories for experiential objects.
Phenomena as subject-relative representations → categories as laws of their conjunction → nature as formally dependent on understanding.
Formal legislation of nature → exclusion of derivation of particular laws → experience retained as the source of empirical specification.
Nature is reclassified from an independently given law-governed domain into the lawful unity of phenomena under conditions of possible experience.
Categories are reclassified from abstract logical concepts into necessary operations that constitute the unity required for perception and experience.
The opposition between subjective conditions and objective validity is reorganized: subjective conditions become precisely the conditions of phenomenal objectivity.
The opposition between a priori necessity and empirical inquiry is redistributed: the former governs nature in general, while the latter determines particular laws.
Space and time are repositioned as neither merely passive receptivity nor independent objects, but as formal intuitions whose unity presupposes synthesis.
Surface — The text establishes the applicability of categories to all objects that can be presented in sensuous experience.
Structural — Perception is produced through the coordinated functions of sensibility, apprehension, imagination, and understanding.
Metastrategic — The deduction secures objectivity by reconstructing its conditions of possibility rather than by deriving concepts from objects.
Ontological/Temporal — Phenomena have being only in relation to sensibility and understanding, while temporal succession becomes objectively determinable only through categorial synthesis.
Epistemic-Limiting — The same argument that grounds necessary laws for experience limits cognition of nature to appearances and leaves things in themselves indeterminate.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central deduction from perceptual synthesis to the universal validity of categories for possible experience.
The system depends critically on identifying the unity of apprehension with categorial unity while distinguishing formal intuition from the empirical forms apprehended within it.
The strongest transition is from the dependence of perception on synthesis to the dependence of experience on categories.
The main compression occurs in the claim that the unity belonging a priori to space and time nevertheless presupposes a synthesis not belonging to sense.
A structural tension remains between assigning formal-intuitive unity to space and time and locating the relevant synthetic unity in understanding through categories.
A second tension remains between the subject-relativity of phenomenal laws and the claim that things in themselves must independently possess law-conformity.
The argument remains coherent if its conclusion is restricted to the formal conditions of possible experience rather than extended to particular empirical laws or things in themselves.

identity.title: Transcendental Deduction of the universally possible employment in experience of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding § 22

units.title: Result of this Deduction of the Conceptions of the Understanding § 23

items.text: The argument seeks to explain how necessary a priori concepts can validly govern experience without being derived from experience.
It distinguishes thinking an object through categories from cognizing an object through a corresponding intuition.
Because human intuition is sensuous, cognition of given objects is empirical and therefore belongs to experience.
Experience nevertheless contains a priori elements, so its conformity with the categories must be explained transcendental-ly rather than empirically.
The alternatives are reduced to empirical derivation, a priori constitution, or a preformation model; empirical derivation and preformation are rejected because they cannot preserve necessity.

The deduction concludes that categories are principles of the possibility of experience, grounded in the synthetic unity of apperception and related to space and time, while their concrete application is deferred to transcendental judgment.
An object can be thought only through categories.
A thought can be cognized only through an intuition corresponding to its conception.
Human intuitions are sensuous.
Cognition of an object insofar as it is given is empirical, and empirical cognition is experience.
Pure intuitions and pure conceptions of the understanding contain a priori elements of cognition.
Necessary harmony between experience and the conceptions of its objects must arise either because experience makes the conceptions possible or because the conceptions make experience possible.
The categories are a priori conceptions independent of experience.
An empirical origin cannot account for the categories without reducing their origin to an unintelligible generation from experience.
The categories contain the grounds of the possibility of all experience.
Determination of an object requires intuition, although the exercise of thought through the categories is not itself limited to sensuous intuition.
Thought without intuition can have consequences for the subject’s reasoning and volition without constituting cognition of an object.
The necessity expressed by the categories must possess objective validity rather than merely subjective psychological necessity.
A preformation account treats the categories as subjective aptitudes harmonized with nature by contingent constitution and thereby removes their genuine necessity.

Pure conceptions of the understanding function as principles of the possibility of experience, whose ultimate formal ground is the original synthetic unity of apperception in relation to space and time.
Categories alone do not cognize an object without corresponding intuition.
Human a priori cognition does not extend to objects outside possible experience.
The categories are not derived entirely from experience.
The categories are not explained by an empirical generatio aequivoca.
The categories are not merely subjective aptitudes implanted alongside human existence.
Necessity is not reducible to the fact that a subject is constitutionally compelled to connect representations in a certain way.
Useful consequences of thought for reason or volition do not amount to cognition of the thought object.
This section does not yet provide the principles governing the concrete application of the categories to phenomena.
Human object-cognition is restricted to possible experience because cognition requires intuition and human intuition is sensuous.
The empirical character of experience does not imply that all of its constitutive elements originate empirically.
Since the categories are independent of experience and empirical origin is unavailable, they must be conditions under which experience is possible.
An empirical account of the categories would fail to explain the necessary conformity between experience and the categories.
The preformation hypothesis converts objective necessity into a contingent fact about subjective organization.
Once category-connections are treated as merely subjective, objective knowledge becomes vulnerable to the status of illusion and loses a basis for rational dispute.
The absence of intuition blocks object-determination but does not block every rational use of thought.
The deduction presents the categories as principles of experience rather than as contents acquired from experience.
The grounding of experience in synthetic unity, space, and time establishes the framework within which the categories must later be applied to phenomena.
Objectivity is secured immanently within the conditions of possible experience rather than by appeal either to empirical acquisition or to cognition beyond experience.
The system produces an epistemic asymmetry in which categorical thought can exceed intuition while determinate cognition cannot exceed possible experience.
Necessity functions as the decisive criterion separating transcendental validity from both empiricism and subjective psychological compulsion.
The argument is transcendental because it infers the conditions of experience from the necessary conformity of experience with cognition rather than reconstructing a causal history of the categories.
Synthetic unity of apperception functions as the formal bridge between the understanding’s categories and the spatiotemporal field in which experience is given.
The argument preserves a rational domain beyond theoretical object-cognition while formally excluding that domain from the present deduction.
The system depends on the falsity of the claim that experience is the sole source of every element present in cognition.
The system excludes the identification of all nonempirical thought with cognition of an object.
The system excludes any account in which the necessity of the categories is merely a contingent feature of human psychology.
The system excludes a genetic or causal explanation of the categories as sufficient to establish their validity.
The system excludes objective validity from being independent of the conditions under which objects can be experienced.
The system excludes the reduction of rationality to theoretical determination of objects, since reason may also determine the subject and its volition.
Unconditioned cognition of objects beyond sensibility is rendered inadmissible.
The possibility that categories disclose objects independently of the conditions of possible experience is foreclosed.
The opposition between subjective form and objective validity is rendered untenable when the subject’s a priori structures are treated as conditions of objectivity.
The positive account of how the categories operate in experience remains absent from this section and appears only as a deferred task.
Object thought → categories; object cognition → corresponding intuition.
Sensuous intuition → empirical cognition → experience; therefore human a priori cognition is restricted to objects of possible experience.
Necessary harmony between experience and categories → empirical-origin alternative or a priori-condition alternative; empirical origin rejected → categories as conditions of experience.
Preformation alternative → subjective aptitude → loss of necessity → loss of objective validity → skeptical consequence.
Categories plus pure intuition plus synthetic unity of apperception → experience understood as the determination of phenomena in space and time.
General transcendental grounding → deferred inquiry into the principles governing the categories’ application to phenomena.

Problem of necessary conformity → distinction between thought and cognition → sensuous limitation of intuition → separation of empirical cognition from a priori conditions → elimination of empirical origin → rejection of subjective preformation → categories as conditions of possible experience → deferral to transcendental judgment.
A priori cognition is reclassified from cognition of a supersensible object to cognition of the conditions governing possible experience.
Thinking and cognizing are separated into distinct operations rather than treated as equivalent.
Objectivity is relocated in necessary validity for possible experience rather than in empirical derivation or private subjective constitution.
The apparent opposition between empiricism and a priori cognition is reorganized as a question of the conditions that make experience possible.
The epistemic field is divided between unrestricted categorical thought and intuition-bound object-determination.
The investigation of category validity is redirected from origin theories toward the transcendental exercise of judgment.
Surface: The text establishes the relation among categories, intuitions, cognition, and experience.
Structural: The categories are positioned as conditions that make the necessary organization of experience possible.
Metastrategic: The argument secures objective validity by exhausting and rejecting competing origin models rather than by describing the psychological acquisition of concepts.

Ontological/Temporal: Reality as experienced is constituted as phenomena determined within space and time, while the unity of apperception provides the formal relation between understanding and sensibility.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the central argument from the distinction between categories and intuition through the conclusion that categories condition possible experience.
The extracted sequence preserves the actual movement from epistemic limitation to transcendental grounding and then to the rejection of rival origin accounts.
The system remains underdetermined regarding the specific principles by which each category makes experience possible.
The argument is internally coherent only if thought without intuition is distinguished from cognition rather than treated as meaningless.
The strongest inference is the incompatibility between subjective preformation and the necessity required by objective validity.
The system depends on treating the two principal origin alternatives as exhaustive and on using necessity as the criterion of transcendental status.
A structural tension remains between the categories’ unbounded sphere of thought and the strict restriction of cognition to possible experience.

identity.title: Result of this Deduction of the Conceptions of the Understanding § 23

items.text: The problem is to determine which higher cognitive faculties can supply objectively valid principles within transcendental logic.
The division of general logic cannot be transferred unchanged to transcendental logic because transcendental logic has a determinate content: pure a priori cognition.
Understanding, judgement, and reason must therefore be separated according to their distinct modes of transcendental employment.
Understanding and judgement can yield objectively valid cognition of phenomena, whereas reason becomes dialectical when it seeks cognition beyond possible experience.
The analytic of principles is consequently restricted to the valid application of pure concepts of understanding to phenomena.
The chapter reframes itself as a doctrine of the faculty of judgement because its governing task is the application of principles rather than the mere inventory of principles.
General logic is organized according to the higher faculties of cognition: understanding, judgement, and reason.
General logic abstracts from all content of cognition and concerns only the form of discursive thought.
The form of reason has a law that can be discovered a priori by analysing the operations of reason.
Transcendental logic concerns the determinate content of pure a priori cognition.
A division valid for general logic cannot be transferred without modification to transcendental logic.
Understanding and judgement possess objectively valid functions within transcendental logic.
Pure concepts of the understanding provide necessary conditions for establishing a priori laws concerning phenomena.
Reason becomes dialectical when it seeks a priori cognition of objects beyond the bounds of possible experience.
Illusory assertions of reason cannot constitute a canon of objectively valid cognition.
The analytic of principles is a canon for the faculty of judgement.
The proper object of the doctrine is the application of pure concepts of the understanding to phenomena.
Transcendental dialectic is the proper department for the illusory transcendental employment of reason.
Transcendental logic is not a merely formal logic that abstracts from every determinate content.
The transcendental analytic is not a canon for reason in its attempt to determine objects beyond possible experience.
Reason’s transcendental employment is not objectively valid.
The analytic of principles is not an unrestricted theory of all a priori cognition.
Pure concepts of the understanding are not self-applying principles whose validity is independent of judgement.
The principles of the understanding are not valid as determinations of objects outside possible experience.
Transcendental dialectic is not part of the logic of truth, although it belongs to the systematic treatment of transcendental logic.
The faculties must be assigned different logical functions because transcendental logic retains determinate cognitive content.
The a priori analysis of reason’s formal operations does not establish the objective validity of reason’s transcendental conclusions.
The existence of a formal law of reason does not entail the existence of a valid transcendental canon for reason.
The validity of pure concepts depends on their application within the field of phenomena.
The analytic of principles must instruct judgement in the application of concepts rather than merely describe the concepts themselves.
The boundary of possible experience separates objectively valid understanding from dialectical reason.
The distinction between analytic and dialectic is determined by objective validity rather than by the mere presence of a priori reasoning.
Transcendental logic is internally stratified into a logic of truth for understanding and judgement and a logic of illusion for reason’s overextension.
The boundary of possible experience functions as the jurisdictional limit that converts otherwise unified cognition into separate regimes of validity.
The analytic of principles is an operation of controlled application: it transforms pure conceptual conditions into valid laws only through judgement’s relation to phenomena.
A priori necessity is divided between valid conditions of phenomenal cognition and invalid claims about objects transcending experience.

The same systematic architecture that orders cognition also produces its critical boundary by showing that reason cannot occupy the same valid role in transcendental logic as understanding and judgement.
The system excludes the assumption that a priori form alone guarantees objective reference.
The system excludes the assumption that every faculty recognized by general logic has an equally valid transcendental employment.
The system excludes a unitary conception of reason in which formal rational necessity and objective cognition coincide.
The system excludes the possibility that pure concepts establish laws without a determinate domain of application.
The system excludes the identification of systematic completeness with unrestricted cognitive legitimacy.
The system excludes cognition of supersensible objects as a possible extension of the analytic of principles.
The system excludes the reduction of judgement to a passive intermediary between concepts and objects.
The system denies that cognition can secure objectivity merely by extending formal necessity beyond experience.
The system leaves no valid analytic route from pure reason to objects that cannot be given in experience.
The system forecloses the possibility of a single canon governing understanding, judgement, and reason without differentiating their objective reach.
The system makes the absence of an experiential field decisive: without possible experience, a priori synthesis loses its status as objectively valid cognition.
The system treats unbounded metaphysical cognition not as an incomplete science but as a structurally different and illusory employment of reason.
Higher faculties of cognition → division of logical functions → distinction between understanding, judgement, and reason.
Formal abstraction from content → general logic → a priori analysis of the form of thought.
Determinate content of pure cognition → transcendental logic → restriction of validity conditions.
Pure concepts of understanding + application to phenomena → necessary conditions of a priori laws.
A priori attempt to cognize objects beyond possible experience → loss of objective validity → transcendental dialectic.
Objective validity of understanding and judgement + invalid transcendental employment of reason → division between analytic of truth and dialectic of illusion.
Need to regulate application rather than merely enumerate concepts → analytic of principles → doctrine of the faculty of judgement.
Faculty-based division of general logic → mismatch with determinate-content transcendental logic.
Mismatch → differentiation of valid and invalid transcendental employments.
Differentiation → restriction of objective validity to understanding and judgement.
Restriction → confinement of pure concepts to their application to phenomena.
Confinement → exclusion of reason’s beyond-experience claims from the analytic of truth.
Exclusion → designation of the analytic of principles as a doctrine of judgement.
The conceptual field is reorganized from a uniform hierarchy of faculties into differentiated regimes of objective validity.
The boundary between analytic and dialectic is relocated from the presence of a priori reasoning to the possibility of valid application to phenomena.
Pure concepts are reclassified from independently sufficient forms into conditions whose lawful force depends on judgement and phenomenal application.
Reason’s metaphysical overreach is reclassified from failed analytic cognition into a distinct logic of illusion.
The analytic of principles is shifted from a static catalogue of principles to a regulatory theory of their use.
Possible experience becomes the boundary-marker determining whether a priori cognition belongs to truth or illusion.
Surface — The chapter identifies the proper subject and scope of the analytic of principles.
Structural — Transcendental logic is divided according to the different validity conditions governing understanding, judgement, and reason.
Metastrategic — The argument prevents the analytic from being captured by metaphysical claims that exceed the domain of possible experience.
Ontological/Temporal — Objective cognition is restricted to objects as they can stand within possible experience, while a priori necessity is denied unrestricted access to transcendent objects.
Epistemic — Validity is produced by the relation among pure concepts, judgement, and phenomena rather than by formal cognition in isolation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the distinction between general logic and transcendental logic.
The axioms are sufficient to derive the separation of analytic truth from transcendental dialectic.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the restriction of objective validity to understanding and judgement.
The structure remains underdetermined regarding the specific principles that the subsequent analytic will establish.
The system is internally coherent if formal reason and objectively valid transcendental cognition are treated as distinct functions.
Its central fault line is that reason possesses an a priori formal law while lacking a valid transcendental canon for objects beyond experience.
A second tension remains between the chapter’s designation as an analytic of principles and its final reclassification as a doctrine of judgement.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement from faculty-based classification through validity restriction to the regulation of application.

units.title: INTRODUCTION. Of the Transcendental Faculty of judgement in General

items.text: Understanding operates through rules, whereas judgment determines whether a particular case falls under a rule.
General logic cannot instruct subsumption because any rule for applying rules would itself require judgment.
Judgment is therefore an irreducible talent that formal learning cannot guarantee and that exercise alone can develop.
Examples train judgment but can weaken the understanding’s grasp of rules in their universal form.
Transcendental logic differs from general logic because it can determine the conditions under which pure concepts may be correctly applied.
Philosophy must abandon positive expansion of pure cognition in favor of critique that negatively prevents misuse of pure concepts.
This critique proceeds from conditions of possible object-givenness to schematism and then to the principles of the pure understanding.
Understanding is the faculty of rules.
Judgment is the faculty of subsuming a given case under a rule and distinguishing whether the case belongs under it.
General logic abstracts from the content of cognition and establishes only formal rules of concepts, judgments, and conclusions.
Any rule intended to direct subsumption would itself require judgment for its correct application.
Judgment is a natural talent that cannot be supplied by tuition and can be developed only through exercise.
Education can transmit rules borrowed from other minds but cannot guarantee their correct application when judgment is deficient.
Examples sharpen judgment but can weaken the understanding’s apprehension of rules in their universality.
Transcendental logic is charged with securing and directing the employment of pure understanding through determinate rules.
Philosophy as a doctrine aimed at enlarging pure a priori cognition yields little or no gain.
Philosophy as critique can guard against errors of judgment in the employment of pure concepts.
Transcendental philosophy can indicate both the general condition of a rule and, a priori, the case to which the rule applies.
Pure concepts must relate a priori to objects if they are to possess objective validity.
Objective validity requires general conditions under which objects can be given in conformity with pure concepts.
The transcendental doctrine of judgment proceeds from schematism to the synthetic a priori principles of the pure understanding.
General logic is not a doctrine that directs the act of subsumption.
Possession of general rules is not equivalent to correct judgment in particular cases.
Scholastic discipline cannot compensate for a deficiency in natural judgment.
No prescribed rule can guarantee correct application in the absence or deficiency of judgment.
Examples are not adequate substitutes for the universal apprehension of rules.
Philosophy is not justified here as a positive enlargement of pure a priori cognition.
Critique is not primarily a positive production of new pure cognition but a guard against error.
Pure concepts are not objectively valid merely as formal logical structures.
Objective validity cannot be established by a posteriori demonstration alone.
General logic cannot provide a non-circular rule for subsumption because such a rule would itself have to be subsumed and applied by judgment.
A person may possess extensive scientific rules and still fail to apply them correctly to concrete cases.
Exercise and examples are compensatory supports for judgment but cannot create the judgmental faculty itself.
Examples have a divided function: they improve the application of rules while risking dependence on particular circumstances.
The impossibility of directing judgment through general logic does not preclude a restricted direction of judgment within the domain of pure understanding.
The philosophical task shifts from expanding pure cognition to preventing invalid applications of the pure concepts already possessed.
The employment of pure concepts requires an a priori account of the conditions under which objects can be given.
The doctrine must first determine the sensuous conditions of application and only then derive the synthetic a priori principles that depend upon them.
Rule possession, rule formulation, and rule application are distinct cognitive functions that cannot be reduced to one another.
Formal education can increase understanding without producing reliable judgment, creating a structural gap between learnedness and correct use.
Transcendental logic functions as a bounded exception to the general non-teachability of judgment: it does not manufacture judgment but specifies conditions governing the use of pure understanding.
Critique acquires methodological force through negation: it secures cognition by excluding invalid applications rather than by enlarging the stock of pure concepts.
Examples occupy an intrinsically ambivalent pedagogical position because they are necessary for exercising judgment while potentially obstructing apprehension of universal rules.
Objective validity is generated by the relation among pure concept, object, and conditions of possible givenness, not by the concept in isolation.
The transition from judgment to schematism and principles converts the problem of application into a doctrine of the conditions governing pure cognition.
The system remains dependent on an incompletely formalized boundary between the general impossibility of teaching judgment and the transcendental possibility of directing its pure employment.
The system excludes a complete algorithm for determining every case of subsumption.
It excludes the reduction of judgment to the possession or manipulation of rules.
It excludes an educational mechanism capable of reliably manufacturing judgment where natural judgment is absent.
It excludes the equivalence of theoretical mastery and competent application.
It excludes empirical examples as sufficient grounds for the universal validity of rules.
It excludes positive philosophical construction as a secure route to the enlargement of pure a priori cognition.
It excludes objective validity from formal conceptual structure without conditions of possible object-givenness.
It excludes an unrestricted employment of pure understanding independent of sensuous conditions.
A complete formal closure of judgment is unavailable; the system requires an irreducible act of distinguishing.
A transferable educational technology capable of guaranteeing judgment is unavailable.
Positive philosophical sovereignty over pure cognition is foreclosed; critique retains authority only as a regulator of misuse.
Unconditioned conceptual access to objects is impossible; pure thought cannot supply object-givenness by itself.
The text leaves no fully articulated criterion for where ordinary non-teachability of judgment ends and transcendental direction of judgment begins.
Rule-governed understanding produces the problem of subsumption because a rule does not determine its own application.
General logic abstracts from content and therefore retains only the formal structure of cognition.
Any attempt to add a general rule for subsumption reproduces the original problem at a higher level and presupposes judgment again.
The resulting gap between rule possession and rule application is expressed pedagogically as the difference between learnedness and judgment.
Exercise and examples can train the operation of judgment but cannot replace the natural capacity required for it.
The domain of pure understanding introduces a restricted alternative in which transcendental logic specifies conditions for the employment of concepts.
Because pure concepts must relate a priori to objects, their validity is tested through conditions under which objects can be given in conformity with them.
The resulting doctrine proceeds from sensuous conditions of application to schematism and from schematism to synthetic a priori principles.
Rule-governed understanding → subsumptive judgment → abstraction of general logic → recursive failure of a rule for subsumption → irreducibility of judgment.
Irreducibility of judgment → exercise and examples → persistent gap between learned rules and correct application.
Gap in application → distinction between positive doctrine and negative critique → prevention of misuse of pure concepts.
A priori conditions of object-givenness → schematism → synthetic a priori principles of the pure understanding.
Judgment is reclassified from rule acquisition to the determination of whether a particular case falls under a rule.
Logic is divided into formal general logic, which cannot direct subsumption, and transcendental logic, which can specify conditions for the pure employment of concepts.
Examples are reclassified from evidentiary instances of rules into instruments for exercising judgment, with a simultaneous risk to universality.
Philosophy is reclassified from a constructive expansion of pure cognition into a critique that prevents invalid use.
Objective validity is relocated from logical form alone to the relation between concept and conditions of possible object-givenness.
The problem of judgment is transformed into a two-stage doctrine: conditions of application first, principles of pure understanding second.
Surface: The text distinguishes understanding, judgment, rules, subsumption, examples, schematism, and principles.
Structural: The argument separates rule production, rule possession, rule application, and the conditions that make application valid.
Metastrategic: The proper philosophical strategy is shifted from constructing more pure cognition to critically policing the use of existing pure concepts.
Ontological/Temporal: Objectivity depends on a priori conditions under which objects can be given, and the doctrine advances sequentially from sensible conditions to principles.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the distinction between understanding and judgment to the architecture of transcendental doctrine.
The precise nature of schemata, principles, and the a priori determination of cases remains underdetermined because those elements are announced rather than developed here.
The system is internally coherent if transcendental direction is treated as a restricted domain-specific exception rather than as a universal teachability of judgment.
Its strongest structural claim is the non-equivalence of rule possession and correct subsumption.
Its principal fault line lies between the asserted non-teachability of judgment and the claimed capacity of transcendental logic to direct its employment.
The argument relies on compressed assertions concerning the failure of positive doctrine and the necessity of a priori conditions for objectivity.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the actual movement from formal insufficiency, through critique, to schematism and principles.

identity.title: INTRODUCTION. Of the Transcendental Faculty of judgement in General

units.title: Chapter I. Of the Schematism at of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding

items.text: The application of pure concepts to sensible objects requires an account of how heterogeneous representations can enter into subsumption.
A third representation must mediate between categories and phenomena by being homogeneous with both.
Transcendental time-determinations supply this mediation as schemata produced by the imagination.
Each category receives objective applicability only through its rule-governed temporal schema.
The same sensible mediation that realizes categories also confines their objective use to possible experience.
The argument moves from heterogeneity, through temporal mediation, to empirical restriction of pure understanding.
Subsumption requires homogeneity between the concept and the object represented under it.
Categories are heterogeneous with empirical intuition and cannot be found in sensation.
A mediating representation must be intellectual in relation to categories and sensible in relation to phenomena.
Time is the formal condition of inner sense and is present in every empirical representation.
A transcendental time-determination is homogeneous with categories through its a priori rule and with phenomena through temporal sensibility.
The transcendental schema is a pure product of imagination that determines inner sense according to a rule.
A schema represents a general procedure for producing intuition in conformity with a concept rather than an image of an object.
Pure concepts attain objective significance only when an object can be given under the formal conditions of sensibility.
Objects can be given to cognition only through modifications of sensibility.
The schemata of categories are a priori determinations of time ordered by the categorical functions.
The unity of schematized intuition indirectly grounds the unity of apperception required for experience.
Categories without schemata retain logical function but lack determinate objective meaning.
Categories are not sensible contents that can be intuited in phenomena.
Schemas are not images, because an image is singular whereas a schema governs the production of possible images.
A pure concept is not objectively meaningful merely by being thinkable.
Categories are not validly applicable to things in themselves as objects independently given beyond sensibility.
The schema is not an empirical representation, because it must mediate a priori.
The schema of a category is not reducible to a spatial figure or any other image.
The category of substance is not a determinate object-concept once its temporal condition of permanence is removed.
Transcendental truth is not cognition of supersensible objects but the condition of possible empirical truth.
The problem of applying categories is transformed from a question of resemblance between concept and object into a question of rule-governed temporal mediation.
Imagination is assigned a transcendental function because it produces the temporal rule that connects understanding with sensibility.
Quantity becomes objectively applicable through number as the successive generation of homogeneous time.
Quality becomes objectively applicable through degrees of temporal filling, including the continuous transition between reality and negation.
Relation becomes objectively applicable through temporal rules of permanence, succession, and rule-governed coexistence.
Modality becomes objectively applicable through temporal determination of possibility, actual existence, and existence in all time.
Experience is possible only as a unified field in which intuitions are synthesized under temporal rules and connected in one apperception.
The empirical restriction of categories is not an external limitation added after their formation but follows from the conditions required for their objective use.
Objectivity is constituted as the lawful temporal synthesizeability of appearances rather than as access to objects independently of sensibility.
The categories possess a double status: they are unrestricted logical functions in abstraction but objectively valid rules only within sensible experience.
Time functions as the universal conversion medium through which intellectual unity acquires phenomenal determinacy.
The unity of experience depends on a hidden productive operation that cannot itself be replaced by either discursive concepts or empirical images.
Transcendental truth precedes empirical truth by establishing the formal conditions under which empirical judgments can form one connected experience.
No direct intellectual intuition of categories in objects is available.
No object can be objectively determined by a category outside the temporal form of sensibility.
No singular sensible presentation can exhaust the universality of a concept.
No purely logical determination supplies the material criteria by which an object can be cognized.
No account of experience can dispense with a mediating synthesis between receptivity and spontaneity.
Cognition of things as they are independently of the conditions under which they are given is foreclosed.
A category’s apparent metaphysical extension beyond experience is denied objective content while remaining thinkable in a merely logical sense.
The source of the mediating synthesis remains unavailable to transparent theoretical inspection, because schematism is posited as an obscure art of the soul.
The hoped-for coincidence of pure thought with objecthood without sensible mediation is structurally inadmissible.
Heterogeneity of category and intuition → impossibility of immediate subsumption.
Requirement of homogeneity → necessity of a third, mixed representation.
Universality of time in sensibility + rule-governed unity of categories → transcendental temporal schema.
Schema as imaginative rule → temporal specification of quantity, quality, relation, and modality.
Temporal specification → lawful synthesis of appearances into possible experience.
Dependence on temporal sensibility → realization and restriction of categories.
Removal of sensibility → residual logical function without objective object-determination.
Heterogeneity of pure concepts and intuition → demand for homogeneous mediation.
Demand for mediation → identification of transcendental time-determination.
Time-determination → schema as rule of productive imagination.
Schema-rule → categorical ordering of appearances in time.
Temporal ordering → unified possible experience and transcendental truth.
Sensible condition of validity → exclusion of objective categorical knowledge of things in themselves.
The category is reclassified from a self-sufficient object-concept into a function requiring sensible schematization for objective employment.
Imagination is reclassified from a merely reproductive image-making faculty into the mediator of understanding and sensibility.
Time is reclassified from one form of intuition among others into the universal field in which every categorical schema receives applicability.
The image/concept opposition is displaced by a threefold structure of image, schema, and concept.
The opposition between unrestricted metaphysical use and empirical use collapses into a distinction between logical significance and objective validity.
Transcendental truth is located in the architecture enabling experience rather than in a correspondence claim about things beyond experience.
Surface — The chapter explains how categories such as quantity, causality, substance, possibility, actuality, and necessity can apply to phenomena.
Structural — Schematism organizes categorical application through rule-governed determinations of time produced by imagination.
Metastrategic — The argument resolves the threat of a gap between pure thought and experience by relocating validity in mediation rather than direct conceptual possession.
Ontological/Temporal — Objects of cognition are determinable only insofar as they enter temporal conditions of appearance and unified consciousness.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the necessity of schematism from the heterogeneity of categories and intuitions.
The system reconstructs the schema’s role only if time is retained as universally present in empirical representation.
The categorical schemata reconstruct the movement from abstract functions to determinate temporal rules.
The system is internally coherent insofar as objective validity is made conditional upon possible sensible givenness.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the positive mechanism by which imagination generates specific schemata, since that operation is declared obscure rather than derived.
The strongest structural closure is the reciprocal thesis that sensibility both enables and limits understanding.
A residual tension persists between the categories’ asserted logical significance apart from sensibility and the claim that no object-concept remains once schematization is removed.

identity.title: Chapter I. Of the Schematism at of the Pure Conceptions of the Understanding

units.title: Chapter II. System of all Principles of the Pure Understanding

items.text: The task is to exhibit systematically the pure a priori judgments actually produced by the understanding.
The categories provide the natural and secure basis for identifying these judgments.
Their application to possible experience determines the complete catalogue of transcendental principles belonging to the understanding.
A priori principles require proof even when no higher principle can objectively ground them.
The required proof proceeds from the subjective conditions that make cognition of an object possible.
The inquiry is delimited by excluding principles grounded in sensibility or intuition while retaining their possibility as an issue of transcendental explanation.
The distinction between analytical and synthetical judgments is introduced to delimit and clarify the proper subject of the investigation.
Pure a priori cognition of the understanding arises through the application of the categories to possible experience.
The relation between the categories and sensibility determines the systematic catalogue of the understanding’s transcendental principles.
A principle may ground other judgments without being grounded in a higher or more general cognition.
Foundational status does not exempt an a priori principle from the need for proof.
The possibility of cognition of an object can be established through the subjective conditions of that cognition.
The categories govern the principles within the present system, whereas space and time belong to the conditions supplied by transcendental sensibility.
Mathematical principles are synthetic a priori but derive from intuition rather than from pure concepts of the understanding.
The possibility of mathematical synthetic a priori cognition can be treated without making mathematical proof itself the subject of this system.
Analytical judgments must be considered as a contrastive boundary for identifying synthetic judgments.
The principles under investigation concern the use of the understanding in relation to possible experience, not objects considered as things in themselves.
The system is not an inventory of every a priori principle whatsoever.
The present inquiry does not investigate the principles of transcendental aesthetics as its proper subject.
Principles concerning space and time are not treated as principles of the pure understanding.
The principles of transcendental aesthetics cannot be applied to objects as things in themselves.
Mathematical principles are not derived from pure concepts of the understanding.
The inquiry does not aim to prove the accuracy or apodeictic certainty of mathematical principles.
Analytical judgments are not the proper subject of the investigation.
A foundational a priori principle is not thereby a gratuitous assertion exempt from justification.
The categories do not license cognition of objects independently of their relation to possible experience.
The categories can function as a complete classificatory guide for the principles of the pure understanding because their application to possible experience exhausts the relevant domain.
A system of principles can be both foundational for object-cognition and subject to transcendental proof.
The proof of a first principle need not appeal to a still higher objective principle.
The relevant proof establishes the conditions under which cognition of an object is possible rather than deducing the principle from an externally superior proposition.
The system distinguishes the source of a principle from the conditions under which its application is legitimate.
Mathematical cognition can be included as an object of transcendental possibility without being assimilated to cognition generated by the categories.
The opposition between analytical and synthetical judgment prevents the theory of synthetic a priori principles from being left conceptually ambiguous.
The scope of the system is determined by the intersection of pure understanding, categorical form, and possible experience.
The system converts the question of first principles from a search for higher premises into an analysis of the conditions that make object-cognition possible.
The categories function simultaneously as principles of synthesis, a rule for systematic classification, and a boundary on legitimate application.

The system produces a layered architecture in which sensibility supplies conditions of appearance, intuition supplies the basis of mathematics, and the categories supply principles for the understanding’s synthesis.
The possibility of a complete catalogue depends on restricting completeness to the domain of the understanding’s categorical relation to possible experience.
The distinction between analytical and synthetical judgment operates as a control mechanism that prevents foundational analysis from collapsing into mere conceptual unpacking.
The system cannot be grounded on an unrestricted theory of all a priori cognition.
The understanding cannot claim principles whose validity is detached from their relation to possible experience.
The categories cannot be treated as interchangeable with the forms of sensibility or the sources of mathematical intuition.
Objectivity cannot be secured solely by positing a principle as foundational.
Transcendental proof cannot be reduced to derivation from a higher empirical or metaphysical proposition.
Systematic completeness cannot mean inclusion of every form of synthetic a priori cognition under one faculty.
The distinction between appearance and thing in itself cannot be suspended when specifying the valid domain of transcendental principles.
Unconditioned cognition of things in themselves is unavailable to the principles established through the categories.
No single undifferentiated source of a priori cognition is admissible; sensibility, intuition, and understanding must remain functionally distinct.
The legitimacy of first principles cannot rest on authority, assertion, or mere absence of a higher ground.
Completeness cannot be achieved by erasing the boundary between the conditions of appearance and the conditions of conceptual synthesis.
The system presupposes that cognition requires a finite field of possible application rather than access to reality without conditions.
Categories + possible experience → domain of pure understanding.
Domain of pure understanding + relation to sensibility → systematic catalogue of transcendental principles.
Foundational status + absence of higher cognition → need for transcendental rather than higher-level proof.
Subjective conditions of object-cognition → proof of the objective validity of foundational principles.
Separation of sensibility, intuition, and understanding → exclusion of aesthetic and mathematical principles from the category-system proper.
Excluded mathematical principles + synthetic a priori status → investigation of their possibility without mathematical demonstration.
Contrast with analytical judgment → determinate identification of synthetic a priori principles.
Restricted domain + transcendental proof + categorical ordering → system of the principles of the pure understanding.
General conditions for using pure concepts → systematic exhibition of actual a priori judgments.
Categories → catalogue of principles governing the understanding’s relation to possible experience.
Foundational status without higher ground → requirement of proof from subjective conditions.
Separation of sensibility, intuition, and understanding → restriction of the system’s proper object.
Mathematical exception → transcendental treatment of possibility without mathematical proof.
Analytical/synthetic opposition → clarification of the system’s proper subject.
Delimited domain + categorical structure + transcendental justification → system of the principles of the pure understanding.
A priori principles are reclassified from unsupported foundations into objects requiring transcendental justification.
The categories become the organizing grid for the understanding’s principles rather than merely a list of concepts.
The boundary between sensibility and understanding becomes a condition of systematic completeness.
Mathematical cognition is relocated from the category-system proper to a neighboring domain whose possibility still requires transcendental explanation.
The opposition between analytical and synthetical judgment becomes a methodological instrument for determining the field of inquiry.
The valid scope of object-cognition is mapped onto possible experience rather than onto objects considered independently of conditions of appearance.
Surface — The text announces a systematic inventory of the pure a priori judgments produced by the understanding.
Structural — The inventory is generated by correlating categories with their application to possible experience and their relation to sensibility.
Metastrategic — The argument replaces appeal to higher principles with transcendental proof from the conditions of cognition, while using exclusions to delimit the system.
Ontological/Temporal — Cognition is restricted to objects as phenomena within possible experience; things in themselves remain outside the valid application of the principles.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s central movement from categorical classification to a systematic theory of principles.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between the source of a principle, the proof of its validity, and the domain of its application.
The structure remains coherent because completeness is restricted to the principles of the pure understanding in relation to possible experience.
The main unresolved tension is that a priori principles are foundational yet require justification, which the text resolves by shifting from objective derivation to transcendental grounding.
A second tension remains between excluding mathematical principles from the system and treating their possibility as necessarily relevant to it.
The chapter’s final system depends on the maintained separation of analytical and synthetical judgment, sensibility and understanding, and phenomena and things in themselves.

identity.title: Chapter II. System of all Principles of the Pure Understanding

units.title: Section I. Of the Supreme Principle of all Analytical Judgements

items.text: The central problem is to determine what the principle of contradiction can and cannot establish about judgment.
Every judgment is first subjected to noncontradiction as a universal negative condition of cognition.
Noncontradiction is then separated from correspondence with the object and from the possession of grounds.
The principle receives a positive function only within analytical cognition, where the predicate belongs to the subject-concept.
Synthetic cognition remains outside the principle’s capacity to establish truth, although it remains bound by its prohibition of contradiction.
The temporalized formula of contradiction is rejected because it confuses logical contradiction with the successive alteration of predicates.
