The corrected formulation must express contradiction through the relation between a predicate and the subject-concept rather than through temporal simultaneity.
A judgment that contradicts itself is nullified as cognition independently of its relation to an object.
Noncontradiction is a universal negative condition of judgment.
A noncontradictory judgment may nevertheless be false or groundless.
The principle of contradiction is formal and applies to cognitions merely as cognitions, without regard to their content.
In an analytical judgment, the predicate is contained in or constitutive of the conception of the subject.
In an analytical judgment, the contrary of a constituent predicate conflicts with the subject-concept.
The principle of contradiction is sufficient for recognizing the truth of analytical cognition.
The principle of contradiction is a necessary condition of truth but not, in general, the determining ground of truth.
The principle of contradiction cannot directly establish the truth of a synthetic proposition.
The formula that a thing cannot be and not be at the same time introduces both a temporal condition and a synthetic relation between predicates.
Predicates that cannot belong to the same thing at the same time may belong to it at different times.
Logical contradiction must not be restricted to simultaneous temporal relations.
An analytical negative judgment does not require a temporal qualification when the negated predicate is excluded by the subject-concept itself.
The absence of contradiction is not equivalent to truth.
The absence of contradiction is not equivalent to correspondence with the object.
The absence of contradiction is not equivalent to the possession of grounds, whether a priori or a posteriori.
The principle of contradiction is not a content-bearing or object-determining principle.
The principle of contradiction is not a sufficient criterion for synthetic truth.
Logical contradiction is not identical with the incompatibility of predicates at one moment in time.
The temporalized formula is not an adequate formulation of the purely logical principle.
An analytical contradiction is not produced by separating a predicate from the subject-concept and opposing that predicate to its contrary.
The principle of contradiction functions as a preliminary nullification test before any question of object-relation arises.
A judgment that survives the contradiction test remains epistemically admissible but not thereby established as true.
The principle acquires positive cognitive force when contradiction with the subject-concept is sufficient to exclude the contrary predicate.
Analytical truth can be recognized through contradiction because conceptual containment supplies the missing relation between predicate and subject.
The same principle operates negatively for all cognition but positively only where the judgment is analytical.
The distinction between analytical and synthetic judgment determines whether contradiction can function as a truth-recognition procedure or only as a prohibition.
Temporal succession shows that opposed predicates do not by themselves constitute a contradiction in the subject.
An analytical negative proposition is atemporal in its logical force when the predicate’s exclusion follows from the subject-concept.
Correcting the formula requires removing the temporal condition and restoring contradiction to the subject-predicate structure of analytical cognition.
The principle of contradiction is simultaneously universal as a boundary condition and restricted as a truth-producing principle.
The positive use of logic does not abolish its formal character; it becomes possible only when the content of the judgment is already structurally contained in the subject-concept.
The analytical–synthetic distinction marks two different epistemic powers of contradiction: determination in the first case and constraint in the second.
The temporalized formula commits a category error by treating a change in predication as though it were the self-nullification of a judgment.
Truth is internally stratified into logical admissibility, analytical recognizability, and synthetic determination.
The system depends on the falsity of the equation between consistency and truth.
The system excludes the derivation of object-correspondence from formal logical validity alone.
The system excludes the reduction of grounds of cognition to the principle of contradiction.
The system excludes the use of temporal succession as the defining structure of logical contradiction.
The system excludes the detachment of predicates from their conceptual relation to the subject when determining analytical contradiction.
The system excludes a single undifferentiated operation of contradiction across analytical and synthetic judgments.
A purely formal principle cannot by itself bridge cognition and the object cognized.
No general positive criterion of synthetic truth is supplied by the principle of contradiction.
The unification of analytical and synthetic truth under one formal rule is structurally foreclosed.
Temporal change is inadmissible as the ground of logical contradiction, even though it remains relevant to changing predicates.
The determining ground of synthetic cognition remains external to the logical principle and is left unprovided in the passage.
Any judgment enters the system through a contradiction test: judgment → self-consistency check → nullification if contradiction is present.
Survival of the contradiction test produces only formal admissibility: noncontradiction → continued status as cognition → unresolved truth-status.
The unresolved truth-status is divided by judgment type: analytical judgment versus synthetic judgment.
Analytical cognition activates conceptual containment: subject-concept → contained predicate → exclusion of contrary predicate → recognizable truth.
Synthetic cognition activates only logical restriction: proposition → noncontradiction requirement → no direct truth-establishment.
The temporal formula is tested against succession: simultaneous predicate opposition → possible successive compatibility → failure of the formula as a general logical principle.
The corrected formulation restores the subject-concept as the site of contradiction and removes temporal qualification from analytical negation.
Universal demand for self-consistency → nullification of contradiction → insufficiency of consistency for truth.
Formal logical principle → distinction between analytical and synthetic cognition → restricted positive use in analytical judgments.
Temporalized contradiction formula → distinction between predicate incompatibility and conceptual contradiction → reformulation through the subject-concept.
Truth is reclassified from a single criterion into differentiated levels of logical admissibility, analytical recognition, and synthetic grounding.
The principle of contradiction is repositioned from a universal truth-generator to a universal boundary condition with a limited positive application.
The opposition between “true” and “contradictory” is separated from the opposition between “grounded” and “groundless.”
Temporal change is removed from the definition of logical contradiction and reassigned to the domain of successive predication.
The analytical judgment becomes identifiable through conceptual containment rather than through the mere simultaneity of predicates.
Synthetic truth is redrawn as a separate epistemic problem that logic can constrain but cannot solve.
Surface: The argument evaluates the principle that a subject cannot possess a contradictory predicate and corrects its temporalized formulation.
Structural: The argument differentiates formal logic, analytical judgment, synthetic judgment, object-correspondence, and epistemic grounds.
Metastrategic: The argument converts a seemingly universal truth criterion into a bounded instrument whose function depends on the type of cognition being assessed.
Ontological/Temporal: The argument separates logical contradiction from temporal succession, allowing predicates to change across time without making the cognition self-contradictory.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the central distinction between noncontradiction as a necessary condition and truth as a further determination.
The extracted structure preserves the argument’s movement from negative logical validity to the restricted positive function of contradiction in analytical cognition.
The system is strongest where it differentiates subject-conceptual contradiction from successive changes in predication.
The apparent tension between calling the principle a criterion of truth and denying its sufficiency is resolved by restricting its positive authority to analytical judgments.
The boundary between conceptual containment and synthetic predication remains compressed rather than fully formalized in the passage.
The grounds of synthetic truth are structurally excluded from the principle but not independently supplied, leaving the larger epistemological problem open.
Reconstruction preserves the internal coherence of the passage, including its deliberate refusal to make logical noncontradiction the determining ground of all truth.

identity.title: Section I. Of the Supreme Principle of all Analytical Judgements

units.title: Section II. Of the Supreme Principle of all Synthetical Judgements

items.text: The possibility and objective validity of synthetic a priori judgement cannot be determined by general logic because such judgement exceeds conceptual containment.
Synthetic judgement requires a mediating field in which heterogeneous representations can be combined rather than merely compared by identity or contradiction.
The mediating conditions of synthesis are a priori intuition, imagination, and the unity of apperception.
A representation acquires objective reality only through possible experience, in which an object can be given in intuition.
Possible experience requires rules that synthesize appearances into a unified consciousness of objects.
Synthetic a priori judgements are valid only as conditions necessary for the possibility of experience and therefore for objects of experience.
The supreme principle subjects every object of possible experience to the necessary synthetic unity of the manifold of intuition.
Analytic judgement determines a concept without exceeding what is already thought in it.
Synthetic judgement connects a concept with something not already thought in that concept.
The truth or falsity of a synthetic judgement cannot be determined from the judgement’s concepts alone.
Every synthesis of representations requires a mediating domain in which the representations can be combined.
Time, as the a priori form of inner sense, contains the representations whose combination makes synthesis possible.
Imagination performs the synthesis of representations.
Apperception supplies the unity required for synthesized representations to constitute judgement.
Cognition has objective reality only if its object can be given in intuition within real or possible experience.
Concepts without possible experiential application are empty of objective meaning.
Experience is possible only through a rule-governed synthesis of appearances under the unity of apperception.
A priori principles have objective validity only insofar as they express necessary conditions of possible experience.
Objects of experience are necessarily subject to the conditions that make unified experience possible.
The possibility of synthetic judgement is not a problem for general logic.
Synthetic judgement is not reducible to conceptual identity, conceptual containment, or contradiction.
Synthetic truth is not decidable through formal inspection of concepts alone.
A synthesis is not possible through two concepts alone without a mediating third term.
Mere thinking is not cognition of an object.
Pure concepts, including space and time, are not objectively valid merely because they are represented a priori.
Experience is not an aggregate or rhapsody of perceptions lacking necessary unity.
Synthetic a priori propositions detached from possible experience are impossible as objectively valid cognitions.
A priori synthesis is not valid when it claims more than the necessary unity of possible experience requires.
The investigation of synthetic a priori judgement becomes an investigation of the conditions under which representations can be objectively unified.
The conditions of a priori intuition, imagination, and apperception jointly supply the architecture required for pure synthetic judgement.
The objective validity of space and time depends on their functioning as conditions under which objects can appear in possible experience.
Experience becomes cognition only when perceptions are synthesized according to rules into one possible consciousness.
The possibility of experience confers objective reality on a priori cognition because such cognition articulates experience’s necessary form.
The supreme principle of synthetic judgement follows because an experiential object cannot be given except under the conditions of unified synthesis.
Objectivity is relocated from correspondence between an isolated concept and an independent object to lawful synthesizability within possible experience.
The same transcendental conditions ground both the unity of experience and the objecthood of what is experienced.
Pure cognition is constrained rather than expanded by its a priori status, because its validity ends where the conditions of possible experience end.
The question of whether synthetic a priori knowledge is possible is transformed into the question of how a unified experience of objects is possible.
Objective cognition is not grounded in concepts whose relation to objects can be established independently of intuition.
Objects of cognition are not available prior to, or apart from, the formal conditions under which they can be experienced.
Necessity is not licensed by mere conceptual coherence; it requires grounding in the necessary form of possible experience.
A priori knowledge is not a route to objects beyond possible experience.
Empirical multiplicity is not self-unifying and cannot yield cognition without transcendental synthesis.
The system excludes a cognition of things as objects independently of the conditions through which a subject can receive and unify them.
The system forecloses an unconditioned standpoint from which the validity of synthetic cognition could be established outside possible experience.
The system denies that an object can serve as a cognitive ground while remaining unavailable to intuition and synthesis.
The system disallows a separation between the conditions of experiential objecthood and the conditions of valid objective judgement.
Conceptual non-containment → need for synthetic connection → impossibility of purely logical validation.
Need for synthetic connection → mediating intuition → imaginative synthesis → apperceptive unity.
Intuition plus synthesis plus unity → possible experience as connected cognition rather than perceptual aggregate.
Possible experience → conditions for objects to be given → objective validity of a priori representations.
Objective validity of a priori synthesis → restriction to necessary conditions of possible experience.
Restriction to experiential conditions → every object of experience is subject to the synthetic unity of intuition’s manifold.

Synthetic judgement exceeds conceptual analysis → a mediating synthesis is required → intuition, imagination, and apperception provide its conditions → possible experience supplies objectivity → necessary experiential conditions define valid a priori synthesis → objects of experience fall under synthetic unity.
The problem of synthetic a priori knowledge is reclassified from a logical problem of concepts to a transcendental problem of experiential objectivity.
Space and time are reclassified from independently meaningful representations to forms whose objective significance depends on possible experience.
Experience is reclassified from received perception to rule-governed synthesis under unified consciousness.
Objectivity is mapped as dependence on conditions of possible givenness rather than as a property secured by thought alone.
The boundary between legitimate a priori cognition and empty speculation is drawn at the limits of possible experience.
Surface — The text establishes the supreme principle governing all synthetic judgements concerning objects.
Structural — The text grounds judgement in the coordinated functions of intuition, imagination, apperception, and rule-governed experiential synthesis.
Metastrategic — The text displaces the validation of a priori knowledge from conceptual analysis to an account of the conditions of possible experience.
Ontological/Temporal — Objects are cognizable only as appearances ordered within a priori forms of intuition and unified in temporal inner sense.
Limitative — The text restricts every objectively valid synthetic a priori claim to what is necessary for possible experience.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from the insufficiency of conceptual analysis to the principle governing synthetic a priori judgement.
The system depends decisively on the claim that possible experience is the sole source of objective reality for a priori representations.
The argument is internally coherent if objectivity means valid applicability to possible experience rather than access to objects independently of experience.
The principal compression occurs in the transition from the unity required for experience to the claim that the same unity necessarily governs every object of experience.
A structural tension remains between time as the stated universal mediating field of representation and space as an indispensable form of external experiential objectivity.
A further tension remains between the claim that an object must be given and the appeal to merely possible experience as sufficient for objective validity.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the limiting function of possible experience is retained alongside its grounding function.

identity.title: Section II. Of the Supreme Principle of all Synthetical Judgements

units.title: Section III. Systematic Representation of all Synthetical Principles of the Pure Understanding

items.text: The chapter determines how synthetic a priori principles can govern every object of possible experience.
It locates the source of such principles in pure understanding because object-cognition requires necessary rule-governance.
It separates principles of pure understanding from empirical laws and from mathematical principles derived through pure intuition.
It derives the system of principles from the category table as rules for the categories’ objective employment.
It divides categorical synthesis into mathematical determination of intuition and dynamical determination of phenomenal existence.
It proves the first two mathematical principles by deriving extensive quantity from spatial-temporal apprehension and intensive quantity from the graduated reality of sensation.
The movement is transcendental-systematic: objectivity requirement → principial source → categorical classification → quantitative proofs → empirical constraints and limits.
Cognition of an object of possible experience requires necessary rules governing its presentation.
Pure understanding is the source of the principles supplying these necessary rules.
Pure understanding is the faculty of concepts, so its proper principles proceed from pure concepts.
Empirical laws of nature apply higher a priori principles and cannot ground their own necessity.
Principles of pure understanding are rules for the objective employment of the categories.
Quantity, quality, relation, and modality generate respectively the Axioms of Intuition, Anticipations of Perception, Analogies of Experience, and Postulates of Empirical Thought.
Mathematical principles originate in pure intuition, but their possibility and objective validity for experience depend on pure understanding.
Categorical synthesis is mathematical when directed to intuition and dynamical when directed to phenomenal existence.
Mathematical synthesis composes homogeneous manifolds, whereas dynamical synthesis connects heterogeneous existences as necessarily related.
Conditions of intuition are absolutely necessary, whereas conditions of phenomenal existence are necessary only under the condition of empirical thought.
The form of every phenomenon is given a priori through continuous intuition in space and time.
Apprehension of determinate space or time requires successive synthesis of a homogeneous manifold.
A quantity is extensive when representation of its parts necessarily precedes and makes possible representation of the whole.
All intuitions, and therefore all phenomena considered as intuitions, are extensive quantities.
Perception contains sensation as empirical matter, while the determinate quality of sensation is cognizable only a posteriori.
Sensation is apprehended as a unity rather than successively composed from parts and therefore has no extensive quantity.
Every sensation permits continuous diminution from its given reality toward negation at zero.
The real in every phenomenon has intensive quantity because sensation is representable by a degree relative to zero.
Extensive empirical validity does not confer the necessity characteristic of a pure principle.
Empirical laws are not coordinate with the higher principles that make their rule-governed application possible.
Principles originating in pure intuition are not themselves principles of pure understanding, even when their objective validity depends on understanding.
“Mathematical” and “dynamical” designate modes of application, not the substantive principles of mathematics or physical dynamics.
Discursive and mediated certainty is not thereby incomplete or uncertain.
Phenomena are not things in themselves.
Objects of sense cannot be exempted from the formal conditions of sensibility.
Neither analytical equality rules nor singular numerical formulae qualify as synthetic universal axioms.
The determinate quality of sensation cannot be anticipated a priori.
Sensation is not an objective spatial or temporal representation and does not possess extensive quantity.
Points and moments are not simple constituents of space and time but boundaries presupposing continuous intuitions.
Repetition of interrupted syntheses produces an aggregate of phenomena, not one phenomenon as a continuous quantity.
The continuity of change is not established here because determination of its cause would exceed the available pure principles.
Failure to perceive reality does not constitute experiential proof of empty space or empty time.
Variable intensive filling is presented as a possible explanation of material difference, not as an established physical fact.
Necessity distinguishes principles of pure understanding from empirical generalizations.
Higher principles provide the necessary form of a rule, while experience supplies the particular case falling under it.
The category table functions as the systematic generator rather than merely the classifier of pure principles.
The quantity and quality principles possess intuitive and apodeictic evidence, while relation and modality possess mediated but complete discursive certainty.
Every phenomenon must be apprehended through part-to-part synthesis as an extensive quantity.
What pure mathematics establishes concerning spatial-temporal intuition applies necessarily to phenomena.
A phenomenal whole cannot antecede the synthesis of the homogeneous parts through which it is apprehended.
Every phenomenal reality possesses degree despite lacking extensive composition within the sensation itself.
The quality of a sensation remains empirical, but the fact that it has a degree is anticipatable a priori.
Phenomena are continuous both as extensive intuitions and as intensive realities.
Neither spatial-temporal extension nor phenomenal reality contains a smallest possible positive part.
Experience cannot prove a void because complete negation is not itself perceived and arbitrarily diminished reality remains possible.
Equal extensive spaces can be completely filled while differing through the intensive degrees of their realities.
Transcendental principles determine the possibility-space of empirical explanation without determining sensation’s qualities, actual causes, or physical facts.
Objectivity consists in necessary conformity to the synthetic rules under which an appearance can become an object of cognition.
The objective applicability of mathematics is secured because the synthesis determining pure space and time also determines possible phenomenal apprehension.
A priori cognition reaches the matter of experience only through an invariant quantitative condition, not through prior knowledge of what is sensed.
The phenomenal field is doubly quantitative: form is extensive and sensible reality is intensive, while both dimensions are continuous.
Nonperception underdetermines the distinction between absolute absence and reality below the degree required for perception.
Transcendental analysis can invalidate a claimed necessity in physical explanation while leaving the competing empirical explanation undecided.
The system stratifies evidence by mode of synthesis without stratifying truth or certainty into secure and insecure forms.
An object cannot become cognizable independently of necessary synthetic rule-governance.
Necessity cannot be generated by induction from repeated empirical cases.
The system cannot tolerate an incomplete or non-exhaustive category table without losing the systematic completeness of its principles.
Spatial-temporal predicates cannot be treated as properties of things independently of the conditions of sensibility.
Space and time cannot be constructed from antecedently given simple points or moments.
Sensation cannot consist of indivisible least positive degrees.
Absence of perception cannot be identified with perception of absence.
Differences among phenomenal realities cannot be reduced necessarily to multiplicity, aggregation, or extensive quantity.
Pure understanding cannot determine the empirical quality of sensation or select an actual physical cause from transcendental conditions alone.
Unmediated cognition of objects apart from sensibility and categorical synthesis is structurally unavailable.
The qualitative content of empirical reality remains absent from a priori cognition.
Absolute nothing cannot appear as a positive datum; zero functions only as the limiting negation of possible degree.
No ultimate phenomenal simple is available either as a spatial-temporal constituent or as a least degree of reality.
A completed physical ontology cannot be extracted from the transcendental conditions of possible experience.
Object-cognition → necessary rule-governance → pure understanding → a priori principles.
Empirical regularity / pure intuition / pure concept → exclusion of empirical and mathematical principles from the proper principles of understanding.
Category table → objective-use rules → quantity/Axioms, quality/Anticipations, relation/Analogies, modality/Postulates.
Intuition-directed composition → mathematical principles → immediate apodeictic evidence; existence-directed nexus → dynamical principles → mediated conditional necessity.
Space-time form → homogeneous manifold → successive synthesis → antecedent parts → extensive phenomenal quantity.
Perception → sensation → non-extensive unity → continuous variation from zero → intensive degree.
Extensive continuity + intensive continuity → no smallest phenomenal parts → no experiential proof of absolute void.
Transcendental condition → exclusion of false necessity → enlarged empirical possibility-space → suspension of factual physical determination.

Need for principles → pure understanding as source → separation from empirical and mathematical principles → categorical systematization → mathematical/dynamical division → proof of extensive quantity → validation of mathematical application → proof of intensive quantity → continuity → restriction of void-inferences → empirical restraint.
Laws of nature are reclassified from self-grounding necessities into empirical applications of higher principles.
Mathematics is repositioned from an independently applicable science to a body of pure-intuitive cognition whose objective use requires transcendental grounding.
The category table becomes a generative map of possible principial forms rather than a static taxonomy of concepts.
Quantity divides into extensive composition and intensive degree, preventing the quantitative field from being reduced to aggregation.
Sensation divides into an empirically unknowable quality and an a priori knowable structure of degree.
Nonperception is reclassified from evidence of nothingness into an indeterminate relation between zero and imperceptibly small reality.
Points, moments, and zero are reclassified as limits or boundaries rather than constitutive phenomenal elements.
Differences in material filling become conceivably intensive rather than necessarily products of empty intervals.
Immediate and mediated evidence become distinct modes of certainty rather than opposing degrees of truth.
Surface: The chapter classifies the principles of pure understanding and proves that phenomenal intuition is extensive while phenomenal reality is intensive.
Structural: The category table and the modes of synthesis determine the architecture, evidence, and domain of each principial class.
Metastrategic: The argument regulates legitimate a priori claims by separating formal conditions of experience from empirical qualities, causes, and physical hypotheses.
Ontological/Temporal: Phenomena exist for cognition only through spatial-temporal synthesis, part-to-part succession, continuous magnitude, and graduated sensible reality.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s taxonomy and its developed arguments for the first two principle classes.
The Analogies of Experience and Postulates of Empirical Thought remain underdetermined because they are classified but not developed in the supplied text.
The structure is internally coherent only if the completeness of the category table and the prior doctrines of pure intuition and phenomena are accepted.
The strongest inferential junction is the identity of the synthesis determining space and time with the synthesis required for apprehending phenomena.
The anticipation argument depends on the asserted continuous diminutability of every sensation, which is not independently demonstrated here.

The account treats sensation as apprehended in one moment while grounding its degree in a temporal rise of consciousness from zero; the relation between instantaneous degree and diachronic synthesis remains compressed.
“Aggregate” shifts between an internally synthesized extensive phenomenon and a mere collection of separate phenomena, leaving the criterion of phenomenal unity partly implicit.
The polemic against exempting sensible objects from geometry adds no independent ground beyond the imported doctrine that phenomena conform to pure intuition.
The anti-void conclusion is epistemic rather than ontological, and the intensive account of material difference is modal rather than factual.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if mediated certainty, empirical underdetermination, and the distinction between possibility and actuality remain intact.

identity.title: Section III. Systematic Representation of all Synthetical Principles of the Pure Understanding

units.title: Chapter III Of the Ground of the Division of all Objects into Phenomena and Noumena

items.text: The chapter asks whether pure understanding can validly determine objects beyond possible experience and thereby ground a division into phenomena and noumena.
Its central claim is that categories and principles possess objective use only under the conditions of sensibility within possible experience.
Objective cognition requires both an intuition that gives an object and a schema that permits categorial subsumption.
The ambiguity of noumenon is resolved by distinguishing a negative limit-concept from a positive object of intellectual intuition.
Positive noumena are unavailable because human cognition lacks intellectual intuition, while negative noumena remain necessary to bound sensible cognition.
The argument is critical, transcendental, diagnostic, and reconstructive: it grounds empirical validity by restricting transcendental pretension.
The movement proceeds from the secured territory of experience through the conditions of objective meaning to the collapse of transcendental use and the retention of a merely limitative beyond.
The unity of experience is produced by the understanding’s a priori synthesis of the sensible manifold in relation to apperception.
Pure concepts and principles possess objective validity through their function as conditions of possible experience.
Objective reference requires that an object be given through intuition.
The only intuition available to human cognition is sensuous intuition.
Space and time possess objective validity only as forms of empirical intuition.
Categories are forms for uniting a given manifold and do not themselves supply that manifold.
Categorial judgment requires a schema as the formal condition for subsuming an intuited object.
Noncontradiction establishes only logical possibility; real objective possibility requires a corresponding intuition.
Empirical use refers concepts to phenomena, whereas transcendental use would refer them to things in general as things in themselves.
Designating an object as phenomenon distinguishes it from the thing considered apart from the human mode of intuition.
A noumenon in the negative sense is a thing considered insofar as it is not an object of sensuous intuition.
A noumenon in the positive sense is an object of nonsensuous intellectual intuition.
Human cognition possesses neither intellectual intuition nor a determinate conception of its possibility.
The negative noumenon is necessary only as a problematic concept limiting sensible cognition.
Every synthetic principle requires a third term connecting concepts that are not analytically related.
Possible experience is the only available mediator for synthetic categorial principles.
The a priori origin of a concept does not authorize its application beyond experience.
Pure categories separated from sensibility do not determine objects.
Logical noncontradiction is not proof of real possibility or existence.
A merely transcendental meaning does not constitute a valid transcendental use.
A noumenon is not a determinate intelligible object for human understanding.
The negative noumenon is neither an arbitrary fiction nor a source of positive supersensible data.
Phenomena and noumena do not form two positively cognizable classes of objects or worlds.
Human sensibility cannot be asserted to be the only possible mode of intuition absolutely.
The lawful conceptual organization of phenomena is not an intelligible world in the noumenal sense.
The claim that understanding represents objects “as they are” cannot signify cognition of things in themselves.
A synthetic ontology of things in general cannot be constructed from pure categories.
Pure understanding can anticipate only the formal structure of possible experience, not the intrinsic constitution of things.
Every objectively valid use of the categories is empirical even though the categories originate a priori.
Transcendental use of a category is no determinate use because it lacks an object capable of subsumption.
Without sensible and temporal schemata, categories collapse into indeterminate logical functions.
Ontology must be replaced by an analytic of the understanding’s contribution to possible experience.
Positive noumenal cognition is unavailable because its required mode of givenness is absent from human cognition.
The negative noumenon is admissible and necessary while yielding no positive cognition beyond phenomena.
A positive division of objects into sensible and intelligible classes is invalid because the alleged noumenal class has no determinable objects.
Categories extend beyond sensibility only as forms for thinking an object in general, not as means of determining a wider domain.
Sensibility without understanding and understanding without sensibility each fail to produce cognition of a determinate object.
No synthetic principle about noumena can be demonstrated because no non-empirical mediator connects its concepts.
The phenomena–noumena distinction is asymmetrical: phenomena constitute a cognizable domain, while noumena mark only that sensible cognition is not cognition of things as such.
Understanding acquires a negative extension by limiting sensibility while simultaneously renouncing any determination of what lies beyond it.
Transcendental illusion arises when independence from sensibility in categorial origin is mistaken for independence from sensibility in categorial application.
Metaphysical inquiry is redirected from determining supersensible objects to determining the conditions under which object-reference has meaning.
Possible experience exhausts the domain of human objective cognition without exhausting every possible mode of reality or intuition.
The thing in itself functions as a necessary unknown remainder that limits appearance but cannot receive positive predication from the categories.
Pure thought cannot generate the givenness of its own object.
Logical forms such as subject, consequence, and combination cannot function as an ontology without sensible conditions of application.
The distinction between appearance and thing in itself cannot support a symmetrical two-world model.
The conditions of human givenness cannot be converted into conditions of all possible being.
Generic thinkability cannot substitute for determinate cognition.
Ignorance of noumena cannot be converted into proof of their nonexistence.
The systematic intelligibility of phenomena cannot resolve the question of supersensible cognition by terminological reclassification.
The constitutive absence organizing the system is intellectual intuition: without it no positive beyond can be given.
No standpoint is available from which human cognition can compare an object as appearance with the same object as it is independently of sensibility.
A positive human science of supersensible objects is structurally foreclosed rather than merely incomplete.
The noumenal place must remain empty: filling it violates the critical boundary, while eliminating it erases the distinction that bounds sensible cognition.
A priori synthesis of the sensible manifold → unity of possible experience → empirical objective validity.
Concept + corresponding intuition + schema → subsumption → determinate object-reference.
Category − sensible manifold − schema → logical form without objective application.
A priori origin → apparent unrestricted range → attempted transcendental use → indeterminacy and illusion.
Designation as phenomenon → abstraction from the sensible mode of intuition → negative noumenon → limitation of sensibility.
Positive noumenon → requirement of intellectual intuition → absence of that faculty → impossibility of positive noumenal cognition.
Noumenal synthetic claim → requirement of a mediating third term → absence of a non-empirical mediator → failure of transcendental ontology.
Secured territory of experience → question of jurisdiction and boundary → recapitulation of the ground of empirical validity.
Conditions of concept-use → necessity of intuition and schema → restriction of categories to possible experience.
Abstraction from sensibility → loss of determinate meaning → collapse of pure ontology.
Phenomenon–thing-in-itself distinction → ambiguity of noumenon → separation of negative and positive senses.
Absence of intellectual intuition → rejection of positive noumena → retention of the negative limit-concept → self-limitation of understanding.
The distinction between a concept’s origin and its range of valid application becomes decisive.
Possibility divides into logical consistency and objective possibility grounded in intuition.
The apparent division between two worlds is redrawn as an asymmetry between a domain of cognition and a boundary-concept.
Ontology is reclassified as an illicit expansion of what can legitimately be only an analytic of understanding.
Cognitive extension beyond experience is reclassified from acquisition of territory to negative delimitation.
Objectivity is relocated from either sensibility or understanding alone to their schematized conjunction.
**Surface —** The immediate issue is whether pure categories can determine noumena and support a division of objects into sensible and intelligible kinds.
**Structural —** Objective cognition is generated through the conjunction of sensible givenness, categorial synthesis, and schematic subsumption.
**Metastrategic —** Critique secures the jurisdiction of empirical knowledge by diagnosing transcendental claims as misapplications of valid cognitive forms.
**Ontological/Temporal —** Object-determination is conditioned by sensible givenness in space and time, while reality apart from those conditions remains thinkable only as an indeterminate limit.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the restriction of pure understanding, the noumenal distinction, and the final rejection of transcendental ontology.
The ontological status of things in themselves and the possibility of nonhuman intellectual intuition remain intentionally underdetermined.
The system is internally coherent only if logical thinkability, objective possibility, transcendental meaning, and objective use remain strictly distinct.
Its strongest inferential mechanism is the requirement that categorial application have both an intuited object and a schema of subsumption.
The universal restriction to possible experience depends on earlier transcendental deductions that this chapter recapitulates rather than independently reproduces.
A structural tension remains between the necessity of thinking the thing in itself and the prohibition against determining it as an object.
A semantic fault line remains between attributing transcendental meaning to pure categories and declaring their separation from sensibility devoid of meaningful use.
Reconstruction preserves the actual movement from empirical grounding through semantic restriction to the negative, non-territorial function of noumena.

identity.title: Chapter III Of the Ground of the Division of all Objects into Phenomena and Noumena

items.text: The argument addresses the false objective judgments produced when conceptions of comparison are used without determining their cognitive source.
Objective comparison requires transcendental reflection because sensibility and understanding condition representations differently.
The procedure is critical-diagnostic: legitimate comparison is reconstructed by locating the amphiboly generated through faculty-confusion.
The argument moves from the distinction between logical and transcendental reflection to four source-dependent modes of comparison.
The four comparisons expose Leibnitz’s intellectualization of phenomena as the common generator of his metaphysical system.
The diagnosis establishes that categories acquire objective validity only under conditions of sensuous intuition.
The restriction of cognition to phenomena yields the noumenon as a negative boundary-concept and culminates in a categorical division of nothing.
Reflection determines the relation of representations to their cognitive sources.
Sensibility and understanding are irreducibly distinct sources of representation.
Logical reflection compares conceptions while abstracting from their cognitive source.
Transcendental reflection assigns representations to sensibility or understanding and thereby grounds objective comparison.
Identity and difference, agreement and opposition, internal and external, and matter and form acquire objective significance only relative to transcendental place.
Conceptions of the understanding acquire objective validity only through corresponding sensuous intuition.
Space and time are primitive a priori forms of sensibility that condition phenomena and experience.
Human objective cognition is restricted to phenomena.
Spatial difference is sufficient for the numerical difference of phenomena even when their internal conceptions are identical.
Phenomenal realities can oppose and reciprocally cancel their effects without logical contradiction.
Matter as phenomenon is cognized through relations and need contain no absolutely internal determination available to cognition.
Pure understanding places the determinable before determination, whereas sensible cognition presupposes formal intuition before sensory matter.
Transcendental amphiboly substitutes an object of pure understanding for a phenomenon when transcendental place remains undetermined.
The precedence of thought over determinate intuition permits logical form to appear as a determination of an object in itself.
A noumenon is legitimate only negatively and problematically as a boundary marking the non-exhaustiveness of sensuous intuition.
Understanding limits sensibility without thereby acquiring a positive non-sensuous domain of objects.
The division into possible and impossible presupposes the problematic conception of an object in general.
The categorical order generates four distinct modes of nothing.
Reflection is not the direct acquisition of conceptions from objects.
Logical comparison alone is not sufficient for objective comparison.
Sensibility is not a confused or analytically deficient form of understanding.
Understanding does not cognize things in themselves by immediate application of its pure conceptions.
Phenomena are not things in themselves.
Space and time are not determinations of things in themselves.
Conceptual indiscernibility does not establish the numerical identity of phenomena.
The absence of logical contradiction between realities does not establish their real agreement.
The external relations of phenomenal matter do not require a cognizable absolutely internal substrate.
Categories without schemata or sensuous data do not constitute cognition.
The representation of an object in general is not sufficient to present an object.
Critique does not authorize the construction of intelligible worlds beyond phenomena.
A negative noumenon is not asserted to be actual, possible, impossible, or cognizable.
What is absent from a general conception is not thereby absent from its particular objects.
Negation and the pure forms of intuition are not self-standing objects.
A transcendental topic is required to assign conceptions to their proper faculties and prevent equivocal objective use.
Omitting transcendental reflection converts merely logical comparisons into pretended synthetic propositions about objects.
Leibnitz intellectualizes phenomena by treating sensibility as confused understanding and objects of sense as things in themselves.
Locke’s sensualization of conceptions and Leibnitz’s intellectualization of phenomena are inverse reductions of the two-source architecture of cognition.
The identity of indiscernibles is an analytical rule for conceptions but not a law governing spatial phenomena.
The non-opposition of affirmative conceptions is logically valid, phenomenally false when generalized, and cognitively empty when asserted of noumenal realities.
Leibnitz’s restriction of substances to an absolutely internal character generates simple representational monads.
Within Leibnitz’s construction, internally self-contained representational substances exclude physical interaction and require a universal coordinating cause for their correspondence.
Leibnitz’s reduction of space to substantial coexistence and time to causal succession follows from treating sensible forms as intellectual relations among things in themselves.
No synthetic cognition of things in themselves can be produced by pure understanding.
Analysis of phenomena may penetrate indefinitely into nature, but it cannot become cognition of the non-sensuous internal nature of things.
The noumenon preserves the limitation of sensibility while withholding every positive determination of a supersensible object.
The transcendental object marks an unknown ground or cause of phenomena while remaining unavailable to categorial determination.
An ens rationis is a non-self-contradictory empty conception without a corresponding object and is neither established as possible nor condemned as impossible.
A nihil privativum is the conceived absence of an object and depends upon the contrast supplied by something real.
An ens imaginarium is an empty intuition without an object, as in pure space or pure time considered apart from appearances.
A nihil negativum is an impossible object because its conception annihilates itself through contradiction.
Any reduction of sensibility and understanding to a single faculty produces systematic metaphysical error rather than an isolated false judgment.
Empirical plurality and real antagonism cannot be derived from logical analysis because their differentiating conditions enter through sensibility.
Leibnitzian indiscernibility, monadology, predetermined harmony, and relational space-time form a coordinated system generated by one amphibolous substitution.
Restriction to phenomena secures objective cognition because sensuous intuition supplies the object-reference that pure thought lacks.
The understanding’s legitimate transcendental function is self-limitation rather than expansion into a supersensible ontology.
A phenomenon may be constituted by relations without licensing inference to an analogous relational or non-relational constitution of the thing in itself.
The fourfold division of nothing prevents non-givenness, privation, formal conditionality, and contradiction from collapsing into a single notion of nonbeing.
The cognitive faculties cannot form a continuum differentiated only by degrees of clarity.
Logical conditions of thinkability cannot serve as constitutive conditions of being.
Abstraction from conditions of intuition cannot eliminate those conditions from the objects given through intuition.
Mere representability by thought cannot establish objective possibility.
The forms of human sensibility cannot legitimately be extended to all possible being.
The independence of thought from sensation does not authorize an intuition-free employment of thought.
Human cognition cannot leave its own conditions in order to compare phenomena directly with things in themselves.
The demand for an explanatory ground cannot convert an unknown ground into a positively determined entity.
The unavailable possibility of non-sensuous intuition is the constitutive absence around which the noumenon is organized.
The transcendental ground unifying subjective forms of cognition with objective givenness remains inaccessible.
No standpoint is available from which the subject can cognize itself otherwise than as phenomenon.
The absolutely internal nature demanded by metaphysics is absent from every possible empirical presentation.
A supersensible field is left open as an empty logical space while being foreclosed as a domain of human cognition.
Representation → reflection on cognitive source → assignment of transcendental place → legitimate objective comparison.
Transcendental place + four conceptions of comparison → source-relative determinations of identity, opposition, internality, and form.
Omitted source-assignment → homogeneous intellectual comparison → substitution of noumenon for phenomenon → transcendental amphiboly.
Reiterated amphiboly → indiscernibility principle + non-opposition of realities + representational monads + predetermined harmony + intellectualized space-time.
Restoration of sensible form + categorial synthesis → objective cognition → restriction to phenomena.
Restriction to phenomena → limitation of sensibility → negative noumenon → no enlargement of understanding.
Problematic object in general + categorical modes of emptiness → ens rationis / nihil privativum / ens imaginarium / nihil negativum.

Unreflected comparison → faculty distinction → transcendental-place assignment → four bifurcated relations → diagnosis of Leibnitzian amphiboly → phenomenal restriction of cognition → negative noumenon → fourfold classification of nothing.
Cognitive provenance becomes a necessary component of every legitimate objective comparison.
Logical relations and objective relations are separated into distinct levels of validity.
Numerical identity is reclassified from conceptual indiscernibility to source-relative individuation through space.
Opposition is expanded beyond contradiction to include the reciprocal cancellation of phenomenal forces.
Internality is divided into the absolute internal demanded by pure conception and the comparative internal available within phenomenal relations.
The priority of matter over form in pure conception is displaced by the priority of sensible form over empirical matter.
Leibnitz’s doctrines are reclassified as coordinated effects of faculty-confusion rather than independent metaphysical discoveries.
The noumenon is reclassified from a supersensible object into a problematic marker of cognitive limitation.
Nothing is pluralized into distinct failures of object, datum, intuition, and conception.
Surface: The argument determines the legitimate use of four conceptions of comparison and tests their misuse in Leibnitzian philosophy.
Structural: Objective cognition is generated by the conjunction of irreducible faculties, while amphiboly results from suppressing their difference.
Metastrategic: Metaphysical construction is replaced by transcendental topic, which regulates claims through source-assignment and boundary enforcement.

Ontological/Temporal: Phenomena are conditioned by a priori forms that antecede empirical data, while things in themselves remain indeterminate and noumenal temporality or spatiality remains unavailable.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the distinction between logical comparison, transcendental reflection, amphiboly, phenomenal cognition, and noumenal limitation.
The relation among thing in itself, transcendental object, and negative noumenon remains underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent if the irreducibility of the two faculties and the intuition-dependence of objective validity are granted.
The structure is strongest where the four reflection-concepts demonstrate concrete divergences between logical and sensible determination.
The argument compresses rather than independently establishes the exhaustiveness of sensibility and categories for human cognition.
The noumenon must be thought to mark sensibility’s limit even though the categories required for determinate object-thought are denied application to it.
The description of the transcendental object as the cause of phenomena employs causal language where categorial determination is otherwise prohibited.
The fourfold table of nothing is reconstructible from the categorical order but remains only loosely integrated with the main diagnosis of amphiboly.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the actual movement from reflective provenance through metaphysical error to critical limitation and modal classification.
The chapter addresses how contingent perceptions can yield objective cognition of phenomena in one time.
Objective temporal determination requires necessary connections that perception itself cannot supply.
The synthetic unity of apperception supplies these connections through temporally schematized categories.
Permanence, succession, and coexistence generate respectively the rules of substance, causality, and reciprocal community.
These rules regulate relations of phenomenal existence without constructing particular existents or reaching things in themselves.
The argument is transcendental and reconstructive, moving from the possibility of experience to its necessary temporal conditions and thence to the unity of nature.
Experience is object-determining empirical cognition constituted by the synthetic unity of perceptions in one consciousness.
Perception and apprehension supply only contingent conjunctions and contain no necessity of connection.
Empirical cognition of an object requires relations of existence to be represented as objective relations in time.
Time itself is not an object of perception.
Phenomena receive determinate temporal positions only through a priori rules of connection.
The a priori unity of apperception requires all perceptions belonging to one cognition to be synthesized according to temporal rules.
Permanence, succession, and coexistence exhaust the modes under which phenomenal existence is temporally determined.
Analogies are regulative rules for relations of phenomenal existence rather than constitutive procedures for constructing existence.
The analogies are valid only for empirical use, and categories apply to phenomena only through temporal schemata.
A permanent phenomenal substratum is necessary for the representation of duration, coexistence, and change.
The total quantum of phenomenal substance is permanent and can neither increase nor diminish.
Empirical change is the alteration of determinations belonging to a permanent substance.
Objective succession exists only where an antecedent state determines a succeeding state necessarily according to a rule.
The law of cause and effect is an a priori condition of experiencing events.
Objective coexistence requires reciprocal temporal determination grounded in interaction.
All phenomenal substances perceived as coexistent stand, mediately or immediately, in complete dynamical community.
Time and phenomenal reality are continuous magnitudes without smallest parts.
Synthetic a priori principles governing phenomenal existence can be justified only by deduction from the possibility of experience, not by dogmatic analysis of concepts.
Experience is not mere intuition, sensation, apprehension, or an aggregate of perceptions.
Necessary connection is not discoverable within perceptions themselves.
Absolute time, void time, and temporal position considered apart from phenomena are not objects of perception.
The existence or determinate character of a phenomenon cannot be constructed a priori.
Philosophical analogy is not a mathematical proportion from which an unknown term can be constructed.
The analogies do not constitute phenomenal existence as mathematical principles constitute intuition.
The analogies do not authorize transcendental application to things in themselves.
Categories are not applied directly to phenomena independently of their temporal schemata.
The permanence of substance cannot be proved by tautology or by analysis of the concept of substance.
Succession in apprehension is not by itself succession in the object.
Causal necessity is not a generalization produced by repeated observation of similar sequences.
Absolute origination or extinction of substance is not an empirically possible event.
The empirical exclusion of creation does not decide whether things considered in themselves depend on a foreign cause.
Simultaneity of cause and effect does not abolish their asymmetrical temporal order.
Reversible apprehension or location in an assumed common time is insufficient to establish objective coexistence.
Empty space is not denied absolutely, but space inaccessible to perception is denied status as an object of possible experience.
The unity that converts perceptions into experience must be supplied by synthesis rather than extracted from perception.
Every empirical determination of time must be subordinated to an a priori rule of general temporal determination.
Permanence, causal succession, and reciprocal coexistence exhaust the rules required to assign phenomenal existence a position in one time.
A philosophical analogy determines the necessary relation to an empirically sought but a priori unspecified counterpart.
The permanent functions as the empirical representation of time by supporting duration, succession, and coexistence.
Substantial existence subsists while accidents positively determine its changing modes.
Absolute generation or annihilation cannot be experienced because change presupposes one enduring subject across opposed states.
Necessary temporal ordering, rather than mere succession of representations, confers objective significance on an event.
An experienced event indicates an antecedent state that determines it according to a universal rule.
Cause and effect may be simultaneous in elapsed time while remaining asymmetrically ordered by which state determines the other.
Action is an empirical criterion of substance because causality produces change and the ultimate subject of change must be permanent.
Every change is generated through intermediate degrees by causality acting continuously throughout its temporal interval.
Reciprocal perceptual order counts as objective coexistence only when each substance can determine the temporal position of the other.
All phenomena belonging to one possible experience form one nature under permanence, causality, and community.
Empirical laws presuppose rather than ground the primitive laws that make experience possible.
The analogies anticipate only the form of temporal connection; particular existents, states, magnitudes, and powers remain empirically discoverable.
Objective significance arises when synthesis is constrained by a necessary rule that excludes alternative temporal orderings.
Phenomena determine one another’s temporal positions relationally, allowing one objective time to be represented without perception of absolute time.
The triad converts categories of relation into temporal conditions of experience: substance into inherence, causality into consequence, and community into composition.
The system combines a priori determination of experiential form with empirical openness of experiential content.
The unity of nature is a precondition for objects to share one experience rather than an empirical totalization assembled after their discovery.
Complete isolation is not merely empirically unknown but uncognizable as coexistence because no temporal relation could connect the isolated perceptions.
The principles that authorize objective empirical judgments simultaneously restrict those judgments to phenomena.
No phenomenal existence is cognizable except as enduring substance, causally ordered event, or coexistent member of a reciprocal whole.
Time cannot function as a self-ordering container independently of rule-governed relations among phenomena.
Change cannot be fundamental without a permanent phenomenal bearer.
A temporally ordered but non-rule-governed sequence cannot count as an objectively experienced event.
Causally independent coexistents cannot be cognized as members of one empirical world.
Mutually disconnected temporal domains cannot be synthesized as one possible experience.
An independently accessible object cannot supply the criterion distinguishing objective connection from subjective association.
Repetition cannot generate the strict universality and necessity presupposed by empirical objectivity.
Formal a priori principles cannot determine which empirical powers, states, or existents occur.
Conditions necessary for experiencing phenomena cannot be converted into determinations of noumenal reality.
Unmediated access to objective temporal reality is unavailable; only rule-governed phenomenal relations can represent it.
The nonappearance of time itself is the absence around which permanence, causality, and community are organized.
Absolute becoming from nothing and absolute disappearance into nothing are foreclosed within experience.
Isolated existence is unavailable as a member of one empirically cognizable nature.
The thing in itself remains the inaccessible remainder that prevents empirical objectivity from becoming absolute ontology.
A priori cognition of temporal form is purchased by renouncing a priori cognition of determinate empirical existence.
The insufficiency sequence is: contingent perceptual manifold → no represented necessity → unperceivable time → no objective temporal position.
The objectivity sequence is: unity of apperception → a priori temporal rule → necessary synthesis → object of possible experience.
The permanence branch is: temporal duration → required permanent correlate → phenomenal substance → alteration of accidents.
The succession branch is: successive apprehension → irreversible rule → cause and effect → objectively experienced event.
The coexistence branch is: reversible apprehension → reciprocal temporal determination → dynamical interaction → compositum reale.
The regulative operation is: given perception + temporal mode + analogy → necessary relation to an unspecified counterpart → directed empirical search without construction.
The totalizing operation is: three temporal analogies + one apperception → unified experience → law-governed empirical nature.
The validation procedure is: assume possible experience → isolate its necessary condition → show that denial eliminates objectivity → restrict the resulting principle to phenomena.
Contingent perceptions → failure of perceptual necessity → unperceivability of time → a priori synthesis under apperception → objective temporal determination.
General regulative principle → permanence and substance → succession and causality → coexistence and reciprocity → unity of nature → transcendental restriction to possible experience.
Experience is reclassified from an accumulation of perceptions into a necessary synthesis that makes objects empirically cognizable.
Temporal position is relocated from an absolute time-container to lawful relations among phenomena.
Substance is reclassified from a noumenal entity into the permanent phenomenal correlate required for duration and change.
Causality is reclassified from an observed regularity into the condition under which succession can count as an objective event.
Coexistence is reclassified from mere simultaneous placement into membership in a dynamical community.
Analogy is reclassified from a constructive quantitative proportion into a regulative qualitative relation.
Nature is reclassified from an aggregate of phenomena into the single law-governed unity required by possible experience.
A priori cognition is restricted to formal relations of existence while determinate empirical content remains unconstrued.
Surface: The chapter establishes permanence, causality, and reciprocal action as the three principles governing temporal relations among phenomena.
Structural: The principles operate through apperception, imagination, temporal schemata, and rule-governed synthesis to distinguish objects from subjective sequences.
Metastrategic: The argument replaces dogmatic proof and empirical induction with transcendental deduction from the possibility of experience.

Ontological/Temporal: Phenomenal reality is presupposed as one temporally unified field of enduring substances, causally ordered changes, and reciprocally connected coexistents, without extension to things in themselves.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the general principle, the three analogies, their scope, and the concluding unity of nature.
The empirical identification of particular substances, causes, powers, and reciprocal influences remains underdetermined by design.
The structure is internally coherent when every principle remains restricted to phenomena and possible experience.
The strongest inference is the distinction between subjective perceptual succession and objective event-order through a necessary rule.

The designation of the analogies as merely regulative stands in tension with their role as conditions making empirical objects possible; the distinction holds only if constitution is restricted to construction of intuition or existence.
The First Analogy compresses the transition from the need for some permanent correlate of time to the conservation of the total quantum of substance.
The Third Analogy moves from an epistemic condition for cognizing coexistence to an assertoric claim of complete dynamical reciprocity among coexistent substances.
The continuity of change depends on inherited premises concerning continuous time and phenomenal magnitude rather than on causality alone.
Simultaneous causation is preserved by replacing temporal lapse with asymmetric order, but the ground of that asymmetry remains compressed into the determining relation.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s real movement if it retains the sequence from perceptual insufficiency through the three temporal rules to phenomenal nature and the final restriction of scope.
The argument determines how possibility, reality, and necessity can possess objective validity without being inferred from conceptual completeness or extended beyond possible experience.
Modal predicates express an object’s relation to the faculties and procedures of cognition rather than additional determinations of the object.
Possibility is grounded in formal experiential conditions, reality in perception or lawful connection with perception, and necessity in universal causal determination within experience.
The criterion of reality generates a refutation of problematic idealism by making temporally determined internal experience dependent on external experience.
The dependence of categories on intuition is generalized into the claim that external intuition supplies the indispensable presentation of permanence, change, community, and quantity.

The argument is transcendental-critical and reconstructive, moving from modal predicates through their experiential conditions to the restriction of all principles of pure understanding to possible experience.
Possible experience is the sole domain in which objects can be presented for cognition.
The understanding supplies the a priori formal rules that synthesize intuitions into unified experience.
Categories are forms of thought rather than cognitions and acquire objective reality only through intuition.
Modal predicates determine the relation of a complete conception to the faculty of cognition rather than the object represented by that conception.
The objective use of modal categories is restricted to possible experience.
An object is possible when its conception agrees with the formal conditions of experience.
Freedom from contradiction is necessary but insufficient for objective possibility.
Reality requires conscious sensation, whether through direct perception or through lawful connection with an actual perception.
Existence cannot be established from a conception but only from perception and empirically lawful inference from perception.
Empirically determined consciousness of one’s existence in time presupposes something permanent in perception.
Internal sense contains no permanent intuition capable of determining time; the required permanence is presented through matter in external space.
Determinate internal experience is possible only through the existence of external objects and external experience.
The necessity of external experience in general does not validate every particular representation of an external object.
Material necessity concerns causally determined states and effects rather than the existence of substances as such.
Necessity within nature is conditioned and intelligible, and empirical synthesis excludes lawless chance, blind fate, leaps, and hiatuses.
External spatial intuition supplies the presentations required to establish the objective reality of relational categories and to represent internal change.
All principles of pure understanding are a priori principles of the possibility of experience and apply only to experience.
Modal predicates do not enlarge or further determine the conception of an object.
Logical noncontradiction does not establish the objective possibility of an object.
Arbitrary recombinations of empirically borrowed concepts do not acquire possibility merely because they are thinkable.
Existence is not contained in even a complete conception of a thing.
Space is not a property of things in themselves from which Berkeleyan idealism could infer the impossibility of spatial objects.
Internal experience is not the sole immediate experience from which external existence must be uncertainly inferred.
The dependence of experience on external objects does not make dreams, hallucinations, or every apparent perception veridical.
Material necessity is neither logical necessity nor absolute necessity nor the necessary existence of substances.
Absolute possibility is not a conception that the understanding can employ empirically.
A postulate is not an indemonstrable speculative assertion entitled to acceptance through self-evidence alone.
Categories alone cannot produce cognition or establish synthetic propositions about objects.
A synthetic conception has objective possibility only when its synthesis is borrowed from experience or constitutes an a priori formal condition of experience.
A conception assembled from empirical materials without conformity to experiential laws remains a chimera lacking a criterion of possibility.
A priori mathematical construction establishes objective possibility only because its formative synthesis is identical with a synthesis governing possible external experience.
An unperceived entity can be cognized as real when empirical laws connect it to an actual perception within one possible experience.
Problematic idealism reverses its own priority because temporally determined self-consciousness presupposes rather than proves from itself the external field of permanence.
Particular external representations require comparison with the criteria of coherent experience because external experience is necessary in general without every representation being real.
Natural necessity is hypothetical: given a cause under empirical law, its effect is necessary, but neither cause nor substance is thereby absolutely necessary.
Questions concerning whether possibility exceeds reality or whether several all-embracing experiences are possible cannot be decided by the understanding from experiential data.
Modal postulates are subjectively synthetic procedures that classify a conception according to formal conformity, perceptual connection, or lawful determination.

The proposition that every contingent thing has a cause is objectively valid only within possible experience; if contingency already means existence solely as a consequence, the proposition becomes analytic.
Objective validity is constituted neither by conceptual coherence nor by access to things in themselves, but by constructibility or lawful connectability within possible experience.
The progression from possibility to reality to necessity adds determinations of cognitive relation rather than additional content to the object itself.
Externality is a constitutive condition of empirically determinate subjectivity rather than a doubtful object inferred from an independently complete interior consciousness.
The same experiential restriction that legitimates a priori cognition also blocks its conversion into a transcendent ontology.
Nature is rendered law-governed without being rendered absolutely necessary because necessity attaches to conditioned phenomenal transitions rather than self-subsisting things.

The understanding can unify what is given into possible experience but cannot determine whether the total modal field contains other forms of intuition, other experiential wholes, or unrealized possibilities.
Pure concepts cannot authenticate their own objective reference.
Conceivability cannot function as a sufficient criterion of being or possibility.
Internal consciousness cannot provide a self-sufficient temporal foundation for empirical knowledge.
Existence cannot be treated as conceptual content added to a possible object.
Phenomenal nature cannot contain brute events, unconditioned transitions, or ruptures that evade the unity of understanding.
Modal domains cannot be measured or compared independently of the conditions under which objects are experientially given.
Alternative forms of intuition or understanding cannot extend cognition for us beyond the conditions of possible human experience.
No standpoint is available from which possibility, reality, and necessity can be surveyed as absolute domains independent of cognition.
No permanent inward presence exists through which the subject could determine itself temporally without externality.
No object can attain cognitive validity while remaining unrelated to every possible mode of givenness.
The modal constitution of things in themselves remains unavailable because every usable modal criterion terminates at the boundary of possible experience.
The possibility circuit is: candidate conception → formal synthesis test → agreement with possible experience → objective possibility; failed agreement → emptiness or chimera.
The reality circuit is: possible object → direct perception or lawful connection with perception → empirical givenness → reality; absence of perceptual connection → merely conceived existence.

The necessity circuit is: real state → universal empirical law → determination by a given cause → hypothetical necessity of the effect; absence of lawful determination → no cognizable material necessity.

The anti-idealist circuit is: temporal self-consciousness → requirement of permanence → absence of permanent internal intuition → external spatial permanence → external experience as condition of internal experience.

The critical closure is: category → corresponding intuition → objective reality → experiential principle; category without intuition → empty form; application beyond experience → illegitimate transcendence or a problem reserved for reason.
Modal predicates → cognitive-relational reinterpretation → formal criterion of possibility → perceptual criterion of reality → causal criterion of necessity → empirical restriction of modality.

Reality criterion → idealist challenge → temporal analysis of self-consciousness → dependence on external permanence → general dependence of categories on external intuition → reduction of pure principles to conditions of possible experience.
Modality is reclassified from a set of intrinsic object-properties into a set of relations between conceptions and cognitive procedures.
The boundary between the thinkable and the possible is redrawn through formal compatibility with possible experience.
Reality is relocated from conceptual completeness to the perceptually connected field of experience.
The epistemic priority of inner over outer experience is reversed by making temporal self-determination depend on external permanence.
Necessity is narrowed from absolute or substantial being to law-governed dependence among phenomenal states.
Categories are reclassified from self-sufficient representations of being into formal operators requiring intuition for objective use.
Questions about absolute possibility, alternative experiential worlds, and modal totality are transferred from understanding to reason and transcendental dialectic.
At the surface level, the text establishes distinct criteria for possibility, reality, and necessity.
At the structural level, modal validity is generated by the cooperation of understanding, intuition, perception, judgment, and empirical law.
