Self-consciousness cannot be treated as immediate self-intuition.
Formal continuity of consciousness cannot guarantee the diachronic persistence of a substantial person.
Removing empirical conditions from a representation cannot remove those conditions from the represented being’s existence.
The thinking subject cannot occupy an unconditioned standpoint from which it cognizes the ground of its own cognitive functions.
Logical thinkability cannot exhaust the conditions of real possibility.
Failure to establish one metaphysical account cannot establish its contrary.
Practical necessity cannot be converted into theoretical determination of the soul’s constitution.
An immediately self-present and theoretically transparent substantial Ego is unavailable.
The noumenal constitution of the thinking subject is excluded from speculative adjudication.
Neither immortality nor extinction beyond life is available as an object of dogmatic theoretical knowledge.
The subject cannot complete theoretical reason by turning the presupposed unity of reason into its own self-grounding object.
The purity requirement removes all empirical predicates and leaves “I think” as the sole datum of rational psychology.
The category table is projected onto that datum to generate substance, simplicity, identity, and external relation.
Combinations of those projected determinations generate immateriality, incorruptibility, personality, spirituality, communion with bodies, and immortality.
Critical analysis separates the determining unity of consciousness from the determinable self that alone could be given as an object.
Each metaphysical predicate is tested against its required intuition and fails because pure apperception supplies no corresponding object.
The central paralogism is exposed as an equivocation between existence only as subject and use only as the subject of judgment.
Auxiliary proofs are neutralized by intensive diminution, contrary possibilities, and the absence of permanent inner intuition.
The failed doctrine is converted into a reciprocal prohibition against materialist and spiritualist dogmatism.
Claims extending beyond life are relocated from speculative cognition to practical orientation.

Transcendental illusion → empirical exclusion → “I think” as sole datum → categorical construction of the soul → distinction between logical function and object-determination → exposure of equivocation → collapse of speculative soul-ontology → reciprocal dogmatic restraint → practical relocation.
Error is reclassified from defective logical form to an unavoidable transcendental misuse of valid form.
The Ego is reclassified from a cognized substance to the formal vehicle of cognition and an indeterminate transcendental subject.
Substance, simplicity, personality, and separability are reclassified as illicit metaphysical expansions of logical functions.
Materialism and spiritualism cease to be exhaustive theoretical alternatives and become equally unsupported determinations.
Rational psychology is reclassified from a positive science into a boundary-discipline of speculative reason.
Immortality is displaced from demonstrable soul-property to an object of practical reason protected from speculative disproof.
The soul–body problem is redrawn from a presumed interaction between heterogeneous substances to an unknowable relation beneath differently structured appearances.
Surface: The argument tests the derivation of substance, simplicity, personality, separability, permanence, and immortality from “I think.”
Structural: The argument identifies a categorical transfer from logical self-consciousness to metaphysical object-determination without mediating intuition.
Metastrategic: The critique converts failed speculative doctrine into symmetrical limits on opposed dogmatisms and redirects reason toward practical employment.
Ontological/Temporal: The self is necessary as the unity of cognition, given empirically only through temporal inner sense, and indeterminate regarding its noumenal constitution and persistence.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from pure self-consciousness through categorical projection to critical limitation and practical relocation.
The exact correspondence between every category and every traditional predicate of the soul remains compressed.
The structure is internally coherent if objective cognition requires intuition and the categories are restricted to possible experience.
The argument is structurally strongest in its distinction between determining consciousness and the determinable self and in its diagnosis of the syllogistic equivocation.
The proof depends on results imported from the Analytic concerning categories, permanence, noumena, and the limits of objective validity.

The status of “I think” shifts among pure apperception, empirical existential proposition, and undetermined perception; the distinction between intellectual form and empirical occurrence manages but does not eliminate this ambiguity.
The use of the real simplicity of apperception against materialist definition approaches the ontological use of simplicity rejected elsewhere, although it is restricted to a negative conclusion.
The practical admission of future life depends on moral and teleological premises not established within this chapter.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the text’s actual transition from transcendental diagnosis to disciplinary closure rather than reducing it to a denial of the soul.

identity.title: Chapter I. Of the Paralogisms of Pure Reason

units.title: Chapter II. The Antinomy of Pure Reason

items.text: Transcendental illusion is generated by dialectical arguments whose forms correspond to the formal species of syllogism.
The dialectical sequence progresses from the unconditioned unity of the thinking subject to the unconditioned unity of phenomenal conditions and then to the conditions of possible objects in general.
Unlike the paralogism, which produces only a partial illusion, the application of reason to phenomenal synthesis produces an apparently valid principle that turns into contradiction.
The antinomy is a natural and unavoidable conflict of reason rather than an error introduced by sophistical reasoning.
The conflict forces either skeptical renunciation or dogmatic insistence, and both responses destroy sound philosophy.
The proper method is to treat cosmical conceptions as ideas generated by reason but irreconcilable with phenomena and experience, rather than as valid cosmological doctrine.
Transcendental illusion of pure reason arises from dialectical arguments.
The formal species of syllogism provide the logical schemas for the principal dialectical arguments of reason.
The first dialectical argument concerns the unconditioned unity of the subjective conditions of representation.
The second dialectical argument concerns the unconditioned unity of objective conditions in phenomena.
The third dialectical argument concerns the unconditioned unity of the objective conditions of the possibility of objects in general.
The paralogism concerning the subject of thought produces only a partial illusion and does not establish its contrary proposition.
The theory of pneumatism gains the argumentative advantage in the paralogism but ultimately fails before pure reason.
Reason applies a principle of unconditioned unity to the objective synthesis of phenomena.
The application of unconditioned unity to phenomenal synthesis generates contradictions within reason itself.
The antinomy arises naturally and unavoidably from the operation of reason.
The antinomy prevents both one-sided conviction and stable philosophical resolution through unqualified assertion.
Cosmical conceptions concern the absolute totality of the empirical synthesis of phenomena.
The ideal of pure reason concerns the absolute totality of the conditions of all possible things and is distinct from, though related to, the cosmical conception.
The antinomy supplies principles for a pretended pure rational cosmology rather than a valid cosmology.
Cosmical conceptions must be presented as ideas irreconcilable with phenomena and experience rather than appropriated as valid objects of knowledge.
The antinomy is not a merely sophistical conflict introduced by subtle argument.
The cosmological illusion is not merely a one-sided illusion of the kind produced by the paralogism.
The unconditioned unity of phenomenal conditions is not secured by the plausibility of the principle that generates it.
The antinomy is not resolved by granting one side of the conflict exclusive authority.
Skeptical surrender is not a sound philosophical resolution.
Dogmatic confidence and obstinate persistence are not sound philosophical resolutions.
The cosmical conception is not identical with the ideal of pure reason.
Rational cosmology is not to be declared valid or appropriated as doctrine.
Absolute totality in the synthesis of phenomena is not reconciled with phenomena and experience.
The formal structure of syllogistic reasoning determines the ordered taxonomy of transcendental illusions.
The movement from subjective conditions to phenomenal conditions marks a transition from dialectical psychology to dialectical cosmology.
The cosmological case is more destabilizing than the paralogical case because the principle of unity appears plausible before producing contradiction.
The natural origin of the antinomy prevents its dismissal as a contingent defect in reasoning.
The antinomy exposes a conflict between reason’s demand for unconditioned unity and the conditions of phenomenal synthesis.
The two immediate responses to antinomy convert a cognitive conflict into either renunciation of reason or illegitimate closure.
The distinction between cosmical conception and ideal of pure reason prevents different forms of totality from being treated as one object.
The proper result of the cosmological analysis is a restriction of doctrinal validity rather than the elimination of the idea that generates the conflict.
Reason’s demand for unconditioned unity is both the generative source of cosmological thought and the source of its self-contradiction.
The contradiction functions diagnostically by revealing that the totality demanded by reason cannot be straightforwardly converted into an object within phenomenal experience.
The text relocates cosmology from the level of doctrine to the level of critical analysis of reason’s totalizing activity.
The same rational architecture that organizes valid inference also produces transcendental illusion when its demand for totality is extended to phenomenal conditions.
The argument preserves the necessity of reason’s demand for unity while denying that this demand yields a coherent phenomenal world-whole.
Sound philosophy requires a position that neither abandons reason in skepticism nor satisfies its demand through dogmatic assertion.
The completed totality of phenomenal conditions is not assumed to be directly available as an object of experience.
The formal schema of reasoning is not assumed to guarantee legitimate ontological reference for the ideas generated through it.
Contradiction in cosmology is not treated as an accidental defect removable by improved sophistical technique.
No single cosmological assertion is permitted to suppress the opposing assertion merely by persistence or confidence.
The analogy among dialectical forms does not entail equal validity for the objects or totalities associated with them.
The demand for absolute totality does not entail the existence of a corresponding phenomenal totality.
Pure reason is not permitted to transform its regulative demand for unity into an experience-grounded cosmological possession.
A fully experience-compatible world-whole is structurally unavailable to the cosmological use of pure reason.
A final reconciliation between absolute totality and phenomenal experience is excluded within the disputed cosmological framework.
A stable doctrinal settlement of the antinomy is foreclosed by the internal conflict of reason’s own principles.
The possibility that reason could transparently master the totality it demands is excluded.
Logical forms of judgment and syllogism → schemas of transcendental reasoning → dialectical production of totalizing ideas.
Subjective conditions of representation → unconditioned unity of the subject → paralogism → partial illusion.
Objective conditions in phenomena → unconditioned unity of phenomenal synthesis → cosmological principle.
Plausible cosmological unity → mutually conflicting consequences → natural antinomy.
Natural antinomy → skeptical renunciation or dogmatic persistence → destruction of sound philosophy.
Cosmical conception distinguished from the ideal of pure reason → cosmological totality restricted to an idea → refusal of doctrinal appropriation.
Conflict of pure reason → exposure of non-reconciliation with phenomena and experience → critical presentation without cosmological validation.
Dialectical form → transcendental illusion → ordered domains of totality → plausible unconditioned unity → unavoidable contradiction → skepticism or dogmatism → critical non-appropriation.
Partial paralogical illusion → stronger cosmological antinomy → failure of both unilateral alternatives → cosmical conception retained as irreconcilable idea.
Antinomy is reclassified from an accidental argumentative failure into a necessary structural effect of reason’s operation.
Contradiction becomes evidence about the limits of cosmological cognition rather than merely an obstacle to be overcome.
Subjective dialectic and objective cosmological dialectic are separated by the different strength and structure of their illusions.
The world-whole is distinguished from the totality of conditions for all possible things.
Rational cosmology is moved from the status of asserted science to the status of a critical object generated by reason.
The opposition between skepticism and dogmatism is collapsed as a false alternative for dealing with antinomy.
Surface — Reason’s synthesis of objective phenomenal conditions produces contradictory cosmological claims.
Structural — Syllogistic forms organize a hierarchy of totalizing demands concerning the subject, phenomena, and possible objects.
Metastrategic — The proper response to contradiction is neither to select a side nor to abandon reason, but to diagnose the status of the idea producing the conflict.
Ontological — Absolute totality belongs to reason’s conception of conditions but cannot be reconciled as a phenomenal object with experience.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from dialectical form through cosmological antinomy to critical restriction.
The reconstruction preserves the decisive distinction between the partial illusion of the paralogism and the contradictory structure of the antinomy.
The system is internally coherent as a diagnosis of reason’s totalizing demand and its phenomenal limit.
The system remains underdetermined regarding the concrete antinomies and the subsequent positive resolution of the conflict.
Its strongest point is the rejection of both skeptical surrender and dogmatic closure as responses to necessary contradiction.
Its central unresolved tension lies between the necessity of the demand for unconditioned unity and the impossibility of satisfying that demand within phenomenal experience.
Reconstruction depends on retaining the formal analogy between syllogistic species and dialectical ideas without treating that analogy as proof of cosmological validity.

identity.title: Chapter II. The Antinomy of Pure Reason

units.title: Section I. System of Cosmological Ideas

items.text: The text seeks a systematic principle for enumerating transcendental ideas rather than treating them as an unstructured set of metaphysical questions.
It grounds transcendental ideas in categories supplied by understanding and transformed by reason through the demand for unconditioned completeness.
It restricts legitimate cosmological ideas to categorial syntheses that form subordinated serial conditions for a given conditioned phenomenon.
It reorients rational inquiry from consequences to antecedent conditions because only regressive synthesis is necessary for explaining what is given.
It derives four cosmological ideas by applying regressive totalization to composition, division, causality, and existential dependence.
It suspends the empirical realizability of absolute totality while distinguishing two possible forms of the unconditioned: an infinite whole of conditioned members or a first unconditioned member.
Understanding originates pure concepts, while reason does not originate concepts but releases concepts from the limits of possible experience.
Reason demands absolute totality of conditions whenever a conditioned is given.
A category becomes a transcendental idea when reason extends its conditioned synthesis toward the unconditioned.
Only a synthesis ordered as a series of subordinated conditions can support a transcendental idea.
Reason necessarily demands completeness only in the ascending regress from a conditioned to its antecedent conditions.
The progressive series of consequences is not required for the possibility or explanation of a given conditioned.
Cosmological ideas concern the totality of conditions for phenomena and do not concern a totality of things independently of phenomenal intuition.
Time supplies a genuine antecedent series because a present moment is conditioned by preceding time.
Space is an aggregate of coexisting parts, but its apprehension and limitation require a successive synthesis that permits regressive totalization.
Matter supplies a regressive series because its parts condition the given real whole and each part can be further divided.
Causality supplies a regressive series because an effect is conditioned by causes antecedent to it.
Contingent existence supplies a regressive series because it requires a condition through which it becomes necessary.
The four admissible cosmological ideas concern absolute completeness in composition, division, origination, and dependence.
Absolute totality is an idea whose possibility in phenomenal synthesis remains unestablished.
The unconditioned can be represented either as the complete infinite series of conditioned members or as an unconditioned first member within the series.
World denotes the mathematical totality of phenomena, while nature denotes their dynamical unity under internal causal connection.
Cosmological ideas remain directed to phenomena while extending synthesis beyond every possible empirical completion.
Mathematical cosmological ideas concern composition and division, while dynamical cosmological ideas concern origination and dependence.
Reason is not an independent source of pure concepts.
A transcendental idea is not a concept detached from categories or from empirical synthesis.
A category does not generate a cosmological idea merely by being a category.
Co-ordinated aggregates do not constitute the serial subordination required for rational regression.
The descending series of consequences does not impose a necessary demand for absolute totality.
Substance and accident do not form the required series of conditions because accidents are modes of substance rather than antecedent conditions of it.
Substances in reciprocal community do not form a cosmological series because they are aggregated rather than subordinated conditions.
Possibility, actuality, and necessity do not independently yield cosmological ideas unless contingency introduces a conditioned existence.
Cosmological totality is not a totality of noumenal things.
Absolute completeness is not established as an empirically realizable synthesis merely because reason necessarily thinks it.
Infinite regress is not equivalent to a completed empirical traversal of infinitely many conditions.
Nature is not merely a spatial-temporal aggregate when it is considered as a causal whole.
The systematic table of cosmological ideas must be derived from the categorial table by selecting only categories capable of expressing regressive serial conditioning.
Rational completeness concerns explanatory grounds rather than an exhaustive prediction or enumeration of future consequences.
The totality of past time is necessarily thought as conditioning the present, whereas the termination or infinitude of future time is indifferent to the present’s possibility.
Spatial magnitude becomes a cosmological problem only through the successive synthesis of delimitation, not through space considered merely as a simultaneous aggregate.
Division of matter directs reason toward the simple because exhaustive division is the only route by which the conditionality of material parts could terminate.
Causal inquiry directs reason from a given effect toward an antecedent ground capable of terminating the regress in causation.
Inquiry into contingent existence directs reason toward an unconditioned necessity because contingency cannot provide its own sufficient condition.
The four cosmological ideas divide into two mathematical questions concerning phenomenal quantity and two dynamical questions concerning phenomenal existence.
The first possible form of the unconditioned permits a series without a first member while requiring that the entire series be thought as complete.
The second possible form of the unconditioned yields the concepts of a temporal beginning, spatial limit, simple part, spontaneous cause, and absolutely necessary existence.
Cosmological reason transforms ordinary categorial determination into a demand for a total explanatory ground that no finite empirical inquiry can guarantee.
The system converts metaphysical questions about the world into questions about the form and possible completion of regressive phenomenal synthesis.
The unconditioned is structurally required as the endpoint of explanation even when its instantiation within experience cannot be known.
The four cosmological problems are generated not by four independently discovered objects but by four admissible modes through which conditioned phenomena can be regressed toward completeness.
The mathematical-dynamical division separates questions concerning the completeness of phenomenal magnitude from questions concerning the completeness of phenomenal causal existence.
Reason is internally driven beyond experience without being licensed to leave the domain of phenomena for noumenal objects.
The system depends on the denial that a conditioned phenomenon can be fully intelligible through its immediately given state alone.
The system depends on the denial that explanation can terminate arbitrarily within a series of conditions.
The system excludes the possibility that coexisting elements are explanatory grounds of one another merely because they belong to one whole.
The system excludes a symmetrical treatment of antecedents and consequences because only antecedents are constitutive conditions of what is given.
The system excludes direct intellectual access to an unconditioned object outside phenomenal conditions.
The system excludes the inference that rational necessity establishes empirical existence or empirical completion.
The system excludes any cosmology not mediated by the categorial forms of understanding.
The argument is organized around the unavailable standpoint from which an entire phenomenal series could be empirically given as absolutely complete.
The argument presupposes that the unconditioned is necessary for reason but unavailable as an object of completed experience.
The argument forecloses a final metaphysical inventory of reality by relocating cosmological totality into the problematic form of rational idea.
The argument withholds any guarantee that the rational demand for completion corresponds to a structure actually possessed by phenomena.
A conditioned phenomenon is given, and reason applies the demand that its complete set of antecedent conditions be thought.
A category is eligible for transcendental elevation only if its synthesis orders conditions in a subordinated series.
The eligible series is taken regressively from the given conditioned toward increasingly remote antecedent conditions.
The regressive demand produces an idea of absolute totality rather than an established object of experience.
The idea of totality yields two alternative representations of the unconditioned: an unlimited complete whole or a first unconditioned condition.
The serial filter yields four cosmological problem-fields: composition, division, origination, and existential dependence.
The resulting cosmological ideas remain phenomenal in reference while exceeding every empirically completable synthesis.
The argument moves from the need for a principle of enumeration to the distinction between understanding’s concepts and reason’s totalizing demand.
The distinction between concepts and ideas leads to the criterion of serially subordinated conditions.
The serial criterion leads to the privileging of regressus over progressus.
Regressive synthesis is differentiated across time, space, matter, causality, and contingent existence.
The differentiation excludes nonserial categories and yields four cosmological ideas.
The four ideas are reframed as problematic demands for an unconditioned whose phenomenal realizability remains undecided.
The argument terminates by dividing the resulting ideas into mathematical and dynamical classes within the world of phenomena.
Metaphysical totality is reclassified from a property immediately attributable to the world into a rational demand generated by conditioned experience.
The distinction between regressus and progressus redraws explanation as dependence on antecedent grounds rather than extension toward consequences.
Categories are divided into those that can generate cosmological problems and those that cannot because they lack serial subordination.
Space is made available for cosmological regression despite not being intrinsically temporal or serial.
Infinity is reclassified as the possible form of a complete idea rather than as a completed sequence empirically traversed by cognition.
The opposition between finite first condition and infinite regress becomes internal to the representation of the unconditioned rather than an immediate dispute about empirical objects.
World and nature are separated into mathematical totality and dynamical causal unity.
Cosmological inquiry is confined to phenomenal conditions while being recognized as necessarily trans-empirical in its demand for completeness.
Surface — The text enumerates four cosmological ideas concerning world magnitude, material division, causal origin, and necessary dependence.
Structural — The enumeration is generated by a filter that admits only categories expressing a regressively ordered series of subordinate conditions.
Metastrategic — The text converts speculative questions into an investigation of the rational procedure that produces them and of the limits governing that procedure.

Ontological/Temporal — Phenomenal reality is treated as conditionally ordered in time, spatial delimitation, material parts, causation, and existence, while absolute completion remains only ideationally available.
Epistemic — Reason necessarily represents the unconditioned as required for explanatory completeness but cannot establish whether corresponding phenomenal totality is possible.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the text’s derivation of cosmological ideas from categories through the demand for regressive totality.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the conditions under which an idea of totality could correspond to an actually possible phenomenal synthesis.
The system is coherent insofar as it distinguishes the rational requirement for totality from empirical proof that totality is realizable.
The system is strongest where it derives the admissible cosmological questions from the formal distinction between serial subordination and mere aggregation.
The system relies on an unresolved tension between the claim that the whole series of conditions is required as given and the claim that completion of phenomenal regress may be impossible.
The system also retains tension between space as a nonserial aggregate and spatial limitation as a regressively serial synthesis.
The system preserves a further tension between ideas that remain restricted to phenomena and their necessary extension beyond all possible empirical completion.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the four cosmological ideas are treated as procedural products of reason rather than as independently given metaphysical objects.

identity.title: Section I. System of Cosmological Ideas

units.title: Section II. Antithetic of Pure Reason

items.text: Pure reason necessarily generates contradictory cosmological claims when it extends the demand for completeness beyond possible experience.
Transcendental antithetic treats these oppositions as reason’s self-contradiction rather than as an external contest between unrelated dogmas.
The contradiction arises because reason demands absolute unity while understanding permits only synthesis governed by the conditions of possible experience.
This conflict recurs as opposed determinations of cosmical magnitude, composition, causality, and necessary existence.
Because neither experience nor a priori intuition can adjudicate transcendent claims, unrestricted conflict becomes the diagnostic criterion.
The argument moves from necessary cosmological question to paired demonstration, from paired demonstration to rational deadlock, and from deadlock to the search for a concealed misunderstanding.
The objective employment of understanding is restricted to possible experience.
Pure reason necessarily demands absolute unity and completeness for every conditioned synthesis.
Cosmological synthesis must conform to the rules of understanding while answering reason’s demand for totality.
A synthesis adequate to reason is too great for understanding, while a synthesis adequate to understanding is too small for reason.
Extending reason beyond possible experience generates transcendental cosmological propositions.
The questions answered by dialectical propositions are necessarily encountered by human reason.
Each side of a transcendental conflict is internally consistent and possesses grounds of necessity in reason.
The contrary side possesses grounds that are equally valid and necessary.
Transcendental illusion is natural, unavoidable, and recurrent even after its deception has been exposed.
Transcendental propositions admit neither empirical confirmation or refutation nor exhibition in a priori intuition.
Free and unrestricted conflict is transcendental reason’s only available criterion for locating the source of disagreement.
The sceptical method seeks certainty by diagnosing misunderstanding rather than by destroying the grounds of knowledge.
Space and time are forms of sensible intuition rather than independently existing objects.
The sensible world consists only of phenomena under the conditions of possible experience.
A world abstracted from all conditions of intuition permits no synthetic proposition, whether affirmative or negative.
Empirical nature requires a connected and law-governed causal order.
A regress begun among empirical conditions cannot validly terminate by changing without warrant to an intellectual condition.
Antithetic is not a collection of dogmatic counterassertions and is not a one-sided defence of either proposition.
A dialectical proposition is not an answer to an arbitrarily invented question.
Transcendental illusion is not an artificial sophism that disappears when detected.
The sceptical method is not scepticism and does not institute universal scientific ignorance.
The conflict is not decided by doctrinal allegiance, practical preference, defensive success, or possession of the final attack.
Transcendental disputes cannot be adjudicated by mathematical construction, experimental testing, or practical exemplification.
Infinity is not a maximum magnitude greater than which none can be conceived.
Space and time are not substances, empty containers, or external correlates of phenomena.
The mundus intelligibilis is not a knowable substitute for the phenomenal world.
Failure to perceive a manifold does not establish the absolute simplicity of an object.
Empirical change does not establish intellectual contingency or justify an inference to a transcendent necessary being.
Transcendental freedom is not identical with the complete empirical or psychological conception of freedom.

Treating the world as a completed temporal-spatial whole excludes both an elapsed infinite succession and an infinite coexistent totality requiring completed successive synthesis, thereby generating the first thesis.
Treating the world as phenomenal excludes a beginning preceded by empty time and a spatial boundary related to empty space, thereby generating the first antithesis.

Once composition is treated as a contingent relation among self-subsisting substances, the removal of composition must leave simple substances or annihilate substance altogether, thereby generating the second thesis.
Because every spatially intuited real part occupies further divisible space, no absolutely simple part can be given in possible experience, thereby generating the second antithesis.
The demand for completeness in a causal series whose natural causes are themselves conditioned generates the postulate of a spontaneous causality, thereby producing the third thesis.
A spontaneous event introduced within experience would sever causal connection with preceding states and destroy empirical unity, thereby producing the third antithesis.

The demand for a complete series of conditions for change generates an absolutely necessary condition and, because its efficacy is construed temporally, tends to place that condition within the cosmical series.

Since every temporal member remains conditioned, the aggregate cannot become necessary through conditioned parts, while an extra-world cause that begins to act becomes temporally implicated in the world, thereby producing the fourth antithesis.
The absence of an external criterion makes dogmatic victory indefinitely reversible and allows argumentative sequence to masquerade as truth.
Staging each opposition at full strength converts antinomy from a contest of doctrines into evidence concerning defects in reason’s principles.
The four antinomies are recurrent outputs of one structural mismatch between absolute rational totalization and empirically conditioned synthesis.
Dogmatic opposition is self-sustaining because each side can invalidate the other’s governing standpoint without establishing its own objective reality.
The sceptical method seeks critical certainty concerning cognitive boundaries rather than positive knowledge of cosmological totalities.
The unconditioned is successively instantiated as completed magnitude, simple substrate, spontaneous causality, and necessary existence.
Antinomy functions as a criterion of transcendental legislation by forcing abstract principles to reveal their defective scope through contradiction.
Because transcendental illusion cannot be eliminated, critique must remain a recurrent discipline rather than a completed eradication of error.
Restriction to phenomena conditionally leaves thing-in-itself alternatives open while denying that such alternatives can supply synthetic cognition.

The declared parity of the opposed proofs is strained by the text’s local reliance on mathematical evidence, the transcendental status of space, and the rejection of monadist constructions as inadmissible.
The world as an absolutely completed whole must not be assumed to be an object of possible experience.
Internal consistency and subjective rational necessity must not be equated with objective validity.
Principles valid for members of an empirical series must not be assumed to determine the series as an absolute totality.
Forms of intuition must not be converted into empty objects capable of bounding or preceding phenomena.
The incomprehensibility of an infinite regress must not by itself be treated as proof of its impossibility.
Antinomy must not be interpreted as evidence that the world itself possesses contradictory predicates independently of reason’s mode of representation.
A noumenal redescription must not be used as an answer to a question posed under phenomenal conditions.
The system is organized around the absence of any possible intuition of the world-whole whose properties reason attempts to determine.
No transcendent metacriterion exists from which thesis and antithesis can be directly compared as objects of knowledge.
A single undifferentiated object cannot simultaneously satisfy reason’s demand for the unconditioned and understanding’s demand for empirical conditionedness.
Speculative reason has no final state in which its drive toward the unconditioned is permanently extinguished.
A positive rule assigning the opposed propositions to distinct standpoints remains absent from this section, although the need for such a distinction structures the conflict.
Understanding-rules → possible experience → legitimate but indefinitely conditioned synthesis.
Conditioned synthesis → reason’s demand for absolute completeness → representation of the cosmical series as a totality.
Transgression beyond experience → loss of intuition and empirical test → natural transcendental illusion.
Application of the completion operator yields temporal-spatial limits, simple substances, spontaneous causality, and necessary existence.
Reapplication of sensible and empirical conditions yields temporal-spatial infinity, indefinite divisibility, universal natural causality, and the absence of necessary existence.
Equal rational grounding plus unavailable objective criterion yields dogmatic deadlock.
Unrestricted conflict → exposure of standpoint or level-shift → diagnosis of misunderstanding → attempted neutralization of recurrent illusion.
Necessary demand for the unconditioned → extension beyond possible experience → paired cosmological assertions → equal demonstrations → antinomial deadlock → sceptical diagnosis.
Assumption of the opposite → derivation of contradiction → establishment of thesis → reversal of governing standpoint → renewed assumption of the opposite → establishment of antithesis.
Magnitude of the world → elements of the world → origin of cosmical causality → ground of cosmical existence.
Contradiction is reclassified from disagreement between doctrines to an endogenous self-conflict of pure reason.
The world-whole is reclassified from a possible object of cosmological description to a problematic totality generated by reason.
Thesis and antithesis become symmetrical products of opposed requirements rather than simple truth and error.
Sceptical suspension is divided into destructive scepticism and a diagnostic method directed toward certainty.
Philosophical combat is converted from a mechanism of doctrinal victory into an experiment for detecting defective principles.
Boundaries, simples, freedom, and necessity become variant forms of one demand for the unconditioned.
Space and time cease to function as independent cosmical containers and become conditions governing what can count as a phenomenal claim.

Surface: Four paired conflicts determine whether the world is finite or infinite, simple or indefinitely divisible, freely originated or naturally determined, and grounded in necessary existence or not.
Structural: The antinomies are generated by the incompatibility between reason’s demand for absolute totality and understanding’s restriction to conditioned experience.
Metastrategic: Doctrinal adjudication is replaced by the deliberate production of maximal conflict as a method for exposing illicit assumptions and level-shifts.
Ontological/Temporal: Objects are available only as phenomena under space, time, and causal order, while the unconditioned cannot be temporally or spatially located without becoming conditioned.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the common generator, the four principal outputs, and the sceptical procedure applied to them.
The final rule by which the antinomies are to be resolved remains underdetermined because this section arranges and diagnoses the conflict without completing its general solution.
The structure is internally coherent as an account of why reason produces opposed necessities in the absence of experiential adjudication.
The structure is strongest where it identifies illicit transitions between empirical conditions, absolute totality, and purely intellectual grounds.

The individual proofs depend on compressed assumptions concerning completed synthesis, spatial divisibility, causal completeness, and the relation between aggregate necessity and the necessity of members.
The claim of strict parity depends partly on rhetorical construction because the observations introduce substantive transcendental commitments that locally privilege some arguments.
The freedom thesis establishes at most a cosmological demand for a first causal beginning, then extends that result toward intraworld agency without an equivalent demonstration.
The fourth thesis tends to place necessary existence within the temporal series while its observation leaves the relation between the necessary being and the world unsettled.
Reconstruction preserves the text’s real movement only if it refuses to select either dogmatic side or import a positive resolution not yet supplied.

identity.title: Section II. Antithetic of Pure Reason

units.title: Section III. Of the Interest of Reason in these Self-contradictions

items.text: Reason necessarily generates cosmological ideas by seeking unconditioned totality for conditionally determined experience, although no possible experience can supply their adequate objects.
The four cosmological antinomies are treated as the exhaustive and unavoidable forms in which this demand for unconditioned completion becomes self-contradictory.
The conflict cannot be dismissed because its opposing conclusions bear practical, speculative, popular, and architectonic interests of reason.
The preliminary inquiry suspends logical adjudication in order to diagnose why reason adheres to either side of the conflict.

The thesis is classified as dogmatism because it supplements empirical explanation with intellectual claims about the unconditioned, while the antithesis is classified as empiricism because it universalizes explanation by possible experience.
Empirical restriction is valid as a maxim of speculative inquiry but becomes invalid when transformed into a denial of what lies beyond phenomenal cognition.
The alternation between freedom and natural necessity leaves the conflict unresolved and redirects inquiry toward the origin of reason’s own disunion.
No possible experience can furnish an object adequate to cosmological ideas.
Reason necessarily reaches cosmological ideas when it seeks the unconditioned totality of conditional empirical synthesis.
The cosmological problems are limited to four because only four a priori series of synthetic conditions delimit empirical synthesis.
The thesis supplements empirical explanation with intellectual propositions concerning the unconditioned.
The antithesis applies pure empiricism to transcendental ideas as well as to natural phenomena.
Objective speculative cognition requires a basis in possible experience.
Methodological empiricism directs understanding to indefinitely extend natural inquiry through experience and necessary laws.
Empiricism becomes dogmatic when phenomenal unknowability is converted into a denial of what exceeds phenomenal cognition.
The thesis claims that the conditioned can be derived from an unconditioned terminus.
The antithesis represents every condition as dependent on a further condition without a self-subsistent first basis.
The thesis’s claims function as theoretical supports for morality and religion.
Reason seeks to place cognition within an a priori rational unity of system.
Interest can govern preliminary partisan choice while logical truth is deliberately bracketed.
Practical interest selects principles for action when speculative reason remains undecided.
A proper preliminary inquiry compares the principles from which thesis and antithesis proceed.
Detached speculative judgment oscillates between opposed cosmological conclusions when it presumes that one side alone must be true.
Radical settlement requires inquiry into the origin of reason’s disunion rather than victory by either party.
Cosmological ideas are not arbitrary inventions, despite their lack of adequate experiential objects.
Interest is not a logical criterion of truth.
The thesis is not governed by empirical explanation alone.
The antithesis is not merely a local theory of natural phenomena but an empiricist treatment of transcendental ideas.
Possible experience does not license speculative explanation by a first epoch, a spatial limit, a supersensible free faculty, or a cause beyond nature.
Transcendent concepts do not acquire objective speculative validity without corresponding intuition.
Methodological suspension of supersensible claims is not equivalent to their dogmatic denial.
Infinite regress is not an architectonically complete system of cognition.
Familiarity with a conception is not comprehension of its objective validity.
Practical need is not speculative evidence.
Neither party may claim objective knowledge beyond what its principle can warrant.
The conflict cannot be ended by indifference, suppression, or partisan intimidation.
Cosmological ideas must be diagnosed as unavoidable products of reason rather than rejected as optional errors.
The opposition between thesis and antithesis is determined by their generating principles rather than by the particular cosmological propositions they defend.
The thesis gains its natural attractiveness by promising moral support, terminal explanation, and architectonic completion.
Empiricism retains speculative legitimacy only when it remains a rule for inquiry within experience rather than a doctrine denying the supersensible.
The analysis of interests explains adherence to opposing doctrines without establishing either doctrine as true.
Action can terminate speculative hesitation through practical selection without theoretically resolving the antinomy.
The chapter divides inquiry into a provisional diagnosis of partisan interests and a deferred investigation of the source of contradiction.
The central fault is not attachment either to nature or to practical hope, but conversion of either orientation into unwarranted speculative doctrine.
Reason generates its own cosmological conflict because its necessary demand for unconditioned totality exceeds the conditions under which objects can be given.
The system separates epistemic authorization from practical commitment: possible experience authorizes speculative cognition, while practical interest explains action and allegiance.
Architectonic reason converts the endlessness of empirical conditioning into an apparent defect and thereby gives the thesis a structural advantage independent of proof.
The same empirical principle produces scientific modesty when used methodologically and practical-spiritual damage when used as a dogmatic metaphysical negation.
A resolution requires a third operation that neither dogmatic affirmation nor empirical denial can provide: an account of how reason produces the opposition.
Phenomenal unknowability cannot be silently equated with nonexistence without converting empiricism into dogmatic denial.
Reason’s need for foundation, moral support, and systematic unity cannot by itself establish the objective constitution of the world.
Architectonic demand cannot supply an experiential object for the unconditioned terminus it requires.
Partisan psychology cannot explain the source of self-contradiction, because interest explains adherence after the conflict has already arisen.
Practical indispensability cannot cancel the distinction between what must be assumed for action and what can be known in speculation.
An infinite empirical series cannot be treated as either a completed object or an achieved systematic whole.
Direct speculative possession of unconditioned cosmological totality is unavailable, and this absence structures every cosmological question.
No final speculative choice between thesis and antithesis is supplied within the chapter’s present frame.
No guaranteed correspondence exists between reason’s demand for a final ground and the form in which nature is knowable as an indefinitely conditioned order.
A non-dogmatic relation between practical commitment and speculative limitation is withheld as the unresolved target of the deferred radical inquiry.
Conditional empirical synthesis + reason’s demand for unconditioned totality → necessary production of cosmological ideas.
Cosmological ideas lacking adequate possible objects + their treatment as determinative knowledge → opposed cosmological conclusions.
Opposed conclusions → thesis as intellectual dogmatism / antithesis as universalized empiricism.
Thesis and antithesis + suspension of immediate truth adjudication → comparison of practical, speculative, popular, and architectonic interests.
Empirical restriction as methodological maxim → secure natural inquiry; empirical restriction as metaphysical denial → dogmatic overreach.
Speculative oscillation + practical necessity → practical selection without theoretical settlement → demand for an origin-diagnosis of reason’s disunion.
The movement begins with reason’s necessary search for the unconditioned and reaches the four forms of cosmological self-contradiction.
Cosmological self-contradiction → suspension of immediate truth-claims → comparison of the principles of dogmatism and empiricism.
Principle-comparison → differentiation of practical, speculative, popular, and architectonic interests → explanation of partisan preference.
Qualified empiricism versus dogmatic empiricism + thesis’s architectonic attraction → speculative oscillation and practical selection → deferred inquiry into the source of the conflict.
Cosmological propositions are reclassified from candidate descriptions of the world into unavoidable products of reason’s demand for totality.
Dogmatism and empiricism are reclassified by their relation to possible experience and the unconditioned rather than by their historical or rhetorical identities.
Practical, speculative, popular, and architectonic interests become distinct explanatory variables rather than interchangeable reasons for truth.
The boundary of experience is split into two functions: it constrains objective assertion but does not authorize denial of everything beyond it.
Infinite regression becomes double-coded as a legitimate horizon of empirical inquiry and an obstacle to architectonic completion.
Speculative indecision becomes evidence of a structural defect in the framing of the dispute rather than evidence for either cosmological side.
Surface — The explicit object is the preference between thesis and antithesis concerning world, self, freedom, causality, and supreme being.
Structural — The conflict is generated by the collision between conditional experience, unconditioned reason, empirical objectivity, and architectonic system-building.
Metastrategic — The inquiry brackets truth temporarily in order to distinguish doctrinal proof from the interests that recruit adherents to doctrines.
Ontological/Temporal — Reality is contested as either an indefinitely conditioned natural order or an order grounded in unconditioned beginnings, simple substances, free causes, and ultimate cause.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from necessary cosmological ideas through antinomial conflict to an interest-analysis and deferred origin-diagnosis.
The extraction does not reconstruct the detailed proofs of the four individual antinomies, because this section presupposes their prior dialectical derivation.
The system is most coherent where it distinguishes methodological empiricism from dogmatic empirical denial.
The primary tension is that thesis-side practical and architectonic attractions explain its appeal while being explicitly insufficient to prove its speculative claims.
A second tension is that reason necessarily demands an unconditioned unity while possible experience cannot provide the object required to know such unity.
The final appeal to impartial trial is under pressure because the chapter has already shown that practical and architectonic interests condition preference.
The proposed radical resolution remains underdetermined because the inquiry into the source of the contradiction is announced but deferred.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s actual movement only if it ends in suspended adjudication and diagnostic redirection rather than in victory for either thesis or antithesis.

identity.title: Section III. Of the Interest of Reason in these Self-contradictions

units.title: Section IV. Of the necessity imposed upon Pure Reason of presenting a Solution of its Transcendental Problems

items.text: Pure reason must determine whether its transcendental questions are internally answerable or merely exceed its competence.
Questions generated by a science’s own constitutive concepts require solutions from those same concepts when their objects are determined within that sphere.
Cosmological ideas uniquely concern the absolute totality of an empirical synthesis rather than a transcendent object given independently of experience.
Because no possible experience can present absolute totality, cosmological problems cannot receive dogmatic determinations of their supposed objects.
The proper solution transfers inquiry from the constitution of a presumed object to the dialectical basis and legitimate employment of the idea that generates the question.
Reason’s apparent failure is therefore diagnosed as an internal illusion that mistakes its own idea for an empirically determinable object.
A question arising from concepts constitutive of a pure science must be answerable from those concepts.
Transcendental philosophy contains questions whose source is pure reason itself.
Cosmological ideas demand the absolute totality of the synthesis of phenomena.
Absolute totality cannot be given in any possible empirical experience.
Cosmological questions concern the required progress of empirical synthesis toward an idea, not the constitution of a thing in itself.
An object not presentable in possible experience cannot be determined by predicates whose application requires experiential conditions.
A question concerning such an indeterminable object is null rather than merely unanswered.
The ideas of reason are not required for the explanation of particular phenomena because no empirical intuition can exhibit their unconditioned object.
Dogmatic solutions treat an idea as though it represented an empirically given object.
Critical solutions investigate the cognitive ground and dialectic of the question rather than determine its supposed object.
Reason cannot discharge its obligation by appealing to the limitation of its faculties when the problem originates in reason’s own ideas.
Transcendental cosmological questions are not questions about a transcendent thing in itself.
Necessary ignorance is not an admissible response to a genuine question generated by pure reason.
Absolute totality is not an empirical whole obtainable through the accumulation of perceptions.
The unconditioned is not discoverable at any point within a series of conditioned appearances.
A transcendental object is not a legitimate object of categorical determination.
A dogmatic answer is not a deficient version of a critical answer; it is impossible for the relevant problems.
The cosmological idea is not a principle required to explain any determinate phenomenon.
The failure to determine an unconditioned object is not evidence that such an object remains obscurely available to cognition.
Cosmological problems require resolution despite the impossibility of empirically exhibiting their unconditioned object.
The answer to a cosmological question must be drawn from the idea’s conditions of use rather than from experience or transcendent metaphysical knowledge.
Questions concerning the soul as a simple thing or a necessary being as a thing in itself fail by lacking an object to which the relevant categories could apply.
The antinomial demand for an absolute beginning, absolute infinity, ultimate simplicity, freedom, or an unconditioned necessary being cannot be settled by further empirical investigation.
The adequate resolution of transcendental problems consists in exposing the idea’s dialectical overreach rather than choosing among rival object-level claims.
The distinction between a legitimate and a null transcendental question depends on whether the question concerns the synthesis of possible experience or an object beyond possible experience.
Pure reason’s necessity to answer its own questions is fulfilled reflexively: it resolves its problems by determining the limits and illusion of the concepts that generate them.
The unconditioned functions as a regulative demand for completeness of synthesis while being unavailable as an object of determinate cognition.
The apparent alternative between metaphysical knowledge and skeptical suspension is displaced by a critical verdict on the legitimacy of the question itself.
Transcendental error arises when reason converts a necessary subjective demand for totality into a claim about an independently existing total object.
Pure reason is not licensed to infer an object’s existence from the mere intelligibility or necessity of an idea.
The totality sought by cosmological reason is not a hidden empirical datum awaiting more complete observation.
Conceptual origin does not authorize objective application beyond the conditions under which an object can be given.
The limit of cognition is not merely an external boundary imposed by deficient evidence but an internal boundary generated by the form of reason’s own demand.
A question’s grammatical form does not guarantee that it has a valid object or admits an object-level answer.
No completed standpoint can occupy the absolute totality that reason necessarily thinks but cannot experience.
No final metaphysical object corresponds to the demand that every conditioned series be grounded in the unconditioned.
Reason cannot become theoretically complete by extending cognition beyond possible experience; its completion consists only in critical self-limitation.
Pure reason generates an idea of unconditioned totality from the demand to complete conditioned synthesis.
The idea is misread as representing an independently given object capable of empirical or categorical determination.
This misreading produces cosmological problems that demand an absolute determination unavailable in experience.
The impossibility of empirical determination redirects inquiry from the supposed object to the idea’s cognitive source, function, and dialectical illusion.
Critical analysis dissolves dogmatic object-claims while preserving reason’s obligation to account for the necessity of its own questions.
Reason’s demand for answers to its own questions → distinction between internally generated and externally contingent questions.
Internally generated questions → isolation of cosmological ideas as demands for absolute totality.
Absolute totality beyond experience → impossibility of dogmatic determination of a cosmological object.
Dogmatic impossibility → diagnosis of the idea-object confusion that generates transcendental dialectic.
Dialectical diagnosis → critical resolution through analysis of the cognitive basis of the question.
The field of transcendental questions is divided between legitimate questions about possible experience and null questions about transcendent objects.
Ignorance is reclassified: it is legitimate in empirical inquiry, inadmissible for genuine questions of pure reason, and replaced by nullity where no object can be given.
Cosmological antinomies are reclassified from disputes about the world’s hidden constitution into effects of reason’s demand for unconditioned completion.
The opposition between empirical solution and metaphysical speculation is displaced by critical examination of the conditions under which a question counts as meaningful.
The object of transcendental inquiry shifts from the world as totality to reason’s representation of totality.
Surface — The text addresses whether reason can answer questions concerning the world’s beginning, magnitude, composition, freedom, and necessary ground.
Structural — The questions arise because reason requires the conditioned synthesis of appearances to be completed through an unconditioned totality.
Metastrategic — The text replaces evasive ignorance and dogmatic metaphysical decision with critique of the question-producing concepts themselves.
Ontological/Temporal — The world as an absolute whole, whether temporally begun or beginningless and spatially finite or infinite, cannot be constituted as an experiential object.
Epistemic — Objective validity depends not on the thinkability of an object but on the possibility of giving that object under conditions of experience.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the transition from reason’s obligation to answer its questions to the critical dissolution of dogmatic cosmology.
The system depends principally on the distinction between an idea of totality and an object given in possible experience.
The structure is coherent if “solution” includes diagnosing a question as null or exposing the dialectical source of its apparent object.
The decisive compression occurs when the text treats the concept that generates a question as also supplying the resources for its resolution.
A structural tension remains between the claim that reason must answer its own questions and the claim that certain such questions receive only a verdict of nullity.
A further tension remains between cosmological ideas as necessarily generated demands for totality and their exclusion from any constitutive determination of an object.
Reconstruction preserves the argument only if critical limitation is treated as reason’s positive self-resolution rather than as skeptical refusal.

identity.title: Section IV. Of the necessity imposed upon Pure Reason of presenting a Solution of its Transcendental Problems

units.title: Section V. Sceptical Exposition of the Cosmological Problems presented in the four Transcendental Ideas

items.text: Dogmatic answers to cosmological questions are irrational when either answer intensifies incomprehensibility or yields contradiction.
The mutual failure of opposed cosmological answers requires criticism of the question’s presupposition rather than adjudication between its alternatives.
Cosmological ideas demand an unconditioned totality within a regressive synthesis of phenomena.
Every cosmological alternative makes the demanded totality either exceed or fall short of the conditions of possible empirical regress.
Possible experience is the sole criterion by which a conception can possess objective reality.
Cosmological antinomy therefore exposes a fictitious conception of how its alleged object is presented, not a conflict between two knowable objects.
A conception has objective reality only through possible experience.
An empirical conception must be adequate to the conditions of a possible empirical synthesis.
Cosmological ideas seek the unconditioned for the regressive synthesis of conditioned phenomena.
A successive empirical regress cannot complete an infinite elapsed series as a given whole.
A conditioned empirical beginning, limit, simple part, cause, or contingent existence requires regress to a further condition.
The unconditioned required as an empirical totality must itself be available within possible experience.
In each cosmological antinomy, one alternative exceeds the empirical synthesis and the opposed alternative leaves that synthesis conditionally incomplete.
When both opposed answers fail the criterion of possible experience, the question rests on a groundless presupposition concerning its object.
Sceptical examination functions critically by converting dogmatic conflict into diagnosis of its generating illusion.
Cosmological questions are not to be settled by a dogmatic affirmative or negative answer.
An infinite temporal, spatial, causal, or divisional regress is not a completed object available to empirical conception.
A finite beginning, boundary, simple, spontaneous event, or contingent existence is not unconditioned when it still demands a further condition.
Absolute void is not an empirical object or a final empirical condition.
Spontaneous causality is not cognizable as an empirical exception that terminates the demand for causal grounds.
A conception lacking relation to possible experience is not knowledge of an object.
Antinomy is not evidence that opposed cosmological doctrines are jointly valid.
The alternatives of world-beginning and world-eternity both fail because the former remains conditioned and the latter cannot be completed in successive regress.
The alternatives of finite and infinite world-extension both fail because finite limits demand determination and infinite extension cannot be empirically synthesized as a whole.
The alternatives of infinitely divisible matter and simple ultimate parts both fail because infinite division exceeds completed synthesis and a simple member still permits regress into its parts.
The alternatives of universal natural causality and free spontaneous events both fail as cosmological totalities because each preserves an unclosed demand for conditions.
The alternatives of an absolutely necessary being and universal contingency both fail because the former exceeds empirical regress and the latter indefinitely renews it.
Cosmological ideas lack objective significance when their alleged objects cannot be made adequate to possible experience.
Scepticism becomes a cathartic criticism when the incoherence of answers is used to expose the false construction of the question.
The antinomies are generated by applying a valid demand for conditions beyond the domain in which empirical synthesis can supply an object.
The conflict of thesis and antithesis is a symptom of transcendental illusion rather than a contest between equally established cognitions.
The empirical regress becomes the normative measure of cosmological thought, while the alleged totality becomes answerable to the conditions of that regress.
Critique displaces metaphysical decision by testing whether the question can present an object under the conditions it itself invokes.
The unconditioned is not available as an empirically given completion of the regress through conditioned appearances.
The world is not legitimately cognized as a thing whose total temporal, spatial, material, causal, or modal constitution can be given as an object.
The demand for a final condition is not authorized merely because empirical understanding requires conditions for each given appearance.
The form of a question does not guarantee that its object, alternatives, or presupposed mode of presentation are valid.
No standpoint is available within possible experience from which the whole series of conditions can be surveyed as unconditionally complete.
No dogmatic resolution can convert the absence of an empirically presentable cosmological object into knowledge of such an object.
The final exclusion is the possibility of universal science founded on cosmological totalities treated as objects of theoretical cognition.
Demand for an unconditional cosmological answer → examination of the opposed answers’ cognitive yield.
Opposed answers → either an infinite regress exceeds possible synthesis or a finite terminus remains conditioned.
Double inadequacy → failure of the alleged object to meet the criterion of possible experience.
Failure of objectivity → diagnosis of a false presupposition about the presentation of the cosmological object.
Diagnosis of transcendental illusion → replacement of dogmatism with sceptical-critical limitation.
Dogmatic demand for cosmological decision → recognition that either answer can be meaningless or contradictory.
Failure of both answers → critical interrogation of the question’s presupposed object.
Cosmological idea of the unconditioned → application to temporal, spatial, divisional, causal, and modal regress.
Infinite alternative exceeds empirical conception; finite alternative remains conditionally deficient.
Possible experience as criterion of reality → cosmological object loses objective significance.
Loss of objective significance → antinomy is reclassified as transcendental illusion requiring criticism.
Cosmological antinomies are reclassified from disputes over the world’s determinate constitution into tests of the objective validity of cosmological ideas.
“Too large” and “too small” become measures of adequacy to possible empirical synthesis rather than comparative properties of independently given objects.
The unconditioned is detached from empirical objecthood, because every empirical object remains within the order of conditional regress.
Scepticism is transformed from suspension between rival doctrines into an instrument for exposing invalid question-formation.
The demand for totality is shown to produce illusion when it converts a rule of regress into a completed empirical whole.
Surface — The text examines four pairs of opposed cosmological claims concerning the world’s beginning and extent, divisibility, causality, and necessity.
Structural — Each pair reproduces one mechanism: infinite regress cannot be completed, while an alleged terminus remains subject to further conditioning.
Metastrategic — The text redirects philosophical procedure from defending a thesis or antithesis toward examining the validity of the object presupposed by both.
Ontological/Temporal — Objects of experience are treated as conditionally given within regress, while unconditional totality is denied empirical presentation.
Epistemic — Possible experience supplies the standard of objective reality and disqualifies ideas that cannot be related to a possible object.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the argument because they generate both poles of each antinomy and the critical transition from contradiction to illusion.
The system depends principally on the claim that possible experience is the exclusive source of objective reality.
The system is coherent if the demand for conditions is valid only within empirical synthesis and invalid when converted into an object of completed totality.
The strongest compression occurs in the common formal structure assigned to all four cosmological ideas: excess through infinity and deficiency through conditional termination.
The system leaves underdetermined how an idea can regulate inquiry without acquiring the objective significance denied to cosmological totality.
The system also relies on, rather than fully establishes here, the boundary between a legitimate empirical regress and an illegitimate demand for its unconditioned completion.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if scepticism is treated as a diagnostic procedure that dissolves the question’s false object rather than merely withholding judgment.

identity.title: Section V. Sceptical Exposition of the Cosmological Problems presented in the four Transcendental Ideas

units.title: Section VI. Transcendental Idealism as the Key to the Solution of Pure Cosmological Dialectic

items.text: Pure cosmological dialectic arises when objects of possible experience are treated as self-subsistent things existing independently of the conditions under which they can be given.
Transcendental idealism preserves the empirical reality of objects while denying that space, time, and phenomena belong to things in themselves.
The text advances a diagnostic and dissolutive argument that locates cosmological illusion in a misapplication of empirical concepts beyond possible experience.
Reality is reframed from independent subsistence into lawful givenness within perception and the possible progression of experience.
Unperceived, past, distant, and future objects are rendered empirically meaningful only as determinable nodes in a possible experiential regress.
The transcendental ground of appearances is retained as an unknowable correlate, preventing phenomenal order from being converted into knowledge of things in themselves.
Cosmological totality is reduced from an independently existing object to the idea of a completed possible experience.
Space and time are pure forms of human sensibility.
Everything intuited in space and time is phenomenon rather than thing in itself.
Phenomena are representations without self-subsistent existence apart from the mind.
An empirical object is real insofar as it is given in perception or lawfully connected to possible perceptions.
The unity of experience supplies the criterion distinguishing empirical reality from dream, fancy, and illusion.
The temporally determined inner self is appearance rather than the transcendental subject as it exists in itself.
The non-sensuous cause of appearances cannot be intuited or known as an object.
The transcendental object is only a mental correlate of sensibility and not a knowable phenomenal object.
Claims about unperceived objects are meaningful only through a possible lawful progression of experience.
The transcendental condition determining the course and endpoint of empirical regress is necessarily incognizable.
The representation of all objects in all space and time is only the idea of possible experience in absolute completeness.
Cosmological illusion results when phenomenal objects are treated as things in themselves outside possible experience.
Transcendental idealism is not empirical idealism, because it does not deny the reality of external bodies in space.
Empirical reality is not self-subsistent reality independent of experience.
Space and time are not determinations of things in themselves.
The object of inner sense is not the proper self as it exists in itself.
The non-sensuous ground of appearances is not an object available to intuition.
A phenomenon not given in perception or in a possible empirical progression is not an object for cognition.
A past event is not affirmed as a self-subsisting fact detached from the possible regress of experience.
The totality of objects in space and time is not given as an already constituted object prior to experience.
Cosmological concepts are not legitimate when severed from the conditions of possible experience.
Empirical realism and transcendental idealism are compatible because phenomenal objects can be fully real within experience without being things in themselves.
The reality of an unobserved object consists in its lawful possible discoverability rather than in its independent phenomenal presence outside experience.
Assertions about the past express the possible extension of present experience through a law-governed regress to temporal conditions.
Assertions about indefinitely distant objects retain meaning only as assertions about the possible extension of experience.
The empirical self can be known only as a succession of appearances and cannot ground knowledge of the transcendental subject.
The transcendental object can mark the dependence of appearances on an unknown ground without furnishing knowledge of that ground.
A cosmological absolute whole cannot be cognized as an object because its alleged objecthood exceeds the possible regress through which objects acquire empirical reality.
Cosmological dialectic is generated by an equivocation between empirical reality within experience and transcendental reality independent of experience.
The world is cognitively available only as an open rule-governed field of possible regress, never as a completed object standing before cognition.
Transcendental idealism dissolves rather than answers cosmological claims that require a standpoint external to possible experience.
Objectivity is relocated from independent ontological subsistence to lawful integration within the unity of experience.
The system preserves an unknowable ground of appearances while prohibiting that ground from explaining cosmological objects as knowable things in themselves.
The system excludes a correspondence model in which cognition compares appearances with spatial-temporal things as they exist independently of sensibility.
The system excludes an ontological inventory of objects whose existence can be determined independently of their possible relation to experience.
The system excludes the inference from the continuity of empirical regress to the existence of a completed cosmological totality.
The system excludes the possibility that temporal self-consciousness yields direct knowledge of a noumenal self.
The system excludes any cognitive passage from the lawful order of appearances to knowledge of their non-sensuous cause.
The system excludes a determinate empirical endpoint at which the regress of experience could become unconditioned knowledge.
No standpoint exists from which the whole of space, time, and objects can be known as a completed reality outside the conditions of possible experience.
No phenomenal object can possess the mode of absolute being required by dogmatic cosmology.
No self-transparent subject remains available beneath the temporal succession through which the empirical self is given.
No final empirical regress can convert the transcendental condition of experience into an object of experience.
Sensibility structured by space and time → appearances constituted as representations.
Appearances plus lawful unity of experience → empirical objects and empirical reality.
Present perception plus possible empirical regress → warranted reference to past, distant, and unperceived phenomena.
Unknown non-sensuous ground → transcendental object as limiting correlate rather than cognized object.
Possible experience considered as complete → cosmological idea without a given cosmological object.
Phenomenal reality misread as independent reality → cosmological dialectic.
Restoration of the distinction between phenomenon and thing in itself → dissolution of the dialectical object.
Apparent conflict over the reality of external and cosmological objects → distinction between empirical and transcendental reality → validation of phenomena through lawful experience.
Lawful experience → possible regress from perception → conditional legitimacy of claims about past, distant, and unobserved objects.
Possible regress mistaken for completed totality → attribution of independent reality to phenomena → cosmological illusion.
Transcendental idealist restriction of objectivity to possible experience → removal of the alleged cosmological object → dissolution of pure cosmological dialectic.
Reality is divided into empirical validity within experience and forbidden transcendental attribution to phenomena as things in themselves.
The past, the distant, and the unobserved are reclassified from absent entities to possible termini of lawful experiential progression.
The external world is preserved as empirically real without being granted independent spatial-temporal existence.
The self is split between an empirically knowable temporal appearance and an unknowable transcendental subject.
Cosmological totality is reclassified from an object to be known into an idea generated by the demand for completed experience.
