items.text: Finite reason must authorize necessary objective cognition while preserving its demands for totality and orientation without converting those demands into knowledge of supersensible objects.
Rational authority is reconstructed as a differentiated constitution in which possible experience grounds theoretical objectivity and distinct jurisdictions govern reason’s remaining functions.
Objective experience arises through the synthesis of sensible multiplicity under concepts whose authority extends only to the conditions under which objects can be presented.
The successful legislation of lawful nature produces conditioned cognition, which necessarily generates a further demand for unconditioned completion.
Critique becomes a reflexive tribunal that secures cognition by diagnosing contradiction and proof failure as effects of unauthorized object-construction.
Negation becomes generative when the exclusion of transcendent knowledge redistributes reason’s demands into empirical, regulative, practical, and architectonic functions.
The movement is spiral: each recovered condition enables cognition, generates a new demand or excess, and returns that excess through another jurisdictional mediation.
Closure is asymmetrical: phenomenal lawfulness and formal jurisdiction close, while empirical inquiry, practical realization, criticism, and systematic construction remain open.
[Persistent] Finite cognition requires irreducibly differentiated sensible presentation and conceptual synthesis under the common restriction of possible experience.
[Attractor] Mediation is the operative center through which cognitive functions acquire authority only by being coordinated within their proper jurisdictions.
[Attractor] Possible experience is simultaneously the constituted field of objective cognition and the tribunal testing every theoretical claim to object-reference.
[Mutating] Objectivity changes from presumed correspondence with independent being into universally necessary, temporally enacted, and jurisdictionally restricted synthesis.
[Mutating] The subject is generated as an apperceptive integrating function and subsequently divided into projector, legislator, accused party, critic, and finite believer.
[Attractor] The field of conditioned experience necessarily activates reason’s demand for complete determination, systematic unity, and an unconditioned ground.
[Emergent] Transcendental illusion is generated when valid conceptual or inferential functions are detached from sensible authorization and transferred to unpresentable total objects.
[Emergent] Contradiction and proof collapse acquire critical force by exposing an invalid completed object-model shared by opposed metaphysical claims.
[Emergent] Critique is a positive governance mechanism that produces valid cognition by allocating, restricting, and coordinating heterogeneous rational functions.
[Persistent] Rational validity is topological because differentiated faculties and functions support irreducibly distinct modes of authorization rather than one homogeneous scale.
[Mutating] Limitation changes from apparent deprivation into the condition protecting objective validity, empirical openness, practical commitment, and systematic orientation.
[Terminal] Supersensible objects remain theoretically indeterminate, and their regulative or practical recovery cannot restore theoretical objecthood.
[Terminal] Formal legislation and jurisdiction can close while particular empirical determinations and the realization of rational ends remain unfinished.
[Attractor] Rational autonomy consists in recursively legislating and criticizing authority through the same finite powers whose legitimacy remains under examination.
[Stable identity with expansion] Experience remains cognition’s field but expands from constituted outcome into the central jurisdictional pole governing theoretical reference.
[Serial mutation] Synthesis escalates from the prior operation of object-constitution into lawful natural legislation and becomes dialectical totalization when extended beyond presentation.
[Functional recurrence] Faculty differentiation migrates from an account of cognitive production into a constitutional prohibition against jurisdictional substitution.
[Subject mutation] Subjectivity reverses from suspected distortion into a universal formal condition, then becomes a divided architect implicated in its own projections.
[Domain expansion] Time develops from sensible form and schematic medium into the recursive asymmetry of incomplete self-presence, regress, criticism, and prospective completion.
[Valence reversal] Critique and negation change from restraint into the constructive, institutional, and procedural governance of positive rational production.
[Reversal] Contradiction changes from an apparent collision within reality into a diagnostic instrument for exposing valid forms operating through an invalid object-model.

[Absorption] Noumenal objecthood and the unconditioned are absorbed into a differentiated boundary architecture of negative limit, regulative horizon, practical concern, and architectonic destination.
[Terminal transformation] Completion ceases to mean possession of total content and becomes formal completeness in the allocation of permanently open inquiry.
Detailed logical inventories, temporal schemata, reflection-concepts, proofs, examples, and hypothesis tests remain local instruments rather than the whole-book architecture.
Faculty differentiation scales upward because it governs both the production of objects and the constitutional separation of rational jurisdictions.
Synthesis, apperception, judgment, and schematism bridge object-constitution to the universal criterion separating objective cognition from nonobjective orientation.
The completion of phenomenal constitution catalyzes the transition to dialectic because every constituted object remains conditioned and therefore reactivates the demand for completion.
The underived inventory of cognitive forms and the underdetermined force of regulative and practical principles scale upward as limits of transcendental self-explanation.
Ready-made correspondence, substantial soul, completed world-totality, and supreme object lose terminal authority and survive only as critically recoded positions or functions.
Empirical recurrence and association cannot generate the necessity required for universally valid objective cognition.
Concepts and categories cannot determine objects without sensible givenness and the conditions of possible experience.
Sensible multiplicity cannot constitute an object before synthesis because an unsynthesized manifold lacks objective conjunction and unity.
Logical consistency, formal validity, and conceptual completeness cannot establish material truth, objective possibility, or existence.
Neither the world-whole nor intrinsic reality can be surveyed from an external or unconditioned standpoint.
Theoretical reason can neither affirm nor deny supersensible objects when categorial application lacks sensible authorization.
Regulative utility and practical necessity cannot become evidence for theoretical objecthood or existence.
Neither an exhaustive application algorithm nor a single successful critique can abolish judgment, recurrent illusion, or the need for renewed criticism.
The architecture requires the falsity of any model in which independently constituted objects arrive already unified and can be inspected from outside finite cognition.
Receptivity and spontaneity cannot be dissolved into a homogeneous faculty or validity continuum without eliminating the mediations that generate cognition.
Finite reason cannot possess intellectual intuition because immediate presentation of complete conditions would dissolve both synthesis and critical jurisdiction.
No transparent or substantial subject can convert its integrating activity into cognition of itself as an independently subsisting entity.
Universal formal order cannot determine particular existence or guarantee the empirical coincidence of nature, freedom, virtue, and happiness.
No external authority can validate critique, yet self-validation cannot confer unconditioned sovereignty on the finite powers being examined.
The deepest absent capacity is an intellectual intuition that would disclose the common ground of receptivity and spontaneity while presenting complete conditions immediately.
The system circles an unavailable all-sufficient ground that would terminate conditioning without becoming another conditioned object.
The unavailable identity of thinkability, knowability, and complete possession of reality prevents the complete world and all its conditions from becoming one object.
The absent empirical unity of nature, freedom, virtue, and happiness gives practical hope its orientation while withholding theoretical completion.
Final completion and an external guarantor must remain absent because criticism, inquiry, and practical approximation derive their force from nonpossession.
The conditions constituting objective experience also generate its boundary, so authorization and restriction are two operations of one critical structure.
The same categories that generate lawful nature produce dialectical illusion when their constitutive use is extended into complete totalization.
Successful phenomenal constitution internally generates an unknown remainder whose withdrawal from objecthood permits regulative and practical use without restoring theoretical cognition.
Temporal schematization and recursive noncompletion jointly make finitude appear as both incomplete self-presence and the impossibility of possessing total conditions at once.
Positive object-constitution and negative criticism form a feedback system in which valid production depends on recurrent exclusion of unauthorized transitions.
Because nature is formally legislated but materially open, regulative totality can guide empirical inquiry only as a procedure that prevents arbitrary arrest.
Domain-indexed theoretical authority and practical necessity form distinct attractors, preventing practical authorization from becoming supersensible evidence.
Since reason judges itself through the powers under judgment, criticism must remain recurrent and publicly reproducible rather than privately or finally completed.
Epistemic authority becomes a conditioned and procedural achievement established through provenance, application, scope, and jurisdiction rather than direct possession of being.
Subject and object become differentiated effects of distributed synthesis, while the subject’s later rational roles remain irreducible to a knowable substance.
Reality-for-cognition becomes a formally legislated field of conditioned appearances whose material laws remain empirical and whose totality remains an unpossessed task.
Time becomes a layered recursive operator joining succession, schematic application, regress, retrospective diagnosis, and prospective completion.
Error is an internally recurrent jurisdictional effect because valid rational forms generate illusion when detached from their authorized conditions.
Metaphysics becomes a constitutional topology of grounding, application, recurrent error, differentiated validity, and regulated function.
Critical authority acquires a public and institutional dimension because recurrent illusion cannot be governed by specialist sovereignty or private correction alone.
Rational agency becomes disciplined action under noncompletion rather than sovereign command over objects, history, or the totality of conditions.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Experience provokes a demand for necessity, necessity triggers a regress to conditions, those conditions constitute experience, and every determination returns for renewed jurisdictional testing.
Faculty separation enables cooperation, cooperation produces cognition, and reason then resubmits both its operations and restrictions to criticism.
Conditioned cognition generates demand, demand becomes projection, and projection passes through reification into paralogism, antinomy, or theological proof.
Valid forms generate illusion, but contradiction or proof collapse converts that illusion into a diagnostic phase change from object-dispute to object-critique.
Phenomenal constitution intensifies the unknown, while the resulting boundary returns excluded totalizing demand as empirical, regulative, practical, or architectonic work.
Rules reproduce the application regress, and criticism reproduces the authorization regress, so judgment and public review interrupt but never abolish recursive mediation.
Practical belief is recursively contained because speculative limitation enables it, while belief reactivates that same limitation against theological inflation.
Possible experience, synthesis, moral law, and unavailable completion form coupled attractors that repeatedly redistribute reason’s operations without terminal convergence.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Necessary cognition plus metaphysical contradiction → demand for synthetic a priori authorization → critique of finite rational competence.
Receptive presentation plus irreducibly distinct conceptual activity → prior synthesis → objectively unified sensible multiplicity.
Synthesis plus apperception plus judgment → category → temporal schema → authorized objective application.
Schematized categories → principles of experience → universal lawful nature → materially open and conditioned cognition.
Conditioned cognition plus recursive inquiry → demand for total conditions → illusory objectification of subject, world, and supreme ground.
Antinomial contradiction plus proof dependency → exposure of reification → invalidation of procedural unity converted into existence.
Withdrawal of the invalid object-model → speculative suspension → redistribution into constitutive cognition, regulation, practical legislation, and architectonic placement.
Public criticism plus architectonic integration → formally bounded authority → reopening of empirical, practical, and systematic tasks.
Scientific necessity and metaphysical conflict → synthetic a priori demand → transcendental regress from objects to enabling conditions.
A priori sensible field → manifold requiring synthesis → original apperception → co-generation of self-ascription and object-relation.
Judgmental function → category → temporal schema → principles of experience → lawful but empirically open nature.
Conditioned experience → unavoidable demand for completion → projected subject, world, and supreme ground → transcendental illusion.
Paralogism, antinomy, and proof collapse → diagnosis of shared reification → withdrawal of constitutive totality.
Speculative restriction → empirical continuation → regulative systematization → practical commitment → architectonic allocation → recurrent public criticism.
Objectivity is reclassified from correspondence with ready-made objects into necessary synthesis compatible with empirical realism and the deobjectification of totality.
The subject–object opposition becomes an internal differentiation of one synthetic architecture whose subject occupies multiple irreducible roles without becoming a substance.
A priori origin is separated from unrestricted range, making boundaries enabling instruments rather than external restraints on an otherwise unlimited reason.
Truth and validity become stratified and topological, requiring each claim to be located by presentation, function, scope, object, and mode of assent.
Contradiction becomes a metacritical method for testing the validity of the alleged object and question before evaluating competing answers.
Nature divides into invariant formal lawfulness and empirical material determination, while world-totality is withdrawn as an object.
Metaphysics and history become recursive audits of reason’s claims, errors, jurisdictions, and future-oriented construction rather than inventories of transcendent being.
At the surface level, mathematics, natural science, selfhood, world-totality, freedom, theology, morality, and system are coordinated around the validity and limits of rational claims.
At the structural level, receptivity, synthesis, imagination, apperception, understanding, judgment, and reason form a distributed circuit that constitutes objects and projects totalities.
At the metastrategic level, inquiry shifts from doctrinal assertion to provenance-testing, object-model criticism, jurisdictional allocation, and governance of claim-production.

At the ontological and temporal level, reality-for-cognition is a lawfully synthesized field of conditioned appearances, while time mediates constitution, regress, correction, and unavailable completion.

At the methodological and performative level, the system constructs rational mechanisms, generates their excesses, reclassifies their functions, and derives limitations from their enabling conditions.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Reason must validate criticism through the powers under examination even though universal criticizability denies the tribunal an unrevisable foundation.
Cognition presupposes affection by independently constituted objects whose passage into formal representation remains underexplained.
Claims of categorial and architectonic completeness depend on inventories whose completeness is asserted while substantive inquiry remains permanently unfinished.
Possible experience is constituted by transcendental principles while simultaneously serving as their validating field, producing reflexive dependence rather than external proof.
Judgment must remain irreducible to rules, while regulative principles exercise axiom-like force whose precise authority over inquiry remains underdetermined.
Speculative limitation enables practical authority but does not itself establish the efficacy, necessity, or exclusivity of particular practical postulates.
Practical freedom and intelligible grounding must remain compatible with empirical lawfulness despite the absence of any guaranteed harmony or resolved relation between them.
The a priori mutates from independence from experience into the structural condition, juridical boundary, and differentiated authorization of possible experience.
Synthesis mutates from a logical relation into the operation generating objecthood and then into dialectical totalization when absolutized.
Objectivity mutates from apparent correspondence into invariant synthesis, valid application, and temporally procedural constitution.
The subject mutates from presumed bearer into an integrating function and then into a finite architect, accused party, legislator, critic, and believer.
Time mutates from intuitive form into schematic transformation medium and then into a vector of recursive diagnosis and future completion.
Critique and negation mutate from limitation into the positive governance that generates, secures, and differentiates cognition, belief, and system.
Closure mutates from possession of substantive totality into formal self-limitation, open inquiry, and prospective practical-architectonic completion.
Reality-for-cognition is a gated recursive court-engine that receives multiplicity, synthesizes objects, generates totalizing claims, and adjudicates them across stratified jurisdictions.
The subject is a finite switching-center, regressor, legislator, defendant, and critic situated inside the system it attempts to judge.
Time is the transformation medium and recursive vector through which succession becomes objectivity, renewed conditioning, retrospective correction, and never-present completion.
Struggle consists in routing claims through presentation and jurisdiction while navigating between dogmatic possession and sceptical suspension.
The resulting world is a lawful but empirically open interior whose unity depends on adjudicated coordination and whose boundary generates an unknowable remainder.

The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from synthetic a priori authorization through phenomenal constitution to dialectical projection, critical restriction, and functional redistribution.
The system is coherent only if receptivity, synthesis, apperception, theoretical cognition, regulation, practical necessity, and architectonic legitimacy remain distinct but recursively coordinated.
The architecture is strongest where phenomenal object-generation and dialectical diagnosis converge on one boundary logic that simultaneously authorizes and restricts reason.
The affection–form relation, exact mediation mechanism, categorial completeness, regulative force, practical postulation, and intelligible grounding remain underdetermined.
Reconstruction preserves the actual movement only by retaining recursive sequencing, projection, conflict, restriction, functional return, and renewed criticism.
Finite reason’s capacity to discipline itself without an external standpoint remains the indispensable element resistant to complete axiomatic reduction.

works.title: A Treatise of Human Nature
works.author: David Hume
works.edition: Original English · Gutenberg eText #4705 · retained 2012 transcription
works.description: How do perceptions become beliefs, a self, and a world held in common?

items.text: The governing problem is the absence of evidentially secure and internally coherent foundations across the sciences.
Scientific disorder displaces rational adjudication with controversy and rhetorical persuasion, thereby discrediting philosophy.
The resulting rejection of abstruse reasoning mistakes previous failure for proof that difficult inquiry is illegitimate.
Human nature is the common epistemic center of the sciences because every science is cognized and judged through human faculties.
The science of human nature must itself be reconstructed through experience and observation rather than speculation about mental essence.
Moral experimentation must use naturally occurring conduct because deliberate self-experiment alters the operations under investigation.

The argument is diagnostic, polemical, and reconstructive: foundational crisis → anti-metaphysical prejudice → anthropological recentering → experimental method → epistemic limit → observational protocol.
Inherited philosophical systems rest on inadequately warranted and incoherently connected principles.
Where decisive evidence is absent, eloquence can govern assent more effectively than reason.
Repeated failure in abstruse inquiry produces indiscriminate aversion to metaphysical reasoning.
If truth is within human capacity, its depth makes sustained abstruse inquiry necessary rather than dispensable.
Every science is cognized and judged through human powers and faculties.
The most humanly important sciences directly concern reasoning, ideas, sentiments, tastes, and social dependence.
Every important scientific decision depends on prior acquaintance with human nature.
The science of human nature can be securely founded only on experience and observation.
The essence of mind is no more cognitively available than the essence of external bodies.
Mental powers and qualities are knowable only through their effects under differing circumstances and situations.
Observed effects should be reduced to maximally universal principles and the simplest, fewest causes compatible with experience.
Inquiry into human nature cannot legitimately pass beyond experience.
Hypotheses claiming access to the ultimate original qualities of human nature are presumptuous and chimerical.
The experiential limit is common to every science and art.
Recognition that reason has reached its utmost extent dissolves the demand for further explanation.
Premeditated production of moral phenomena alters the natural principles being observed.
Ordinary human conduct is the proper evidential field for moral experiments.
Judicious collection and comparison of ordinary-life observations can establish a science of human nature with non-inferior certainty and superior utility.
Established credit does not supply secure warrant for philosophical principles.
The proliferation and intensity of disputes do not constitute certainty.
Rhetorical attractiveness is not rational evidence.
Metaphysical reasoning is not confined to a particular subject matter; the prejudice targets abstruse argument generally.
Previous failures in difficult inquiry do not justify abandoning it without embracing comprehensive scepticism and indolence.
Ease and obviousness are not presumptions in favor of philosophical truth.
Mental powers cannot be deduced from speculative knowledge of mental essence.
The pursuit of universal principles does not license passage beyond experience.
Ultimate qualities of human nature are not legitimate objects of explanatory hypothesis.
Moral experiments cannot be validly produced by deliberately placing oneself in the condition under examination.
Ignorance of ultimate principles is not a defect peculiar to the science of human nature.
Systemic evidential disorder both discredits philosophy and generates overbroad rejection of difficult reasoning.
Past failure supplies no warrant for methodological indolence if truth remains humanly attainable.
Reform of the science of human nature becomes the precondition for reforming the sciences dependent upon human reasoning, sentiment, and sociality.
Investigation of mind must proceed from circumstance and effect to powers and operations, not from essence to deduced consequences.
Empirical generalization may compress effects into simple causes but may not convert causal economy into an account of ultimate origins.
Confessed ignorance at the experiential boundary constitutes legitimate closure rather than a unique failure of moral philosophy.
Moral experimentalism must be naturalistic and observational rather than deliberately interventionist.
Comparison across ordinary circumstances supplies the variation from which general principles of human nature may be inferred.
A successful science of human nature acquires exceptional utility because its closest dependent sciences govern reasoning, evaluation, and social life.
The science of human nature becomes a metascience governing the possible security of other sciences while remaining empirically constrained itself.
Foundational security is redefined from access to essence into disciplined knowledge of recurrent effects within experiential limits.
Reflexivity does not defeat moral science; it relocates experimentation from constructed situations to naturally occurring social life.
Scepticism receives a selective function: it destroys inherited pretensions and ultimate hypotheses but cannot license abandonment of abstruse inquiry.
Scientific certainty and ultimate ignorance can coexist because certainty concerns observed regularities while ignorance concerns their final origin.
Humanity becomes both the medium through which science operates and the object whose investigation is required to secure that operation.
Scientific objects and standards are not intelligible independently of the faculties by which humans apprehend and judge them.
Knowledge of mental operations does not require prior access to an underlying mental substance.
Human conduct cannot be irreducibly singular or unstable; recurrent relations across circumstances must be available to comparison.
Controlled intervention cannot be a necessary condition of all scientific warrant.
Premeditated introspection cannot be assumed to leave the operations under inspection unchanged.
A science need not justify its most general experiential principles through a deeper non-experiential ground.
Ultimate original qualities remain unavailable, and their absence functions as the terminal boundary of legitimate explanation.
No science can occupy an unmediated standpoint outside human nature from which human cognition could be judged independently.
A pure moral experiment separating observer, intervention, and observed operation is unavailable.
The proposed foundation of the sciences has no further foundation beyond experienced reality and the regularities abstracted from it.
Insecure principles → defective deductions → unresolved controversy → rhetorical assent → philosophical discredit.
Philosophical discredit → indiscriminate anti-metaphysical prejudice → conditional attainability of deep truth → reinstatement of abstruse inquiry.
Mediation of every science by human faculties → common dependence on human nature → strategic redirection toward the science of man.
Unavailable mental essence → observation of effects across circumstances → inference to powers and operations.
Comparative observations → causal simplification → maximally general empirical principles → bounded scientific system.
Claim to ultimate qualities → transgression of experiential limits → rejection of hypothesis → confessed ignorance as closure.
Deliberate moral intervention → reflexive disturbance → ordinary conduct as experimental field → judicious comparison → moral science.

Foundational disorder → rhetorical controversy → anti-metaphysical prejudice → defense of difficult inquiry → human nature as common center → experience as foundation → ultimate explanation excluded → ordinary life converted into the field of moral experiment.
Disciplinary disorder is reclassified from a plurality of local failures into a common foundational deficit.
Human nature is repositioned from one scientific object among others to the epistemic center of the sciences.
Metaphysics is divided into legitimate abstruse empirical reasoning and illegitimate speculation about ultimate qualities.
Philosophical foundation is reclassified from knowledge of essences into observed regularities and constrained causal generalization.
Ordinary social life becomes an experimental archive rather than merely the domain to which theory is applied.
The difference between natural and moral science becomes a difference in experimental access rather than a difference in possible scientific status.
The opposition between certainty and confessed ignorance collapses once certainty is assigned to experienced relations and ignorance to ultimate origins.
Surface — Existing sciences lack secure principles, coherent deductions, and rationally decisive outcomes.
Structural — Human faculties mediate every scientific judgment, making human nature the common dependency beneath disciplinary plurality.
Metastrategic — Inquiry is redirected from piecemeal disciplinary conquest toward the central investigation of human nature and its downstream sciences.

Ontological/Temporal — Essences and ultimate origins remain inaccessible; reality enters inquiry as effects under circumstances, while experimental philosophy extends historically from nature to humanity.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from disciplinary crisis through anthropological recentering to observational moral science.
The specific taxonomy of human faculties, the rules of observational comparison, and the criterion of adequate certainty remain underdetermined.
The structure is coherent insofar as inaccessible essence, empirical method, causal compression, and explanatory limitation mutually constrain one another.
The strongest mechanism is the conversion of reflexive interference from an objection against moral science into a reason for naturalistic observation.
The transition from human mediation of science to the exclusive foundational priority of the science of man is asserted more strongly than it is demonstrated.
The promise of non-inferior certainty depends on ordinary-life observations supplying sufficient control, representativeness, and comparability despite the prohibition on constructed experiments.
The universal prohibition on passing beyond experience risks functioning as a methodological principle whose own experiential warrant is not supplied.
Foundational recursion remains unresolved because the science intended to secure human cognition must already employ cognition, observation, and comparison.
Reconstruction preserves the real argumentative movement without the martial, patriotic, and honorific rhetoric, none of which generates the methodological conclusion.

units.title: Sect. I. Of The Origin Of Our Ideas

items.text: Problem: determine the kinds of mental perception and the direction of origin between them.
Core thesis: simple ideas, on first appearance, derive from prior corresponding simple impressions.
Argument type: introspective taxonomy → empirical genealogy → anti-innatist reconstruction.
Initial impression–idea resemblance is restricted through the simple–complex distinction.
Correspondence plus constant conjunction establishes dependence; temporal priority fixes impression-to-idea causation.
Deprivation and recursive copying qualify the maxim; the missing-shade anomaly is contained rather than permitted to revise it.
Every mental perception is either an impression or an idea.
Impressions are perceptions at first appearance marked generally by greater force and liveliness.
Ideas are fainter perceptions operating in thinking and reasoning.
Every impression and idea is either simple or complex.
Simple perceptions admit no distinction or separation.
Complex perceptions are formed from distinguishable simple parts.
Every simple perception has a correspondent in the other perception class that matches its content and differs only in force and liveliness.
Complex ideas and complex impressions need not correspond as exact wholes.
Constant conjunction between corresponding perceptions establishes dependence.
Within a dependent pair, temporal priority identifies causal direction.
A simple impression precedes its corresponding idea on first appearance.
Unavailable operation of an impression-producing faculty entails absence of the corresponding idea.
Every simple idea on first appearance derives from its corresponding simple impression.
Secondary ideas may copy prior ideas while remaining mediately derived from impressions.
A missing shade can be imaginatively supplied as a simple idea without its corresponding prior impression.
A singular counterinstance is insufficient to alter the generally established derivation maxim.
Impression does not name the mechanism by which a lively perception is produced.
Idea does not name every mental perception indiscriminately.
The impression–idea distinction is not infallibly discriminable by vivacity in every exceptional state.
Exact whole-to-whole correspondence is not universal among complex perceptions.
Merely thinking an idea does not ordinarily produce its corresponding sensation, passion, or emotion.
The conjunction of impressions and ideas is not treated as accidental or causally neutral.
Secondary ideation is not a reversal of the impression-to-idea genealogy.
The missing-shade case is not allowed to repeal the general maxim.
Ideas preceded by corresponding lively perceptions are not innate.
The perception field is organized by two intersecting distinctions: impression versus idea and simple versus complex. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A1 + CH_THN_SIOO:A4 + CH_THN_SIOO:A5 + CH_THN_SIOO:A6)
Failure of exact complex correspondence does not defeat exact correspondence at the simple level. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A6 + CH_THN_SIOO:A7 + CH_THN_SIOO:A8)
Corresponding simple impressions and ideas form dependent rather than accidental pairs. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A7 + CH_THN_SIOO:A9)
Impressions are causes and first ideas are effects. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A9 + CH_THN_SIOO:A10 + CH_THN_SIOO:A11)
Normal acquisition of a simple idea requires operative access to its corresponding impression. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A12 + CH_THN_SIOO:A13)
Complex imagination may exceed experienced wholes without exceeding impression-derived simple content. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A6 + CH_THN_SIOO:A7 + CH_THN_SIOO:A8 + CH_THN_SIOO:A13)
Ideas may generate further ideas without becoming the ultimate source of their simple content. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A13 + CH_THN_SIOO:A14)
The admitted missing-shade case converts the derivation principle logically into an exception-tolerant general maxim. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A13 + CH_THN_SIOO:A15 + CH_THN_SIOO:A16)
The dispute over innate ideas is reconstructed as a question of whether ideas are preceded by livelier perceptions. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIOO:A2 + CH_THN_SIOO:A3 + CH_THN_SIOO:A11 + CH_THN_SIOO:A13)
Empirical restriction at the level of simple content coexists with recombinatorial freedom at the level of complex ideas.
The origin of an idea becomes a temporal-causal question rather than a question settled by its apparent content alone.
The missing-shade case reveals that relations among acquired ideas may generate an unexperienced simple candidate, but the system quarantines this generativity.
The proof of the copy principle employs constant conjunction and succession as causal criteria before the promised full examination of causation.
Where force and liveliness cease to discriminate impressions from ideas, genealogical order must carry the classificatory burden.
Simple ideational content cannot generally originate from an autonomous productive intellect.
Complex wholes cannot function as irreducible primitive contents independent of simple perceptions.
Causal symmetry between impressions and ideas cannot hold.
Ideas cannot normally compensate for the total absence of the faculties required to produce their corresponding impressions.
A singular counterexample cannot be permitted the logical force ordinarily sufficient to defeat an unrestricted universal proposition.
Foreclosed possibility: the mind as an original source of primitive simple representational content.
Quarantined possibility: relations among acquired perceptions constitute a general power for synthesizing genuinely new simple qualities.
Unavailable foundation: an exceptionless demonstration of the copy principle independent of introspective induction and challenge to produce a counterexample.
Mental perception → force-and-liveliness partition → impression / idea.
Each perception class → separability test → simple / complex.
Initial universal resemblance → complex counterinstances → restriction of exact correspondence to simple perceptions.
Simple correspondence + constant conjunction → dependence; first-appearance priority → impressions cause ideas.
Obstructed impression-faculty → absent impression + absent corresponding idea → confirmation of derivation.
Idea → secondary idea → recursive copying without reversal of ultimate impression-origin.
Missing-shade counterinstance → concession → singularity filter → maxim retained → innateness dispute translated into perceptual genealogy.

Undifferentiated perceptions → impression–idea distinction → simple–complex distinction → failure of universal complex copying → exact simple correspondence → causal dependence → impression priority → derivation maxim → anomaly containment → anti-innatist reframing.
Mental contents become classifiable along two independent axes: vivacity and compositional separability.
Feeling and thinking become different intensities of corresponding perceptual content rather than wholly different kinds of content.
Novel complex imagination is separated from the production of novel primitive content.
Sensory or affective deprivation becomes a genealogical test for the availability of ideas.
Innateness is reclassified from an obscure metaphysical status into a question of perceptual precedence and derivation.
Surface: perceptions are classified as impressions or ideas and as simple or complex.
Structural: simple correspondence, conjunction, and temporal priority produce a causal-copy model of mental content.
Metastrategic: the vocabulary of innate ideas is displaced by an empirically testable genealogy of perceptions.
Ontological/Temporal: mental content is modeled as a succession of perceptions whose causal status depends on order of appearance, while corresponding thought and feeling differ primarily by degree.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the taxonomy, causal derivation, qualification, and anti-innatist reframing.
The criteria for simplicity, exact correspondence, and measurable force or liveliness remain underdetermined.
The structure is coherent as a general empirical genealogy but not as an exceptionless universal system.
The argument is strongest where temporal priority and deprivation converge on the same direction of dependence.
The causal inference compresses dependence into constant conjunction and succession before causation itself has been examined.
The missing-shade case directly conflicts with the unrestricted wording of the first principle and is managed by rarity rather than resolved.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement only if the missing-shade anomaly and the deferred theory of causation remain explicit structural fault lines.

identity.title: Sect. I. Of The Origin Of Our Ideas

units.title: Sect. II. Division Of The Subject

items.text: The argument is classificatory, genealogical, and methodological.
The problem is to determine the proper order for examining impressions and ideas.
The general priority of simple impressions over correspondent ideas initially requires impressions-first inquiry.
The division of impressions into sensation and reflection replaces undifferentiated priority with a stratified genealogy.
The operative sequence is sensation → idea-copy → reflective impression → reflective idea → possible recurrence.
Because sensations are disciplinarily deferred and reflective impressions mostly arise from ideas, the inquiry must begin with ideas.
Simple impressions generally precede their correspondent ideas, notwithstanding rare exceptions.
Impressions divide into impressions of sensation and impressions of reflection.
Impressions of sensation arise originally in the soul from unknown causes.
An idea is a mental copy that remains after its originating impression ceases.
Returned ideas of pleasure and pain produce desire, aversion, hope, and fear as impressions of reflection.
Memory and imagination copy impressions of reflection into correspondent ideas.
Resulting ideas may generate further impressions and ideas.
An impression of reflection is posterior to and derived from sensation while antecedent to its own correspondent idea.
Passions, desires, and emotions are the principal objects of the present inquiry.
Impressions of reflection arise mostly from ideas.
Examination of sensations belongs to anatomy and natural philosophy rather than the present moral inquiry.
Method requires the operative antecedents of the focal object to be examined before that object.
Ideas are not ordinarily prior to their correspondent simple impressions.
The original causes of sensory impressions are not known.
Impressions of reflection are not original sensory occurrences.
Reflective impressions are not prior to the sensations from which they derive.
Ideas are not causally inert copies; returned ideas can produce new impressions.
The present inquiry is not an anatomical or natural-philosophical investigation of sensation.
General impression-priority does not require every kind of impression to precede ideas in the order of exposition.
Impressions-first inquiry is the default method when simple impressions and their correspondent ideas are considered without further division.
Priority cannot be assigned uniformly to impressions as an undifferentiated class.
Ideas mediate the derivation of reflective impressions from sensory impressions.
The copy relation can enter a recursive production sequence rather than terminate in a single idea.
Sensations can be deferred without abandoning the principal objects of the inquiry.
Ideas must be examined before the reflective impressions principally under investigation.
Ideas are derivative relative to sensation but productive relative to reflection.
Temporal priority is relational: each item may be posterior to one stratum while anterior to another.
The methodological reversal changes the relevant reference class rather than contradicting the priority of simple impressions.
The perception-chain is recursively extensible but asymmetrically grounded in sensation.
Moral inquiry begins from an intermediate representational mechanism while leaving the ultimate sensory origin unexplained.
Explanation of reflective life must not require prior resolution of the unknown causes of sensation.
The principal reflective impressions cannot be predominantly independent of antecedent ideas.
Chronological firstness alone cannot determine method once the object and disciplinary scope are restricted.
Rare exceptions must not invalidate the general precedence of simple impressions.
Recursive production must not be mistaken for a self-originating circle detached from sensation.
A complete account of the first cause of perception is unavailable within the system.
A purely immediate and representation-free account of passion is foreclosed as the primary moral model.
A single invariant order governing every relation between impressions and ideas is inadmissible.
Exceptionless closure is withheld by the qualifiers governing priority, derivation, and recurrence.
General precedence: simple impression → correspondent idea → default impressions-first method.
Class division: impression → sensation or reflection.
Genetic sequence: unknown cause → sensory impression → idea-copy → returned pleasure-or-pain idea → reflective impression.
Recursive extension: reflective impression → memory-or-imagination copy → reflective idea → possible further impression or idea.
Scope filter: sensation → anatomy and natural philosophy; reflection → present moral inquiry.
Local methodological output: ideas as antecedents of reflection → ideas-first exposition.
General impression-priority → division of impressions → stratified genealogy → relative-priority correction → disciplinary exclusion of sensation → concentration on reflection → ideas-first method.
“Impression” is reclassified from a uniform category into kinds distinguished by origin and dependency.
“Idea” is reclassified as both a copy of an antecedent impression and a cause of subsequent reflective impressions.
Priority becomes indexed to a specific correspondence and genealogical stratum rather than assigned absolutely to a whole class.
Order of exposition is detached from absolute origin and governed by the dependencies of the selected object.
Surface: impressions are divided, and ideas are selected as the starting point of inquiry.
Structural: copying and return mediate a recursive sequence between sensation, idea, reflection, and further ideas.
Metastrategic: disciplinary jurisdiction converts the natural impressions-first order into an ideas-first method.
Ontological/Temporal: perception has an unknown sensory origin, layered temporal precedence, and recursively productive mediation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the classification, genealogy, and methodological reversal.
The causes of sensation and the rare exceptions to impression-priority remain underdetermined.
The mechanism by which an idea “returns” and produces reflection is asserted rather than explained.
The structure is coherent if genetic order, correspondent order, and expository order remain distinct.
The strongest inferential joint is the derivation of ideas-first inquiry from the idea-dependence of the focal reflective impressions.
The principal fault line is that sensation supplies the indispensable foundation while being excluded from present analysis.
The argument depends on compressed qualifiers—rarely, mostly, and perhaps—that prevent universal closure.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if the final reversal is treated as local and methodological rather than as a denial of sensory precedence.

identity.title: Sect. II. Division Of The Subject

units.title: Sect. III. Of The Ideas Of The Memory And Imagination

items.text: The problem is to distinguish memory from imagination when both consist of impressions returning as ideas.
The argument is empirical-taxonomic and reconstructive: experienced differences among ideas are assigned to distinct faculties.
Both faculties remain subject to a common antecedent-impression constraint.
The first differential is vivacity: memory retains considerable force, whereas imagination loses it.
The second differential is relational fidelity: memory conserves original form and order, whereas imagination can transpose them.
Imaginative liberty is generated from copy-dependence combined with distinction, separability, and simple-complex composition.
The movement is recurrence → common origin → force distinction → order distinction → combinatorial explanation.
A previously present impression can later reappear in the mind as an idea.
Every idea is copied from a corresponding impression.
Memory repeats an impression as an idea retaining a considerable degree of its original vivacity.
Imagination repeats an impression as an idea after its original vivacity has been lost.
Proper memory preserves the original form, order, and position of its objects.
A departure in recollection from the original arrangement arises from defect or imperfection in memory.
Imagination is free to transpose and change copied ideas.
No two impressions are perfectly inseparable.
Any difference perceived by imagination among ideas permits their separation.
Ideas are divided into simple and complex forms.
Neither memory nor imagination can supply an idea without a prior corresponding impression.
Memory is not free to alter the original relations among remembered objects.
Imagination is not bound to reproduce the original conjunction or order of impressions.
Imaginative freedom is not the creation of unprecedented simple ideas.
An altered order of exposition is not an altered remembered order when the original positions remain acknowledged.
Memory and imagination differ by mode of recurrence rather than by the origin of their contents. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A1 + CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A3 + CH_THN_SIIM:A4)
Memory ideas are more forceful, lively, distinct, and stable than imagination ideas. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A3 + CH_THN_SIIM:A4)
Memory’s characteristic work is preservation of relational order and position rather than preservation of simple contents as such. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A5 + CH_THN_SIIM:A10)
Deliberate narrative reordering remains compatible with memory when due positions are retained. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A5 + CH_THN_SIIM:A6)
Imagination can form unexperienced complexes by separating and rearranging impression-derived components. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A7 + CH_THN_SIIM:A9 + CH_THN_SIIM:A10)
Perceived difference becomes compositional liberty because distinguishable components are separable rather than necessarily conjoined. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A7 + CH_THN_SIIM:A8 + CH_THN_SIIM:A9)
Mental recurrence is organized along two axes—vivacity and relational fidelity—rather than by differences in elemental source.
Memory conserves experienced temporal and positional order, while imagination releases copied contents from that order.
Imagination is dependent at the level of elements but free at the level of arrangement.
The faculty boundary is maintained asymmetrically: mnemonic disorder counts as failure, while imaginative disorder counts as successful liberty.
Copy-dependence is not relational determinism; derivation from impressions does not require preservation of their conjunctions.
A component idea’s identity is not constituted by the complex whole in which its impression originally appeared.
Distinguishability cannot coexist with an unbreakable necessary union among ideas.
Mnemonic variation cannot count as an equally proper mode of memory without dissolving the fidelity criterion.
Absolute mental spontaneity is unavailable: productivity begins only after impression-given materials.
Necessary continuity between experienced world-order and thinkable world-order is foreclosed.
Mixed cases in which vivacity and order-fidelity point toward different faculties remain unformalized.
Independent access to the original arrangement by which mnemonic fidelity is judged is absent from the system.
Present impression → later recurrence as corresponding idea.
Recurrence with considerable retained vivacity → memory → force, distinctness, and relative stability.
Recurrence after loss of original vivacity → imagination → faintness and instability.
Preservation of original form, order, and position → proper memory; altered remembered order → mnemonic defect.
Perceived difference + absence of perfect inseparability → separable idea-components.
Separable components + simple-complex composition → transposition and changed conjunction.
Copy-fixed elements + variable arrangement → imaginative fiction without novel elemental content.

Experienced return of impressions as ideas → bifurcation by vivacity → common copy constraint → bifurcation by fidelity to original order → memory as positional conservation → imagination as transposition → separability as the ground of fiction.
Ideas are reclassified from a homogeneous derivative class into faculties differentiated by force and operation.
Common provenance is separated from divergent treatment: identical source materials can support conservation or recombination.
Memory is reclassified as an archive of relations and positions rather than merely a repository of simple ideas.
Imaginative liberty is localized in arrangement rather than in the origination of content.
Unnatural fictional objects become evidence of recombination rather than exceptions to impression-origin.
Surface: Memory and imagination are distinguished by vivacity and fidelity to original arrangement.
Structural: The mind applies conservation or separation-recombination to common impression-derived materials.
Metastrategic: The faculty distinction is secured by coding mnemonic variation as defect and fictional anomaly as lawful recombination.
Ontological/Temporal: Ideas are posterior copies; memory preserves experienced succession and position, while imagination detaches contents from that succession without escaping derivation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the two faculties, their dual criteria, and the bounded liberty of imagination.
The vivacity threshold remains underdetermined; memory is both an idea and intermediate between impression and fully diminished idea.
The relation between vivacity and order-fidelity is unspecified, leaving mixed cases unresolved.
The structure is coherent if copy-dependence governs elements while separability governs arrangements.
The tightest inference is the derivation of novel complexes from copied but rearrangeable components.
The memory principle depends on compressed appeal to common phenomena rather than an independent derivation.
The move from perceived difference and non-inseparability to easy separation is asserted without specifying limits.
Mnemonic fidelity lacks an independent standard for recovering original order, while the classification of deviations as defects partially insulates the principle.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the text’s movement from experiential recurrence through dual differentiation to combinatorial closure.

identity.title: Sect. III. Of The Ideas Of The Memory And Imagination

units.title: Sect. IV. Of The Connexion Or Association Of Ideas

items.text: The central problem is how freely separable and recombinable ideas nevertheless form regular sequences and complexes.
Uniformity requires universal associative principles that guide imagination without determining it.
The argument is empirical, reconstructive, taxonomic, and methodologically anti-speculative.
Free combination → inadequacy of chance → non-necessary associative force → three relational operators.
Direct association expands into attenuated relational chains, with causation extending from production to power and social influence.
Inquiry terminates at original qualities of human nature and redirects itself from unknown causes to complex ideational effects.
Every simple idea is separable and recombinable by imagination.
The regular recurrence of simple ideas in complex formations requires a universal bond rather than chance.
Association is a gentle prevailing tendency that introduces one idea through another without compelling the transition.
Resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect are the three associative qualities.
Resemblance alone is sufficient to facilitate an imaginative transition.
Custom transfers the regular contiguity of sensory succession into the imagination’s method of transition.
Cause and effect produce the strongest and most extensive associative relation.
Association propagates through relational intermediaries while weakening at each remove.
Causal association includes the production of an object’s existence, action, or motion.
A power to produce action establishes causal relation because its exertion through will remains possible and often probable.
Relations of interest, duty, government, and subordination arise from powers by which persons influence one another.
Associative cohesion supplies within imagination the role played by inseparable connexion within memory.
The causes of associative attraction are mostly unknown and terminate here in original qualities of human nature.
Once a principle is experimentally established, inquiry should examine its effects rather than pursue obscure ultimate causes.
Complex ideas, as the common objects of thought and reasoning, generally arise from associative union among simple ideas.
Complex ideas divide into relations, modes, and substances.
Association is not an inseparable or necessary connexion.
Association is not a condition without which imagination becomes unable to join ideas.
Regular ideational composition is not attributable to chance alone.
Associative connexion is not confined to objects standing in an immediate relation.
Causation is not restricted to actual production or to the production of existence.
The theory does not claim to explain the ultimate causes of associative principles.
Philosophical inquiry should not continue into obscure and uncertain speculation after experimental sufficiency is reached.
Mental order is compatible with combinatorial freedom because association governs probabilistically rather than necessarily.
Correspondence among languages follows from shared associative tendencies toward similar complex formations.
Relational proximity is inversely proportional to the number of intermediaries, making kinship distance representable as causal-chain length.
Social offices and hierarchies become associatively causal wherever positional power can be converted into another person’s action.
Association is admissible as an experimentally supported original principle even when its underlying mechanism remains unknown.
The investigation must proceed from the associative mechanism to the classes of complex ideas it generates.
The imagination is neither mechanically determined nor randomly discontinuous; it is free under recurrent natural tendencies.
The ideational field forms an attenuating network in which relation type and relational distance jointly regulate recall.
Causation becomes a bridge between natural production, counterfactual capacity, and institutional authority.
A science of mind can map the production of complex thought through observable associative effects without possessing an ultimate metaphysics of mental connexion.
Radical cross-contextual idiosyncrasy in the succession of ideas must be false.
The opposition between necessary determination and pure chance must be false.
No independent fourth principle may be required to explain ordinary associative transitions.
Relational force cannot remain unchanged across indefinitely extended mediation.
Social interest and duty cannot require an irreducibly normative bond wholly outside causal power.
Adequate empirical explanation cannot depend upon access to the ultimate mechanism of every observed principle.
The system is organized around the absence of necessary mental connexion, whose functional place is occupied by gentle attraction.
The origin of associative attraction remains unavailable; “original qualities of human nature” names the terminal explanatory absence.
The possibility of further primitive associative sources is excluded by the triadic taxonomy without being independently refuted.
The nature of causation remains deferred even while causation carries the greatest explanatory scope within the chapter.
Free separability and recombination + recurrent complex formations → demand for a non-random ordering principle.
Ordering without compulsion → gentle associative force.
Associative force → resemblance / contiguity / cause and effect.
Immediate relation + intermediary relations → extended but progressively weakened associative chains.
Causal production → action and existence → power to produce → social influence and hierarchy.
Observable effects + unknown ultimate causes → methodological arrest at original human qualities.
Associative cohesion → complex ideas → relations / modes / substances.

Freedom of combination → recurrent uniformity → insufficiency of chance → gentle universal association → triadic operators → mediated attenuation → causal expansion into power → methodological limit → taxonomy of complex effects.
Imagination is reclassified from an arbitrary combinatorial faculty into a free faculty regulated by natural tendencies.
Necessary connexion and random succession cease to exhaust the possible models of mental order.
Ideational connexion becomes graded and transmissible rather than merely present or absent.
Causation expands from actual event-production to latent power and institutional command.
Complex ideas become generated effects of associative operations rather than primitive mental units.
Philosophical explanation is redirected from inaccessible origins toward experimentally observable effects.
Surface: One idea regularly recalls another, and simple ideas regularly form complexes.
Structural: Three relational operators organize transitions through direct and attenuated chains.
Metastrategic: The inquiry expands causation into social power while restricting philosophy to experimentally warranted effects.
Ontological/Temporal: Human nature supplies universal but non-necessary tendencies, while sensory succession and custom sediment spatial-temporal order into imagination.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s central account of regularity within a freely combinatorial imagination.
The core structure is coherent insofar as gentle tendency mediates between necessity and chance.
The exhaustiveness and universality of the three associative relations remain underdetermined rather than demonstrated.
Causation is assigned maximal explanatory force before its own nature is examined.
Contiguity is explained through acquired custom, while associative causes are classified as original qualities; the relation between acquisition and originality remains unresolved.
The argument is strongest in its graded model of mediated association and its separation of regularity from necessity.
Its extension into social relations depends on compressing interest, duty, authority, and obedience into causal power.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the movement from combinatorial freedom through associative regulation to complex ideational effects.

identity.title: Sect. IV. Of The Connexion Or Association Of Ideas

units.title: Sect. III. Of The Other Qualities Of Our Idea Of Space And Time

items.text: Problem — Determine the impression-origin and internal composition of the ideas of space and time.
Thesis — Space and time are not distinct impressions but ordered manners in which sensible or perceptual contents appear.
Argument type — Empiricist genealogy joined to eliminative, separability, and compositional tests.
Spatial movement — Sensible points → disposition → extension → abstraction across variable sensible qualities.
Temporal movement — Successive perceptions → noncoexistent order → duration → exclusion of time without change.
Closure — Indivisible spatial and temporal components remain conceivable only when filled by sensible quality or real existence.
Every idea is preceded by a correspondent impression that it copies.
Only sight and touch supply impressions from which extension can be derived.
An extended sensible impression consists of indivisible colored or tangible points disposed in a determinate order.
Every abstract idea is a particular idea considered under a shared aspect and attached to a general term.
The idea of time originates in the succession of perceptions of every kind.
Time is the manner in which successive perceptions appear, not an additional impression.
The parts of duration are noncoexistent.
The parts of extension are coexistent.
Whatever is different is distinguishable.
Whatever is distinguishable is separable in idea.
What is not distinguishable cannot be separated in idea.
An idea can properly represent only the objects or impressions from which it derives.
The compound ideas of extension and duration resolve into simple indivisible component ideas.
A real compound idea cannot be composed of nonentities.
An indivisible spatial point is conceivable only through retained color or tangibility.
The idea of extension is not derived from passions, emotions, desires, or aversions.
Extension is not an impression additional to colored or tangible points and their disposition.
An abstract idea is not an indeterminate or contentless universal.
Time cannot appear to the mind alone.
A steady and unchangeable object cannot originate the idea of time.
Time is neither an additional sensation nor an additional impression of reflection.
Duration cannot properly be predicated of an unchangeable object without fiction.
A simple spatial point is neither itself extended nor a nonentity.
A point deprived of every visible or tangible quality is unavailable to thought.
The idea of extension copies sensible points together with their relative disposition.
Abstract extension suppresses variable sensible peculiarities only while retaining their shared disposition in a particular sensible representation.
One abstract idea of extension can represent both visible and tangible configurations because their parts share a disposition.
Abstract time ranges over sensations, reflections, impressions, and ideas while remaining represented by a determinate succession.
Without successive perceptions there is no notion of time, even where objects undergo real succession.
Apparent duration varies with the rate and discriminability of successive perceptions.
Coexistence and noncoexistence provide the constitutive distinction between extension and duration.
Time may be abstracted from particular successive objects but cannot be separated from some succession of objects.
Applying duration to an unchangeable object exceeds the impression from which duration derives and is therefore fictional.
The indivisible component of extension must be qualitatively sensible rather than extended or nonexistent.
No idea of space or extension remains when all visible and tangible content is removed.
An indivisible moment must be filled by a real object or existence whose succession makes duration conceivable.
Space and time are higher-order arrangements of content rather than additional contents: space orders coexistent sensible points, while time orders successive existences.
Abstract universality is representational rather than imagistic: a determinate particular represents heterogeneous cases through selective regard and general denomination.
Experienced temporality is constrained by the mind’s resolution and rate of perception rather than determined immediately by objective succession.
Pure spatial and temporal minima are conceptually unavailable because every minimum must retain sensible quality or existential filling.
The genealogy of an idea functions as a limit on its legitimate application: predication cannot properly outrun the originating impression.
Space and time cannot be innate or independently given ideas.
Repeated contemplation cannot generate a new simple idea unless a new original impression occurs.
Abstraction cannot remove every particular determination while leaving a positive idea intact.
A manner of appearance cannot be reified as an additional constituent of what appears.
Common linguistic application cannot establish conceptual legitimacy independently of impression-origin.
Objective occurrence alone cannot furnish an idea when the corresponding order is not perceivable.
Pure empty spatiality is the absent object around which the spatial argument is organized.
Bare duration without successive existence is excluded from possible conception.
Absolute time capable of measuring changeless being is foreclosed except as fiction.
Direct cognitive access to space or time independently of perceptual content is unavailable to the system.
Copy principle → impression audit → elimination of reflective sources → restriction to sight and touch.
Sensible minima → relative disposition → compound extension → spatial idea.
Recurrent disposition across variable qualities → selective omission → particular representative → abstract space.
Heterogeneous perceptions → perceivable succession → noncoexistent order → temporal idea.
Absence of distinct temporal impression → non-distinguishability → non-separability from succession.
Genetic restriction → absence of temporal source in changeless objects → fictional application of duration.
Compound decomposition → indivisible component → exclusion of nonentity → sensible or existential filling.

Copy principle → source elimination → spatial derivation → abstraction mechanism → temporal derivation → separability test → exclusion of changeless duration → indivisible-component test → content-filled space and time.
Space is reclassified from an independent receptacle into the disposition of visible or tangible minima.
Time is reclassified from an independent medium into the perceivable succession of changing contents.
Abstraction is reclassified from production of a contentless universal into selective use of a particular idea.
Coexistence and noncoexistence replace independent substances as the primary distinction between space and time.
Changeless duration and qualityless spatial points are relocated from proper ideas to fiction or nonconception.
Questions concerning space and time are made answerable through impression-tracing rather than through unrestricted metaphysical postulation.
Surface — The immediate inquiry identifies the impressions and component qualities represented by ideas of extension and duration.
Structural — Copying, abstraction, separability, and decomposition govern the formation and limits of both ideas.
Metastrategic — Conceptual disputes are adjudicated by tracing ideas to impressions and rejecting applications that exceed that genealogy.
Ontological/Temporal — Spatiality and temporality become orders of existent content: coexistence for sensible points and succession for changing objects.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the parallel genealogies of extension and duration.
The claim that the senses present only sensible points and their disposition is asserted phenomenologically rather than independently demonstrated.
The terminal argument depends on the prior establishment of indivisible component ideas.
Internal coherence is strongest where the copy principle, absence of a distinct impression, and inseparability test converge.
The exact-copy principle strains against abstraction: abstract extension omits determinate color while every spatial representative must retain color or tangibility.
Temporal abstraction separates time from particular perceptions while denying its separation from some perceptions; the type-token mechanism remains compressed.
The denial of duration to changeless objects depends on treating genetic origin as a binding semantic limit.
The argument establishes conditions of conception more securely than conditions of independent existence; its closing language partially compresses that distinction.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s movement only if spatial disposition and temporal succession remain parallel but nonidentical structures.

identity.title: Sect. III. Of The Other Qualities Of Our Idea Of Space And Time

units.title: Sect. VI. Of The Idea Of Existence, And Of External Existence

items.text: Problem: determine the origin and content of the ideas of existence and external existence.
Argument type: empiricist genealogy conducted through an exhaustive dilemma, elimination, and conceptual boundary test.
The impression-copy principle and the universal conception of perceptions as existent force existence to be either a distinct accompanying perception or identical with the object conceived.
The absence of a distinct impression inseparably accompanying every perception eliminates the first alternative.
Existence is identical with the idea of the object and adds nothing to its conceived content.
Because only perceptions are present to the mind, no positive idea can represent an existence specifically different from perceptions.
Impression-origin test → exhaustive dilemma → elimination of distinct existence-content → identity thesis → perceptual closure → relative conception of externality.
Every idea arises from a similar antecedent impression.
Every impression or idea available to consciousness or memory is conceived as existent.
No distinct impression is inseparably conjoined with every perception.
The idea of existence is identical with the idea of the object conceived as existent.
A distinction without real difference requires one simple idea to bear different resemblance-relations to other ideas.
Nothing is present to the mind except perceptions: impressions and ideas.
External objects are known only through the perceptions they occasion.
An external object supposed specifically different from perceptions can be conceived only relatively, without comprehension of its intrinsic nature.
External objects are ordinarily differentiated from perceptions by attributed relations, connections, and durations rather than by a specifically different content.
Existence is not derived from a distinct impression attached to every perception.
Existence is not an additional quality inserted into an object-idea.
Reflecting on an object simply is not distinct from reflecting on it as existent.
Existence cannot be rescued as a distinction without difference, because presented objects supply no differential resemblance with respect to existence.
Loving, hating, thinking, feeling, and seeing are not modes of mental presence beyond perception.
No specifically extra-perceptual kind of existence can be positively represented.
Directing attention outward does not move conception beyond the universe of perceptions.
Relative reference to external objects is not comprehension of those objects.
Conscious awareness supplies the maximal idea and assurance of being available within the argument.
The idea of existence must arise either from a distinct impression universally conjoined with perception or from the perception itself.
The distinct-impression alternative fails, leaving identity between existence and the conceived object.
Conjoining existence with an object-idea produces no conceptual enlargement.
No contrast class permits existence to function as a distinction of reason.
Every positive conception remains composed of perceptual content already available within the mind.
Knowledge of external objects is necessarily mediated and cannot become direct presence of those objects to the mind.
Externality is available either as an uncomprehended relative correlate or as a redistribution of relations, connections, and durations.
Being functions at the conceptual level as the universal status of presentation rather than as discriminating content.
Conceivability guarantees existence-as-conceived but supplies no additional content establishing independent external actuality.
Positive ontology is bounded by the inventory of possible perceptions; whatever exceeds that inventory cannot be conceived according to its specific nature.
External realism remains thinkable only through mediation, relational attribution, or an intrinsically unfilled correlate.
An intellectual idea of being independent of impressions is excluded.
Existence cannot be both universally attached to perceptions and positively distinguishable from them.
Presented objects cannot differ in kind merely through possession or absence of conceived existence.
Attention and imagination cannot generate access to a domain specifically heterogeneous to perception.
Merely positing a specifically different external object cannot generate positive content for that object.
The requirement that relative reference comprehend its relatum is excluded by the permitted conception of external existence.
The positive essence of mind-independent being is the governing absence: external existence is retained only where intrinsic comprehension is withdrawn.
No bare existential marker separates an imagined object from an independently existing object.
No representational passage connects the perceptual universe to a positively conceived heterogeneous realm.
The external source said to occasion perceptions remains named through relation but unavailable as a comprehended kind of being.
The intrinsic nature of external objects remains neither positively affirmable nor eliminable within the chapter’s conceptual resources.
Copy principle + universal existential conception → exhaustive origin dilemma.
Candidate universal existence-impression → test for distinctness and inseparability → failure.
Elimination of distinct impression → identity of existence with object-conception → zero conceptual addition.
Proposed distinction without difference → differential-resemblance test → absence of an existence contrast class → rejection.
Perceptions alone present + ideas copied from prior perceptions → closure of positive conception within perception.
Specifically different external object posited → no qualitative comprehension → relative idea only.
Ordinary external attribution → altered relations, connections, and durations → no specifically different object-content.

Question of existence-content → impression-origin dilemma → elimination of a distinct existence-impression → identity and non-addition → rejection of distinction by resemblance → perception-only horizon → impossibility of specifically external conception → relative or relational externality.
Existence is reclassified from a detachable predicate or quality into identity with conceived content.
Existential predication loses the power to enlarge an idea or distinguish kinds of conceived objects.
The internal/external distinction is displaced from specific qualitative difference to mediation and relational organization.
The universe of imagination becomes the boundary of all positive conceptual content.
External-object discourse divides into comprehensible relations and an incomprehensible related term.
Surface: the chapter determines what the ideas of existence and external existence contain and from which impressions they derive.
Structural: the copy principle, separability test, and perception-only presence rule regulate admissible concepts.
Metastrategic: metaphysical claims are converted into demands for an originating impression, with unsupported positive content eliminated.
