Private consciousness cannot independently determine vanity without comparative and social mediation.
Momentary possession cannot constitute durable evidence of personal excellence or defect.
Untutored passion cannot be presumed to assign stable values correctly on first encounter.
Hedonic condition and self-estimation cannot be coextensive.
General rules cannot remain merely cognitive; the system requires them to organize passion itself.
There is no unmediated passage from the reality of good or evil to a corresponding judgment of self.
There is no guaranteed recognition of suffering within the economy of pride and humility.
There is no self-sufficient measure of personal worth insulated from comparison, publicity, and customary classification.
There is no invariant intrinsic scale capable of explaining the passions independently of familiarity and contrast.
There is no assured equilibrium between particular affective reality and general rules, because custom both regularizes and exceeds particular grounds.
Valenced object → primary pleasure or pain.
Primary affect + relation to self → candidate transition toward pride or humility.
Relational test: closeness sufficient, competing relation subordinate.
Comparative test: cause peculiar, unfamiliar enough to retain value, and capable of distinguishing self.
Discernibility test: cause apparent to self and others.
Temporal test: cause sufficiently constant and proportionate to the duration attributed to self.
Customary-rule operation → stabilized valuation, facilitated passion, possible extension beyond particular warrant.
Successful tests + association of ideas and impressions → pride or humility; failed tests → pleasure or pain without corresponding self-directed passion.
Unrestricted general system → overgeneration problem → necessity of limitations.
Joy/pride distinction → graded relation → peculiarity → public discernibility → temporal constancy.
Variable first-order responses → custom and practice → general maxims → regularized passion.
Qualified causal system → separation of self-estimation from welfare → rejection of any necessary pride–happiness or humility–misery alignment.
A universal causal claim is redrawn as a threshold-dependent transformation model.
Hedonic affect and self-evaluative passion become distinct classes of response.
Relation is reclassified from simple presence into graded, competitive, and interruptible force.
Value is relocated from intrinsic quality alone to familiarity, comparison, rarity, and distinction.
Public appearance becomes a causal condition of self-directed passion rather than an incidental accompaniment.
Real evil is separated from the mechanisms by which evil becomes a basis of humility.
Custom appears simultaneously as an affective regularizer and a source of overextension.
Surface — Five qualifications restrict or enlarge the production of pride and humility from agreeable and disagreeable objects.
Structural — A dual-object passion requires a stronger transition than a direct pleasure or pain and is therefore more vulnerable to failed mediation.
Social — Peculiarity, comparison, shared possession, and visibility to others determine whether a quality distinguishes self.
Metastrategic — General rules explain how delicate causal principles can operate with sufficient regularity to sustain the larger system.
Ontological/Temporal — A relatively durable self functions as the comparator against which transient causes lose self-defining force.
Ontological/Temporal — The reality of good and evil remains independent of whether representational conditions convert them into pride or humility.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the restriction of the general causal system and its concluding separation of welfare from self-estimation.
The exact degree of relational closeness required for pride or humility remains underdetermined.
The causal basis of public discernibility is deferred rather than demonstrated within the section.
The formation and authority of general rules depend on a prior account of custom that is imported in compressed form.
The system is internally coherent where it distinguishes direct pleasure and pain from their conversion into self-directed passion.
Its strongest operation is the explanation of cases in which pleasure or misery persists while pride or humility fails.
A fault line remains between familiarity as a depreciator of value and custom as a stabilizer of value; no priority rule resolves their interaction.
General rules can exceed particular warrant, but their capacity to override the other limitations is not formally bounded.
The claim that the most solid evils often evade humility is structurally licensed but not demonstrated.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the movement from unrestricted law through limitation and enlargement to affective dissociation.

identity.title: Sect. VI Limitations Of This System

units.title: Sect. XI Of The Love Of Fame

items.text: Problem: explain why reputation governs pride and humility and amplifies their otherwise original causes.
Thesis: love of fame is secondary; praise and blame affect self through sympathetic communication, while authority governs uptake of the judgment.
Another’s expressed sentiment becomes an idea whose vivacity is increased through its relations to the persistently vivid self.
Sufficient vivacity converts the represented sentiment into an impression experienced as one’s own affection.
Variations in esteem, acquaintance, self-concurrence, proximity, and relational convergence test the mechanism against an undifferentiated instinct for fame.
Explanatory-reconstructive movement: reputational effect → sympathy mechanism → application to self-evaluation → differential tests → assimilation of apparent objections.
Ideas and impressions share representational content and differ in force and vivacity.
Consciousness supplies an invariably intimate and maximally lively impression of self.
Relations enable the imagination to transfer vivacity from a present impression to a related idea.
External signs produce an idea of another person’s affection.
Causal inference establishes the represented affection as real.
General human resemblance relates another person’s mental structure to one’s own.
Peculiar resemblance, contiguity, kinship, and acquaintance strengthen the relation between self and another.
A sufficiently enlivened idea of an affection becomes the corresponding impression.
Pride and humility require a self-related source of independent pleasure or pain.
Praise and blame represent another person’s favorable or unfavorable sentiment toward a quality attributed to self.
Reasoning treats another person’s judgment as evidence for the attributed quality.
Evaluative influence increases with the authority accorded to the evaluator.
Praise yields substantial pleasure only when its attribution concurs with, or can alter, the recipient’s own opinion.
Relations amplify sympathy when they converge upon the same evaluator.
Sympathetic impressions remain divided when supporting relations are distributed across different evaluators.
Passion gives additional force to related ideas.
Conscious self-partiality favors confirming evaluations and resists opposing evaluations.
Love of fame is not an original instinct responding equally to every favorable or unfavorable opinion.
National uniformity of sentiment is not adequately explained by soil or climate.
Sympathy is not immediate access to another’s passion; the passion first appears as an idea inferred from signs.
Conversion between idea and impression is not a change in representational content.
Approbation is not equally effective regardless of its source.
Abstract esteem for a quality is not sufficient to make praise pleasurable when possession of that quality is disbelieved.
Relations do not operate merely by existing; they must facilitate associative transition and vivacity transfer.
Relations distributed across different persons do not produce the unified force achieved when they converge upon the same persons.
Blame from a despised or unserious source is not affectively equivalent to credible blame.
Sympathy occurs when signs and causal inference form an idea of another’s sentiment and self-related relations enliven it into the corresponding impression.
Common humanity makes sympathy generally possible, while specific similarity and proximity regulate its intensity.
Praise generates pride when another’s favorable sentiment is sympathetically reproduced, accepted as evidence, and attached as pleasure to a self-related quality.
Preference for the approval of competent judges over indiscriminate approval follows from unequal authority and contradicts an undifferentiated fame instinct.
Intimate acquaintance strengthens approbation by increasing both associative proximity and the evidential weight of judgment.
Praise incongruent with self-attribution cannot ordinarily establish the pleasure required for pride.
Separating kinship from contiguity across different evaluators prevents their contempt from forming a unified sympathetic impression.
Concealment of prior rank suppresses unfavorable comparison in observers and prevents private misfortune from being affectively doubled through sympathy.
Numerical accumulation can compensate for low individual esteem by conferring aggregate authority upon popular opinion.
Undeserved praise can please when imagination fabricates a provisional self-attribution and sympathetic agreement stabilizes it.
Contempt can wound without securing assent because the sympathetically received passion conflicts with antecedent pride; the effect disappears when the critic lacks credibility or seriousness.
Reputation is mediated self-affection: an external evaluation becomes causally effective only by being internally reproduced.
The self is both the source of vivacity and the eventual object of the sentiment that vivacity imports, producing a recursive self–other–self circuit.
Social evaluation has a relational topology: proximity, authority, convergence, separation, and multiplicity determine affective force more than bare evaluative content.
Individual self-esteem and collective uniformity are generated by the same mechanism of communicated sentiment.
Social opposition can alter affect without altering belief because sympathetic reception and intellectual assent are separable.
The distinction between original and secondary causes of pride is functionally porous because communicated opinion amplifies the qualities nominally capable of producing pride independently.
Other minds cannot be affectively sealed from one another.
Ideas cannot be permanently separated from impressions by an absolute difference of kind.
Self-evaluation cannot be sovereign or insulated from socially transmitted sentiment.
Evaluative influence cannot be reduced to propositional content independently of relational configuration.
Relations cannot be inert classifications; they must alter transitions and vivacity.
Reason cannot remain neutral when its judgments are connected with passion and self-partiality.
The system forecloses an autonomous self whose passions originate wholly within its private judgment.
Fame has no independent affective substance apart from communicated sentiments and their authority.
A neutral tribunal of self-worth is unavailable because both external testimony and internal judgment are modulated by passion.
Expression → external sign → causal certification → idea of another’s sentiment.
Vivid self-impression → human resemblance plus contingent relations → associative transition → transferred vivacity.
Enlivened idea → idea–impression threshold crossed → corresponding affection reproduced → sympathy.
Evaluative sentiment about self → sympathetic affect plus testimonial evidence → pleasure or pain attached to a self-quality → pride or humility.
Judge authority plus relational proximity plus self-concurrence plus relational convergence plus numerical accumulation → degree of reputational influence.
Distance plus disesteem plus nonconcurrence plus divided relations plus perceived jest → attenuation or interruption of reputational influence.
Apparent counterexample → identify compensating authority, imaginative supplementation, or passion-conflict → return variation to the sympathy mechanism.

Reputational power → rejection of undifferentiated fame instinct → general sympathy principle → vivacity-transfer mechanism → application to praise and blame → differential phenomena → assimilation of objections → communication-of-sentiments thesis.
Fame is reclassified from an original appetite into a secondary effect of sympathetic communication.
Opinions are reclassified as both propositions carrying evidential authority and sentiments capable of affective transmission.
Resemblance, contiguity, kinship, and acquaintance become conductors of vivacity rather than merely descriptive relations.
Reputation becomes a topological phenomenon governed by the arrangement of evaluators around the self.
Affective injury is separated from intellectual assent, making resisted contempt psychologically operative.
Relocation, anonymity, and concealment become mechanisms for altering shame without altering the underlying material condition.
Surface: praise, blame, reputation, and infamy produce differential pride and humiliation.
Structural: relational networks regulate the conversion of others’ sentiments into self-affection.
Metastrategic: controlled variations in authority, proximity, concurrence, and relational convergence test sympathy against the rival instinct model.
Ontological/Temporal: ideas and impressions occupy a continuum of vivacity, while sympathy unfolds as the compressed sequence sign → idea → enlivening → impression.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from sympathy’s perceptual mechanism to the secondary production of pride and humility through reputation.
The quantitative threshold for idea–impression conversion and the relative weights of authority and relational proximity remain underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent across variations in evaluator status, acquaintance, concurrence, and relational distribution.
Its strongest discriminator is the unequal influence of opinions that an original, undifferentiated fame instinct would treat equally.
Reconstruction depends on the prior theories of association and of independent pleasure or pain as causes of pride and humility.
The case of consciously undeserved praise requires imaginative fiction to preserve the concurrence condition, introducing an auxiliary mechanism.
The response of pride to rejected contempt leaves an unresolved boundary between communication of sentiment and adoption of judgment.
The claim of lossless conversion under perfected sympathy coexists with graded ordinary influence without a specified threshold or measure.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s real movement only if these qualifications remain visible rather than being absorbed into an unrestricted sympathy principle.

identity.title: Sect. XI Of The Love Of Fame

items.text: Problem: reconcile apparent exceptions to the pleasure–pain account of love and hatred and explain their conjunction with further passions.
Core thesis: affection arises when pleasure or uneasiness is joined to a sufficiently vivid and durable imaginative relation to a person.
Argument type: diagnostic, eliminative, and reconstructive.
Momentary causation → intention/durability distinction → explanation of transient versus lasting passion.
Relation, acquaintance, and resemblance → increased vivacity → agreeable agitation → affection, modulated by directional association.
Candidate causes of wealth-esteem → elimination of object-pleasure and expected advantage as primary → sympathy → recursive amplification.
Passion-mixture → rejection of identity between love and benevolence → contingent natural conjunction → constructive sympathy as the basis of pity.
Love and hatred vary in valence and intensity with the pleasure or uneasiness received from another.
Love and hatred require both a relation of ideas to a person and a relation of impressions between pleasure or pain and passion.
An enduring personal quality connects its pleasure or uneasiness to the person independently of intention.
A momentary action requires intention to remain connected to its author after the action disappears.
Intention intensifies injury or service by signifying contempt, hatred, kindness, or esteem toward the recipient.
A sufficiently forceful pleasure or pain can activate passion despite only a weak relation of ideas to its personal cause.
An established passion tends to generate judgments that prevent its diminution.
Ideas and impressions differ principally in force and vivacity, permitting a sufficiently lively idea to become an impression.
Lively conceptions are agreeable, and conceptions of passions produce especially strong mental agitation.
Relation, acquaintance, and resemblance increase the force of conception through association, custom, or dispositional correspondence.
A personal relation is strongest when imaginative transition between its terms is easy in both directions.
Sympathy converts a vivid idea of another’s sentiment into a corresponding impression through resemblance between persons.
Extension by a general rule requires predominantly uniform experience connecting the relevant condition and effect.
Possession, power, and utility produce actual or represented satisfaction in their possessor or beneficiary.
Power and riches elicit esteem even where the observer can expect no benefit from their possessor.
Sentiments communicated between persons can be reciprocally reflected and amplified.
Passions can blend into a compound impression, whereas ideas combine without losing their distinctness.
Love and hatred stand in an original but contingent conjunction with benevolence and anger rather than in identity with them.
Sympathy can construct the passion customarily associated with a condition even when that passion is absent from the person observed.
Imaginative proximity and contrast intensify sympathetically constructed emotion.
Mere causal production of pleasure or pain is not sufficient for durable love or hatred.
Intention is not universally necessary for affection toward personal qualities.
Accidental and involuntary harm is not incapable of producing immediate anger.
Acknowledged justice does not necessarily extinguish anger caused by harm.
The opinion of iniquity is not always the antecedent cause of hatred.
Affection arising from relation or acquaintance is not proportioned solely to objective merit.
Logical reciprocity between objects does not guarantee equal psychological transition in both directions.
Esteem for riches is not principally caused by contemplation of agreeable possessions.
Esteem for riches is not principally caused by expected personal advantage or a general rule derived from such expectation.
Love is not identical with desire for another’s happiness, nor hatred with desire for another’s misery.
The conjunction of love with benevolence and hatred with anger is not conceptually necessary.
Pity does not require antecedent friendship or reflection on one’s own vulnerability to misfortune.
Sympathy does not require the observed person actually to feel the passion communicated to the observer.
Enduring qualities produce stable affection without design, whereas transient actions require design to disclose enduring character.
Intention strengthens passion twice: by connecting the action to the person and by adding communicated esteem or contempt to its effect.
Accidental harm can produce violent but short-lived anger because the impression remains strong while the personal relation remains weak.
Recognized justice diminishes but need not erase anger because it opposes the painful impression without annihilating it.
Harm can first produce hatred, after which hatred produces an opinion of injury that stabilizes it.
Relation and acquaintance produce affection by making the related or familiar person unusually vivid and therefore agreeable to contemplate.
Resemblance facilitates affection both by transferring vivacity and by predisposing the observer toward the corresponding emotion.
A competing relation weakens an existing tie when it redirects imagination and obstructs the return transition.
Agreeable possessions generate esteem chiefly when imagination passes from the possessions to the satisfaction of their possessor.
Expected advantage cannot principally explain wealth-esteem because esteem persists where benefit is impossible and the uniformity required for a general rule is absent.
Sympathy remains the general cause of wealth-esteem because it communicates the proprietor’s satisfaction independently of benefit to the observer.
The perceived beauty of utility is pleasure communicated from the beneficiary rather than pleasure intrinsic to sensible form.
Wealth produces a feedback circuit in which possession causes satisfaction, communicated satisfaction causes esteem, and perceived esteem increases the possessor’s satisfaction.
Love and hatred acquire practical tendencies through their conjunction with benevolence and anger, not through their own conceptual essence.
Pity for strangers follows from the general human resemblance that permits their sorrow to become a vivid impression in the observer.
An observed misfortune can produce stronger pity when the sufferer feels less sorrow because general expectation supplies the absent passion and contrast heightens it.
Personal attribution is temporally organized: durable passion requires either a durable quality or a sign of durable character.
Moral accusation can function as an endogenous preservation-mechanism of prior affect rather than as its independent rational cause.
Kinship, acquaintance, resemblance, and sympathy form one economy of transmitted vivacity whose recurrent output is affection.
Social attachment depends on the topology of imaginative passage, not merely on the existence of an objective relation.
Economic rank and utility-based beauty are affective appropriations of satisfaction located initially in another person.
Wealth reproduces its own desirability through recursive exchanges between possessed power, observer esteem, and proprietary vanity.
The benevolent or destructive direction of love and hatred is naturally installed but not logically or morally entailed by those passions.
Sympathy is a constructive simulation capable of exceeding, supplementing, or replacing the actual emotion of its apparent source.
Rational judgment of guilt cannot be the exclusive ground of anger or hatred.
Deliberate intention cannot be the universal gate through which affective attribution passes.
Objective merit cannot independently determine affection against the force of familiarity and associative vivacity.
The mind cannot be affectively self-sufficient; its animation depends on lively relations to external objects and other minds.
Relations cannot be treated as static, symmetrical properties without regard to the direction and interruption of imaginative movement.
Social esteem cannot be reduced to calculated self-interest or probable exchange.
The practical tendencies of passions cannot all be deduced from their conceptual content; some conjunctions remain irreducibly constitutional.
Sympathetic communication cannot be assumed to reproduce another’s inner state with veridical fidelity.
An affectively neutral standpoint from which persons are judged independently of pleasure, pain, association, and prior passion is unavailable within the system.
Intrinsic social or aesthetic value independent of communicated satisfaction is structurally displaced.
No necessary moral order guarantees that love seeks happiness or hatred seeks misery; the alignment rests on contingent nature.
Transparent correspondence between the actual emotion of one mind and the sympathetic emotion of another is foreclosed.
A closed individual mind capable of sustaining pleasure, passion, and value without reflective dependence on other minds is excluded.
Pleasure or uneasiness from another → agreeable or disagreeable impression.
Enduring quality ∨ intention-as-character-sign → strong person-relation; momentary accident → weak person-relation.
Impression-relation × person-relation → love or hatred; strong impression × weak relation → acute but unstable passion.
Intention → communicated esteem or contempt → vanity or mortification → amplified affection.
Pain-generated passion → threat of diminution by innocence or justice → justificatory injury-judgment → partial stabilization.
Self-vivacity → relation, custom, or resemblance → lively idea of another → agreeable agitation → affection.
Easy outward transition + easy return → strong tie; competing transition + obstructed return → weakened tie.
Possession or power → proprietor satisfaction → sympathetic esteem → perceived esteem → vanity → renewed satisfaction and esteem.
Love or hatred + original constitutional coupling → benevolence or anger → blended compound affection.
Observed condition + human resemblance + customary affect-rule + proximity or contrast → vivid constructed impression → pity despite absent original sorrow.
Pleasure–pain rule → intentionality difficulty → quality/action distinction → explanation of passion duration → passion-generated injury judgment.
Love of relations and acquaintance → search for common cause → force and vivacity → reciprocal-transition model.
Wealth-esteem → competing causal hypotheses → failure of direct object-pleasure and expected advantage → sympathy → recursive status amplification.
Compound passions → identity hypothesis → experiential rejection → original contingent conjunction of love with benevolence and hatred with anger.
Pity without friendship → sympathy through resemblance → communication of sorrow → passion without an actual original → constructive imagination.
Agency is reclassified from immediate causal authorship to durable attribution through character or intention.
The judgment of injury becomes potentially an effect of hatred rather than its necessary antecedent.
Kinship, familiarity, and resemblance become variants of one vivacity-producing mechanism.
Relations become directional pathways of imagination rather than merely reciprocal logical connections.
Esteem for wealth is relocated from rational advantage to vicarious participation in proprietary satisfaction.
Utility-based beauty is relocated from sensible form to sympathetic apprehension of another’s benefit.
Love and hatred are separated from the benevolent and destructive desires that ordinarily accompany them.
Sympathy is expanded from emotional transmission to affective construction under association, general rules, and contrast.
Surface: variations in anger, affection, social esteem, benevolence, and pity are treated as test cases for the passion-system.
Structural: double relations, force and vivacity, directional association, sympathy, and recursive reflection generate the observed passions.
Metastrategic: apparent counterexamples are converted into discriminating tests that eliminate rival mechanisms and qualify the governing hypothesis.
Ontological/Temporal: ideas and impressions differ by degree of force; enduring qualities sustain personal attribution, while transient events produce unstable passions unless mediated by intention.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the principal transitions from personal causation through association and sympathy to compound affection and pity.
Reconstruction preserves the operative movement: anomaly → distinction → rival elimination → revised mechanism → extension.
Internal coherence depends on accepting force and vivacity as the common currency connecting association, pleasure, impression, and passion.
The structure is strongest where rival explanations generate discriminating cases, especially intention, impossible benefit, and love–desire identity.
The relative weights of harm, justice, intention, associative strength, and individual disposition remain underdetermined.
Appeal to an original constitutional conjunction preserves the phenomenon of benevolence and anger at the cost of further causal derivation.
Sympathy shifts from reproducing actual emotion to constructing absent emotion without a fully specified criterion governing the shift.
Malice is classified as a secondary affection but is not derived with the completeness given to pity.
Compression removes illustrative cases without removing the distinctions, eliminations, feedback structures, or terminal tensions required to regenerate the argument.

units.title: Sect. VIII Of Malice And Envy

items.text: Problem: explain unprovoked pleasure in another’s misery and pain in another’s enjoyment.
Core thesis: malice and envy arise when comparison converts another’s condition into an inverse estimate of one’s own.
Argument type: reconstructive psychological diagnosis grounded in affective succession and associative transition.
Comparative judgments vary because comparison alters an idea’s attendant emotion, which custom then attributes to the object.
Comparison becomes affectively operative only where relations permit easy transition between ideas and their impressions.
Movement: comparative distortion → altered self-estimate → reverse affect → malice/envy differentiation → relation-conditioned general law.
Human sentiments ordinarily assign value through comparison rather than intrinsic assessment.
Every sensed object or imagined idea is accompanied by an emotion proportioned to it.
A succeeding emotion is magnified or diminished by contrast with the preceding emotion.
Habitual general rules carry the mind from a degree of emotion to the object’s customary corresponding degree.
Satisfaction with one’s condition varies with its apparent fortune.
In comparison, one term alters the felt value of the other in a direction contrary to its own direct affective effect.
Associative relation between ideas enables an easy transition of imagination.
Easy transition preserves the first object’s impression during passage to the second.
Preserved impressions can modify one another through comparison or affective contrariety.
Envy is pain produced when another’s present enjoyment comparatively diminishes one’s own apparent condition.
Malice is the unprovoked desire to produce another’s misery for the pleasure of comparative self-advantage.
A predominant passion assimilates affective additions to its own direction.
Malice is not hatred caused by antecedent offense or injury.
Affective judgment is not governed chiefly by reason or intrinsic value.
Comparative variation is not produced by alteration of the immediate impression, image, or idea.
The direct survey of another’s condition is not affectively equivalent to comparison with that condition.
Envy is not proportionate to the absolute magnitude of another’s superiority.
Proximity in merit alone is not sufficient for envy without supporting relations.
Unrelated ideas cannot substantially affect one another merely through juxtaposition.
Contrary passions do not encounter or neutralize one another when their objects remain associatively separate.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A2 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A4) Comparison can change judgment while leaving representation unchanged because contrast alters the attendant emotion and custom attributes that alteration to the object.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A5 + CH_THN_SVME:A6) Another’s misery elevates one’s apparent happiness and produces pleasure, while another’s happiness diminishes it and produces pain.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A6) The same misery can be painful under direct survey and pleasurable under comparative survey.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A5) Past pain becomes agreeable when contrasted with present satisfaction, while past pleasure becomes painful when contrasted with present deficiency.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A12) Self-inflicted suffering can remove a contrast that would otherwise intensify predominant grief or the imagined punishment of remorse.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A1 + CH_THN_SVME:A3 + CH_THN_SVME:A5 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) An inferior’s approach converts decreased comparative pleasure into positive pain by comparing the reduced advantage with its former degree.

(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A9 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) Nearby or resembling rivals provoke more envy than remote superiors because proximity sustains the transition required for comparison.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A9) Separating related objects into distinct conceptual units prevents their attendant passions from influencing or contradicting one another.
(from CH_THN_SVME:A7 + CH_THN_SVME:A8 + CH_THN_SVME:A10) The mind seeks relief from related superiority either by breaking the association or by removing the superiority itself.
Evaluative magnitude is relationally produced even where the perceived object and its representation remain invariant.
Malice converts another’s suffering into an instrument for changing one’s own apparent position.
Envy follows associative proximity more reliably than absolute inequality.
Comparative passions are recursively temporal: a loss of former comparative pleasure can itself become a new source of pain.
Associative organization governs whether passions interact across personal, social, political, and aesthetic domains.
Emotional distance can be produced by weakening relations even when objective superiority remains unchanged.
Affective self-estimation is not insulated from the fortunes of comparable others.
Identity of representation does not entail identity of judgment.
Objective inequality cannot by itself generate envy without an associative route of comparison.
Natural contrariety between passions cannot ensure their interaction without continuity between their ideas.
Sensory invariance cannot reliably correct judgments imposed by habitual effect-to-cause association.
Evil need not be desired as an independent end for malicious action to arise.
The system supplies no affectively operative intrinsic baseline capable of stabilizing self-worth against comparison.
No autonomous faculty of malevolence is required; comparative self-augmentation occupies its explanatory place.
The boundary of operative relation has no independent metric and appears only where transition succeeds or fails.
The system does not fully specify what determines whether another’s condition is surveyed directly or comparatively.
Object O → attendant emotion E(O) proportioned to O.
Relation R(O1,O2) → easy transition O1→O2 → preservation of E(O1).
Preserved E(O1) + succeeding E(O2) → contrast → altered E′(O2).
Altered E′(O2) + habitual emotion–magnitude rule → altered judgment of O2 despite invariant representation.
Another’s misery compared with self → augmented apparent self-condition → pleasure.
Another’s enjoyment compared with self → diminished apparent self-condition → pain → envy.
Anticipated misery of another → anticipated comparative elevation of self → desire to produce misery → malice.
Strong relation → sustained comparison and impression interaction; broken relation → affective separation.
Former comparative advantage A0 → reduced advantage A1 → comparison A1<A0 → lost pleasure converted into pain.
Same object/different estimate → attendant-emotion hypothesis → contrast amplification → habitual projection of altered emotion onto the object.
Comparative self-estimation → inverse response to others’ fortunes → envy/malice distinction → proximity and relation as affective gates → general law of impression transition.
Malice and envy are reclassified from responses to moral injury as products of comparative self-estimation.
Evaluative change is relocated from the object or idea to its attendant impression.
Social hierarchy is redrawn through associative proximity rather than absolute rank alone.
Distance becomes an affective mechanism capable of disabling comparison.
Direct valence and comparative valence become distinct: what is painful in itself may become pleasurable through contrast.
Personal envy, political rivalry, aesthetic consistency, and passion-conflict become instances of one relation-mediated transition law.
Surface: malice and envy are differentiated by whether another’s misery is already present or deliberately sought for comparative pleasure.
Structural: comparison, emotional succession, habitual attribution, and associative relation jointly produce altered judgments and passions.
Metastrategic: explanation shifts from rational or moral appraisal to the formation, severance, and manipulation of comparative relations.
Ontological/Temporal: ideas carry attendant impressions whose effects depend on sequence, preserved transition, present comparison, and remembered prior condition.
CH_THN_SVME:A1–CH_THN_SVME:A12 are sufficient to reconstruct the perceptual mechanism, passion differentiation, and relational boundary.
The relative activation of direct survey and comparative survey remains underdetermined.
The kinds and degrees of relation required for effective comparison lack a formal threshold.
The structure is internally coherent if proportional attendant emotion and habitual effect-to-cause attribution are granted.
The strongest explanatory linkage is the relation-conditioned transfer from stable representation to variable affective judgment.
The extension from magnitude and number to virtue, wealth, happiness, and misery depends on analogical generalization.
The inference from absent relation preventing an effect establishes relation as contributory or necessary, not independently sufficient.
The self-affliction cases require the auxiliary predominance principle rather than following from comparison alone.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from comparative perception through reverse affect to the general associative law.

identity.title: Sect. VIII Of Malice And Envy

units.title: Sect. XII Of The Love And Hatred Of Animals

items.text: Problem: whether the preceding causal system of love and hatred extends beyond humanity.
Thesis: animal affections arise from simple, species-general principles continuous with those governing human passions.
Argument type: comparative, empirical, and confirmatory.
Movement: reduced animal reflection → isolation of sensible causes → qualified relational causes → instinct → sympathy → comparative passion prevalence.
Cognitive demand determines which affective mechanisms operate strongly in animals.
The recurrence of the predicted passions under reduced cognition corroborates the foregoing system.
Love and hatred are common to the whole sensitive creation.
The operative causes of love and hatred require no force of reflection or penetration.
The springs governing love and hatred are not peculiar to humanity or any single animal species.
Animals are only weakly susceptible to pleasures and pains of imagination.
Animals judge affective objects by the sensible good or evil those objects produce.
Animal love is not restricted to members of the animal’s own species.
The affective force of relation is limited by the animal’s capacity to trace relations.
Cognitively obvious associative relations generate affection in animals.
Parental affection toward offspring arises from a peculiar instinct.
Sympathy communicates passions among animals without knowledge of the initiating cause.
Animals possess a sense of one another’s pain and pleasure.
Sympathetic conjunction intensifies animal passion.
Envy and malice require less thought and imagination than pity.
Love and hatred are not exclusively human passions.
Their production does not require reflective penetration.
Animal love is not bounded by identity of species.
Animal affection is not governed primarily by imagined goods and evils.
Relation is not wholly absent from animal affection, though its influence is cognitively restricted.
Parental affection is not reduced to acquired benefit or traced relation.
Sympathy does not require cognition of the original cause of a passion.
Restraint toward companions is not explained solely by fear of retaliation.
Pity is not assumed to be more primitive or prevalent than envy and malice.
Benefits generate animal love and injuries generate animal hatred.
Relation is weaker in animals than in humans but remains effective through acquaintance, resemblance, and other obvious associations.
Species identity is neither a necessary nor sufficient boundary for an animal’s objects of affection.
Parental attachment constitutes an instinctive branch distinct from ordinary sensible and associative causation.
Passions can organize animal social conduct without shared knowledge of their originating object.
Collective animation exceeds isolated passion when animals act in sympathetic conjunction.
Envy and malice may be more common among animals than pity because their cognitive threshold is lower.
The persistence of love, hatred, and sympathy under diminished reflection supports their derivation from simple, species-general springs.
Animal psychology functions as a cognitive-subtraction test: mechanisms surviving reduced reflection cannot depend essentially on reflective human faculties.
Affective universality is compatible with unequal cognitive complexity because common passions can be produced through differently available channels.
The chapter treats lower cognitive cost as a condition of wider animal prevalence among passions.
Social intensification of affect precedes and exceeds conscious representation of its causal origin.
The unity of the system lies in species-general springs rather than in a single uniform route of affective production.
Reflective self-consciousness cannot be a necessary condition of love and hatred.
Species-specific human faculties cannot constitute the ultimate source of the passions shared with animals.
Abstract relation-tracing cannot be required for every form of associative attachment.
Affective communication cannot depend on propositional knowledge of what caused the communicated passion.
Animal social restraint cannot be exhausted by retaliation avoidance if it evidences sensitivity to another’s pain.
A wholly acquired or associative account cannot explain parental affection if peculiar instinct is irreducible.
Greater moral valuation cannot be assumed to entail greater natural prevalence; pity may be rarer because it is cognitively costlier.
An ontological rupture between human and animal affective life is foreclosed.
Direct animal self-testimony is unavailable; behavioral analogy must bear the attribution of internal passion.
Conscious causal representation is unavailable as the universal ground of social affect.
A unitary reduction of affection to sensible reward and injury is foreclosed by relation, instinct, and sympathy.
Species-general causes + cognitive simplicity → prediction of animal applicability.
Reduced reflection and imagination → isolation of sensible affective causation.
Sensible good or benefit → love; sensible evil or injury → hatred.
Limited relation-tracing + obvious association → restricted relational affection.
Parent–offspring configuration → instinctive affection.
Perceived passion or suffering → sympathetic communication → coordinated or intensified affect.
Reduced imaginative demand → greater probable prevalence of envy and malice relative to pity.
Convergence of animal mechanisms with prior predictions → confirmation of the foregoing system.

Foregoing causal system → animal test case → cognitive restriction → sensible causation → qualified association and instinct → sympathetic transmission → cognitive-cost comparison → systemic corroboration.
The human–animal opposition is redrawn as continuity of affective mechanism with variation in cognitive degree.
Species membership ceases to define the possible object-range of love.
Animal affection is reclassified into sensible, associative, instinctive, and sympathetic causal channels.
Relation becomes cognitively graded rather than simply present or absent.
Collective animal animation becomes visible as transmitted and amplified passion rather than mere aggregation.
Comparative prevalence among passions becomes explicable through differing demands on thought and imagination.
Surface: animals exhibit love, hatred, sympathy, envy, malice, and sensitivity to one another’s suffering.
Structural: sensible effects, obvious associations, instinct, and sympathetic transmission form distinct affective mechanisms.
Metastrategic: animal conduct tests whether the preceding theory depends on specifically human reflection.
Ontological: sensitive life forms a continuous affective domain across species.
Epistemic: internal animal passions are inferred from patterned conduct and analogy with human experience.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s movement from cross-species continuity to confirmation of the prior system.
The precise mechanisms converting sensible good, resemblance, and communicated emotion into affection remain underdetermined.
The structure is coherent only if patterned animal conduct warrants attribution of passions analogous to human passions.
The argument is strongest where reduced animal reflection independently tests the claimed simplicity of affective causes.
The restriction of animal judgment to sensible good and evil is not explicitly reconciled with acquaintance and resemblance as additional causes.
Peculiar parental instinct introduces a causal exception without integration into the foregoing system.
Cross-species preference and conspecific preference are both asserted, but the conditions governing their relative strength remain unspecified.
Human analogy explains animal sympathy while animal sympathy confirms the human system, creating a partially reciprocal evidential structure.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if its universal claims are retained despite their compression from selective observations.

identity.title: Sect. XII Of The Love And Hatred Of Animals

units.title: Sect. V Of The Effects Of Custom

items.text: The problem is to explain how custom can intensify or diminish passion and reverse pleasure and pain.
All effects of custom are reduced to facility and subsequent inclination.
The argument is a causal-psychological reduction through variations in mental motion.
Unfamiliarity produces difficulty, agitation, novelty, and amplified passion.
Repetition removes novelty and produces tranquillity before generating pleasurable facility.
Moderate facility can reconcile the mind to pain, whereas excessive facility destroys interest and can reverse pleasure.
Facility and inclination jointly weaken passive habits while strengthening active habits.
Facility and inclination exhaust the original effects of custom.
Repetition first produces facility in action or conception.
Repetition subsequently produces inclination toward the repeated action.
Unaccustomed action or conception encounters resistance from unpliable faculties.
Mental resistance excites the spirits and generates the emotions of novelty.
Moderate enlivening of the mind is pleasurable.
An emotion attending a passion is readily converted into and augments that passion.
Repetition extinguishes novelty, agitation, and their amplification of passion.
Moderate facility produces pleasure.
The pleasure of facility consists in orderly motion rather than agitated motion.
Excessive facility renders mental action faint, languid, and unable to sustain interest.
Custom-induced aversion ordinarily requires an object naturally attended by emotion.
Extinction of an expected agreeable emotion disposes the mind toward the opposite affection.
An entirely disagreeable action cannot become an object of inclination.
Facility weakens passive habits by rendering the motion of the spirits faint.
Active performance supplies independent support to the spirits.
Customary inclination adds force to active performance.
Custom does not affect passion monotonically.
The pleasure of novelty is not the pleasure of facility.
Orderly facility does not augment painful affection as novelty-agitation does.
Frequent repetition does not ordinarily make affectively neutral objects disagreeable.
Custom cannot create inclination toward what remains entirely disagreeable.
Active and passive habits are not strengthened or weakened by the same mechanism.
Novel objects produce more pleasure or pain than their intrinsic affective character supplies.
Early repetition diminishes passion by removing the agitation that had amplified it.
Moderate facility can convert initial harshness into relish because its pleasure counteracts rather than inflames pain.
Excessive repetition can convert pleasure into pain by extinguishing the emotion required to sustain interest.
Affectively neutral repeated objects normally remain non-aversive because custom has no natural emotion to destroy.
Custom produces inclination only where residual disagreeability does not amount to complete repugnance.
Passive habits decline under repetition, while active habits acquire additional force.
The affective trajectory of repetition is non-linear: amplification gives way to tranquillity, pleasure, languor, and possible reversal.
Experienced valence depends on the history and degree of encounter, not solely on the object’s natural affective character.
Custom operates through successive regimes rather than through cumulative reinforcement alone.
Difficulty and facility are affectively reversible: either can support or weaken the mind according to degree and mode of operation.
Repetition redistributes affective force between passive receptivity and active tendency rather than merely increasing familiarity.
Intrinsic pleasure or pain cannot by itself determine the experienced strength or direction of passion.
Facility cannot be inherently pleasurable, because its excess must be capable of producing languor and aversion.
Diminished excitation cannot have a uniform effect across passive reception and active performance.
Repetition cannot explain its own effects without distinctions of degree, affective endowment, and activity type.
A fixed subject-object relation of affect, insulated from temporal repetition, is unavailable.
A single continuous law by which increasing custom always increases or always decreases passion is foreclosed.
Custom is denied unlimited transformative power by the irreducible boundary of complete disagreeability.
Custom/repetition → facility + subsequent inclination.
Unfamiliarity → resistance → excitation → novelty-pleasure → conversion into the predominant passion → affective amplification.
Repetition → novelty-decay → tranquillity → moderate facility → orderly motion → pleasure → possible pain-to-pleasure reversal.
Continued repetition → excessive facility → faintness and languor → destruction of sustaining emotion → indifference → possible opposite affection.
Inclination + complete disagreeability → blocked tendency; inclination + tolerable action → strengthened tendency.
Passive mode + facility → weakened habit; active mode + self-supported spirits + inclination → strengthened habit.

Opposed effects of custom → reduction to facility and inclination → novelty-agitation mechanism → repetition and tranquillity → moderate facility and relish → excessive facility and affective reversal.
Inclination effect → disagreeability boundary → active/passive distinction → active strengthening and passive weakening.
Repetition is reclassified from a uniform influence into a threshold-dependent process with contrary phases.
Affective force is divided between the object’s natural valence and the mental motion attending its apprehension.
Novelty and familiarity cease to be simple opposites and become distinct regimes of excitation and order.
Habit is divided into passive diminution and active reinforcement.
Pleasure and pain become reversible outcomes of altered mental operation rather than fixed responses to objects.
Surface: Custom increases, diminishes, and reverses passions while differentiating active from passive habits.
Structural: Resistance, agitation, orderly motion, languor, and tendency mediate custom’s effects.
Metastrategic: Diverse and apparently contradictory phenomena are reduced to two primary operations governed by degree and mode.
Ontological/Temporal: Affect is a path-dependent process whose present force is constituted by successive encounters.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s principal causal sequence.
The boundary between moderate and excessive facility remains quantitatively undetermined.
The language of the spirits supplies a causal vocabulary without a fully specified mechanism.
The transition from acquired facility to inclination is asserted more strongly than it is derived.
The structure is strongest where one graded mechanism explains both affective reconciliation and affective exhaustion.
The active/passive divergence depends on the compressed claim that active performance supports its own excitation.
The scope boundary between pain convertible by facility and complete disagreeability resistant to inclination remains unresolved.
The system is internally coherent if attendant-emotion conversion and degree-sensitive facility are granted.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from dual-effect reduction through facility’s phases to the final habit bifurcation.

identity.title: Sect. V Of The Effects Of Custom

units.title: Sect. X Of Curiosity, Or The Love Of Truth

items.text: Problem: explain why truth motivates inquiry when truth and assurance alone do not reliably produce pleasure.
Thesis: scientific curiosity is generated by qualified acts of discovery, not by truth considered intrinsically.
Argument type: differential psychological genealogy reinforced by cross-domain analogy.
Active inquiry derives its principal pleasure from exercised understanding, while perceived importance fixes attention and success completes the pursuit.
Passion originating in pursuit transfers affective concern to the pursued end.
Non-investigative curiosity has a distinct source: belief vivifies and stabilizes an engaging idea, relieving the pain of doubt.
Movement: intrinsic-truth hypothesis → differential test → composite pursuit mechanism → analogical validation → bifurcation of curiosity.
Equal truth and equal assurance can yield unequal pleasure.
Exercised genius and understanding in difficult discovery are the principal source of scientific pleasure.
Attention is necessary for cognitive exercise to produce satisfaction.
Perceived importance functions as a condition for fixing attention.
Perceived importance contributes little direct pleasure independently of its effect on attention.
Imagined utility can operate through faint sympathy without genuine concern for its beneficiaries.
Some success in attaining the pursued end is required to complete the pleasure of inquiry.
Passion originating in action and pursuit naturally produces derivative concern for the related end.
The active-inquiry mechanism applies both to abstract relations and to real connections and existence.
Non-investigative curiosity arises from a principle distinct from exercised inquiry.
Belief vivifies an idea in the imagination.
Belief fixes an idea against hesitation and uncertainty.
A vivid idea gives pleasure by affecting the imagination like a moderate passion.
Doubt produces pain by rapidly varying thought among competing ideas.
Instability generates curiosity when interest, relation, greatness, or novelty makes an idea sufficiently forceful and proximate.
Truth is not desired merely as truth.
Demonstrative superiority or increased assurance is not sufficient to increase epistemic pleasure.
Objective difficulty is not valuable when knowledge is acquired without cognitive exertion.
Exercised understanding alone is not sufficient without attention-fixing importance and some success.
A requirement that inquiry appear publicly useful does not establish public spirit in the inquirer.
Utility is not the primary direct passion sustaining scientific inquiry.
Concern for an end need not precede the activity directed toward it.
Informational curiosity is not reducible to self-interest or active study.
Curiosity attaches neither to every fact nor exclusively to facts of practical interest.
Variations in epistemic pleasure must be attributed to qualities of discovery rather than to correctness or certainty alone.
Scientific enjoyment requires the conjunction of demanding cognitive activity, engaged attention, and partial attainment.
A philosopher can require belief in public utility while remaining indifferent to the public good because imagined sympathy supplies attention rather than a terminal motive.
Error and disappointment become painful even when the pursued end was initially indifferent.
Philosophy, hunting, and gaming instantiate a common architecture in which a represented stake activates attention and difficult pursuit generates concern.
The affective structure of active inquiry remains constant across mathematical, moral, political, and natural-philosophical objects.
Non-investigative curiosity seeks a vivid and settled conception when an already engaging idea remains unstable.
Familiarity increases curiosity by strengthening relation and ideational force, while fading representation extinguishes it.
Conditions can be motivationally indispensable without being original sources of pleasure: importance engages attention, and success consummates an independently generated pursuit.

Epistemic motivation forms a recursive circuit: represented importance fixes attention → cognitive activity becomes pleasurable → concern transfers to the end → success and error acquire affective force.
Apparently disinterested inquiry can arise without benevolence or material interest through the conjunction of imaginative sympathy and exercised understanding.
Truth functions affectively in two distinct ways: as the endpoint of active achievement and as the content of stabilizing belief.
Operational uncertainty can intensify active pursuit, while doxastic vacillation produces pain and demands closure.
Epistemic value within the system depends less on an object considered alone than on its relation to effort, attention, imagination, and temporal stability.
Epistemic motivation cannot transparently track truth as an intrinsic good.
Cognition cannot be affectively self-sufficient or independent of attention.
Objective utility cannot be identical with subjective concern.
Every passion cannot originate in the antecedent value of its end.
Belief cannot be treated as merely representational; it modifies pleasure, pain, and ideational stability.
Curiosity cannot be determined by informational content alone, independently of relation, novelty, familiarity, and memory.
The system excludes an autonomous, purely truth-directed intellect.
The singular name “love of truth” does not correspond to a single causal passion.
No object-side property of truth guarantees attention, pleasure, or pursuit.
The account of informational curiosity contains no explicit truth-sensitive discriminator between true belief and a false belief that equally vivifies and fixes an idea.
A normative reason why truth ought to be pursued remains absent; the system supplies an affective genealogy rather than an epistemic justification.
Truth and assurance held constant + pleasure varied by mode of attainment → truth-as-such excluded as sufficient cause.
Perceived utility → faint imaginative sympathy → attention fixed; difficulty → exercised understanding; attention × exercise × success → scientific pleasure.
Pleasure in pursuit → relational transfer of passion → acquired concern for end → pain at error or failure.
Philosophy / hunting / gaming → represented stake + demanding pursuit → conjoint effect unavailable from either factor alone.
Abstract relations or real existence → same active-inquiry architecture → general scientific curiosity.
Interest, relation, greatness, or novelty → forceful unstable idea → doubt and painful alternation → demand for belief → vivification + fixation → pleasure and relief.

Neglected passion → division of truth → intrinsic-truth explanation falsified → mental exercise identified → importance reclassified as attentional support → success added → concern transferred to the end → analogical confirmation → extension across sciences → separate informational curiosity diagnosed.
Curiosity → active discovery branch: exertion + attention + success → pleasure; informational branch: ideational force + instability → painful doubt → stabilizing belief.
Truth is reclassified from an intrinsically desired object into an endpoint mediated by affective and cognitive operations.
Utility is reclassified from terminal motive to imaginative support for attention.
Disinterested inquiry becomes intelligible without attribution of benevolence or material self-interest.
Philosophy, hunting, and gaming become structurally comparable as stake-mediated pursuits.
Curiosity divides into active challenge-seeking and passive uncertainty-relief.
Belief becomes visible as an affective operation of vivification and stabilization, not merely assent to content.
Surface — Variable pleasure in scientific discovery and the desire to know otherwise irrelevant facts.
Structural — Attention mediates between represented importance and pleasurable cognitive exertion; belief mediates between unstable ideas and affective relief.
Metastrategic — The argument decomposes motivation into principal source, enabling condition, completion condition, and acquired end-concern.
Ontological/Temporal — The mind is treated as a succession of ideas whose vivacity, fixation, rapid alteration, and relational transfer generate passions over time.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct both the active-inquiry mechanism and the distinct informational-curiosity mechanism.
Reconstruction depends on prior theories of belief, sympathy, attention, and the relational transfer of passions.
The structure is coherent where it distinguishes original pleasure from attentional conditions and acquired concern for ends.
Its strongest operation is the controlled separation of truth and assurance from cognitive exertion.
The role of faint sympathy is compressed: its capacity to support attention without genuine concern is asserted more than generated.
The informational branch explains desire for settled belief more directly than desire for truth.
The opposed valences of pursuit-uncertainty and belief-instability remain differentiated but not fully unified.
Reconstruction preserves the argument only if the final bifurcation of curiosity is retained rather than reduced to a single truth-drive.

identity.title: Sect. X Of Curiosity, Or The Love Of Truth

units.title: Part II Of Justice And Injustice

items.text: The problem is to explain both the establishment of justice and the subsequent attribution of moral virtue to its observance.
Justice is an artificial but necessary and non-arbitrary virtue generated by human convention under determinate social conditions.
The argument is eliminative, genealogical, functional, and sentimentalist.
Semantic disambiguation of nature leads to an affective criterion of morality, which leads to the priority of motive over action.
The circularity of making regard for justice its own first motive forces the elimination of self-love, public benevolence, and private benevolence as original motives.
Human weakness, partial affection, transferable scarcity, and social dependence generate a reciprocal convention stabilizing possession.
Common interest generates observance; sympathy with public interest generates moral approval; education, reputation, and government reinforce the result.
Virtue is marked by satisfaction and vice by uneasiness produced under general contemplation.
Moral merit belongs ultimately to the motive signified by an action.
The first virtuous motive for an action must precede and differ from regard for that action’s morality.
Standards of duty track the ordinary force and direction of passions in human nature.
Human affection ordinarily prioritizes self, relations, acquaintances, and strangers in descending order.
Society is necessary to compensate human weakness and secure the satisfaction of human wants.
External goods are scarce relative to desire, transferable, and insecure against appropriation.
Uncultivated moral judgment conforms to natural partiality rather than correcting it.
Acquisitive self-interest can be restrained only by its reflective redirection toward the greater advantages of social preservation.
Stability of possession arises through mutually known and conditionally reciprocal resolutions grounded in common interest.
Convention does not depend upon a prior promise.
Convention acquires force gradually through repeated experience and increasing confidence in reciprocal conduct.
Justice, injustice, right, and obligation arise only after possession has been stabilized by convention.
Property is a moral relation constituted by the laws of justice.
The whole scheme of justice is socially and individually advantageous even when particular just acts are harmful.
Interest in preserving the general scheme supplies the natural obligation to justice.
Sympathy with public interest supplies the moral approbation of justice.
The rules of justice are artificial without being arbitrary because their invention is necessary and obvious under human circumstances.
Natural and unnatural do not mark the boundary between virtue and vice.
The external performance is not itself the bearer of moral merit.
Regard for the justice of an action cannot be that action’s first virtuous motive.
Justice is not an innate passion capable of originally producing equitable conduct.
Unrestrained private interest is not a universal motive to honest action.
An affection for humanity merely as humanity is not an operative universal passion.
Private benevolence cannot ground invariant property rights or obligations.
Direct concern for public interest is not the original ordinary motive of just conduct.
Justice is not founded upon eternal and immutable relations of ideas discovered by reason.
Convention is not a promise and cannot be founded upon promises.
Property, right, and obligation do not exist naturally before justice.
Justice is not required under universal benevolence or complete abundance.
The solitary state of nature is not an actual historical condition.
Artificiality does not entail arbitrariness.
Political inculcation is not the sole cause of moral distinctions.
The absence of property before convention does not mean that violating another’s property was permissible; the relevant property relation did not yet exist.
Duty can secondarily motivate an action only because an antecedent natural motive has already made that kind of action morally intelligible.
A natural sense of justice cannot be the first cause of just conduct; justice becomes intelligible only after the convention it evaluates.
Partial generosity both forms close associations and generates conflict between those associations.
Social instability arises from the conjunction of partial affection with scarce and transferable goods, not from either condition alone.
Immediate self-interest threatens society, while reflected self-interest preserves society by accepting reciprocal restraint.
Non-promissory convention avoids regress by grounding coordination in reciprocal expectations rather than antecedent obligation.
Justice and property are co-generated; property cannot be invoked to explain the origin of justice.
Removing either confined generosity or scarcity removes the functional conditions that make justice necessary.
The justice of a particular act is determined by its place within a beneficial general scheme rather than by its isolated consequences.
Compliance precedes moralization: interest first establishes observance, and sympathy later converts observance into virtue.
As society expands and direct awareness of common interest weakens, sympathy and general rules preserve moral disapproval of injustice.
Political rhetoric can extend an existing moral sentiment but cannot create moral intelligibility without natural affective materials.
Education and reputation internalize established conventions as durable sentiments of honor.
A pre-conventional condition contains neither justice nor injustice because it contains no moral relation of property.
Normative order emerges from non-moral coordination: interested restraint produces convention, and convention becomes morally charged through sympathy.
The universality of justice is rule-general and reciprocal rather than metaphysical or consequence-sensitive at the level of individual acts.
Property and right are socially constituted relations sustained by stabilized expectations rather than intrinsic features of persons or objects.
The same partial interest that generates social conflict also supplies the only passion capable of resolving it when redirected by understanding.
Justice is conditionally necessary: contingent relative to scarcity and limited generosity, yet effectively inseparable from humanity while those conditions persist.
Artificial rules become second-nature through sympathy, custom, education, public judgment, and reputational interest.
Justice converts long-range systemic advantage into stable obligations capable of overriding contrary local advantage.
Moral and institutional emergence are temporally ordered but mutually reinforcing once established: convention enables approval, and approval stabilizes convention.
A moral predicate cannot generate the first passion that makes its own application possible.
Natural impartial benevolence cannot be sufficiently strong or general to stabilize possession.
Property cannot be a pre-institutional relation waiting merely to be recognized.
Reason cannot independently create concern, motivation, or moral obligation from relations of ideas.
The consequences of isolated acts cannot determine the justice of those acts independently of general rules.
Neither a sovereign command nor an antecedent promise is necessary for conventions to emerge.
The genealogy of society does not require an actual period of solitary human existence.
Stable restraint cannot persist without confidence that others will regulate their conduct by the same rule.
Justice occupies the absence of a direct natural route from partial passion to impartial social order.
Property occupies the absence of natural stability in scarce and transferable possessions.
Moral approbation occupies the gap between interested compliance and disinterested evaluation.
The system excludes self-grounding normativity: every moral obligation depends upon antecedent passions, interests, and sentiments.
Stable property forecloses case-by-case redistribution according to immediate merit, benevolence, need, or public advantage.
The system contains no primordial rights-bearing individual prior to convention; the pre-social subject lacks the relations that would make such rights intelligible.
Naturalness disambiguated → morality detached from nature/unnature classification → pleasure and uneasiness installed as evaluative criteria.
Action treated as sign → motive identified as moral object → regard for morality rejected as first motive.
Candidate natural motives tested → private interest, public benevolence, private benevolence, and universal humanity eliminated → artificial origin required.
Human wants and weakness → sexual and familial association → habit-mediated recognition of social advantage.
Partial affection + scarce transferable goods → unstable possession → threat to socially necessary cooperation.
Reflection on long-range interest → redirection of acquisitive passion → reciprocal rule of abstinence.
Mutual expression of conditional restraint → non-promissory convention → repeated experience → stable expectation.
Stable possession → justice and injustice → property, right, and obligation.
Advantage of the whole scheme → interested observance → sympathy with public effects → moral approval.
Moral approval → education, political reinforcement, and reputation → internalized probity → increased institutional stability.
Ambiguity of nature → affective moral criterion → priority of motive → prohibition of motivational circularity.
Failure of natural motives → anthropological and material diagnosis → reflected self-interest → reciprocal convention → artificial justice.
Stability of possession → property and obligation → systemic advantage → sympathetic approval → reinforced moral practice.
The natural/artificial distinction replaces the natural/unnatural distinction as the relevant classification of justice.
The primary object of moral judgment shifts from external action to motivating passion.
Justice is reclassified from an innate virtue into a convention-dependent practice subsequently moralized.
Self-interest is divided into an impulsive form destructive of society and a reflective form capable of sustaining it.
Property shifts from being the presumed ground of justice to being an effect of justice.
Utility shifts from the isolated act to the coordinated system of general rules.
Convention becomes visible as decentralized reciprocal coordination rather than promise, command, or explicit contract.
The state of nature shifts from historical origin to analytical fiction produced by separating passions from understanding.
Moral obligation is separated from natural obligation: sympathy explains approval, while interest explains initial observance.
Surface: Justice is tested as a natural or artificial virtue, and its rules and moral valuation are assigned distinct origins.
Structural: Partial affection, scarcity, transferability, reciprocal expectation, general rules, and social reinforcement constitute the mechanism of justice.
Metastrategic: Explanation must proceed from motive and convention to property and obligation, prohibiting the use of established moral categories to explain their own genesis.

Ontological/Temporal: Property and right are emergent relations formed gradually through coordinated expectations; their contingency coexists with their practical inseparability from enduring human conditions.
CH_THN_PIJI:A1–CH_THN_PIJI:A18 are sufficient to reconstruct the argument’s semantic, motivational, genealogical, institutional, and sentimental stages.
The structure is coherent only if the establishment of rules, interested observance, and moral approbation remain distinct explanatory moments.
The strongest transition is from motivational circularity and failed natural motives to reciprocal convention grounded in reflected interest.
The shift from rejected private interest to accepted common interest depends upon distinguishing immediate unilateral gain from conditional systemic advantage.
The co-generation of justice and property risks circularity unless physical possession is kept distinct from morally constituted property.
The account of moral obligation remains underdetermined because the full mechanism of sympathy and the natural virtues is explicitly deferred.
General-rule utility explains adherence despite harmful particular acts but leaves the limits, revision, and exception conditions of those rules unresolved.
The artificial-versus-natural tension is contained by assigning different senses to nature, but the resolution depends upon controlled semantic variation.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the movement from conceptual clearing through genealogy to moral internalization.

identity.title: Part II Of Justice And Injustice

units.title: Sect. III Of The Rules Which Determine Property

items.text: Problem: the necessary convention of stable possession does not determine which goods belong to which persons.
Thesis: particular assignments require general, society-wide rules insulated from case-specific judgments of fitness or utility.
General utility necessitates determinate property, while imagination principally selects the relations through which titles are assigned.
Argument type: genealogical reconstruction joined to psychological and jurisprudential diagnosis.
Instability of possession → convention of stability → initial assignment by present possession → restriction of that founding rule.
Established society differentiates acquisition into occupation, prescription, accession, and succession.
Gradual relations and conflicting criteria defeat complete natural determination, requiring municipal law to close residual disputes.
Stable possession is necessary to human society.
The general rule of stable possession cannot by itself assign particular goods to particular persons.
Particular fitness or utility is too contestable and partial to serve as a peaceful rule of property.
Property assignments must be governed by general and inflexible rules.
Property is constant possession secured by social rules, not a real quality inhering in objects.
The imagination tends to complete an existing relation between objects by adding further resembling relations.
General utility requires determinate settlement, while imagination principally fixes the specific forms of property rules.
At society’s first formation, property is assigned to the present possessor.
The rule favoring present possession is valid only for initial social settlement.
After society is established, occupation attaches property to first possession.
Possession consists in a causal power to use, alter, move, or destroy an object.
Possessory power varies by degrees of probability and therefore lacks universally precise boundaries.
Prescription transfers title toward long and uninterrupted present possession as temporal distance weakens the first possessor’s relation.
Accession extends ownership from a principal object to an intimately connected and inferior object.
Municipal law must determine cases in which natural criteria of relation and comparative importance remain balanced or contradictory.
Succession directs property toward near relations through presumed consent and public interest, reinforced by associative relation.
Property is not to be distributed through case-by-case judgments of personal fitness.
Justice does not vary title according to the owner’s character, need, or effective use.
Property is not an intrinsic or perceptible feature of the owned object.
Present possession does not remain a perpetual source of title after society has been established.
Occupation is not grounded in a literal incorporation of labor into an object.
Possession is not reducible to immediate physical contact.
Reason and public interest do not supply exact boundaries for every possessory dispute.
Mere connection does not produce accession symmetrically; the principal draws the inferior, not the inferior the principal.
Natural associative principles do not constitute a complete code for deciding compound and borderline cases.
Justice must disregard whether property is useful to its owner because individualized adjustment would restore the contention that stability was instituted to prevent.
Present possession becomes the founding title because custom strengthens attachment and because present possession resembles the constant possession constituted as property.
Permanent adherence to present possession would authorize seizure and exclude restitution.
Occupation supplies the default title to previously unassigned goods because rejecting first possession leaves no non-arbitrary basis for preferring a later possession.
The extent of possession varies with imaginative boundedness, salience, and proportionality between possessor and object.
