Time produces prescription by changing the influence of relations upon sentiment, not by producing a new real feature in the object.
Accession can confer title before actual possession because ownership travels through an established chain of relations.
The apparent ease of transition from a small object to a great one does not make the great object an accession; the compound whole is imaginatively dominated by its most considerable part.
When inseparable properties are combined, the whole tends toward the proprietor of the most considerable part; when components remain distinguishable, distinct or proportional claims persist.
Succession can follow the line from which goods originated even when neither presumed consent nor public interest specifies that division.
Property is generated by a dual mechanism: utility creates the demand for settled rules, while imagination supplies their concrete relational form.

The property regime is temporally layered: present possession governs founding, occupation governs first acquisition, prescription revises obscured origins, accession extends existing title, and succession resolves death-created vacancy.
Legal determinacy is practical closure rather than the discovery of an independently precise natural boundary.
A title can change without any corresponding real alteration in its object because property depends upon socially stabilized sentiment and relation.
Juridical attribution follows salience, continuity, proximity, scale, and associative ease rather than distributive optimality.
Municipal rules may be mutually inconsistent at the level of principle while remaining systemically necessary as devices for terminating controversy.
The system requires pre-social property rights independent of convention to be false.
The system requires public utility alone to be incapable of deriving every particular title.
The system requires historical facts not to retain unchanged psychological force across temporal distance.
The system requires durability, value, extent, visibility, and independence not to form a universally commensurable hierarchy.
The usefulness of a natural-seeming property rule does not entail its universal or permanent validity.
Social peace and continuously revised allocation by individual suitability cannot operate as coequal governing principles.
“Natural” property rules cannot mean intrinsic rights antecedent to society; they depend upon natural psychological propensities operating within convention.
No final adjudicative measure exists beneath convention, imagination, and positive legal stipulation.
No property bond remains as an objective feature once social recognition, law, and sentiment are removed.
Stable justice forecloses continuous correction of ownership according to need, merit, or optimal use.
Complete recovery of original title is unavailable as a permanent foundation of present ownership.
The system contains no natural procedure capable of eliminating every borderline dispute without authoritative closure.
Changeable possession → insecurity and conflict → convention of stable possession.
General stability → unresolved allocation problem → demand for modifying rules.
Case-specific fitness → controversy and partiality → rejection in favor of general rules.
Antecedent person-object relation + associative completion + social security → property relation.
Initial social settlement → present possession + custom + resemblance → founding title.
Established society → rejection of perpetual present-possession title → differentiated acquisition rules.
Unassigned object → first possessory power → occupation → title.
Obscured original title + prolonged current possession → weakened first relation + strengthened present relation → prescription.
Owned principal + intimate inferior connection → imaginative union → accession.
Death-created vacancy + kinship association + presumed consent and public interest → succession.
Graded relation or conflicting salience criteria → natural indeterminacy → municipal stipulation → terminated dispute.

Necessary stability → allocation gap → rejection of particular utility → general-rule requirement → imaginative attachment to antecedent relations → founding title by present possession → restriction of that title → occupation, prescription, accession, and succession → municipal closure of residual indeterminacy.
Property is reclassified from an inherent object-quality into a socially secured moral relation.
General utility and particular title-generation are separated: utility explains why settlement is needed, while imagination explains how goods become connected to persons.
The natural/artificial opposition is reorganized: artificial conventions acquire their form through natural habits of association.
Spatial proximity, causal power, temporal duration, comparative scale, and kinship become juridically productive relations.
Occupation, prescription, accession, and succession become variants of one mechanism: the extension or redistribution of property through antecedent relations.
Municipal law is reclassified from discovery of natural right to authoritative completion of naturally underdetermined judgments.
Surface: the argument determines the recognized sources by which particular goods become assigned to particular persons.
Structural: conventions transform unstable possession into a rule-governed property regime whose residual ambiguities are closed by municipal law.
Metastrategic: jurisprudential explanation shifts from personal fitness and abstract reason toward the interaction of public utility, imagination, and authoritative settlement.
Ontological/Temporal: property has no object-inherent reality, and title changes as time alters the force of relations upon sentiment rather than the object itself.
CH_THN_SIRW:A1 through CH_THN_SIRW:A16 are sufficient to reconstruct the allocation problem, the dual explanatory mechanism, and the four established titles.
The relative causal weight of public utility and imagination remains explicitly underdetermined.
The thresholds of possession, temporal prescription, inferiority, and comparative importance remain naturally indeterminate.
The structure is coherent once founding rules are distinguished from rules governing an established society.
The strongest mechanism is the division between utility’s demand for determinate settlement and imagination’s production of particular relational titles.
The argument depends on analogy and comparative psychological plausibility when identifying imagination as the predominant cause.
Its principal tension is that inflexible legal rules are generated from fluid, context-sensitive, and sometimes contradictory relations.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from general stability through differentiated titles to the necessity of municipal closure.

identity.title: Sect. III Of The Rules Which Determine Property

units.title: Sect. VI Some Farther Reflections Concerning Justice And Injustice

items.text: Problem: whether justice and its juridical relations precede convention or are constituted by it.
Thesis: justice is an artificial virtue generated by human convention rather than an original natural principle.
Argument type: reconstructive genealogy joined to conceptual, modal, and motivational reductio.
Presumed antecedence of property → analysis of property → dependence of property upon justice.
Gradable natural morality → non-gradable juridical relations → exclusion of justice from natural virtue.
Variable natural motives → socially destructive particular judgment → institution of universal and inflexible rules.
Coordinated interest → conventional observance → social utility → subsequent moral approval.
Human well-being requires society.
Social peace and security require strict observance of stability of possession, consensual transfer, and performance of promises.
Self-love is the originating passion of the laws of justice.
The self-love of different persons is naturally conflictual.
Convention adjusts conflicting interests into a common system of conduct.
Property consists in the influence of object-person relations upon minds and actions as duties.
Duties of justice constitute property; property does not antecedently constitute justice.
Rules determining property, right, and obligation display contrivance through multiplicity, legal mutability, and orientation toward civil utility.
Natural moral qualities pass into one another by imperceptible degrees.
Property, right, and obligation are integral rather than gradable within their stipulated scope.
Property, right, and obligation depend upon justice and injustice for their variations.
Natural moral conduct inherits the particularity and variability of its motivating passions.
The laws of justice are universal and inflexible.
Unregulated particular judgment, under avidity and partiality, produces social disorder.
Convention institutes invariant rules to prevent that disorder.
The first foundation of justice is recognized interest in the possibility and preservation of society.
The second foundation of justice is the moral approval that arises after the social utility of its rules is established.
Justice is not a natural virtue grounded in a peculiar original principle.
“Giving every one his due” cannot define justice without presupposing the property and right that justice constitutes.
Property is not independent of moral sentiment and convention.
Property is not a sensible quality of an object, a relation among external objects, or a merely corporeal relation.
Bare possession, occupation, or transfer does not naturally carry an original sentiment of moral approval.
Regard for public good is not the originating motive of the rules of justice.
Imperfect property or dominion is not a rationally grounded intermediate juridical state, but a civil fiction.
Justice is not the flexible application of immediate private or public motives to particular cases.
Social indispensability does not entail natural origin.
Property changes without sensible or corporeal alteration because its constitutive change occurs in duties governing conduct.
The vulgar definition of justice reverses the order of dependence and becomes circular.
The adjustment of opposed self-interests can produce public advantage without public advantage being intended.
Even deliberate orientation toward public good would establish artifice rather than naturality.
If justice admits degrees, its dependent juridical relations must admit degrees, contradicting their integral form.
If justice does not admit degrees, it lacks the gradual form attributed to natural virtue and vice.
Gradated justificatory pressures underdetermine binary juridical verdicts, forcing adjudication to impose decisive closure.
Without convention, circumstance-sensitive natural motives could authorize partial conduct because no antecedent property relation would be violated.
Universal justice is a remedial constraint upon ordinary motivation rather than its immediate expression.
Moral obligation is posterior to interest-based conventional stabilization.
Artificiality and natural genesis are compatible: convention is a second-order strategy by which passion secures satisfaction against the destructive effects of its first-order operation.
Property has no independent object-ontology; it is a normative effect of institutionally stabilized expectations and duties.
Juridical impartiality is produced by suppressing the case-sensitive responsiveness characteristic of natural motivation.
Legal determinacy exceeds the determinacy of its gradual utilitarian and imaginative grounds, creating recurrent pressure for arbitrary boundary decisions.
Justice has a dual genealogy: interested coordination produces the rule-system, while contemplation of its social effects produces its moral sanction.
Necessity attaches to the social function of justice, not to an innate moral source.
What is necessary for human life need not be naturally implanted.
What is artificial need not be arbitrary, dispensable, or opposed to human passion.
The moral status of justice cannot itself supply the pre-moral motive required to establish just conduct.
No normative fact of mine and thine survives the subtraction of conventionally organized duty.
No immediate natural motive possesses the universality and invariability required by juridical order.
Collective benefit does not require collective benevolence or a consciously shared public end.
The system excludes a pre-social normative world in which objects intrinsically belong to persons.
The system forecloses spontaneous social stability through unrestricted case-sensitive equity.
Nature supplies no impartial legislative motive capable of directly generating the formal structure of justice.
No stable middle term reconciles gradated grounds of entitlement with the binary verdicts required by juridical decision.
Social necessity + opposed self-love → coordination problem.
Particular motives + avidity + partiality → variable judgment → social confusion.
Recognition of common interest → voluntary convention → universal and inflexible rules.
Inflexible rules → duties of abstention, restoration, transfer, and performance → property, right, and obligation.
Coordinated private interests → unintended public utility → peace and social security.
Perceived social utility → pleasure in observance and uneasiness at violation → moral sanction.
Constitutive-priority test + gradation test + motive-rule mismatch test → justice classified as artificial virtue.
Social necessity of the three laws → question of their origin → artificial-virtue thesis.
Vulgar definition → presumed antecedent property → relational analysis → priority of justice over property.
Gradable natural morality → integral juridical relations → dichotomous reductio → exclusion of natural justice.
Particular natural motivation → partial judgment → social disorder → conventional inflexibility.
Interest-based convention → stable social utility → natural moral approval → dual foundation of justice.
Necessity and naturality are separated: an institution may be indispensable without being innate.
Property is reclassified from a quality of objects into an effect of norm-governed relations among persons.
Justice is reclassified from an original sentiment into a conventional rule-system that later receives moral approval.
Self-interest is reclassified from a mere source of disorder into the generative material of social order.
Public good is reclassified from an originating intention into an emergent effect of coordinated private interests.
Adjudication is reclassified as the forced production of binary closure over grounds that often appear continuous.
Moral motivation divides into a pre-moral motive of interest and a post-institutional sentiment of approval.
Surface: the three laws of possession, transfer, and promise are necessary but artificial rules of justice.
Structural: convention redirects opposed self-interests into invariant conduct capable of sustaining society.
Metastrategic: the naturality claim is defeated through inversion of conceptual priority, mismatch of gradation, and mismatch of motivational form.
Ontological/Temporal: property exists as a norm-mediated relation, while interest-based institution temporally precedes moral approbation.
CH_THN_SVSF:A1–CH_THN_SVSF:A17 are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s three proofs and final two-foundation model.
The exact historical mechanism by which voluntary convention first stabilizes is underdetermined.
The structure is coherent if natural passion is distinguished from the second-order arrangements generated by passion.
The strongest support lies in the constitutive priority of justice over property and the mismatch between variable motives and invariant rules.
The gradation argument depends on the broad and insufficiently demonstrated premise that all natural moral qualities vary continuously.
The inference from the multiplicity of juridical rules to their non-natural origin is compressed rather than independently established.
The insistence on integral rights remains in tension with the acknowledged graduality of utility, imagination, and ordinary judgments of half-right.
The claim that justice is both an offspring of passion and contrary to ordinary passionate conduct is resolved only by an implicit distinction between first-order impulse and second-order strategy.
Reconstruction preserves the operative movement: necessity → conceptual inversion → modal reductio → motivational diagnosis → convention → moralization.

identity.title: Sect. VI Some Farther Reflections Concerning Justice And Injustice

units.title: Sect. IX Of The Measures Of Allegiance

items.text: Problem: determine when allegiance ceases and resistance becomes morally permissible.
Contract theory reaches the correct anti-tyrannical conclusion through the false premise of an original promise.
Promise reduces genealogically to convention and interest and therefore cannot be the ultimate source of allegiance.
Public interest in security and protection is the original motive and immediate sanction of government and obedience.
Intolerable oppression destroys that interest and thereby terminates the natural obligation of allegiance.
Moral obligation may outlive its natural cause through general-rule inertia, but recurrent abuses of power establish a general exception permitting resistance.
Reconstructive-genealogical movement: valid conclusion → false contractual ground → interest-ground → moral persistence objection → generalized resistance exception → common-judgment confirmation.
A promise is a human convention invented for the sake of interest.
Government is a human invention ordered to the interest of society.
Political security and protection are unattainable under perfect freedom and independence.
Public interest is the immediate natural sanction of allegiance.
The natural obligation of allegiance lasts no longer than the public interest that causes it.
The moral obligation of allegiance is founded on the natural obligation of interest.
Human beings extend general moral rules beyond the reasons that originally established them.
An exception to a general moral rule ordinarily requires its own general-rule form, grounded in numerous and common cases.
The frailties and passions of human nature persist in rulers.
Political office gives rulers a more immediate interest in preserving order and executing justice.
Rulers can be driven by passion to neglect that immediate interest and pursue cruelty or ambition.
Human nature, history, and present experience make severe abuses of ruling power recurrent and foreseeable.
Settled moral practice approves resistance to flagrant tyranny and rejects passive obedience.
The general opinion of mankind is authoritative and, in morals, infallible.
Imitation and custom cannot originate submission because both presuppose prior instances of submission.
Public interest is the only original motive capable of overcoming natural ambition and producing political submission.
The justified exception to allegiance does not depend on an original contract.
Promise is not a natural, preconventional, or self-grounding source of political obligation.
Government need not be derived through reflective institution followed by a promise of obedience.
The cessation of a natural cause does not by itself guarantee the immediate cessation of moral obligation.
A general moral rule is not exceptionless merely because it has become habitual.
Political authority does not transform rulers into beings of superior nature.
A ruler’s situational interest in justice does not guarantee just conduct.
Imitation and custom are not original motives of allegiance.
Passive obedience is not a coherent moral absolute.
Resistance is not authorized by every partial, private, or isolated disadvantage.
Promise cannot be the ultimate foundation of allegiance because its own authority derives from convention and interest.
When intolerable oppression removes political security, it removes the natural obligation to obey.
Moral allegiance may persist temporarily after its originating interest has ceased because general rules exceed their original causes.
Recurrent rulerly abuse gives the anti-tyrannical exception the generality required to correct the rule of obedience.
Once loss of public interest is grave and generalizable, conscience no longer binds submission to violent tyranny.
Resistance to flagrant tyranny is neither criminal nor unjust within the prevailing moral judgment of mankind.
Custom and imitation can transmit allegiance but cannot explain its first production.
The operative measure of resistance is conjunctive: public interest must fail in a great degree, and the failure must belong to a considerable class of cases.
Allegiance is conditionally binding without being contractually founded: its condition is the continued public function of government.
The same general-rule mechanism that stabilizes ordinary obedience also generates the exception to obedience when abuses become recurrent.
A ruler who systematically destroys security is reclassified from magistrate into tyrant and public enemy because authority is functionally sanctioned.
Legitimate resistance is internal to the rule-governed structure of allegiance rather than an arbitrary suspension of political morality.
Common moral practice can embody the causal logic of political obligation implicitly without articulating its philosophical genealogy.
Political obligation cannot possess an independent normative foundation severed from public security.
Elevation to office cannot eliminate the passions that make institutional failure foreseeable.
General-rule inertia cannot be absolute, or moral allegiance would survive the destruction of its own foundation.
A singular private grievance cannot constitute the public-interest failure required for resistance.
Correct moral judgment cannot require explicit theoretical knowledge of its generating principles.
Custom cannot be self-originating or explain the first act that later becomes customary.
No transcendent, natural, or unconditional residue of allegiance remains once public interest and its moral generalization cease.
No ruler possesses an indefeasible title to obedience independently of the protective function of government.
No exact decision procedure measures intolerable tyranny; the threshold remains confined to qualitative severity and recurrence.
A political order from which justified resistance could be permanently excluded is unavailable because rulerly frailty is inseparable from human nature.
Correct anti-tyrannical conclusion → separation from contractual premises.
Promise → human convention → interest → collapse of promise as ultimate foundation.
Need for security → invention of government → public-interest sanction → natural allegiance.
Intolerable tyranny → destruction of protection → cessation of interest → cessation of natural allegiance.
General-rule propensity → persistence of moral allegiance beyond its immediate cause.
Invariant human frailty + rulerly passions + repeated historical abuse → generalizable exception.
Generalized exception + common moral judgment → morally permissible resistance to violent supreme power.
Regress of imitation and custom → exclusion of rival origin motives → public-interest foundation secured.

Correct resistance conclusion → rejection of original contract → reduction of promise to interest → direct grounding of allegiance in public security → natural obligation canceled by severe tyranny → moral-rule persistence objection → recurrent abuse generalized into an exception → resistance morally authorized → custom and imitation excluded as origins.
Political conditionality is relocated from contractual nonperformance to the functional cessation of public protection.
Allegiance is reclassified from an absolute duty to a defeasible effect of public interest.
Tyranny becomes a reversal of political function capable of converting the governor into a public enemy.
General rules acquire a double role: they preserve obedience beyond immediate calculation and authorize resistance through generalized exceptions.
History, common practice, and moral sentiment become evidence for the structure and limits of political obligation.
Custom and imitation are demoted from generative causes to mechanisms that direct or reproduce an allegiance generated by interest.
Surface: the argument identifies the threshold at which subjects may resist supreme power without crime or injustice.
Structural: government converts common insecurity into coordinated submission but remains vulnerable to rulers whose passions override institutional incentives.
Metastrategic: the argument preserves a general rule of allegiance while making resistance an internal, generalizable exception rather than a contractual escape.
Ontological/Temporal: invariant human frailty persists across political positions, while moral rules outlive their causes until repeated experience produces a corrective counter-rule.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the replacement of contractual allegiance by interest-grounded allegiance.
The system is strongest where the same public interest explains both the institution of government and the limit of obedience.
The natural-obligation/moral-obligation distinction preserves the actual movement from direct causal cessation to the general-rule objection.
The precise threshold between tolerable misgovernment and resistance-authorizing tyranny remains underdetermined.
The exclusivity of public interest as original motive is compressed into a regress against imitation and custom rather than established against every possible rival.
The appeal to universal moral approval depends heavily on the asserted infallibility of general opinion in morals.

The central tension lies between moral rules exceeding their causes and moral obligation ultimately ceasing with natural obligation; the general exception mediates but does not quantify this transition.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement provided qualitative severity, recurrent abuse, and common moral judgment are accepted as sufficient to generalize the exception.

identity.title: Sect. IX Of The Measures Of Allegiance

units.title: Part III Of The Other Virtues And Vices

items.text: The problem is to explain how natural qualities become virtues or vices without reducing morality to either rational judgment or political contrivance.
Virtue and vice arise from pleasure and uneasiness produced by surveying durable character from a common evaluative standpoint.
Sympathy communicates the pleasures and pains attached to a quality’s effects on its possessor or on others.
The argument is a sentimental genealogy supported by causal comparison, explanatory parsimony, objection-resolution, and application.
Artificial virtue supplies the controlled case from which the sympathetic basis of approval is extended to natural virtues.
Variability of sympathy and accidental failure of useful dispositions are neutralized by the general point of view and evaluation of natural tendency.
Pride functions as the decisive test: its moral valence changes with its utility, intrinsic agreeableness, comparative effect, degree, and mode of expression.
Moral distinctions are constituted by peculiar sentiments of pleasure and uneasiness elicited by contemplating mental qualities.
A pleasing quality produces virtue, pride, or love; an uneasy quality produces vice, humility, or hatred.
Actions enter morality only as evidence of durable principles of character.
Sympathy converts a sufficiently lively idea of another’s inferred affection into a corresponding sentiment in the spectator.
An object’s natural fitness for an agreeable end can please the imagination even when external circumstances prevent the end.
Moral pleasure has four sources: usefulness to others, usefulness to the possessor, immediate agreeableness to others, and immediate agreeableness to the possessor.
The usefulness of a quality becomes agreeable to a disinterested spectator through sympathy with its beneficiaries.
Qualities agreeable only to their possessor or associates become agreeable to other spectators through sympathy.
Reflection on tendencies determines the principal lines of duty, while immediate taste independently produces lesser moral approvals.
General moral judgment adopts the interests of the person evaluated and of those connected with that person as the common standpoint.
General evaluation corrects variations caused by distance, situation, personal interest, present disposition, and fortune, even when occurrent passions remain unequal.
A disposition’s natural tendency, rather than its accidental actual efficacy, determines its standing as virtue or vice.
Imaginative sympathy can determine moral taste without becoming strong enough to motivate sacrifice or restrain private passion.
Natural and artificial virtues differ in the scale of beneficial operation: natural virtues benefit through particular acts, whereas justice benefits through a general scheme.
A cause demonstrated sufficient for an effect must be extended to analogous effects unless another cause is necessary.
Well-grounded self-esteem derives merit from both its usefulness and its immediate agreeableness to its possessor.
Sympathy and self-comparison respond oppositely to another’s condition: sufficiently vivid and credible representation is shared, while intermediate representation produces a contrary self-feeling.
Moral love and hatred generate benevolence and anger, thereby producing judgments of good and ill desert.
Moral good and evil are not discovered by reason or comparison of ideas.
An isolated action without a constant originating principle is not a proper object of moral praise or blame.
Another person’s passion is not perceived immediately; it is inferred from its causes or effects.
Utility-based beauty and moral approval are not absolute qualities detached from relations to agreeable ends.
Moral distinctions are not inventions imposed wholly by politicians, education, honour, or shame.
Public utility does not exhaust the sources of moral approval.
The spectator’s private advantage cannot serve as the universal standard of character.
Variation in the intensity of sympathy does not entail variation in general moral esteem.
Actual success is not necessary for a disposition to retain virtue.
Extensive moral sympathy does not entail unlimited generosity or practical self-sacrifice.
Pride is not intrinsically vicious, and socially required modesty is not identical with sincere inward self-abasement.
Moral inquiry must infer enduring character from conduct rather than assign final value to isolated events.
A spectator can approve qualities useful or agreeable to strangers without possessing any private interest in them.
The sympathetic explanation established for artificial justice extends to socially useful natural virtues, whose particular benefits facilitate rather than obstruct sympathy.
Equal esteem for near and remote characters signifies corrected counterfactual judgment, not equal intensity of present affection.
Accidental impotence or bad fortune can weaken affective vividness without reducing the virtue attributed to a disposition.
Limited generosity is compatible with extensive moral concern because taste requires only imaginative participation, whereas action requires stronger passion.
Moral evaluation is irreducibly fourfold, although considerations of useful tendency possess priority in major duties.
The constancy and universality required for moral discourse exclude each spectator’s shifting private interest from the speculative standard.
Due self-esteem is virtuous because it enables action and supplies immediate satisfaction to its possessor.
Unsupported self-exaltation becomes vicious when sympathy gives its claim enough vivacity for comparison but not enough credibility for shared admiration.

Haughtiness toward remote or historical others remains blameworthy through a double rebound: the spectator sympathizes with associates whose uneasiness already arose from sympathetic comparison with the proud person.
Good-breeding suppresses direct self-applause while permitting concealed, well-grounded self-esteem.
Heroic pride can remain admirable despite social harm when immediate sympathy with elevation overpowers reflected pain from its public tendency.
Moral approval and blame terminate in desires to benefit the virtuous and punish the vicious.
Moral universality is produced by intersubjective stabilization of sentiment rather than by escape from sentiment.
The authority conventionally attributed to reason is the authority of calm, generalized passion over judgment, not the necessary control of immediate passion.
Moral character is a counterfactual-dispositional object: evaluation concerns what a quality is fitted to produce under adequate conditions.
Natural and artificial virtues share one mechanism of approval while differing in whether utility belongs to the act or to the coordinated system.
The four-source system integrates self-regarding and other-regarding excellence by making sympathetic mobility, rather than direct benefit, the condition of spectator approval.
Good-breeding operates as an artificial coordination system for natural pride, preventing reciprocal comparison from making social intercourse intolerable.
Heroic admiration exposes moral judgment as a conflict among affective sources rather than as the output of a single utility measure.
Moral desert is not an independent rational relation but the practical extension of pleasure into love and benevolence, or uneasiness into hatred and anger.
Radical affective incommensurability among human beings must be false, because sympathy presupposes similarity of passions and operations.
Ideas of another’s condition cannot remain permanently affectless representations, because moral transmission requires their conversion into impressions.
First-person interest cannot possess legitimate universal authority, because its variability would dissolve shared moral language.
Actual outcomes cannot exhaust the value of causes, because fortune may obstruct a disposition without altering its internal fitness.
Moral approval cannot be required to produce corresponding action, because the system distinguishes imaginative taste from motivational force.
General judgment cannot be required to coincide with immediate passion, because correction may regulate judgment or language while leaving affection resistant.
An affect-free foundation of moral universality is unavailable; universality remains dependent on shared constitution and corrected sentiment.
Perfect impartiality at the level of lived passion is unavailable; only judgment and evaluative language can be regularly stabilized.
A single rule for commensurating utility, immediate agreeableness, self-regarding merit, and other-regarding merit is absent.
Unmediated access to character is unavailable; moral evaluation depends on signs, inferred dispositions, general rules, and counterfactual tendencies.
Complete unity between inward virtue and outward presentation is foreclosed by the requirement that legitimate pride conceal itself under conventional modesty.
Conduct or expression → inference to durable character → admission into moral evaluation.
Character → useful or immediately agreeable relation → actual or imagined pleasure or pain.
Useful to others / useful to possessor / agreeable to others / agreeable to possessor → four-source moral classification.
Causes or effects of another’s condition → lively idea → sympathy → corresponding spectator sentiment.
Pleasure in survey → virtue → pride or love; uneasiness in survey → vice → humility or hatred.
Situational sentiment → common standpoint → correction for distance, interest, disposition, and fortune → stable esteem and moral language.
Natural virtue → particular beneficial act → determinate beneficiary → vivid sympathy; artificial virtue → coordinated scheme → general social benefit → diffuse sympathy.
Imaginative sympathy below motivational threshold → moral taste without sacrifice; sympathy touching the heart → practical control of passion.
Another’s self-assessment → sympathetic vivacity → credible superiority produces shared elevation and respect / unsupported superiority produces comparison, humiliation, and dislike.
Moral love or hatred → benevolence or anger → attribution of good or ill desert.

Natural-virtue problem → sentimental criterion → character filter → sympathy mechanism → artificial-virtue experiment → extension to natural virtues → variability objection → general-point-of-view correction → inactive-virtue objection → dispositional correction → four-source taxonomy.

Four-source hypothesis → pride test → sympathy/comparison conflict → condemnation of overweening pride → rehabilitation of due self-esteem → conventional concealment → heroic-source conflict → confirmation with unresolved weighting tension.
The primary moral object shifts from isolated action to durable character and disposition.
Natural and artificial virtues cease to require different sources of approval while retaining different structures of beneficial operation.
Impartiality is reclassified from rational detachment to correction of sentiment through a common standpoint.
Virtue expands beyond public utility to include usefulness and immediate agreeableness to the possessor.
Moral esteem separates from both affective intensity and practical motivation.
Moral value becomes counterfactual: natural tendency remains evaluable when fortune suppresses actual effects.
Pride is reclassified from a unitary vice into a variable quality governed by ground, degree, utility, comparative effect, and expression.
Good-breeding becomes visible as a coordination technology managing conflicts among self-evaluations.
Heroism becomes a conflict-site where immediate elevation can defeat reflected concern for society without ceasing to be morally ambivalent.
Surface — The text classifies natural virtues and vices, then determines the moral limits of pride, humility, modesty, and greatness of mind.
Structural — Sympathy, imagination, comparison, general rules, and standpoint correction generate and stabilize moral evaluation.
Metastrategic — Artificial virtue functions as an experimental baseline, objections isolate corrective mechanisms, and pride serves as a stress test of the four-source system.

Ontological/Temporal — The person is treated as a durable dispositional character whose tendencies extend across conduct and remain distinct from momentary action, situational feeling, and accidental fortune.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the sentimental criterion, sympathetic mechanism, common standpoint, four-source taxonomy, and application to pride.
The structure is internally coherent only if occurrent sentiment, corrected judgment, moral language, and motivating passion remain distinct.
The strongest inferential segment is the movement from artificial virtue as a sufficient-cause case to analogous socially useful natural virtues.
The weighting of the four moral sources remains underdetermined; predominance of useful tendency is asserted without a general aggregation rule.
The scope of the relevant connected persons and the procedure for resolving conflicts among their interests remain unspecified.
Heroic admiration exposes an unresolved fault line between social tendency and immediate sympathetic elevation.
The inference from actions to durable character and the threshold separating comparison from sympathy depend on compressed probabilistic judgments.
Reconstruction preserves the actual movement from causal genealogy through objection-correction to fourfold classification and pride-based verification.
The system supplies an explanatory architecture of moral judgment but not a complete decision procedure for conflicting virtues.

identity.title: Part III Of The Other Virtues And Vices

units.title: Sect. III Of Goodness And Benevolence

items.text: Problem: determine the sources and standard of merit attributed to goodness and benevolence under conditions of limited human generosity.
Thesis: benevolent character receives merit through beneficial tendency and the immediate agreeableness communicated by sympathy.
Argument type: reconstructive moral psychology joined to a diagnostic correction of situated judgment.
Limited generosity → appraisal within the agent’s relational sphere → conflict among private standpoints → socially generalized standard.
Variable sympathy → reflective correction of distance → stable calm judgment without equal emotional concern.
Relational usefulness → benevolence as director of capacities; contagious tenderness → merit independent of utility.
Qualified anger → condemnation of cruelty and incommodiousness → role-complete relational desirability as the final test of character.
Ordinary human generosity is limited to friends, family, and at most country.
Character must be judged within the ordinary relational sphere in which its passions operate.
A passion is approved or blamed according to its tendency to advantage or harm persons connected with its possessor.
Sympathy communicates the pleasures, pains, and sentiments of affected persons to the spectator.
Judgment from private interest produces contradictions among differently situated spectators.
Social intercourse generates a general and stable standard for judging character.
Reflection corrects calm judgment for distance-based variations in sympathetic force.
The general standard can regulate discourse without governing actual love and hatred.
Loving and tender passions are immediately agreeable through sympathy independently of their utility.
Sympathetically reproduced love readily transfers affection from the displayed sentiment to its bearer.
Courage, ambition, judgment, and capacity acquire social valence from the passions directing them.
Angry passions are constitutionally inherent and can be fitting in limited degree.
Cruelty and inhumanity are vicious through the misery and harm they impose on others.
Complete virtue requires desirability in every social relation together with adequate regard for oneself.
Goodness does not require impossible or universally extended generosity.
Moral judgment is not validly fixed to the spectator’s private interest or position.
Raw sympathetic intensity is not the final measure of character.
Benevolence does not derive all its merit from social utility.
Courage, ambition, judgment, and capacity are not intrinsically beneficial.
Angry passions are not categorically vicious merely because they are disagreeable.
The naturalness of anger does not excuse its escalation into cruelty.
Adequacy toward others alone does not constitute complete perfection.
The object of appraisal remains local to the agent, while the standpoint of appraisal is generalized across spectators.
Distance-based variations in sympathy are treated as corrigible appearances rather than differences in character.
Benefits remote from the spectator can ground stable praise despite producing weaker immediate concern.
Benevolent direction converts otherwise indifferent capacities into socially useful powers, while hostile direction converts them into instruments of harm.
Sympathy with displayed love generates love toward the benevolent agent through a transfer of the passion’s object.
A tender excess can remain amiable even when its public utility is negligible.
The mere presence of anger cannot determine vice; degree, necessity, and consequence must intervene.
Sympathy with sufferers converts pity into intensified hatred of the cruel agent.
Any disposition that makes ordinary relations persistently harmful or intolerable constitutes a defect of character.
The system universalizes the standpoint of appraisal without universalizing either benevolent motivation or beneficiary scope.
Moral stability is a reflective-social achievement imposed upon variable sympathy, not constancy of spontaneous feeling.
Benevolence possesses two irreducible routes to merit: beneficial tendency and affective self-communication.
Character becomes a relational risk-and-benefit architecture in which capacities receive value from direction and dispositions from their effects across roles.
Shared moral discourse can persist without convergence between calm verdicts and personal affections.
Moral perfection combines interpersonal harmlessness and usefulness with preservation of the agent’s own good.
Partial sympathy is not epistemically final or incapable of correction.
A shared moral standard does not require equal emotional concern for all persons.
Utility cannot become morally salient to a disinterested spectator without sympathetic access to those affected.
Virtue cannot be identified with maximal public impact, since minute tenderness can possess exceptional merit.
Powerful capacities do not carry self-validating moral worth.
Natural occurrence is not equivalent to moral innocence.
Immediate agreeableness and beneficial consequence are not reducible to a single source of approval.
Universal benevolence is unavailable as an ordinary human motive; generalized judgment substitutes for universal affection.
A view from nowhere is unavailable; moral generality is constructed through correction among situated spectators.
Complete coincidence between moral verdict and actual love or hatred is absent from the system.
No explicit common metric reconciles utility, immediate tenderness, fitting anger, and self-regard when they conflict.
Character conceived apart from relations is excluded from final evaluation; moral identity appears only through effects on others and self.
Experience of human affairs → recognition of limited generosity → restriction of appraisal to feasible relational spheres.
Private interest → contradictory verdicts → conversational pressure → general standard.
Distance-attenuated sympathy → reflective correction → constant calm judgment → possible divergence from actual affection.
Utility channel: passion → advantage or harm to connected persons → sympathetic uptake → approval or blame.
Immediate channel: displayed tenderness → contagious love → agreeable movement → transfer to bearer → affection and merit.
Regulatory channel: capacity → benevolent direction or hostile direction → usefulness or magnified harm.
Anger boundary: constitutional passion → limited degree → excusability or praise; escalation → cruelty → suffering → intensified hatred.
Closure: test every social relation → no relation refused → test self-relation → complete character.

Limited generosity → sphere-bounded appraisal → contradictions among situated judgments → corrected common standpoint → utility-based merit → immediately sympathetic merit → qualified anger → relational test of perfection.
Goodness is relocated from universal benevolent reach to beneficial operation within an agent’s feasible relational sphere.
Distance is reclassified from a moral difference into a perspectival distortion correctable by reflection.
Moral constancy is separated from emotional impartiality.
Benevolence is reclassified as the directing principle that determines the social valence of power and ability.
Merit is expanded beyond useful consequences to include the immediate sympathetic pleasure of tender affection.
Anger is reclassified by degree and relational consequence rather than by a simple agreeable–disagreeable opposition.
Character perfection is transformed into role-complete relational desirability supplemented by adequate self-relation.
Surface: explanation of the merit of benevolent qualities and the vice of cruelty and inhumanity.
Structural: social intercourse converts conflicting situated sympathies into a stable standard of character judgment.
Metastrategic: evaluation proceeds through a generalized relational standpoint and two distinct channels of merit rather than through universal motivation or utility alone.
Ontological/Temporal: human beings possess limited affections, contagious sympathy, and inherent anger, while repeated changes of position and reflection stabilize judgment over time.
CH_THN_SIGB:A1–CH_THN_SIGB:A14 are sufficient to reconstruct the dual-source account of benevolent merit and its relational closure.
The precise mechanism by which conversation produces an inalterable standard remains underdetermined.
No weighting rule determines precedence between beneficial tendency and immediate agreeableness when they conflict.
The structure is coherent insofar as sympathy mediates both consequence-based and immediately affective approval.
The strongest generative linkage runs from positional contradiction through reflective correction to a common relational standpoint.
The optical-distance analogy establishes the need for correction but does not prove the unique content of the corrected moral judgment.
Similarity-based approval reintroduces spectator partiality into the mechanism intended to correct private standpoint.
The merit assigned to excessive tenderness can conflict with the requirement of adequate self-relation unless an unstated threshold limits excess.
The qualified praise of anger prevents immediate agreeableness from functioning as a universal criterion and leaves the system evaluatively plural.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the movement from limited affection through generalized judgment and dual merit to relational perfection.

identity.title: Sect. III Of Goodness And Benevolence

items.text: Scientific insecurity is traced beneath disciplinary disputes to inadequate knowledge of the human faculties through which all sciences are constituted and judged.
Human nature is therefore installed as a metascientific object, but its investigation is denied access to mental essence and restricted to experienced operations and effects.
This restriction is operationalized by decomposing mental life into impressions and ideas, then into simple and complex perceptions.
Simple ideational content is genealogically subordinated to prior impressions, while complex imagination remains free to recombine impression-derived elements.
The linear copy model mutates when impressions divide into sensation and reflection: ideas remain effects of sensation but become causes of passions and further perceptions.
Priority consequently becomes relational rather than absolute, distinguishing original, correspondent, causal, and expository order.
The inquiry begins from ideas not because ideas are ultimately first, but because they are the operative antecedents of the reflective phenomena selected for moral investigation.

The cluster moves by recursive tightening: foundational crisis → empirical restriction → perceptual genealogy → recursive mediation → methodological reversal → bounded closure at unknown sensory origins.
[Attractor] A secure science of human nature is the strategic center of scientific reconstruction because human faculties mediate every scientific judgment.
[Persistent] Mental inquiry must proceed from experienced operations, effects, and relations rather than from speculative access to mental essence.
[Emergent] Empirical investigation of mind requires both a taxonomy of perceptions and a genealogy specifying their dependency and order.
[Persistent] Simple ideas generally derive on first appearance from corresponding prior simple impressions.
[Emergent] Restriction at the level of simple content permits recombination and recursive productivity at the level of complex ideas and later perceptions.
[Mutating] Temporal priority establishes causal direction only within a specified dependency relation; it cannot assign one absolute order to impressions and ideas as total classes.
[Mutating] Ideas are derivative copies relative to sensation but productive mediators relative to impressions of reflection.
[Emergent] Mental life forms an asymmetrically grounded recursive sequence: sensation → idea → reflection → idea → possible further perception.
[Mutating] Proper methodological order follows the operative antecedents of the selected object, not necessarily the chronology of absolute origin.
[Terminal] The ultimate causes of sensation and the original qualities of human nature remain unavailable; legitimate explanation terminates at maximally general experienced relations.
[Mutating] Scientific warrant at this level belongs to stable empirical generalization rather than exceptionless universality.
[Attractor] The human subject functions as both the medium of inquiry and a relay within the perception-chain being investigated.
Stable identity: experience remains the admissible ground of inquiry from the foundational program through the perceptual genealogy.
Functional recurrence: observation of effects becomes classification of perceptions, comparison of correspondences, and reconstruction of temporal dependencies.
Mutation: general impression-priority is restricted from a class-wide hierarchy to indexed relations between particular perceptions and genealogical strata.
Reversal: impressions-first genetic order yields an ideas-first exposition once reflective impressions become the focal object.
Mutation: the idea changes from faint copy and terminal effect into an intermediate cause capable of producing desire, aversion, hope, and fear.
Escalation: the simple copy relation expands into a recursively extensible production machine without losing its asymmetrical sensory grounding.
Displacement: the rejection of speculative metaphysics becomes an operational rejection of innate simple content and self-originating reflective life.
Terminal transformation: ignorance changes from a sign of disciplinary failure into the legitimate endpoint of genealogy at unknown sensory causes.
Partial disappearance: ordinary conduct is declared the proper moral archive, but the subsequent machinery relies chiefly on introspective taxonomy, deprivation, and conceptual genealogy.
Contained anomaly: the missing shade and repeated qualifiers convert strict universal precedence into an exception-tolerant empirical rule without being allowed to reorganize the system.
[Local] The initial diagnosis of philosophical discredit and rhetorical controversy motivates the reconstruction but does not itself govern the later perceptual machinery.
[Local] Force and liveliness provide the initial impression–idea distinction, but exceptional states prevent them from functioning as the complete current-level criterion.
[Local] The missing-shade case remains a concentrated anomaly rather than an alternative generative principle.
[Scales upward] The prohibition on essence-first explanation becomes the common boundary governing both the science of human nature and the origin of perception.
[Bridge] The simple–complex distinction links empirical restriction to imaginative productivity: primitive content is constrained while complex formation remains open.
[Catalyst] Division of impressions into sensation and reflection converts the linear copy model into an asymmetrical recursive system.
[Superseded] Undifferentiated impressions-first method is recoded as a default valid only before object, scope, and internal dependency are specified.
[Scales upward] Disciplinary exclusion of sensory causes becomes a general methodological principle: proximate operations may be investigated securely without resolving absolute origins.
Mental science is not an inquiry from substance or essence to deduced operations.
Simple ideational content is not generally generated by an autonomous productive intellect.
Complex invention does not establish the production of primitive content independent of prior impressions.
Impressions and ideas do not stand in a causally symmetrical or uniformly ordered relation.
Reflective impressions are not predominantly original, immediate occurrences independent of antecedent ideas.
Chronological firstness does not by itself determine the proper order of inquiry.
Scientific security does not require access to ultimate causes, essences, or an exceptionless first principle.
Controlled self-intervention is not the exclusive route to empirical warrant in the science of human nature.
The architecture requires the falsity of any model in which cognition can secure itself from a standpoint outside human faculties and perceptual mediation.
It excludes a foundationalism for which only knowledge of first causes can warrant knowledge of derivative regularities.
It disqualifies the mind as a static receptacle: derivative perceptions must be capable of returning as causes within reflective life.
It rejects a single linear chronology as sufficient to organize origin, causation, correspondence, recurrence, and exposition.
It cannot admit that reflective phenomena are irreducibly singular, because their scientific treatment requires recurrent relations between ideas, circumstances, and passions.
It implicitly rejects strict falsification by isolated anomaly, preserving general empirical rules through rarity and qualification.
The system circles an unavailable absolute origin: sensory impressions ground the genealogy, but the cause of their first appearance remains outside the inquiry.
No unmediated foundation is available: science depends on human faculties, while those faculties are accessible only through their mediated effects.
Purely immediate passion is excluded as the governing model; reflection is structurally dependent on representational return.
Exceptionless closure remains unavailable because the copy principle, impression-priority, and recursive sequence survive only through controlled qualifications.
The absent possibility organizing the cluster is a nonrecursive foundation capable of grounding cognition without already employing cognition, comparison, and perceptual succession.
The impression–idea genealogy operationalizes the introductory science of human nature by replacing speculative anthropology with observable dependencies among perceptions.
Foundational security is reconstructed as a bounded genealogy: reliable order among perceptions can be known even when mental essence and sensory origins cannot.
Because ideas are both impression-derived and reflectively productive, human reasoning is neither self-originating nor causally inert.
The science intended to provide a foundation begins from an intermediate layer—ideas—because absolute origins are both inaccessible and unnecessary for the selected inquiry.
Recursive mental productivity does not abolish empiricism: later perceptions may generate one another while the primitive content of the sequence remains asymmetrically grounded in sensation.

The naturalistic protocol for moral science and the later reliance on introspective perceptual taxonomy remain methodologically misaligned unless introspection is treated as observation of naturally occurring operations.
Empirical certainty must mean robust qualified regularity rather than universality, because the cluster retains both the missing-shade anomaly and rare exceptions to impression-priority.
The proposed causal genealogy incurs a methodological debt: it uses conjunction and succession to establish dependence before the promised analysis of causation secures those criteria.
Foundationalism is converted from discovery of an ultimate ground into disciplined reconstruction of dependency relations within an acknowledged horizon of ignorance.
The science of human nature is necessarily reflexive: faculties investigate the perceptual operations through which those same faculties know and judge.
The operative subject becomes a relay rather than an origin: it receives impressions, retains copies, returns ideas, and produces reflective effects.
Mental temporality is layered: irreversible sensory precedence grounds a downstream field in which derivative perceptions recursively become antecedents.
Ideational creativity is constrained but real: it cannot generally originate simple qualities, yet it can recombine contents and generate new reflective states.
Methodological relevance supersedes absolute origin: an inquiry may begin from the nearest productive condition of its object while leaving the remote ground unexplained.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Foundational recursion: insecure sciences require a science of human nature, but that science must employ the cognition and comparison it is intended to secure.
Perceptual production loop: sensory impression → retained idea → reflective impression → reflective idea → possible further impression or idea.
Restriction–proliferation loop: simple content is empirically restricted, complex ideas recombine it, and returned ideas produce additional reflective states.
Boundary loop: inquiry reaches unknown origin, withdraws to observable effects, compresses them into general principles, and treats the acknowledged limit as closure.
Anomaly-containment loop: universal formulation → counterinstance or qualifier → restriction of scope → retention of the governing maxim.
Ideas become the principal conceptual attractor because they connect sensation to reflection, empirical derivation to productivity, and genetic order to expository method.
Sensation functions as the recessed ground-attractor: every recursive sequence depends on it, yet its causes are deferred beyond the operative system.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Disciplinary insecurity + rhetorical controversy → demand for a common foundation.
Mediation of science by human faculties → human nature installed as the common metascientific object.
Unavailable mental essence → effects, circumstances, and perceptions become the legitimate evidential field.
Perceptual classification → impression/idea distinction + simple/complex distinction → isolable units of genealogy.
Simple correspondence + conjunction + first-appearance priority → general impression-to-idea derivation.
Division of impressions → sensation grounds ideas → ideas generate reflection → recursive downstream production.
Selection of reflective phenomena + exclusion of sensory origins → ideas-first exposition within an asymmetrically sensation-grounded system.
Qualified regularity + terminal ignorance → bounded empirical foundation without essential or absolute closure.
Foundational disorder → human nature identified as the common dependency beneath the sciences.
Human nature as common dependency → experience and observation replace speculation about essence.
Observational restriction → mental life decomposed into impressions, ideas, simple contents, and complex formations.
Perceptual decomposition → simple correspondence and temporal succession establish impression-to-idea genealogy.
Linear genealogy → division of impressions → ideas become mediators between sensation and reflection.
Ideational mediation → recursive production → absolute priority replaced by indexed priority.
Indexed priority + disciplinary scope → ideas-first method → bounded closure at unknown sensory origins.
Scientific disorder is redrawn as a problem of the human medium through which evidence, judgment, and assent operate.
Foundation is reclassified from access to essence into a qualified causal genealogy of experienced perceptions.
Mind is mapped as a field of ordered perceptions rather than approached through an antecedently known mental substance.
The opposition between receptivity and productivity collapses: ideas are received copies at one stratum and productive causes at another.
The opposition between linear and recursive causality is replaced by asymmetrical recursion: one-way grounding supports downstream feedback.
Priority is redistributed among genetic, correspondent, causal, disciplinary, and expository orders.
Certainty and ignorance cease to be opposites: reliable relations may be established precisely by refusing claims about ultimate origins.
Surface level: insecure sciences, disputed metaphysics, impressions, ideas, sensations, reflections, passions, and the correct order of inquiry constitute the explicit objects.
Structural level: perception is organized by classification, copying, conjunction, temporal precedence, return, and recursive mediation.
Metastrategic level: inquiry is redirected from disciplinary disputes and innate-content vocabulary toward a bounded empirical genealogy of the operative antecedents of reflective life.
Ontological/Temporal level: reality enters mental science as successive effects whose priority is relational, whose sensory grounding is asymmetrical, and whose ultimate origin is unavailable.

Methodological/Performative level: the argument performs its empiricism by beginning with a general distinction, submitting it to counterinstances and subdivisions, and revising method without abandoning the governing genealogy.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: The ordinary-life observational protocol is not fully integrated with the later introspective classification of perceptions and hypothetical deprivation tests.
Constant conjunction and temporal succession perform causal work before the system has supplied its full account of causation.
The missing shade contradicts the unrestricted copy principle and is contained by rarity rather than incorporated into a revised theory of simple-content production.
Sensation is indispensable as the ultimate empirical ground but is simultaneously unexplained and excluded from the present inquiry.
The science of human nature remains foundationally recursive because it uses perception, cognition, and comparison to establish the authority of perception, cognition, and comparison.
The mechanism by which an idea returns and generates a reflective impression is structurally indispensable but causally unexplained.
Impression mutates from a uniform class opposed to ideas into a divided category containing both original sensations and idea-dependent reflections.
Idea mutates from derivative effect into causal mediator without becoming the ultimate source of its primitive content.
Priority mutates from class-wide precedence into an indexed relation varying by correspondence, stratum, and selected object.
Methodological order mutates from reproduction of genetic order into selection of the proximate antecedents needed to explain the focal phenomena.
Reality is imaged as an asymmetrically grounded cascade whose lower sensory entry is one-way but whose upper perceptual strata form recursive feedback circuits.
The subject is not operationally an originating substance but a switching relay that receives, copies, returns, recombines, and transmits perceptions.
Time is stratified: first appearance grounds irreversible derivation, while later ideas and reflections repeatedly exchange the positions of cause and effect.
Navigation consists in tracing effects, decomposing complexes, indexing priorities, following operative antecedents, and stopping where experience no longer supplies relations.
The current-level axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from scientific crisis through empirical perceptual genealogy to recursive mediation and ideas-first method.
The criteria for simplicity, exact correspondence, force, adequate observation, causal dependence, and the productive return of ideas remain underdetermined.
The architecture is coherent if ultimate origin, genetic order, correspondent order, recursive production, and expository order remain strictly distinguished.
Its strongest joint is the conversion of an empirically grounded linear copy relation into recursive reflective production without granting autonomous origin to ideas.
Reconstruction depends on sequencing and recursive return: the methodological reversal is intelligible only after sensory precedence, copying, and reflection have been separately established.
The missing shade, rare exceptions, and unexplained return of ideas resist complete axiomatic reduction and prevent exceptionless closure.
The reconstruction preserves the actual movement only by retaining the transition from foundational ambition to bounded genealogy, and from linear derivation to asymmetrical recursion.

identity.kicker: Cluster · A Treatise of Human Nature
identity.title: Chapters 01–03
identity.context: Introduction · Sect. I. Of The Origin Of Our Ideas · Sect. II. Division Of The Subject

items.text: The central problem is to explain how impression-derived ideas can preserve experience, depart from it, form regular complexes, and generate spatial and temporal order without acquiring independent content.
The governing thesis is that ideational differences arise primarily from force, arrangement, recurrence, and relational operation rather than from heterogeneous elemental origins.
The argument becomes an empirical genealogy of mental organization: impressions supply materials, while faculties and relations determine how those materials recur, combine, and appear.
Memory conserves force and experienced order; imagination releases copied elements from that order; association then supplies noncompulsory pathways through the liberated field.
Spatiality and temporality complete the architecture by showing that order itself is not an additional impression but the disposition or succession of content.
Mental freedom is therefore bounded twice: it cannot originate unprecedented simple contents, and its ordinary transitions remain weighted by natural associative tendencies.
The movement is recursive rather than linear: copied order is preserved, dissolved, probabilistically regenerated, and finally exposed as constitutive of the ideas of space and time.
Closure occurs through paired limits: conception terminates in content-filled minima, while explanation terminates at experimentally established principles whose ultimate causes remain unknown.
[Persistent] Every legitimate idea must derive its elemental content from antecedent impression-material.
[Emergent] Elemental provenance and relational organization are distinct explanatory levels: identical copied materials can support preservation, recombination, association, or ordered appearance.
[Attractor] Order is the common object of the cluster: memory conserves it, imagination alters it, association regenerates it, and space and time consist in its coexistent or successive forms.
[Mutating] Difference licenses distinguishability and separability, but separation remains possible only where a positive component can be conceived apart.
[Persistent] Memory is recurrence under retained vivacity and fidelity to the experienced form, order, and position of its objects.
[Persistent] Imagination is dependent at the level of simple contents but free to separate, transpose, and recombine those contents at the level of arrangement.
[Emergent] Associative tendency mediates between compulsory connexion and random succession, producing regularity without abolishing imaginative liberty.
[Persistent] Resemblance, spatiotemporal contiguity, and cause and effect are the primary operators by which one idea introduces another.
[Mutating] Relational efficacy is graded: it propagates through intermediaries, weakens with distance, and expands causally from production to capacity and social influence.
[Emergent] Space and time are ordered manners of appearance rather than independent impressions: extension is coexistent disposition, and duration is noncoexistent succession.
[Mutating] Abstraction produces general representation by selectively regarding a determinate particular, not by generating a contentless universal.

[Attractor] An idea’s genealogy limits its legitimate application: recombination may alter conjunctions, but predication cannot properly exceed the kind of content or order supplied by the originating impression.
[Terminal] Empirical explanation may stop at a recurrent principle established through its effects even when the ultimate cause of that principle remains inaccessible.
[Terminal] Conceptual decomposition cannot terminate in nonentity: spatial minima must retain sensible quality, and temporal minima must be filled by successive existence.
The copy principle retains stable identity across the cluster, functioning first as a faculty constraint and later as a test of spatial, temporal, and predicative legitimacy.
Order mutates from a criterion of mnemonic fidelity into an object of imaginative alteration, an associative product, and finally the constitutive form of extension and duration.
Separability expands from the ground of imaginative liberty to a universal compositional premise, then reverses into a limiting test when no distinct spatial or temporal content can be isolated.
Imagination changes function from a faculty of transposition into a regulated field whose transitions are weighted by resemblance, contiguity, and causation.
Contiguity migrates from the experienced order preserved by memory into a customary associative pathway grounded in spatial and temporal arrangements.
Complex ideas divide into three generative regimes: freely rearranged fictions, associatively stabilized objects of thought, and compounds whose order constitutes extension or duration.
Causation migrates from an associative relation between ideas into a model of production, counterfactual capacity, authority, and social subordination.
Vivacity remains indispensable for establishing the memory–imagination distinction but disappears from the later explanations of associative order and spatiotemporal composition.
Connexion changes valence: memory approximates inseparable conservation, association supplies nonnecessary cohesion, and space and time remain nonseparable from some positive content.
Fiction reverses from a successful exercise of combinatorial liberty into a mark of illegitimate application when duration or spatiality is detached from every possible originating content.
[Local] The precise degree of vivacity distinguishing memory from imagination remains a faculty-specific criterion and does not govern association or spatiotemporal conception.
[Local] The claim that sight and touch alone provide extension’s source is required for spatial genealogy but does not scale into a general theory of all ideational recurrence.
[Local] The asserted exhaustiveness of resemblance, contiguity, and causation remains local to the associative taxonomy; the current level requires only nonnecessary relational regulation.
[Scaled] The copy principle scales upward because it constrains faculty content, abstract representation, spatial and temporal conception, and semantic application.
[Scaled] The distinction between content and arrangement becomes the cluster’s primary architecture, subsuming memory, imagination, association, space, and time.

[Bridge] Separability connects imaginative composition to conceptual analysis, but its cross-unit use requires distinguishing separation from an original complex from separation from every content-bearing instance.
[Catalyst] Imaginative freedom generates the problem solved by association: once ideas can combine arbitrarily, recurrent regularity demands a non-random but noncompulsory principle.
[Superseded] The binary opposition between necessary determination and pure chance is replaced by graded tendency, custom, and attenuating relational force.
[Recoded] Fiction is divided into lawful relational recombination and genealogically unsupported predication; novelty alone no longer determines illegitimacy.
[Transition] The expansion of causal association into social power demonstrates domain migration, but it does not itself govern the spatial and temporal ontology of the cluster.
No faculty, abstraction, or relational operation can originate an unprecedented simple idea independently of prior impression-material.
Copy-dependence does not entail preservation of original conjunctions, positions, or sequences.
Mental regularity is neither necessary determination nor random succession.
Order, extension, and duration are not additional simple impressions superadded to the contents they organize.
Generality cannot consist in an indeterminate or contentless universal representation.
Neither empty spatiality nor bare duration can remain positively conceivable after all sensible or successive existence is removed.
Memory cannot properly vary experienced order as freely as imagination, while imagination cannot escape impression-derived elements.
Empirical adequacy does not require speculative access to the ultimate mechanism producing associative attraction.
The system requires the falsity of any model in which the origin of an idea determines all of its possible arrangements; otherwise imagination and association collapse into mere replay.
It excludes both the passive-copy model of mind and the sovereign-creation model: the mind transforms relations without supplying its own simple materials.
It disqualifies any account that treats relations as independently given substances rather than operations, dispositions, successions, or tendencies among contents.
It rejects an ontology of empty frameworks in which space and time exist for thought independently of sensible points or successive existences.
It excludes semantic autonomy from genealogy: common language, objective occurrence, or habitual predication cannot by themselves legitimate an idea’s application.
It requires that stable mental order be explainable without necessary connexion, because necessity would destroy imaginative freedom while pure chance would destroy recurrence.
It rejects the demand that every empirically usable principle possess an independently known metaphysical substrate or ultimate cause.
The deepest unavailable object is pure order without ordered content: empty space, bare time, relation without relata, and memory without a prior arrangement are structurally inadmissible.
Sovereign mental spontaneity is absent; all available freedom is post-impressional freedom exercised through separation, recombination, and selective regard.
Necessary mental connexion is the missing force around which association is organized: gentle attraction occupies its functional place without acquiring its compulsion.
Ultimate explanatory grounding remains absent; “original qualities of human nature” marks the point where operational regularity survives without disclosed origin.
No independent tribunal verifies original order, absolute succession, or pure spatiality apart from the perceptual materials whose fidelity or arrangement is being judged.
Mental novelty consists primarily in relational transformation: copied elements remain constrained while their conjunction, sequence, emphasis, and representative function vary.
Association supplies default trajectories to a freely recombinable imagination, explaining stable complex thought without converting tendency into necessity.
Memory and associated imagination partially overlap because customary contiguity can lead imagination to reproduce the experienced sequences that memory preserves by fidelity.
Because space and time are arrangements of content, mnemonic fidelity conserves constitutive coexistence and succession rather than merely locating objects inside independent containers.
Customary association by contiguity depends on perceived spatial and temporal order: sensory succession supplies the sequence that custom converts into an imaginative transition.

Separability is conditional rather than absolute: components may be detached from original complexes, but extension cannot be detached from all sensible quality and time cannot be detached from every succession.
Fiction bifurcates into legitimate composition and illegitimate predication: an unexperienced complex can be formed lawfully, whereas duration without change exceeds its genetic basis.
