PORTION HAVING RECEDED: BUT THE SUPERFLUOUS, AND THE POINT OF CONFUSION, HAVING BEEN DAMNED AND REJECTED. O omnipotent Divine Majesty, HOW GREAT A WISDOM, AND AN INFINITY OF INEFFABLE MYSTERIES, WE MORTALS ARE COMPELLED TO CONFESS TO INHERE IN THY TITTLES AND IOTAS, DESCRIBED AND DISPOSED IN THY LAW: IF THE GREATEST EARTHLY SECRETS AND ARCANA, OF THIS ONE POINT, PLACED AND EXAMINED BY ME (BUT IN THY LIGHT), MAY BE EXPLAINED BY VARIOUS INDICATION AND MOST FAITHFULLY DEMONSTRATED; namely, of the POINT in the divine TERNARY, by no means SUPERFLUOUS: BUT OF THE POINT in the KINGDOM OF THE FOUR ELEMENTS
O F
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

C O N S I D E R E D, indeed F O U L, C O R R U P T I B L E, S H A D O W Y. O thrice and four times blessed are those who can A T T A I N that P O I N T of the T E R N A R Y, as it were C O R R E L A T I V E: and can C O N S I G N that T E T R O U S and S U P E R F L U O U S point of the Q U A T E R N A R Y, and leave it to the Prince of Darkness. Thus we shall attain the ornaments of S N O W Y  B R I G H T N E S S and W H I T E  G A R M E N T S: O M A X I M I L I A N, whom God may someday make Greatest (by this mystagogy, or by some one of the Austrian Family), to the honour of His Dread Name—even if I myself be sleeping in Christ—in these, those abominable Darknesses (the Points superfluous on E A R T H), and further, intolerable. But lest I myself now pour forth superfluous words (not
E 4
M O N A S

namely, in a fitting place), let me now betake myself within the bounds of my purpose. And, since I have now finished my discourse for those whose Eyes are in the seat of their Heart: now I must turn my speech to those whose Hearts still protrude in their eyes. What we have said in this place, behold, the figure inscribed upon the C R O S S can in some manner represent. First, concerning the P O I N T, N E C E S S A R Y in Two Equal L I N E S (crossed equally and unequally), as here, at A. Then, at B, you see, as it were, a certain vacancy of the superfluous Point having been removed, distin-
[Visual material: PDF page 76, region 4]
ctly, F O U R straight Lines: S E P A R A T E D from the P O I N T formerly common to them: with no detriment to them resulting therefrom. This is the
way,
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

the way through which Our M O N A S, proceeding through the Binary and the T E R N A R Y,
is restored to itself as One, in the Purified Q U A T E R N A R Y, through the Proportion of E-
quality. (For every Whole is Equal to all its parts.) And while this is done, Our M O N A S meanwhile admits nothing of External Units or Num-
bers: since it most exactly Suffices unto itself, by all its most absolute Num-
bers. Into the Amplitude of which it is spread abroad, now by Magical modes: now, afterward, by the not common Industry of the Artificer, and to the greatest Emolument of the Monad itself (in Dignity and Power), it is Restored to its First and Proper M A T T E R: in the meantime, those things which do not pertain to its genuine and hereditary Proportion having by every means and diligence been cut away, and rejected for ever as Dregs.
MONAS

THEORY XXI.

IF that which, in the recesses of our MONAD, lay hidden inwardly, enfolded, were brought forth into the light; and, positions having been exchanged, its Primary Parts, such as were Exterior, were enclosed in the Middle Place, what Philosophical Transformation of the MONAD would thence result, ye have seen above: but now we shall propose to you another Local Transposition of the Mystical MONAD: those Parts from which the Characters of our Hieroglyphics of the SUPERIOR PLANETS first offered themselves to us, being here raised upward: and, by like reasoning, thereafter assigning to the remaining Planets severally that Position which Plato seems almost to ascribe to them: if they be rightly taken from that Position. For at the very Arietine Summit, Saturn, Jupiter,
[Visual material: PDF page 78, region 5]
Mars:
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

Mars: then, descending, the Cross is inserted for Venus and Mercury. Finally follow the Sun itself, and the lowest MOON. But these matters are to be discussed elsewhere: nevertheless, I did not wish to conceal these Philosophical Treasures of our MONAD. And thus we deemed it advisable to give one reason why the Position of the MONAD should be thus changed. But see and hear other and greater matters concerning this Position, which I know to be to your advantage, and which must be explained in few words. Let us therefore distribute the MONAD (placed in this new manner) into the Anatomical Members B. D. C. Where, in that new TERNARY, D and C themselves are familiar FIGURES, even to rustics. But that THIRD, which is denoted by B, cannot so easily be recognized by all. Nor indeed is that
[Visual material: PDF page 79, region 4]
M O N A D

to be considered lightly: that those three noted FORMS, D and C, separate and different from that B, show ESSENCES: secondly, that the horns of that C are seen to be turned downward, as though toward the EARTH: and that that part of D which illuminates C itself looks downward toward the earth; in the centre of which alone is the Visible POINT: truly TERRESTRIAL. And that, finally, both D and C make their Hieroglyphic indication here toward the lower places rather than does B. Now Earth, hieroglyphically, can denote STABILITY and FIXITY to us. What, therefore, D and C may be, I leave to be concluded thence. Whence anyone can now also note a great SECRET: concerning the former SUN and MOON, of which we have spoken, how they can hence receive a fuller, and most necessary, interpretation,
receive-
HIEROGLYPHICS.

can receive: those, indeed, up to this place having been placed upward, and with the Lunar Horns raised upward. But enough concerning this. Let us now examine the NATURE of that THIRD, according to the Foundations of our Hieroglyphic Art. First, it seems to bear a DOUBLE MOON upon its Head. Or our Aries, (but mystically inverted.) Next, it has attached the Hieroglyphic Sign of the Elements. So far as concerns the Doubled MOON, it can thus be explained (according to the subject matter): A DOUBLE DEGREE OF THE MOON. We speak of those degrees which experts in Natural Philosophy can find to be only four among all created NATURES. Namely, TO BE, TO LIVE, TO SENSE, and TO UNDERSTAND. Therefore, noting that the first Two of these Degrees are present in this, we shall say thus: THE MOON EXISTING, LIVING
M O N A D

But some define Life by Motion. Now there are six most well-known Species of MOTION. Certainly, the CROSS which is joined to it signifies that the Artifice of the Elements is here required. Moreover, in these our Theories, we have very often taught that the SEMICIRCLE is the Hieroglyphic of the MOON: so too, that the entire Circle signifies the SUN: but here there are two Semicircles; yet SEPARATE (nevertheless joined at a common POINT), which, if they be fittingly joined together (as indeed they can be by art), can represent to us a SOLAR and Circular Plenitude. From these things considered together, it is evident that we can thus set forth, summarily and hieroglyphically, this Proposition. THE MOON, EXISTING, LIVING, TO BE DEALT WITH THROUGH THE MASTERY OF THE ELEMENTS: HAVING THE POWER THAT IT MAY REPRE-
SENT
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

FEELS FULLNESS, with its semicircles
at the same time connected by art. Let it therefore be completed: and let that (which we have called) CIRCLE come to be: as we have here marked it by the letter E. Let us therefore remember, first, that this SOLAR DEGREE was not encountered by us in Nature, but is now ARTIFICIAL AND MADE: and indeed, that it presented itself to us at first sight; and by its Nature (namely in B), with its Parts Loose, Fluid, dissolved; not COMPACTED SOLIDLY into a Solar Spe-
cies. Secondly, that the Semidiameter of these Semicircles is not equal to the Semidiameter of D and C (born thus to us, and most well known to all), but much Smaller. Whence it is Clear: that B itself is not of so great an Extent as D and C themselves are. And E itself well confirms this to us: by that Circular operation, from B, advanced into the Species E,

80
M O N A S

there arises for us thence the Character of V E N U S alone. We have therefore now made plain, by these Hieroglyphic Syllogisms: From B, a true D is not to be hoped for. Nor was there at first a true C in the nature of B: whence there was not a T R U E, living M O O N. You may therefore now also doubt concerning L I F E and Motion: whether they are truly and Naturally so disposed: yet, as we have now elucidated for the Prudent, at the least, A N A L O G I C A L indeed are A L L things which are spoken in a similar phrase (concerning B): just as also those things which above we briefly touched upon concerning C and D, A N A L O G I C A L L Y, properly suit B itself with its E L E M E N T S. Those things also which we have adduced concerning the Nature of Aries ought exactly to agree with this: since it bears the same Figure of that one in its head (although inverted): and likewise the same Mystical Mark of the Elements is joined to B itself.
When
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

When nevertheless from this Anatomy we see that, from the single body of our M O N A D (thus dissected by art), this new T E R N A R Y has proceeded. Thence we cannot doubt that MEMBERS of this sort will embrace a mutual S Y M P A T H Y among themselves, and will, as it were of their own accord, admit a MOST ABSOLUTE MONADIC U N I O N: thus in these MEMBERS the M A G N E T I C virtue is vigorous.

Finally, I wished to note this (for the sake of refreshing the mind): that B itself most readily presents to us as many RUSTIC letters as it bears Points, to be beheld above, upon its head, and as it were its Forehead: namely,
[Visual material: PDF page 85, region 5]

those three: as also another, as it were six: (but in sum, thrice three) very ROUGH and unpolished, fluid and turning: so that you may see them to have been made from one or more Semicircles. But, of Experts
M O N A S

in letters, a firmer and more stable method of F O R M I N G T H O S E L E T T E R S is in the hands. I had before my eyes an infinity of Mysteries here: but I wished to break off those matters with this Sportive Theory. Yet I understand that the endeavor of certain persons has advanced me not a little: If, our M O N A D restored to its former Mystical Position, and its individual Members artificially joined together, I should at least admonish and exhort those same persons to investigate more carefully, N O W, W H O that A R I E T I N E F I R E of the F I R S T T R I P L I C I T Y was. W H O that Equinoctial one of ours was. W H O was the cause that the S U N could be E X A L T E D A B O V E I T S C O M M O N D E G R E E: and to run through very many other preceding matters with S E C O N D, W I S E R M E D I T A T I O N S. But we, now hastening to other matters, wish only to point out the way to others with the finger (upon which
they ought to tread
HIEROGLYPHICS.
they ought to tread), not only amicably, but also most faithfully: nevertheless keeping silent, as we have said, concerning the conspicuous infinity of other Mysteries.

THEOREM XXII.

That the Mysteries of our MONAD have not yet been exhausted will readily be clear. If I should now exhibit for the contemplation of Your Royal Serenity certain more secret Vessels of the SACRED ART (indeed wholly Cabalistic ones), to be revealed only to the Initiated, cautiously taken from the workshop of the same MONAD. Therefore, when EVERY BOND of our MONAD has been Wisely DISSOLVED, let us add literal marks to the individual parts (for the sake of distinction): as you will see done here. We warn, therefore, that a is a certain artificial Vessel, from A and B: with what is common to both, and already

by making manifest the SEMIDIAMETER) itself indeed made M, and differing from the first letter of the Greek Alphabet by this letter alone, through a local transposition of the parts: as you see.
[Visual material: PDF page 88, region 4]

For from a Straight Line, a Circle, and a Semicircle, we are the first now to teach its true and mystical Symmetry (although we also warned above that the same can be made from a Circle and a Semicircle: yet all things fall back upon the same mystical proposition). But λ and δ are, first indeed, as it were images of other Vessels: (λ, indeed, of GLASS.
[Visual material: PDF page 88, region 6]
But δ, of Earth.) Yet, in the second place, λ and δ can remind us of a certain Pestle and
Mortar,

Mortar, for preparing such materials (of the old sort), so that with these we may grind into the most subtle powders artificial unperforated Pearls, crystalline and beryl-like Plates; then precious Chrysoliths and Rubies; Carbuncles and other very rare artificial Stones. Finally, that which you see marked with ω is a very small Vessel, most full of Mysteries; and differing from the very last letter of the Greek Alphabet (now restored to its first instituted mystagogy) solely through a manifest local transposition of its parts: it too consisting of two Semicircles. Moreover, concerning the ordinary necessities of Vessels, both their shapes and the Materials (from which they ought to be made), there is no need for us to speak here. translations.title: T H E O R. XXIII.

paragraphs.text: T H E O R E M.  XXIII.

The symmetries now observed by us in the Hieroglyphic Construction of our MONAD, and to be observed by those who will find it pleasing to carry the same in rings or seals, or otherwise to possess it, we here set forth accurately noted. In the Name of JESUS CHRIST, crucified for us (whose Spirit, swiftly, makes me who write these things through Him to be merely a pen, and
I desire,
HIEROGLYPHICS.

I desire and hope.) From the CROSS of our ELEMENTS, we shall now seek all these Measures. Or indeed by this reasoning (according to the subject-matter of the proposed argument): Because, beneath the Heaven of the MOON, whatever takes the beginning of its Generation is either compacted from the FOUR Elements, or is itself an ELEMENTAL ESSENCE; and this in various modes not commonly known. And because in no created thing are the Elements themselves in equal proportion or power, yet by Art they can be reduced to equality in certain things (as in those of the Sophists): in our CROSS we establish equal and unequal parts. Which, by another reasoning, we may call the Same and the Different, or the One and the Many. Admitting in secret the Pro-
M O N A D

perty of the equilateral CROSS (as we have noted above). But if we were to bring forward individually the reasons of the SYMMETRIES set down here (which we maintain), or otherwise demonstrate their causes than we have done sufficiently abundantly throughout this whole little work for the Wise, we should not without cause overstep the limits prescribed to us for our purpose.

Let some point be taken in a plane, for example A: through it let a sufficiently long straight line be drawn on both sides, namely C, A, K. And upon the line K, C, at point A, let a perpendicular be raised, extended on both sides to a sufficient length (Geometers customarily say, to infinity, prudently forestalling inconveniences), which may be admitted to be D, A, E. Now upon A, K let any point be taken, and let it be B. The proportion A, B (that is, the common measure of our work) having now been taken, let its triple be taken from
from A to-
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

ward C, and let it be set as AC. Let AE be made double AB. And let AD be double AB. Thus the whole DE is quadruple AB. Thus, therefore, we have made our ELEMENTAL CROSS, from AB, AC, AD, and AE: that is, from a QUATERNARY of lines. Now from BK let a straight line equal to AD itself be cut off, and let it be BI. With centre I and interval IB, let the circle BR be described, cutting the straight line AK at point R. From point R, toward K, let a straight line equal to AB itself be cut off, and let it be RK. At point K let straight lines of sufficient length be drawn on both sides (at right angles to AK itself), and let them be P, K, F. From that point K, toward F, let there be cut off
[Visual material: PDF page 95, region 4]

a straight line equal to AD itself, and let it be K, F. Then, with centre K and interval KF, let the semicircle F, L, P be described, so that F, K, P is its diameter. Finally, at point C let a perpendicular be drawn to the straight line A, C, extended on both sides to a sufficient length, and let it be O, C, Q. Afterwards, from line C, Q and at point C, let a straight line equal to line A, B be taken, and let it be C, M. With centre M and interval M, C, let the semicircle C, H, O be described, of which C, M, O is the diameter. And finally, by a like method, from the straight line C, Q and at point C let a line equal to AB itself be cut off, and let it be C, N. Therefore, with centre N and length N, C, let the semicircle C, G, Q be made, of which C, N, Q is the diameter. I now assert that all the requisite SYMMETRIES in our M O N A D have been explained and described.
    Yet it is fitting to warn the mechanic
M O N A D

that the entire line C, K consists of nine such parts as our FUNDAMENTAL A, B is one. Whence he may approach by another way to complete this same work. Next, all the diameters and semidiameters ought here to be marked with faint lines (as mechanics speak). Nor should any visible CENTRE be left, except the Solar Centre, which here he sees marked by the letter I. No letters are to be added; then, for ornament (not for any mystical necessity, to be considered by us now on that account), the mechanic may add to the Solar circumference a superficial breadth (one parallel having been drawn within). The distance of the parallels, however, may be made a fourth or fifth part of A, B, or thereabouts. But to the Lunar [circumference], let him assign that appearance which it customarily has first after its conjunction
with-
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.
the Sun.
conjunction-
M O N A S

junction, to appear in Heaven: namely, very horned. This will occur if, from point K, towards R, that fourth or fifth part of the line A B (of which we spoke) is taken; and, upon the end of that line, as centre, but with the lunar semidiameter, this second part of the circumference is drawn, tending towards either contact of the former semicircle. Something similar may be done at points M and N: perpendiculars having been raised there; in which a sixth part, or a smaller part, of A B itself is taken: where, a centre having been made, but with M, C, and N, C, as semidiameters, let those second, as it were semicircles, be drawn externally. Finally, through the straight lines of our Cross themselves, parallels may on either side be extended, distant from the middles by an eighth or a tenth part—
[Visual material: PDF page 98, region 4]
HIEROGLYPHICS.

—of A, B itself: so that our CROSS may thus be composed, as it were, of FOUR linear surfaces, whose width is a fourth or fifth part of the straight line AB itself. I have wished, in the appended figure, to sketch these ornaments in some fashion. Each person may do all these things according to the judgment of his own mind: provided meanwhile that no injury (or the least possible) be inflicted upon our Mystical SYMMETRIES; lest, by that very negligence, in the progress of time, the Discipline of those true (and most necessary) Hieroglyphical Commensurations be disturbed and perish—a discipline far broader and greater than we either could, or indeed wished, to explain in this little book. As the Daughter of Time, by GOD'S NOD, TRUTH will teach.
M O N A S

BUT we shall now methodically set before the eyes certain matters concerning those things which can be obvious to anyone in those necessary Symmetries of the MONAD. Beginning first, indeed, from the QUATERNARY of the Lines of our CROSS, with that respect in which anyone can simply declare that there are FOUR Lines. Then, concerning the QUATERNARY of those same lines, according as they have a particular and Mystical division and relation in another way. Thirdly, by some examples, we shall show to some persons that the Numbers which we have artfully elicited, whether in that place or from other Theories throughout the whole little book, have certain useful Offices appointed by God in NATURE; and we shall introduce other things in suitable places, which, if rightly understood, will bear no small fruit: and we shall dispatch these matters very briefly.
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

GOREAN QUATERNARY.

With however many Numbers described in natural order from the First Monad: if, from the First to the Last, a continued multiplication be made—thus, the product of the First into the Second into the Third; and that product into the Fourth; and in like manner unto the last—the final product determines every Possible
M O N A S

Metathesis in all those places. And by the same reasoning, in any number whatsoever of such diverse things. This Operation I most highly commend to thee, O KING, as most useful both in every examination of Nature and in other affairs of the Commonwealth. I am accustomed to use this in the Hebrew Tziruph (or Thmura) with the greatest delight.
[Visual material: PDF page 102, region 4]
QUA-
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.
[Visual material: PDF page 103, region 3]

I am not unaware that Euclid could have brought forth into light very many other Numbers from the Arithmetic Virtue and FORMALITY of the QUATERNARY. But he who has not perceived that by THESE a great obscurity of Nature is unfolded and illuminated, would not feel his own intellect blunted by their greater multitude. Therefore, in our Numbers (as we have promised)
G 2

how much Authority resides, in WEIGHING THE ELEMENTS, in determining the MEASURES OF TIMES, and finally in prescribing certain DEGREES to the Power and Virtue of Things, we set forth to be weighed from the following Schemas.

From these Schemas, more can be drawn forth (if they are considered more deeply) than it is fitting to express in plain words. Yet, before the rest, one singular thing must be noted: that a Reason has here been set in the middle, on account of which the QUATERNARY, or the DENARY, imposes a certain limit upon Numerations; and we assert that the cause which our Elders adduced was not complete and exact, but rather this one which we shall now relate.
After that MONAD has been restored to itself wholly and fully, physically-
[Visual material: PDF page 107, region 4]
and, (then indeed it is
[Visual material: PDF page 107, region 6]
MONAD, MOST UNITARY,
[Visual material: PDF page 107, region 8]

and UNITY judged by the Magi)
is neither in the power of NATURE, nor of any
ART, TO IMPEL THE SAME
MORE OFTEN THAN FOUR TIMES,
through
G 4
M O N A D

Supercelestial Revolutions, to impel [it]
to make any Progress or MOTION:
(And thence is begotten
That One, which, on account of its
eminence, we wish thus to be marked,)
and for this reason, because neither in the Elemen-
tal world, nor in the Celestial, nor in the SU-
PERCÆLESTIAL, is there any POWER,
CREATED AND INFLUENTIAL: Which,
then, shall not have been most absolutely Enriched
and Endowed.
[Visual material: PDF page 108, region 4]

The true Effect of this [thing],
FOUR most distinguished Men, philosophizing
together (formerly), attained by their Work:
Whence, for a long time, Astonished by the
Greatest Miracle of the Thing, at length they
turned themselves wholly thereafter to singing
and proclaiming the Praises of God, Best and Greatest.
Who, by that means, had bestowed upon them such
Wisdom, and, over the other CREATURES,
Power and most ample Dominion.
THEORY.
HIEROGLYPHICS.

THEORY XXIV.

AS we began the Exordium of this little Book of ours from a Point, a Straight Line, and a Circle: and thus from our MONADIC POINT drew out the extreme LINEAR efflux of our ELEMENTS into a Circle, nearly analogous to the Equinoctial itself, which completes its revolution in 24 hours: SO now at last we shall bring to completion, and shall terminate with this our Twenty-Fourth Theory, THE ALL-MODAL METATHESIS OF THE QUATERNARY (defined by the number 24), AND ITS METAMORPHOSIS: unto the HONOUR AND GLORY of Him WHO (as John, chief priest of the Divine Mysteries, testifies, in the FOURTH part, the LAST, of the FOURTH Chapter of the Apocalypse) sits upon the Throne: in the midst of whose CIRCUIT—
M O N A D

—ARE four living creatures, each having SIX WINGS, which, without rest, DAY and NIGHT, say:
Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty: WHO Was, and WHO Is, and WHO is to come:
WHOM also the 24 ELDERS, falling down from the 24 seats set about in a CIRCUIT (CASTING DOWN THEIR GOLDEN CROWNS), worship, saying: Worthy art thou, O Lord, to receive GLORY and HONOUR and POWER: BECAUSE THOU HAST CREATED ALL THINGS: and because of THY WILL THEY ARE, AND WERE CREATED. AMEN.
SAYS
THE FOURTH LETTER,
A.
To whom,
H I E R O G L Y P H I C S.

To whom God gave the will and ability to consign this Divine Mystery thus to the everlasting memorials of letters, and most peacefully to bring these his labours to completion, begun on the 25th day of January of the same 13th year:
In the year 1564, at Antwerp.

items.text: Quaestio regens est quomodo unus character hieroglyphicus totius sapientiae compendium praebere atque publicationem simul exigere et restringere possit.
Thesis principalis Monadem proponit ut formam exactam, mathematice roboratam et divinitus fundatam, quae litteras, numeros, figuras caelestes, naturam et mysteria metaphysica connectat.
Argumentatio apologetica, reconstructiva, polemica et strategica est: artem restituit, eius legitimam naturam defendit, falsas similitudines excludit et condiciones transmissionis constituit.
Motus incipit a raritate philosophi veri et per gradus physicos, caelestes atque supercaelestes ad raritatem muneris ascendit.
Raritas muneris per exactam compositionem characteris et per eius fecunditatem trans disciplinas comprobatur.
Defensio a distinctione inter corpora doctrinarum verarum et umbras imitationum falsarum pendet.
Conclusio practica coniungit iudicium regium, reproductionem typographicam exactam et circulationem ad lectores idoneos restrictam.
Omnia visibilia invisibiliaque a Deo emanant et eius bonitatem, sapientiam potentiamque significant.
Creatio est scriptum divinum in creaturis exaratum atque humanae investigationi legibile.
Litterae mysticae primariae a Deo procedunt, earumque figurae ex punctis, lineis rectis et circulorum peripheriis componuntur.
In forma Monadis nullum punctum superfluum aut semanticamente vacuum est.
Unitas immota pluralitatem consubstantialem et ordinate distinctam intra se continere potest.
Character Monadis figuras astronomicas dispersas in unam formam symmetricam restituit.
Interpretatio hieroglyphica lumen et robur mathematicum possidet.
Eadem structura monadica per analogiam in pluribus artibus diversas potentias explicare potest.
Cabala realis signa ex tota creatione, non ex una tantum lingua scripta, colligit.
Quo altior est gradus philosophiae, eo rarior est facultas eum sincere comprehendendi.
Iudicium validum de mysteriis perfectam amplitudinis eorum cognitionem praesupponit.
Scientiae honestae sunt corpora solida, artes autem adulteratae earum umbrae inanes sunt.
Corpora et umbrae terminis, figuris atque phrasibus communibus uti possunt.
Demonstratio propria, non auctoritas humana, assensum philosophicum fundat.
Bonitas muneris in fecunditate honesta, sincera, pia et dignitati humanae apta consistit.
Receptio ab hominibus imperitis errorem, imposturam, negationem vel accusationem generare potest.
Exactitudo typographica est condicio integritatis doctrinalis operis.
Iustitia regia veras artes ab earum umbris discernere et contra iudicia imperitorum protegere potest.
Monas non est character mortuus, mutus aut mere barbarus.
Interpretatio hieroglyphica non est violenta, impropria aut formae extrinsecus imposita.
Cabala realis non terminatur litteris ab homine scribibilibus neque finibus unius linguae.
Opus fidem suam ab Hermete, Pythagora aliisque antiquis non mendicat.
Magia vera non identificatur cum impietate, scelere aut superstitione vulgari.
Similitudo nominis non sufficit ut studium honestum cum arte falsa condemnetur.
Mysteria non destinantur indiscriminatae multitudinis usui.
Typographia non est medium semanticamente indifferens.
Occultatio per figuras umbratiles non est necessario deceptio, si veritatem ab usu indigno protegit.
Natura tota fit campus semioticus in quo res creatae simul obiecta et signa divinorum attributorum sunt.
Geometria elementaris pontem constituit inter alphabetum, mathematicam et ordinem rerum.
Monas operatur ut machina compressionis, qua unitas formaliter minima pluralitatem interpretationum ordinatarum generat.
Concordia effectuum per multas disciplinas adductorum rarae fecunditatis atque bonitatis muneris testis efficitur.
Cabala realis linguam sacram universalizat, quia idem Deus omnibus gentibus per creationem signa praebet.
Corruptio umbratilis artis existentiam corporis veri non infirmat.
Iudicium iustum usum, structuram et finem artis examinare debet potius quam vocabulum commune.
Publicatio legitima reproductionem exactam cum delectu recipientium coniungere debet.
Approbatio regia munus tutelae et discriminationis habet, non locum demonstrationis intrinsecae.
Velamentum doctrinale fit instrumentum tutelae, quia communitas figurarum veritatem celare potest sine eius abolitione.
Disciplinae particulares reordinantur ut projectiones analogicae unius ordinis divini et monadici, non ut regiones penitus autonomae.
Accessus epistemicus simul gradualis et moralis est, quia altitudo obiecti, amplitudo cognitionis et sinceritas investigatoris inter se conectuntur.
Corpus materiale libri pars machinae conceptualis fit, quoniam corruptio puncti, lineae aut schematis doctrinam ipsam mutilat.
Universalitas scripturae creationis non producit universalem aequalitatem accessus, sed publicum duplicem: omnes signis circumdantur, pauci ea recte interpretantur.
Potestas regia tamquam ars distinctionis reconstituitur, cui competit corpora doctrinalia ab umbris homonymis separare.
Repudiatio vulgi contra systema non necessario fit contra-testimonium, quia defectus comprehensionis ipsam repudiationem explicare potest.
Falsum esse oportet disciplinas absolutis finibus clausas neque ad commune principium reducibiles esse.
Falsum esse oportet signa esse mera instituta conventionalia rebus quas significant extrinseca.
Falsum esse oportet publicam accessibilitatem esse condicionem necessariam veritatis.
Falsum esse oportet similitudinem vocabuli vel figurae identitatem rei probare.
Falsum esse oportet auctoritatem, antiquitatem aut consensum per se demonstrationem constituere.
Falsum esse oportet materiam typographicam sensui transmisso indifferentem esse.
Falsum esse oportet unitatem et pluralitatem ordinatam mutuo excludi.
Falsum esse oportet abusus artis corpus verae artis tollere.
Expositio omnino perspicua et indiscriminatim omnibus tradita habetur ut possibilitas epistemice et moraliter inadmissibilis.
Tribunal externum, neutrum et a perfecta mysteriorum cognitione solutum, intra systema nullam competentiam ultimam obtinet.
Separatio absoluta inter characterem et rem significatam praecluditur, quia forma hieroglyphica vim realem et operativam continere ponitur.
Divortium absolutum inter contemplationem sacram, scientiam naturalem et operationem technicam excluditur.
Deus → emanatio rerum → creatio ut scriptura → signa visibilia et invisibilia → inquisitio attributorum divinorum.
Signa dispersa → reductio ad punctum, lineam et circulum → compositio monadica exacta → validatio mathematica.
Monas exacta → projectiones analogicae per disciplinas → testimonia concordantia → raritas fecunda → bonitas muneris.
Communitas nominum et figurarum → confusio corporis cum umbra → cognitio integra → discretio iusta → tutela regia.
Arcanum doctrinale → exemplar materialiter exactum → typographia fidelis → lector idoneus → cognitio legitima.
Typographia neglegens aut circulatio promiscua → mutilatio sensus → labyrinthus interpretativus → impostura, negatio vel accusatio.

Raritas philosophi veri → raritas muneris → reductio signorum ad unitatem geometricam → fecunditas trans disciplinas → universalitas Cabalae realis → distinctio corporis et umbrae → iudicium regium → impressio exacta et circulatio selectiva.
Character astronomicus ex nota mortua in condensatum semanticum et operativum reclassificatur.
Grammatica ex disciplina litterarum humanarum in ontologiam signorum creationis dilatatur.
Disciplinae separatae in manifestationes analogicas unius ordinis monadici convertuntur.
Oppositio inter scientiam et magiam substituitur distinctione inter corpus verum et umbram adulteratam.
Typographia ex vehiculo externo in operationem constitutivam sensus mutatur.
Regnum ex patrocinio ornamentali in tribunal distinctionis et tutelam cognitionis reconfiguratur.
Publicum non amplius dividitur inter cognoscentes et omnino exclusos, sed inter eos qui signis communibus recte vel perperam utuntur.
Surface — Praefatio raritatem, bonitatem et dignitatem Monadis defendit atque opus regi et typographo committit.
Structural — Mechanismus consistit in reductione pluralitatis signorum ad formam geometricam exactam et in re-expansione eius per analogias disciplinarias.
Metastrategic — Certamen de magia, Cabala et artibus occultis in quaestionem discriminationis inter corpora et umbras transfertur, simulque accessus et transmissio reguntur.

Ontological/Temporal — Realitas ut emanatio divina et scriptura legibilis ponitur, unitas pluralitatem continet, iar ars praesens simul ut nova constitutio et ut sapientiae priscae restitutio temporalis exhibetur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem a scriptura creationis per compressionem monadicam ad tutelam transmissionis.
Demonstrationes particulares et nexus operativi inter characterem et effectus promissos in hac unitate nondum satis determinantur.
Structura interne cohaeret quatenus forma exacta, analogia disciplinaris et discretio recipientium ex eodem principio significationis necessariae deducuntur.
Firmissima commissura est coniunctio inter minutias formales, integritatem interpretationis et necessitatem typographiae fidelis.
Clausura fragilis oritur ex regula qua nemo nisi amplitudinem mysteriorum iam comprehendens de eis valide iudicare potest.
Universalitas Cabalae realis et inexcusabilitas generis humani cum prohibitione circulationis promiscuae in tensione manent.
Repudiatio auctoritatis humanae cum usu Maximiliani tamquam testis privilegiati et defensoris nondum plene conciliatur.
Ars inter primam constitutionem novam et revocationem traditionis extinctae ambigue collocatur.
Multa effecta disciplinaria vi enumerationis et promissionis potius quam demonstratione intra frontem materiae nituntur.
Restitutio motum verum servat: raritas → unitas formalis → fecunditas universalis → discriminatio → transmissio custodita.
The governing question is how a single hieroglyphic character can provide a compendium of all wisdom and simultaneously require and restrict publication.
The principal thesis presents the Monad as an exact form, mathematically reinforced and divinely grounded, which connects letters, numbers, celestial figures, nature, and metaphysical mysteries.
The argument is apologetic, reconstructive, polemical, and strategic: it restores the art, defends its legitimate nature, excludes false resemblances, and establishes the conditions of transmission.
The movement begins from the rarity of the true philosopher and ascends through physical, celestial, and supercelestial degrees to the rarity of the gift.
The rarity of the gift is demonstrated through the exact composition of the character and through its fruitfulness across disciplines.
The defense depends upon the distinction between bodies of true doctrines and the shadows of false imitations.
The practical conclusion joins royal judgment, exact typographical reproduction, and circulation restricted to suitable readers.
All visible and invisible things emanate from God and signify His goodness, wisdom, and power.
Creation is a divine writing inscribed in creatures and legible to human investigation.
The primary mystical letters proceed from God, and their figures are composed of points, straight lines, and the circumferences of circles.
In the form of the Monad, no point is superfluous or semantically empty.
Immovable unity can contain within itself plurality that is consubstantial and orderly distinguished.
The character of the Monad restores dispersed astronomical figures into one symmetrical form.
Hieroglyphic interpretation possesses mathematical illumination and strength.
The same monadic structure can, by analogy, explicate diverse powers in several arts.
Real Cabala gathers signs from the whole of creation, not from only one written language.
The higher the degree of philosophy, the rarer is the capacity sincerely to comprehend it.
A valid judgment concerning mysteries presupposes perfect knowledge of their scope.
Honest sciences are solid bodies, whereas adulterated arts are their empty shadows.
Bodies and shadows can employ common terms, figures, and phrases.
Proper demonstration, not human authority, grounds philosophical assent.
The goodness of the gift consists in fruitfulness that is honest, sincere, pious, and suited to human dignity.
Reception by unlearned persons can generate error, imposture, denial, or accusation.
Typographical exactness is a condition of the work's doctrinal integrity.
Royal justice can distinguish true arts from their shadows and protect them against the judgments of the unlearned.
The Monad is not a dead, mute, or merely barbarous character.
Hieroglyphic interpretation is not violent, improper, or imposed extrinsically upon the form.
Real Cabala is not confined to letters writable by man or to the boundaries of one language.
The work does not beg its credibility from Hermes, Pythagoras, or other ancients.
True magic is not identified with impiety, crime, or vulgar superstition.
Resemblance of name does not suffice for an honest study to be condemned together with a false art.
Mysteries are not intended for the use of an indiscriminate multitude.
Typography is not a semantically indifferent medium.
Concealment through shadowy figures is not necessarily deception, if it protects truth from unworthy use.
All nature becomes a semiotic field in which created things are at once objects and signs of divine attributes.
Elementary geometry establishes a bridge between alphabet, mathematics, and the order of things.
The Monad operates as a compression machine, by which formally minimal unity generates a plurality of ordered interpretations.
The concordance of effects brought forth across many disciplines becomes a witness to the rare fruitfulness and goodness of the gift.
Real Cabala universalizes sacred language, because the same God provides signs through creation to all peoples.
The shadowy corruption of an art does not weaken the existence of a true body.
Just judgment must examine the use, structure, and end of an art rather than a common term.
Legitimate publication must join exact reproduction with the selection of recipients.
Royal approval has a function of protection and discrimination, not the place of intrinsic demonstration.
The doctrinal veil becomes an instrument of protection, because the communality of figures can conceal truth without abolishing it.
Particular disciplines are reordered as analogical projections of one divine and monadic order, not as wholly autonomous regions.
The epistemic approach is at once gradual and moral, because the height of the object, the scope of knowledge, and the sincerity of the investigator are interconnected.
The material body of the book becomes part of the conceptual machine, since corruption of a point, line, or diagram mutilates the doctrine itself.
The universality of the writing of creation does not produce universal equality of access, but a twofold public: all are surrounded by signs; few interpret them correctly.
Royal power is reconstituted as an art of distinction, to which it belongs to separate doctrinal bodies from homonymous shadows.
Rejection by the vulgar against the system does not necessarily become counter-testimony, because failure of comprehension can explain the rejection itself.
It must be false that disciplines are closed within absolute boundaries and cannot be reduced to a common principle.
It must be false that signs are merely conventional institutions extrinsic to the things they signify.
It must be false that public accessibility is a necessary condition of truth.
It must be false that similarity of word or figure proves identity of thing.
It must be false that authority, antiquity, or consensus in itself constitutes demonstration.
It must be false that typographical material is indifferent to the sense transmitted.
It must be false that unity and ordered plurality mutually exclude one another.
It must be false that abuse of an art removes the body of the true art.
An exposition wholly clear and delivered indiscriminately to all is regarded as an epistemically and morally inadmissible possibility.
An external and neutral tribunal, freed from perfect knowledge of the mysteries, obtains no ultimate competence within the system.
An absolute separation between the character and the thing signified is precluded, because the hieroglyphic form is posited to contain real and operative force.
An absolute divorce between sacred contemplation, natural science, and technical operation is excluded.
God → emanation of things → creation as writing → visible and invisible signs → inquiry into divine attributes.
Dispersed signs → reduction to point, line, and circle → exact monadic composition → mathematical validation.
Exact Monad → analogical projections across disciplines → concordant testimonies → fruitful rarity → goodness of the gift.
Communality of names and figures → confusion of body with shadow → integral knowledge → just discrimination → royal protection.
Doctrinal secret → materially exact exemplar → faithful typography → suitable reader → legitimate knowledge.
Negligent typography or indiscriminate circulation → mutilation of sense → interpretive labyrinth → imposture, denial, or accusation.

Rarity of the true philosopher → rarity of the gift → reduction of signs to geometric unity → fruitfulness across disciplines → universality of real Cabala → distinction of body and shadow → royal judgment → exact printing and selective circulation.
The astronomical character is reclassified from a dead sign into a semantic and operative condensate.
Grammar is expanded from a discipline of humane letters into an ontology of the signs of creation.
Separate disciplines are converted into analogical manifestations of one monadic order.
The opposition between science and magic is replaced by the distinction between true body and adulterated shadow.
Typography is transformed from an external vehicle into a constitutive operation of sense.
The kingdom is reconfigured from ornamental patronage into a tribunal of distinction and a protection of knowledge.
The public is no longer divided between those who know and those wholly excluded, but between those who use common signs rightly or wrongly.
Surface — The preface defends the rarity, goodness, and dignity of the Monad and entrusts the work to the king and the printer.
Structural — The mechanism consists in reducing a plurality of signs to an exact geometric form and re-expanding it through disciplinary analogies.
Metastrategic — The contest concerning magic, Cabala, and occult arts is transferred into a question of discrimination between bodies and shadows, while access and transmission are regulated.

Ontological/Temporal — Reality is posited as divine emanation and legible writing; unity contains plurality; and the present art is exhibited at once as a new constitution and as a temporal restoration of ancient wisdom.
The axioms suffice to restore the sequence from the writing of creation through monadic compression to the protection of transmission.
The particular demonstrations and operative links between the character and the promised effects are not yet sufficiently determined in this unit.
The structure coheres internally insofar as exact form, disciplinary analogy, and discrimination of recipients are deduced from the same principle of necessary signification.
The strongest joint is the connection between formal minutiae, integrity of interpretation, and the necessity of faithful typography.
A fragile closure arises from the rule that no one can validly judge mysteries unless already comprehending their scope.
The universality of real Cabala and the inexcusability of the human race remain in tension with the prohibition of indiscriminate circulation.
The repudiation of human authority is not yet fully reconciled with the use of Maximilian as a privileged witness and defender.
The art is ambiguously situated between a first new constitution and the revival of an extinct tradition.
Many disciplinary effects rest upon enumeration and promise rather than demonstration within the front matter.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement: rarity → formal unity → universal fruitfulness → discrimination → guarded transmission.
