identity.context: Chapters 19–25 · Theor. Xviii. · T H E Ò R. X I X. · T H E O R. X X. · Theor. Xxi. · Theor. Xxii. · T H E O R. Xxiii. · Theor. Xxiiii.

items.text: Systema quaerit quomodo character minimus ordines geometricos, cosmicos, materiales, temporales et numericos in unam machinam contrahere possit sine differentiarum abolitione.
Monas non est obiectum stabile, sed operator relationalis qui distinctiones producit, per media distribuit et per reditum ordinatum ad unitatem reformatam colligit.
Argumentatio est reconstructiva et transductiva: geometria invariantes secernit, analogia campos coniungit, operatio efficaciam probat, numerus autem mutationes commensurat.
Motus procedit a signo manifesto ad principium minimum, inde per differentiationes cosmicas et materiales, postremo ad commensurationem, consignationem et reditum finitum.
Progressio est spiralis, cumulativa et mutatione acta, quia singulus reditus relationem priorem servat dum eius campum, functionem aut statum auget.
Probatio non est deductio uniforme clausa, sed congruentia inter necessitatem formalem, mediationem materialem, operationem rectam, effectum et intellectum interpretis.
Necessitas geometrica in grammaticam translationis amplificatur, sed omnis transitus inter caelum, materiam, figuram et mysterium mediatore indiget quem analogia sola non supplet.
Forma expositionis propriam thesim perficit, quoniam figuras dividendo, convertendo, numerando et recomponendo unitatem transductivam quam affirmat actu constituit.
Clausura totius libri est duplex: potentiam creatam ad proportionem et principium finit, sed mysterium atque relationem occultam tamquam causas ulterioris interpretationis reservat.
[Persistent] Forma vel signum non rem iam constitutam passive imitatur, sed relationes manifestat, distribuit et in apparatum operationis convertit.
[Persistent] Relatio sive proportio identitatem et efficaciam terminorum antecedit; elementum est id quod intra configurationem generatricem agere potest.
[Emergent] Unitas monadica per distinctionem conservatur, quia divisio partes relatas producit quarum recompositio ampliorem unitatem efficit.
[Mutating] Identitas persistit ut invarians relationis per mutationem situs, medii et functionis, non ut substantia immobilis.
[Persistent] Geometria est grammatica ontologica et transductiva qua situs, centrum, sectio, vicinitas, circulatio et proportio in causalitatem convertuntur.
[Emergent] Causalitas est medialis, distributa et asymmetrica: principia, figurae, animae, radii, corpora et receptacula effectum participant, sed non aequaliter fundant.
[Mutating] Materia transit a termino receptivo ad nodum activum qui influxum nutrit, imprimit, reconfigurat et in circulationem remittit.
[Emergent] Tempus non est receptaculum praedatum, sed spiralis recursionis effectus quo apparitio, complementum, operatio et reditus statum relationis mutant.
[Mutating] Numerus ex mensura externa in operator qualitativum transit qui configurationem, permutationem, amplificationem et completionem temporalem ordinat.
[Emergent] Partialitas, subtractio, dissolutio et terminatio generativae fiunt cum relationem originis servant atque differentiam recomponibilem producunt.
[Persistent] Cognitio valida est reconstructiva et operativa: relationes generatrices persequitur atque interpretationem, operationem, effectum et dispositionem interpretis congruere postulat.
[Terminal] Ars potentia realis sed derivata est: configurationes mutat et potentias perficit localiter, neque originem, mensuram aut causalitatem suam absolute producit.
[Emergent] Ordines geometricus, cosmicus, materialis, numeralis, alphabeticus et doctrinalis sunt codices convertibiles, non regiones causaliter seiunctae.
[Terminal] Clausura legitima finitam restitutionem proportionis producit, sed saturationem semanticam impedit atque novum circuitum interpretativum relinquit.
[Attractor] Attractor totius libri est unitas monadica proportionalis, quae dispersionem formarum retrahit sine earum mutationibus in identitatem simplicem redigendis.
Punctum ab ingrediente minimo in centrum ontologicum et fontem fluxus amplificatur, deinde tamquam copula superflua excluditur et ut centrum effusionis restituitur.
Monas a nomine unitatis in functionem distributam, inde in attractorem conversionum et tandem in machinam internam originis, processus et finis mutatur.
Geometria a repertorio formarum transit ad medium commune causalitatum, grammaticam conversionis et instrumentum calibrationis transductivae.
Signum ex manifestatione productiva in operatorium relationum, deinde in apparatum materialiter condicionatum et consignationem disciplinae transmissibilem migrat.
Terra et corpus a locis cosmologicis aut receptaculis transeunt in nodos activos impressionis, nutritionis, compositionis et mensurae.
Circularitas a dependentia peripheriae et circulatione cosmica mutatur in circuitum conversionum, recursionem differentiae et formam finiti reditus.
Numerus ab extensione symbolica ad motorem compositionis, qualitatem configurationis et mensuram metamorphosis temporalis amplificatur.
Occultatio ex statu absentiae in residuum internum conversionis et tandem in mysterium consignabile sed inexhaustum transfertur.
Potentia agendi ex conversione dependentiae in operationem interpretativam transit, deinde ut ars configurativa realis sed causaliter limitata determinatur.
Clausura a peripheria generativa ad impressiones materiales et verbales progreditur, deinde in reditum finitum convertitur qui relationem occultam non consumit.
Exterioritas pura primum negatur, mediatio immediationi substituitur, postremo exterioritas in supplementum illicitum, condicionem ambientalem et causam ontologicam distingui debet.
Patrocinium, constructiones linearum, animalia symbolica et apparatus singulares localia manent; ascendit tantum regula quod relatio exacta condicionibus materialibus et figurativis sustentatur.
Sol, Luna, Mercurius et alii termini cosmici non fiunt substantiae globales; functiones mediationis, complementi, substitutionis et transductionis gradum libri ordinant.
Octonarius, quinarietas, quaternarius et XXIV localia discrimina retinent; globalis est tantum thesis numerum qualitatem configurationis et amplificationis exprimere.
Stillae, impressiones, materias et ambitus singulares non oportet universalizare; ascendit materialitas activa cuius efficacia a situ et compositione dependet.
Dependentia figurae a puncto et planetae a relatione in causalitatem distributam amplificatur, ubi nullum terminum effectum sibi soli appropriare licet.
Connexio inter formam, tempus et signum in machinam translatricem ascendit, cuius figura completa relationem, materiam et consignationem simul continet.
Apertura generativa priorum circuituum a clausura terminali non aboletur, sed per finitudinem causalitatis creatae et reditum ad principium qualificatur.
Correspondentiae particulares valent ut machinae locales translationis; non ascendunt in legem universalem nisi mediatio, mensura et necessitas transitus demonstrari possunt.
Signum passivum, ornamentale aut mere conventionale excluditur, quia figura relationem producere, operationem condicionare vel disciplinam consignare debet.
Autonomia termini excluditur: unitas, figura, materia et agens creatum solum intra relationes centri, mediationis, mensurae et principii operantur.
Materia passiva excluditur, quoniam receptio, nutritio, impressio et configuratio continuationem causalem constituunt.
Identitas fixa et unitas indivisa excluduntur, quia permanentia tantum per translationem functionis et relationem partium conservatur.
Tempus lineare praedatum et progressus creatus indefinitus excluduntur; tempus ex circuitibus finitis transformationis et reditus emergit.
Disciplinae clausae et sensus immediatus excluduntur, quia intellectus per conversionem codicum atque media figurativa procedit.
Numerus nudus et arithmetica a configuratione separata excluduntur, cum vis numeralis e situ, partitione et permutatione nascatur.
Demonstratio totaliter clausa et interpretatio exhaustiva excluduntur, quia mensura occulta et mysterium terminale ulteriorem reconstructionem exigunt.
Ars absoluta excluditur: operatio creata effectum realem efficere potest, sed essentiam naturalem, mensuram et fundamentum causalitatis ex nihilo non producit.
Falsum esse oportet realitatem continere residuum absolute informe aut res mutuo indifferentes, quia systema omne ens intra situm et relationem effectivam collocat.
Falsum esse oportet ordines essendi, significandi, producendi et mensurandi fundamentaliter separatos aut sine mediatore convertibiles esse.
Falsum esse oportet distinctionem unitatem destruere aut partes in substantias autonomas mutare, quia divisio facultatem reunionis conservare debet.
Falsum esse oportet causalitatem ex unica origine efficiente procedere; effectus requirit principium, media, receptaculum et mensuram asymmetrice cooperantia.
Falsum esse oportet absentiam, dislocationem, subtractionem et dissolutionem esse privationes steriles, quia negatio ordinata distinctionem et circuitum sequentem generat.
Falsum esse oportet creaturam sibi originem, mensuram et continuationem infinitam conferre posse; aliter ars derivata in causalitatem absolutam converteretur.
Falsum esse oportet aut analogiam nudam aut deductionem externam solam probationem sufficientem praebere; systema congruentiam inter relationem, operationem et effectum requirit.
Purum exterius relationibus indisponibile est, sed creator ut causa ontologica ultima retinetur; haec exterioritatis asymmetria systema ordinat sine plena resolutione.
Sensus immediate perspicuus impossibilis est, quia nulla perspectiva exterior totam Monadem sine conversione, disciplina et dispositione interpretis possidet.
Autonomia absoluta sive termini sive operatoris ontologice inadmissibilis est; potentia semper intra dependentiam et mensuram exercetur.
Lex universalis quae analogiam, geometriam, causalitatem materialem et auctoritatem cosmicam perfecte convertat desideratur, sed numquam plene praesto est.
Saturatio interpretativa terminalis impossibilis est: completio structuram finit, sed mysterium et relatio occulta iter operationis denuo aperiunt.
Progressus creatus infinitus indisponibilis est, quia omnis potentia legitima terminum, restitutionem proportionis et relationem ad principium requirit.
Monas est invarians relationis per transformationes: unitas eius non praecedit distinctiones tamquam substantia simplex, sed ex coordinatione earum efficitur.
Signum completum simul manifestat, operatur et consignat; significatio igitur est effectus apparatus relationalis et materialis, non additamentum operationi externum.
Efficacia materialis neque receptione passiva neque arte absoluta constat, sed circulatione inter potentiam datam, receptaculum activum et reconfigurationem mensuratam.
Tempus totius libri est spiralis finita: regressum ontologicum, revolutionem convertibilem et terminationem potentiae creatae in eadem recursionis forma componit.
Differentia negativa fit principium productionis, quia partialitas, separatio, dissectio et subtractio repertorium relationum componendarum aperiunt.
Probatio valida est reconstructio congruentiae inter genealogiam formae, seriem conversionum, operationem rectam et effectum intellectum.
Numerus qualitatem relationis formalizat atque conversionem inter figuram, materiam, litteram et tempus efficit, sed non eam ex quantitate sola deducit.
Clausura duplicem statum habet: finem operationis constituit et retroactive condicionem novi circuitus interpretativi efficit.
Translatio analogica est simul instrumentum amplificationis et commissura epistemica fragilis, quia ambitum systematis auget sine lege conversionis ubique demonstrata.
Potentia subiecti est administratio configurativa dependentiarum: lector, operator et artifex agunt eligendo, dividendo et componendo, non originem causalitatis usurpando.
Ontologia libri realitatem constituit ut campum transductionum, in quo res sunt status relative stabiles circuituum formalis, materialis, numeralis et symbolici.
Causalitas fit syntaxis mediationum asymmetricarum: principium sustentat, figura ordinat, medium transfert, materia prolongat et mensura effectum limitat.
Semiosis est circuitus causaliter efficax, quia eadem configuratio rem manifestat, effectum materialem condensat et formam transmissibilem instituit.
Tempus non metitur machinam extrinsecus, sed ex eius differentiationibus, conversionibus, exhaustionibus localibus et reditibus finitis generatur.
Subiectum est operator-interpres intra machinam constitutus, qui relationes administrat sed neque spectator exterior neque dominus causalis fit.
Libertas est facultas configurationis sub mensura: potentia agendi crescit per rectam mediationem et selectionem, non per exemptionem a dependentia.
Historia huius systematis constat ex clausuris localibus quae effectum perficiunt, potentiam finiunt et sub relatione occulta novam extractionem aperiunt.
Veritas fit concordia transmodalis inter invariantem, apparatum, operationem et effectum, sed eius vis minuitur ubi transitus analogicus regulam communem non exhibet.
Auctoritas epistemica simul restringitur et distribuitur: initiatio qualitatem accessus ordinat, consignatio autem operationem ultra praesentiam magistri transmittit.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Compressio formarum in unitatem differentiationem generat; differentiae proportionantur, recomponuntur et ad unitatem redeunt quae novam divisionem iam continet.
Centrum peripheriam constituit, peripheria motum requirit, motus in materiam imprimitur, et impressio tamquam signum causae ad centrum refertur.
Unitas distinctionem parit, distinctio proportionem postulat, proportio coniunctionem efficit, et coniunctio unitatem ut capacitatem ulterioris differentiae restituit.
Dislocatio aut dissolutio repertorium partium aperit; compositio mensurata ordinem restituit, sed restitutio novam differentiam producit.
Latentia per manifestationem solvitur, sed effectus manifestus residuum occultum producit quod ulteriorem interpretationem et conversionem incitat.
Amplificatio numeralis figuram in litteram, potentiam et tempus transfert; singulus gradus maiorem ordinem promittit sed novam regulam conversionis postulat.
Substitutio medii conservat circuitum cum terminus particularis deficit, quia functio inter Lunam, Mercurium, animam, Spiritum, Terram aut codicem transferri potest.
Monas, proportio, Mercurius et inexhaustio attractores diversos constituunt: primi dispersionem colligunt, ultimum prohibet ne collectio in possessionem plenam claudatur.
Terminus operationem sistit, proportionem restituit et principium retroactive manifestat; eadem clausura, quatenus mysterium servat, punctum reingressus fit.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Signum manifestum → reductio ad repertorium geometricum minimum → inventio relationis generatricis.
Punctum sive centrum → extensio et peripheria → unitas distincta in partes operativas.
Distinctio configurata → situs, sectio et vicinitas → proportio invisibilis → identitas relationalis.
Configuratio → mediatio cosmica et spiritualis → circulatio functionis → translatio inter codices.
Influxus configuratus → receptio materialis activa → nutritio, impressio et continuatio causalis.
Corpus compositum → dissectio et subtractio → repertorium partium → metathesis et ars recompositiva.
Recompositio proportionata → commensuratio geometrica → numerus qualitativus → amplificatio temporalis.
Effectus coordinatus → Lux, Verbum aut figura completa → consignatio materialis et doctrinalis.
Exhaustio potentiae creatae → restitutio proportionis → reditus ad principium → mysterium servatum → novus circuitus interpretativus.
Character manifestus → Punctum-Monas → centrum et peripheria → distributio cosmica → mediatio materialis → figura operativa → numerus transformativus → reditus finitus.
Unitas relationalis → differentiatio → proportio → translatio inter codices → impressio et effectus → recompositio mensurata → unitas relecta.
Negatio autonomiae → activatio partialitatis → distributio causalitatis → limitatio artis → terminatio potentiae creatae → relatio ad principium.
Necessitas geometrica → translatio analogica → probatio operativa → congruentia effectus → clausura localis → residuum occultum → nova reconstructio.
Geometria reclassificatur ex instrumento descriptionis in grammaticam ontologicam, causalitatem configurativam et rationem calibrationis inter campos.
Monas reclassificatur ex unitate simplici in centrum transductivum quod distinctiones producit, conversiones colligit et limites earum ordinat.
Materia reclassificatur ex receptaculo passivo in condicionem co-causalem impressionis, nutritionis, operationis et verificationis.
Numerus reclassificatur ex quantitate abstracta in matricem qualitativam quae functiones, permutationes, tempora et metamorphoses coordinat.
Tempus reclassificatur ex successione externa in effectum recursionis, conversionis et finitae restitutionis potentiae.
Oppositio inter signum et rem corruit, quia figura eadem manifestationem, operationem materialem et transmissionem doctrinae efficit.
Oppositio naturae et artis recodificatur: ars potentias naturales configurat et ordinat, sed perfectionem naturalem causaliter non usurpat.
Lectio reclassificatur ex visu aut extractione sensus in participationem reconstructivam quae figuras dividit, operationes probat et invariantes a contingentibus secernit.
Fines disciplinarum reclassificantur ut canales translationis, ita ut differentiae codicum serventur sine autonomia ontologica.
In gradu superficiei punctum, linea, circulus, Sol, Luna, Mercurius, Terra, crux, litterae, animalia et numeri apparent ut obiecta determinata.
In gradu structurali centrum, distinctio, proportio, mediatio, circulatio, dissectio, metathesis et reditus unam machinam transformationis constituunt.
In gradu metastrategico quaestio a significatione termini ad regimen conversionum transfertur, ut interpres invariantia, media et limites operationis discernat.
In gradu ontologico et temporali realitas est reticulum entium dependentium, causalitas transductio distributa, tempus autem spiralis finita mutationis et reditus.
In gradu methodologico et performativo textus figuras comprimit, dividit, convertit et recomponit, ita ut forma expositionis machinam assertam exsequatur.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Necessitas geometrica et amplificatio analogica diversas vires epistemicas retinent, quamquam systema eas tamquam gradus unius translationis tractat.
Exactitudo configurationis et identitas per transformationem tensionem efficiunt, quia regula quae mutationes legitimas a corruptione discernat non semper exhibetur.
Autarkia Monae, dependentia operationis ab ambitu et subordinatio creaturae principio superiori diversos exterioritatis sensus producunt qui non plene conciliantur.
Causalitas distribuitur inter media, receptacula et effectus, sed simul ordinem asymmetricum et hierarchicum retinet; pondus relativum nodorum incertum manet.
Ars effectum realem efficit, sed terminus inter reconfigurationem validam et perfectionem naturalem acquisitam instabilis manet.
Disciplina initiatoria et consignatio transmissibilis simul postulantur, sed criterium communicationis quae neque secreta privat neque universaliter publicat incompletum est.
Clausura finita et inexhaustio interpretationis mutuo indigent, sed incertum est utrum altera terminum ontologicum, altera solum epistemicum significet.
Monas mutatur ab elemento unitatis in functionem coordinationis et tandem in tabulam transductivam originis, differentiae et reditus.
Punctum mutatur ab ingrediente et centro necessario in copulam removendam, deinde in principium effusionis circularis restitutum.
Signum mutatur ex repraesentatione productiva in operatorium, apparatum materialem et consignationem disciplinae.
Numerus mutatur ex enumeratione et extensione figurae in operator qualitativum temporis, permutationis et metamorphosis.
Materia mutatur ex receptaculo cosmico in nodum productivum, sed eius activitas sub condicionibus situs, mensurae et influxus manet.
Circulus mutatur ex figura et circulatione caelesti in motum artis, recursionem differentiae et clausuram finiti reditus.
Realitas implicite est machina scriptoria et transductiva concentrica, in qua centrum formas distribuit, materia eas recipit, numerus commensurat et reditus circuitum claudit.
Monas est centrum quod se in differentias explicat sine dispersione absoluta atque eas per proportionem ad relationem communem retrahit.
Subiectum est lector, operator et artifex initiatus qui intra machinam mensuras, tempora, instrumenta et translationes administrat.
Tempus est spiralis finita effusionis, operationis, occultationis et reditus, cuius circuitus relationem servant sed statum eius mutant.
Navigatio possibilis consistit in conservando canalem proportionalem inter principium et transformationes contra autonomiam partium, corruptionem configurationis et dominium causale absolutum.
Axiomata relationis prioris, unitatis differentiatae, formae operativae, causalitatis medialis, numeri qualitativi, artis derivatae et clausurae inexhaustae sufficiunt ad machinam libri restituendam.
Structura firmissima est ubi dependentia, distinctio, mediatio et commensuratio eandem legem servant: mutatio relationem communem non delet sed manifestat.
Minus determinata manet lex quae necessitatem geometricam in causalitatem cosmicam, efficaciam materialem, litteram, numerum et auctoritatem metaphysicam convertat.
Systema cohaeret per reditum functionalem relationis, non per identitatem terminorum neque per deductionem univocam.
Cohaerentia nititur recursionis ordine et formae performativae vi, quae hiatus inter probationis genera saepe comprimit potius quam formaliter solvit.
Reductioni axiomaticae resistunt differentiae inter analogiam et demonstrationem, operationem artificialem et perfectionem naturalem, clausuram finitam et inexhaustionem interpretativam.
The system asks how a minimal character can contract geometric, cosmic, material, temporal, and numerical orders into a single machine without abolishing their differences.
The Monad is not a stable object, but a relational operator that produces distinctions, distributes them through media, and gathers them through ordered return into reformed unity.
The argumentation is reconstructive and transductive: geometry separates invariants, analogy connects fields, operation tests efficacy, while number measures changes.
The movement proceeds from a manifest sign to a minimal principle, thence through cosmic and material differentiations, finally to commensuration, consignment, and finite return.
The progression is spiral, cumulative, and driven by change, because each return preserves the prior relation while increasing its field, function, or state.
Proof is not a uniformly closed deduction, but congruence among formal necessity, material mediation, correct operation, effect, and the interpreter's understanding.
Geometrical necessity is extended into a grammar of translation, but every transition between heaven, matter, figure, and mystery requires a mediator that analogy alone does not supply.
The form of exposition accomplishes its own thesis, since by dividing, converting, numbering, and recomposing figures it actually constitutes the transductive unity it affirms.
The closure of the whole book is double: it terminates created power in proportion, but reserves mystery and hidden relation as causes of further interpretation.
[Persistent] Form or sign does not passively imitate an already constituted thing, but manifests, distributes, and converts relations into an apparatus of operation.
[Persistent] Relation or proportion precedes the identity and efficacy of terms; an element is that which can act within a generative configuration.
[Emergent] Monadic unity is preserved through distinction, because division produces related parts whose recomposition effects a broader unity.
[Mutating] Identity persists as an invariant of relation through change of position, medium, and function, not as an immobile substance.
[Persistent] Geometry is an ontological and transductive grammar through which position, center, section, proximity, circulation, and proportion are converted into causality.
[Emergent] Causality is medial, distributed, and asymmetrical: principles, figures, souls, rays, bodies, and receptacles participate in effect, but do not ground it equally.
[Mutating] Matter passes from a receptive term into an active node that nourishes, imprints, reconfigures, and returns influx into circulation.
[Emergent] Time is not a pre-given receptacle, but the effect of a spiral of recursion through which manifestation, completion, operation, and return alter the state of relation.
[Mutating] Number passes from external measure into a qualitative operator that orders configuration, permutation, amplification, and temporal completion.
[Emergent] Partiality, subtraction, dissolution, and termination become generative when they preserve the relation of origin and produce recomposable difference.
[Persistent] Valid knowledge is reconstructive and operative: it traces generative relations and requires interpretation, operation, effect, and the interpreter's disposition to be congruent.
[Terminal] Art is real but derivative power: it changes configurations and locally perfects powers, yet does not absolutely produce its origin, measure, or causality.
[Emergent] Geometric, cosmic, material, numerical, alphabetic, and doctrinal orders are convertible codes, not causally separate regions.
[Terminal] Legitimate closure produces a finite restoration of proportion, but prevents semantic saturation and leaves a new interpretive circuit.
[Attractor] The attractor of the whole book is proportional monadic unity, which draws back the dispersion of forms without reducing their changes to simple identity.
The point is amplified from minimal entry into ontological center and source of flow, then excluded as a superfluous copula and restored as a center of effusion.
The Monad changes from the name of unity into a distributed function, thence into an attractor of conversions, and finally into the internal machine of origin, process, and end.
Geometry passes from a repertory of forms to a common medium of causalities, a grammar of conversion, and an instrument of transductive calibration.
The sign migrates from productive manifestation into an operator of relations, then into a materially conditioned apparatus and a transmissible consignment of discipline.
Earth and body pass from cosmological places or receptacles into active nodes of impression, nourishment, composition, and measure.
Circularity changes from dependence of the periphery and cosmic circulation into a circuit of conversions, recursion of difference, and the form of finite return.
Number is amplified from symbolic extension into an engine of composition, a quality of configuration, and a measure of temporal metamorphosis.
Concealment is transferred from a state of absence into an internal remainder of conversion and finally into a mystery that may be consigned but remains inexhausted.
The power to act passes from conversion of dependence into interpretive operation, then is determined as real but causally limited configurative art.
Closure progresses from generative periphery to material and verbal impressions, then converts into a finite return that does not consume hidden relation.
Pure exteriority is first denied, mediation replaces immediacy, and finally exteriority must be distinguished into illicit supplement, environmental condition, and ontological cause.
Patronage, constructions of lines, symbolic animals, and singular apparatuses remain local; only the rule ascends that exact relation is sustained by material and figurative conditions.
The Sun, Moon, Mercury, and other cosmic terms do not become global substances; functions of mediation, completion, substitution, and transduction order the level of the book.
The octonary, quinarity, quaternary, and XXIV retain local distinctions; only the thesis that number expresses the quality of configuration and amplification is global.
Drops, impressions, particular materials, and environments must not be universalized; what ascends is active materiality whose efficacy depends on position and composition.
The dependence of figure on point and of planet on relation is amplified into distributed causality, in which no term may appropriate effect to itself alone.
The connection among form, time, and sign ascends into a translating machine, whose complete figure contains relation, matter, and consignment together.
The generative openness of prior circuits is not abolished by terminal closure, but qualified through the finitude of created causality and return to the principle.
Particular correspondences are valid as local machines of translation; they do not ascend into universal law unless mediation, measure, and necessity of transition can be demonstrated.
The passive, ornamental, or merely conventional sign is excluded, because figure must produce relation, condition operation, or consign discipline.
Autonomy of the term is excluded: unity, figure, matter, and created agent operate only within relations of center, mediation, measure, and principle.
Passive matter is excluded, since reception, nourishment, impression, and configuration constitute causal continuation.
Fixed identity and undivided unity are excluded, because permanence is preserved only through translation of function and relation of parts.
Pre-given linear time and indefinite created progress are excluded; time emerges from finite circuits of transformation and return.
Closed disciplines and immediate sense are excluded, because understanding proceeds through conversion of codes and figurative media.
Bare number and arithmetic separated from configuration are excluded, since numerical force arises from position, partition, and permutation.
Totally closed demonstration and exhaustive interpretation are excluded, because hidden measure and terminal mystery demand further reconstruction.
Absolute art is excluded: created operation can produce a real effect, but does not produce natural essence, measure, and the ground of causality from nothing.
It must be false that reality contains a residue absolutely without form or things mutually indifferent, because the system places every being within effective position and relation.
It must be false that the orders of being, signifying, producing, and measuring are fundamentally separate or convertible without a mediator.
It must be false that distinction destroys unity or turns parts into autonomous substances, because division must preserve the capacity for reunion.
It must be false that causality proceeds from a single efficient origin; effect requires principle, media, receptacle, and measure cooperating asymmetrically.
It must be false that absence, dislocation, subtraction, and dissolution are sterile privations, because ordered negation generates distinction and the following circuit.
It must be false that a creature can confer upon itself origin, measure, and infinite continuation; otherwise derivative art would be converted into absolute causality.
It must be false that either bare analogy or external deduction alone provides sufficient proof; the system requires congruence among relation, operation, and effect.
Pure exteriority is unavailable to relations, but the creator is retained as ultimate ontological cause; this asymmetry of exteriority orders the system without full resolution.
Immediately evident sense is impossible, because no external perspective possesses the whole Monad without conversion, discipline, and the interpreter's disposition.
Absolute autonomy of either term or operator is ontologically inadmissible; power is always exercised within dependence and measure.
A universal law that perfectly converts analogy, geometry, material causality, and cosmic authority is desired, but never fully available.
Terminal interpretive saturation is impossible: completion terminates structure, but mystery and hidden relation reopen the course of operation.
Infinite created progress is unavailable, because every legitimate power requires a limit, restoration of proportion, and relation to the principle.
The Monad is an invariant of relation through transformations: its unity does not precede distinctions as a simple substance, but is effected by their coordination.
The complete sign simultaneously manifests, operates, and consigns; signification is therefore the effect of a relational and material apparatus, not an addition external to operation.
Material efficacy consists neither in passive reception nor in absolute art, but in circulation among given power, active receptacle, and measured reconfiguration.
The time of the whole book is a finite spiral: it composes ontological regression, convertible revolution, and termination of created power in the same form of recursion.
Negative difference becomes a principle of production, because partiality, separation, dissection, and subtraction open a repertory of relations to be composed.
Valid proof is a reconstruction of congruence among the genealogy of form, series of conversions, correct operation, and understood effect.
Number formalizes the quality of relation and effects conversion among figure, matter, letter, and time, but does not deduce it from quantity alone.
Closure has a double status: it constitutes the end of operation and retroactively effects the condition of a new interpretive circuit.
Analogical translation is at once an instrument of amplification and a fragile epistemic seam, because it increases the system's scope without a law of conversion demonstrated everywhere.
The power of the subject is configurative administration of dependencies: reader, operator, and artisan act by selecting, dividing, and composing, not by usurping the origin of causality.
The ontology of the book constitutes reality as a field of transductions, in which things are relatively stable states of formal, material, numerical, and symbolic circuits.
Causality becomes a syntax of asymmetrical mediations: principle sustains, figure orders, medium transfers, matter prolongs, and measure limits effect.
Semiosis is a causally efficacious circuit, because the same configuration manifests a thing, condenses material effect, and institutes a transmissible form.
Time does not measure the machine extrinsically, but is generated from its differentiations, conversions, local exhaustions, and finite returns.
The subject is an operator-interpreter constituted within the machine, who administers relations but becomes neither external spectator nor causal master.
Freedom is the capacity for configuration under measure: the power to act grows through correct mediation and selection, not through exemption from dependence.
The history of this system consists of local closures that complete effect, terminate power, and open a new extraction under hidden relation.
Truth becomes transmodal concordance among invariant, apparatus, operation, and effect, but its force diminishes where analogical transition does not exhibit a common rule.
Epistemic authority is simultaneously restricted and distributed: initiation orders the quality of access, while consignment transmits operation beyond the master's presence.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: The compression of forms into unity generates differentiation; differences are proportioned, recomposed, and return to a unity that already contains new division.
The center constitutes the periphery, the periphery requires motion, motion is impressed into matter, and the impression is referred back to the center as a sign of cause.
Unity begets distinction, distinction demands proportion, proportion effects conjunction, and conjunction restores unity as a capacity for further difference.
Dislocation or dissolution opens a repertory of parts; measured composition restores order, but restoration produces new difference.
Latency is resolved through manifestation, but manifest effect produces a hidden remainder that incites further interpretation and conversion.
Numerical amplification transfers figure into letter, power, and time; each stage promises greater order but demands a new rule of conversion.
Substitution of a medium preserves the circuit when a particular term fails, because function can be transferred among Moon, Mercury, soul, Spirit, Earth, or code.
The Monad, proportion, Mercury, and inexhaustion constitute different attractors: the first three gather dispersion, while the last prevents gathering from closing into full possession.
The limit stops operation, restores proportion, and retroactively manifests the principle; the same closure, insofar as it preserves mystery, becomes a point of re-entry.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Manifest sign → reduction to a minimal geometric repertory → discovery of generative relation.
Point or center → extension and periphery → unity distinguished into operative parts.
Configured distinction → position, section, and proximity → invisible proportion → relational identity.
Configuration → cosmic and spiritual mediation → circulation of function → translation among codes.
Configured influx → active material reception → nourishment, impression, and causal continuation.
Composite body → dissection and subtraction → repertory of parts → metathesis and recompositive art.
Proportioned recomposition → geometrical commensuration → qualitative number → temporal amplification.
Coordinated effect → Light, Word, or complete figure → material and doctrinal consignment.
Exhaustion of created power → restoration of proportion → return to principle → preserved mystery → new interpretive circuit.
Manifest character → Point-Monad → center and periphery → cosmic distribution → material mediation → operative figure → transformative number → finite return.
Relational unity → differentiation → proportion → translation among codes → impression and effect → measured recomposition → reread unity.
Negation of autonomy → activation of partiality → distribution of causality → limitation of art → termination of created power → relation to principle.
Geometrical necessity → analogical translation → operative proof → congruence of effect → local closure → hidden remainder → new reconstruction.
Geometry is reclassified from an instrument of description into an ontological grammar, configurative causality, and a means of calibration among fields.
The Monad is reclassified from simple unity into a transductive center that produces distinctions, gathers conversions, and orders their limits.
Matter is reclassified from passive receptacle into the co-causal condition of impression, nourishment, operation, and verification.
Number is reclassified from abstract quantity into a qualitative matrix that coordinates functions, permutations, times, and metamorphoses.
Time is reclassified from external succession into the effect of recursion, conversion, and finite restoration of power.
The opposition between sign and thing collapses, because the same figure effects manifestation, material operation, and transmission of doctrine.
The opposition of nature and art is recoded: art configures and orders natural powers, but does not causally usurp natural perfection.
Reading is reclassified from sight or extraction of sense into reconstructive participation that divides figures, tests operations, and separates invariants from contingencies.
The boundaries of disciplines are reclassified as channels of translation, so that differences of codes are preserved without ontological autonomy.
At the surface level, point, line, circle, Sun, Moon, Mercury, Earth, cross, letters, animals, and numbers appear as determinate objects.
At the structural level, center, distinction, proportion, mediation, circulation, dissection, metathesis, and return constitute a single machine of transformation.
At the metastrategic level, the question shifts from the meaning of a term to the governance of conversions, so that the interpreter may discern invariants, media, and limits of operation.
At the ontological and temporal level, reality is a network of dependent beings, causality is distributed transduction, while time is a finite spiral of change and return.
At the methodological and performative level, the text compresses, divides, converts, and recomposes figures, such that the form of exposition executes the asserted machine.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Geometrical necessity and analogical amplification retain different epistemic forces, although the system treats them as stages of a single translation.
Exactitude of configuration and identity through transformation produce tension, because the rule that distinguishes legitimate changes from corruption is not always exhibited.

The autarky of the Monad, the dependence of operation on environment, and the subordination of the creature to a higher principle produce different senses of exteriority that are not fully reconciled.
Causality is distributed among media, receptacles, and effects, but at the same time retains an asymmetrical and hierarchical order; the relative weight of nodes remains uncertain.
Art produces real effect, but the boundary between valid reconfiguration and acquired natural perfection remains unstable.
Initiatory discipline and transmissible consignment are simultaneously required, but the criterion of communication that neither privatizes as secret nor makes universally public remains incomplete.
Finite closure and inexhaustion of interpretation mutually require one another, but it is uncertain whether one signifies an ontological limit, the other only an epistemic one.
The Monad changes from an element of unity into a function of coordination and finally into a transductive map of origin, difference, and return.
The point changes from entry and necessary center into a removable copula, then into a restored principle of circular effusion.
The sign changes from productive representation into an operator, a material apparatus, and a consignment of discipline.
Number changes from enumeration and extension of figure into a qualitative operator of time, permutation, and metamorphosis.
Matter changes from cosmic receptacle into a productive node, but its activity remains under the conditions of position, measure, and influx.
The circle changes from figure and celestial circulation into the motion of art, recursion of difference, and closure of finite return.
Reality is implicitly a concentric writing and transductive machine, in which the center distributes forms, matter receives them, number commensurates, and return closes the circuit.
The Monad is a center that unfolds itself into differences without absolute dispersion and draws them back through proportion to common relation.
The subject is the initiated reader, operator, and artisan who administers measures, times, instruments, and translations within the machine.
Time is a finite spiral of effusion, operation, concealment, and return, whose circuits preserve relation but alter its state.
Possible navigation consists in preserving a proportional channel between principle and transformations against the autonomy of parts, corruption of configuration, and absolute causal dominion.
The axioms of prior relation, differentiated unity, operative form, medial causality, qualitative number, derivative art, and inexhausted closure suffice to restore the machine of the book.
The firmest structure is where dependence, distinction, mediation, and commensuration preserve the same law: change does not erase common relation but manifests it.
Less determined remains the law that converts geometrical necessity into cosmic causality, material efficacy, letter, number, and metaphysical authority.
The system coheres through the functional return of relation, not through identity of terms nor through univocal deduction.
Coherence relies on the order of recursion and the force of performative form, which often compresses rather than formally resolves the gaps among kinds of proof.
Differences between analogy and demonstration, artificial operation and natural perfection, finite closure and interpretive inexhaustion resist axiomatic reduction.

sources.text:
## Book I

## Chapter 1

Every skill and every inquiry, and similarly every action and rational choice, [ 1094a ] is thought to aim at some good; and so the good has been aptly described as that at which everything aims. But it is clear that there is some difference between ends: some ends are activities , while others are products which are additional to the activities. In cases where there are ends additional to the actions, the products are by their nature better than the activities. [5]

Since there are many actions, skills, and sciences, it happens that there are many ends as well: the end of medicine is health, that of shipbuilding, a ship, that of military science, victory, and that of domestic economy, wealth. But when any of these actions, skills, or sciences comes under some single faculty – as bridlemaking and other sciences [10] concerned with equine equipment come under the science of horsemanship, and horsemanship itself and every action in warfare come under military science, and others similarly come under others – then in all these cases the end of the master science is more worthy of choice than the ends of the subordinate sciences, since these latter ends are pursued [15] also for the sake of the former. And it makes no difference whether the ends of the actions are the activities themselves, or something else additional to them, as in the sciences just mentioned.

## Chapter 2

So if what is done has some end that we want for its own sake, and everything else we want is for the sake of this end; and if we do not choose [20] everything for the sake of something else (because this would lead to an infinite progression, making our desire fruitless and vain), then clearly this will be the good, indeed the chief good. Surely, then, knowledge of the good must be very important for our lives? And if, like archers, [25] we have a target, are we not more likely to hit the right mark? If so, we must try at least roughly to comprehend what it is and which science or faculty is concerned with it.

Knowledge of the good would seem to be the concern of the most authoritative science, the highest master science. And this is obviously the science of politics, because it lays down which of the sciences there [ 1094b ] should be in cities, and which each class of person should learn and up to what level. And we see that even the most honourable of faculties, such as military science, domestic economy, and rhetoric, come under it. Since political science employs the other sciences, and also lays down [5] laws about what we should do and refrain from, its end will include the ends of the others, and will therefore be the human good. For even if the good is the same for an individual as for a city, that of the city is obviously a greater and more complete thing to obtain and preserve. [10] For while the good of an individual is a desirable thing, what is good for a people or for cities is a nobler and more godlike thing. Our enquiry, then, is a kind of political science, since these are the ends it is aiming at.

## Chapter 3

Our account will be adequate if its clarity is in line with the subject-matter, because the same degree of precision is not to be sought in all discussions, any more than in works of craftsmanship. The spheres of [15] what is noble and what is just, which political science examines, admit of a good deal of diversity and variation, so that they seem to exist only by convention and not by nature. Goods vary in this way as well, since it happens that, for many, good things have harmful consequences: some people have been ruined by wealth, and others by courage. So we should [20] be content, since we are discussing things like these in such a way, to demonstrate the truth sketchily and in outline, and, because we are making generalizations on the basis of generalizations, to draw conclusions along the same lines. Indeed, the details of our claims, then, should be looked at in the same way, since it is a mark of an educated [25] person to look in each area for only that degree of accuracy that the nature of the subject permits. Accepting persuasive arguments from a mathematician is like demanding demonstrations from a rhetorician.

Each person judges well what he knows, and is a good judge of this. So, in any subject, the person educated in it is a good judge of that subject, [ 1095a ] and the person educated in all subjects is a good judge without qualification. This is why a young person is not fitted to hear lectures on political science, since our discussions begin from and concern the actions of life, and of these he has no experience. Again, because of his tendency to follow his feelings, his studies will be useless and to no [5] purpose, since the end of the study is not knowledge but action. It makes no difference whether he is young in years or juvenile in character, since the deficiency is not related to age, but occurs because of his living and engaging in each of his pursuits according to his feelings. For knowledge is a waste of time for people like this, just as it is for those without self-restraint. But knowledge of the matters that concern political science will prove very beneficial to those who follow [10] reason both in shaping their desires and in acting.

Let these comments – about the student, how our statements are to be taken, and the task we have set ourselves – serve as our preamble.

## Chapter 4

Let us continue with the argument, and, since all knowledge and rational choice seek some good, let us say what we claim to be the aim of political science – that is, of all the good things to be done, what is the [15] highest. Most people, I should think, agree about what it is called, since both the masses and sophisticated people call it happiness, understanding being happy as equivalent to living well and acting well. They [20] disagree about substantive conceptions of happiness, the masses giving an account which differs from that of the philosophers. For the masses think it is something straightforward and obvious, like pleasure, wealth, or honour, some thinking it to be one thing, others another. Often the same person can give different accounts: when he is ill, it is health; when [25] he is poor, it is wealth. And when people are aware of their ignorance, they marvel at those who say it is some grand thing quite beyond them. Certain thinkers used to believe that beyond these many good things there is something else good in itself, which makes all these good things good. Examining all the views offered would presumably be rather a waste of time, and it is enough to look at the most prevalent [30] ones or those that seem to have something to be said for them.

Let us not forget, however, that there is a difference between arguments from first principles and arguments to first principles. For Plato rightly used to wonder about this, raising the question whether the way to go is from first principles or to first principles, as in the [ 1095b ] racecourse whether it is from the judges to the post or back again as well. For while we should begin from things known, they are known in two senses: known by us, and known without qualification. Presumably we have to begin from things known by us. This is why anyone who is going to be a competent student in the spheres of what is noble and [5] what is just – in a word, politics – must be brought up well in his habits. For the first principle is the belief that something is the case, and if this is sufficiently clear, he will not need the reason why as well. Such a person is in possession of the first principles, or could easily grasp them. Anyone with neither of these possibilities open to him should listen to Hesiod :

> [10] This person who understands everything for himself is the best of all, And noble is that one who heeds good advice.

> But he who neither understands it for himself nor takes to heart What he hears from another is a worthless man. 1

## Chapter 5

But let us begin from where we digressed. For people seem, not [15] unreasonably, to base their conception of the good – happiness, that is – on their own lives. The masses, the coarsest people, see it as pleasure, and so they like the life of enjoyment. There are three especially prominent types of life: that just mentioned, the life of politics, and thirdly the life of contemplation. The masses appear quite slavish by rationally [20] choosing a life fit only for cattle; but they are worthy of consideration because many of those in power feel the same as Sardanapallus . 2

Sophisticated people, men of action, see happiness as honour, since honour is pretty much the end of the political life. Honour , however, seems too shallow to be an object of our inquiry, since honour appears [25] to depend more on those who honour than on the person honoured, whereas we surmise the good to be something of one’s own that cannot easily be taken away. Again, they seem to pursue honour in order to convince themselves of their goodness; at least, they seek to be honoured by people with practical wisdom, among those who are familiar with them, and for their virtue . So it is clear that, to these people at least, virtue is superior .

One might, perhaps, suppose virtue rather than honour to be the end [30] of the political life. But even virtue seems, in itself, to be lacking something, since apparently one can possess virtue even when one is asleep, or inactive throughout one’s life, and also when one is suffering terribly or experiencing the greatest misfortunes; and no one would call a person [ 1096a ] living this kind of life happy, unless he were closely defending a thesis. But enough of this, because these issues have been sufficiently dealt with in our everyday discussions.

The third kind of life is that of contemplation, which we shall examine in what follows. [5]

The life of making money is a life people are, as it were, forced into, and wealth is clearly not the good we are seeking, since it is merely useful, for getting something else. One would be better off seeing as ends the things mentioned before, because they are valued for themselves. But they do not appear to be ends either, and many arguments have been offered against them. So let us put them to one side. [10]

## Chapter 6

It would perhaps be quite a good idea to examine the notion of the universal and go through any problems there are in the way it is employed, despite the fact that such an inquiry turns out to be difficult going because those who introduced the Forms 3 are friends. It will presumably be thought better, indeed one’s duty , to do away with even what is close to one’s heart in order to preserve the truth, especially [15] when one is a philosopher. For one might love both, but it is nevertheless a sacred duty to prefer the truth to one’s friends.

Those who introduced this idea did not set up Forms for series in which they spoke of priority and posteriority, and this is why they did not postulate a Form of numbers. But the good is spoken of in the [20] categories of substance, of quality and of relation; and that which exists in itself, namely, substance, is naturally prior to what is relative (since this seems like an offshoot and attribute of what is). So there could not be some common Form over and above these goods.

Again, good is spoken of in as many senses as is being: it is used in the [25] category of substance, as for instance god and intellect, in that of quality – the virtues, in that of quantity – the right amount, in that of relation – the useful, in that of time – the right moment, and in that of place – the right locality, and so on. So it is clear that there could not be one common universal, because it would be spoken of not in all the categories, but in only one.

[30] Again, since there is a single science for the things answering to each individual Form, there should have been some single science for all the goods. But as it happens there are many sciences, even of the things in one category. For example, the right moment: in war, it is military science, in illness, medicine; or the right amount: in diet, it is medicine, in exercise, gymnastics.

[35] One might also be puzzled about what on earth they mean by [ 1096b ] speaking of a ‘thing-in-itself’, since the definition of humanity is one and the same in humanity-in-itself and human being. Inasmuch as they are human, they will not differ. And if this is so, the same will be true of good.

Nor will a thing be any the more good by being eternal, since a long-lasting white thing is no whiter than a short-lived one.

[5] The Pythagoreans 4 seem to give a more plausible account of the good, when they place the one in their column of goods; and Speusippus 5 seems to have followed them in this. But let this be the topic of another discussion.

An objection to what we have said might be that they did not speak [10] about every good, and that things which are pursued and valued for their own sake are called good by reference to a single Form, while those that tend to be instrumental to these things or in some way to preserve them or prevent their contraries are called good for the sake of these – in a different way, in other words. Clearly, then, things should be called good in two senses: things good in themselves, and things good for the sake of things good in themselves. So let us distinguish things good in themselves from those that are means to them and see whether the former are called good with reference to a single Form. What sort of [15] things should one put in the class of things good in themselves? Those that are sought even on their own, such as understanding, sight, certain types of pleasure, and honours? For even if we do seek these for the sake of something else, one would nevertheless put them in the class of things good in themselves. Perhaps nothing but the Form? Then the Form [20] would be useless. But if those other things are in the class of things good in themselves, the same definition of the good will have to be exemplified in all of them, as is that of whiteness in snow and white lead. But the definitions of honour, practical wisdom and pleasure are distinct, and differ with respect to their being good. There is therefore no common good answering to a single Form. [25]

But how, then, are things called good? For they do not seem like items that have the same name by chance. Is it through their all deriving from one good, or their all contributing to one good, or is it rather by analogy? For as sight is good in the body, so intellect is in the soul, and so on in other cases. But perhaps we should put these questions aside for the time [30] being, since seeking precision in these matters would be more appropriate to another area of philosophy.

But the same is true of the Form. For even if there is some one good predicated across categories, or a good that is separate, itself in itself, clearly it could not be an object of action nor something attainable by a human being, which is the sort of thing we are looking for. [35]

Perhaps someone might think that it would be better to understand it with an eye to those goods that are attainable and objects of action. For with this as a sort of paradigm we shall know better the goods [ 1097a ] that are goods for us, and if we know them, we shall attain them. This argument has some plausibility, but seems to be inconsistent with the sciences: they all aim at some good and seek to remedy any lack of the good, but they leave to one side understanding the universal good. And if [5] there were such an important aid available, it is surely not reasonable to think that all practitioners of skills would be ignorant of it and fail even to look for it.

There is also a difficulty in seeing how a weaver or carpenter will be helped in practising his skill by knowing this good-in-itself, or how someone who has contemplated the Form itself will be a better doctor [10] or general. For apparently it is not just health that the doctor attends to, but human health, or perhaps rather the health of a particular person, given that he treats each person individually.

That is enough on these issues.

## Chapter 7

[15] But let us return again to the good we are looking for, to see what it might be, since it appears to vary between different actions and skills: it is one thing in medicine, another in military science, and so on in all other cases. What then is the good in each case? Surely it is that for the sake of which other things are done? In medicine it is health, in military [20] science, victory, in housebuilding, a house, and in other cases something else; in every action and rational choice the end is the good, since it is for the sake of the end that everyone does everything else. So if everything that is done has some end, this will be the good among things done, and if there are several ends, these will be the goods.

Our argument, then, has arrived at the same point by a different [25] route, but we should try to make it still clearer. Since there appear to be several ends, and some of these, such as wealth, flutes, and implements generally, we choose as means to other ends, it is clear that not all ends are complete . But the chief good manifestly is something complete. So if there is only one end that is complete, this will be what we are [30] looking for, and if there are several of them, the most complete. We speak of that which is worth pursuing for its own sake as more complete than that which is worth pursuing only for the sake of something else, and that which is never worth choosing for the sake of something else as more complete than things that are worth choosing both in themselves and for the sake of this end. And so that which is always worth choosing in itself and never for the sake of something else we call complete without qualification.

Happiness in particular is believed to be complete without qualification, [ 1097b ] since we always choose it for itself and never for the sake of anything else. Honour, pleasure, intellect, and every virtue we do indeed choose for themselves (since we would choose each of them even if they had no good effects), but we choose them also for the sake of happiness, on the assumption that through them we shall live a life of happiness; whereas [5] happiness no one chooses for the sake of any of these nor indeed for the sake of anything else.

The same conclusion seems to follow from considering self-sufficiency, since the complete good is thought to be self-sufficient. We are applying the term ‘self-sufficient’ not to a person on his own, living a solitary life, but to a person living alongside his parents, children, wife, and friends and fellow-citizens generally, since a human being is by nature a [10] social being. We must, however, set some limit on these, since if we stretch things so far as to include ancestors and descendants and friends of friends we shall end up with an infinite series. But we must think about this later. For now, we take what is self-sufficient to be that which on its own makes life worthy of choice and lacking in nothing. [15] We think happiness to be such, and indeed the thing most of all worth choosing, not counted as just one thing among others. Counted as just one thing among others it would clearly be more worthy of choice with even the least good added to it. For the good added would cause an increase in goodness, and the greater good is always more worthy of choice. Happiness, then, is obviously something complete and self- [20] sufficient, in that it is the end of what is done.

But perhaps saying that happiness is the chief good sounds rather platitudinous, and one might want its nature to be specified still more clearly. It is possible that we might achieve that if we grasp the characteristic activity of a human being. For just as the good – the doing well – of [25] a flute-player, a sculptor or any practitioner of a skill, or generally whatever has some characteristic activity or action, is thought to lie in its characteristic activity, so the same would seem to be true of a human being, if indeed he has a characteristic activity.

Well, do the carpenter and the tanner have characteristic activities and actions, and a human being none? Has nature left him without a characteristic activity to perform? Or, as there seem to be characteristic [30] activities of the eye, the hand, the foot, and generally of each part of the body, should one assume that a human being has some characteristic activity over and above all these? What sort of thing might it be, then? For living is obviously shared even by plants, while what we are looking for is something special to a human being. We should therefore rule [ 1098a ] out the life of nourishment and growth. Next would be some sort of sentient life, but this again is clearly shared by the horse, the ox, indeed by every animal . What remains is a life, concerned in some way with action, of the element that possesses reason. (Of this element, one part has reason in being obedient to reason, the other in possessing it and engaging [5] in thought.) As this kind of life can be spoken of in two ways, let us assume that we are talking about the life concerned with action in the sense of activity, because this seems to be the more proper use of the phrase.

If the characteristic activity of a human being is an activity of the soul in accordance with reason or at least not entirely lacking it; and if we say that the characteristic activity of anything is the same in kind as that of a good thing of the same type, as in the case [10] of a lyre-player and a good lyre-player, and so on, without qualification, in the same way in every case, the superiority of the good one in virtue being an addition to the characteristic activity (for the characteristic activity of the lyre-player is to play the lyre, that of the good lyre-player to play it well); then if this is so, and we take the characteristic activity of a human being to [15] be a certain kind of life; and if we take this kind of life to be activity of the soul and actions in accordance with reason, and the characteristic activity of the good person to be to carry this out well and nobly, and a characteristic activity to be accomplished well when it is accomplished in accordance with the appropriate virtue ; then if this is so, the human good turns out to be activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, and if there are several virtues, in accordance with the best and most complete. Again, this must be over a complete life. For one swallow does not make a summer, nor one day. Neither does one day or a short time make someone blessed and happy.

[20] So let this serve as an outline of the good, since perhaps we have first to make a rough sketch, and then fill it in later. One would think that anyone with a good outline can carry on and complete the details, and [25] that in this task time will bring much to light or else offer useful assistance. This is how skills have come to advance, because anyone can fill in the gaps. But we must bear in mind what we said above, and not look for the same precision in everything, but in each case whatever is in line with [30] the subject-matter, and the degree appropriate to the inquiry. A carpenter and a geometrician approach the right-angle in different ways: the carpenter in so far as it is useful for his work, while the geometrician seeks to know what it is, or what sort of thing it is, in that he aims to contemplate the truth . We should therefore do the same in every other case, so that side-issues do not dominate the tasks in hand. Nor should [ 1098b ] we demand an explanation in the same way in all cases. A good proof that something is the case will suffice in some instances, as with first principles, where the fact itself is a starting-point, that is, a first principle . Some first principles we see by induction, some by perception, some by a kind of habituation , and others in other ways. We must try to investigate each type in the way appropriate to its nature, and take pains to define [5] each of them well, because they are very important in what follows. The first principle seems to be more than half the whole thing, and to clarify many of the issues we are inquiring into.

## Chapter 8

But we must consider the first principle in the light not only of our conclusion and premises, but of the things that people say about it. For [10] all the data harmonize with the truth, but soon clash with falsity.

Goods have been classifed into three groups: those called external goods, goods of the soul , and goods of the body. Goods of the soul are the ones we call most strictly and most especially good, and the actions [15] and activities of the soul we may attribute to the soul. Our conception of happiness , then, is plausible in so far as it is accords with this view, a venerable one that has been accepted by philosophers.

Our account is right also in that we are claiming that the end consists in certain actions and activities. For the end thus turns out to be a good of the soul and not an external good. [20]

Another belief that harmonizes with our account is that the happy person lives well and acts well, for we have claimed that happiness is pretty much a kind of living well and acting well.

Again, all the things that people look for in happiness appear to have been included in our account. Some think that happiness is virtue, some practical wisdom, others a kind of wisdom; while others think it is a combination of these or one of these along with more or less pleasure. [25] Yet others include external prosperity as well. Some of these views are popular and of long standing, while others are those of a few distinguished men. It is not likely that either group is utterly mistaken, but rather that at least one component of their view is on the right track, perhaps even most of them.

Our account of happiness is in harmony with those who say that [30] happiness is virtue or some particular virtue, since activity in accordance with virtue is characteristic of virtue. Presumably, though, it makes a great difference whether we conceive of the chief good as consisting in possession or in use, that is to say, in a state or in an activity [ 1099a ] . For while a state can exist without producing any good consequences, as it does in the case of a person sleeping or lying idle for some other reason, this is impossible for an activity: it will necessarily engage in action, and do so well. As in the Olympic Games it is not the most attractive and the [5] strongest who are crowned, but those who compete (since it is from this group that winners come), so in life it is those who act rightly who will attain what is noble and good.

It is also the case that the life of these people is pleasurable in itself. For experiencing pleasure is an aspect of the soul, and each person [10] finds pleasure in that of which he is said to be fond, as a horse-lover finds it in a horse, and someone who likes wonderful sights finds it in a wonderful sight. In the same way, a lover of justice finds it in the sphere of justice and in general a person with virtue finds pleasure in what accords with virtue. The pleasures of the masses, because they are not pleasant by nature, conflict with one another, but the pleasures of those who are fond of noble things are pleasant by nature. Actions in accordance with virtue are like this, so that they are pleasant to these people as well [15] as in themselves. Their life therefore has no need of pleasure as some kind of lucky ornament, but contains its pleasure in itself, because, in addition to what we have already said, the person who does not enjoy noble actions is not good. For no one would call a person just if he did [20] not enjoy acting justly, or generous if he did not enjoy generous actions; and the same goes for the other virtues. If this is so, it follows that actions in accordance with virtue are pleasant in themselves. But they are also good and noble as well as pleasant; indeed, since the good person is a good judge of goodness and nobility, actions in accordance with virtue have them to a degree greater than anything else; and here he judges in accordance with our views.

Happiness, then, is the best, the noblest and the pleasantest thing, and [25] these qualities are not separate as in the inscription at Delos :

> Noblest is that which is the most just, and best is being healthy. But most pleasant is obtaining what one longs for.

This is because the best activities have all of these qualities. And we say [30] that happiness consists in them, or one of them – the best.

Nevertheless, as we suggested, happiness obviously needs the presence of external goods as well, since it is impossible, or at least no easy matter, to perform noble actions without resources . For in many actions, we employ, as if they were instruments at our disposal, friends, wealth, and [ 1099b ] political power. Again, being deprived of some things – such as high birth, noble children, beauty – spoils our blessedness. For the person who is terribly ugly, of low birth, or solitary and childless is not really the sort to be happy, still less perhaps if he has children or friends who are [5] thoroughly bad, or good but dead. As we have said, then, there seems to be an additional need for some sort of prosperity like this. For this reason, some identify happiness with good fortune, while others identify it with virtue.

## Chapter 9

Hence the problem also arises of whether happiness is to be acquired by learning, habituation, or some other training, or whether it comes by virtue of some divine dispensation or even by chance. [10]

If there is anything that the gods give to men, it is reasonable that happiness should be god-given, especially since it is so much the best thing in the human world. But this question would perhaps be more suited to another inquiry. Even if it is not sent by the gods, however, but [15] arises through virtue and some sort of learning or training, it is evidently one of the most divine things. For that which is the prize and end of virtue is clearly the chief good, something both divine and blessed.

It would also be something widely shared, since everyone who was not incapacitated with regard to virtue could attain it through some kind of learning and personal effort. And if it is better to be happy in this way than by chance, it is reasonable that happiness should be [20] attained like this. For what is in accordance with nature is by nature as noble as it can be, and so is what is in accordance with skill and every other cause, especially that in accordance with the best cause. To entrust what is greatest and most noble to chance would be quite inappropriate.

The answer to our question is also manifest from our account of [25] happiness, since we said that it was a certain kind of activity of the soul in accordance with virtue; and of the other goods, some are necessary conditions of happiness, and others are naturally helpful and serve as useful means to it.

And this agrees with what we said at the beginning. We took the end of political science to be the chief good, and political science is concerned [30] most of all with producing citizens of a certain kind, namely, those who are both good and the sort to perform noble actions.

It is with good reason, then, that we do not call an ox, a horse or any [ 1100a ] other animal happy, because none of them can share in such activity. And for this same reason, a child is not happy either, since his age makes him incapable of doing such actions . If he is called blessed, he is being described as such on account of the potential he has, since, as we have [5] said, happiness requires complete virtue and a complete life. For there are many vicissitudes in life, all sorts of chance things happen, and even the most successful can meet with great misfortunes in old age, as the story goes of Priam 6 in Trojan times. No one calls someone happy who meets with misfortunes like these and comes to a wretched end.

## Chapter 10

[10] Should we then call no one happy while they are alive, but rather, as Solon advises, wait to see the end? 7 Even if we must assume this to be right, is it really the case that he is happy when he is dead? Or is this not quite ridiculous, especially for us, claiming as we do that happiness is some kind of activity?

[15] But if it is not that we call the dead person happy, and Solon meant not this, but that we can at that stage safely call a person blessed in so far as he is now beyond the reach of evils and misfortunes, even this claim is open to dispute. For both good and evil are thought to happen to a dead person, since they can happen to a person who is alive but not [20] aware of them. Take, for example, honours and dishonours, and the good and bad fortunes of his children or his descendants generally. But this view also gives rise to a problem. Though a person may have lived a blessed life into his old age and died accordingly, many reverses may happen in connection with his descendants. Some of them may be [25] good and meet with the life they deserve, others the contrary; and clearly the relation to their ancestors can vary to any degree. It would indeed be odd if the dead person also were to share in these vicissitudes, and be sometimes happy, sometimes wretched. But it would also be odd if the fortunes of descendants had no effect on their ancestors for any [30] time at all.

But we should return to the original question, since considering it might shed light on the one now under discussion. If we must wait to see the end and only then call a person blessed, not as such but as having been so before, surely it is odd that – because we do not wish to call the living happy on account of possible changes in their fortunes, [ 1100b ] and because happiness is understood as something permanent and not at all liable to change, while the living experience many turns of the wheel – when he is happy, he will not be truly described as such? For clearly, if we were to follow his fortunes, we should often call the same person [5] happy and then wretched, representing the happy person as a kind of chameleon, or as having an unsound foundation. Or is following a person’s fortunes the wrong thing to do? For they are not what doing well or badly depend on, though, as we said, they are required as complementary to a fully human life. What really matter for happiness are activities in accordance with virtue, and for the contrary of [10] happiness the contrary kind of activities.

The question we have been discussing is further confirmation of our account, since nothing in the sphere of human achievement has more permanence than activities in accordance with virtue. They are thought to be more lasting even than the sciences, and the most honourable to be the more lasting, because the blessed spend their lives engaged, [15] quite continually, in them above all (which seems to be why there is no forgetting in connection with these activities).
