## Book X

## Chapter 1

After this our next task is presumably to discuss pleasure, because pleasure seems to be especially closely associated with beings like us. This is why [20] people educate the young by steering them in the right direction with pleasure and pain. Also, enjoying and hating the right things seem the most important factors in virtue of character, because pleasure and pain run through the whole of life; and they have weighty significance for virtue and the happy life, since people rationally choose what is pleasant, and [25] avoid what is painful. It would seem, then, that these are the last things that should be ignored, especially since there is much dispute about them: some say that pleasure is the good, while others say on the contrary that it is thoroughly bad.

Some of those who say it is bad presumably say this because they are convinced that this is how things are. Others, however, say it because they believe that it is better with a view to how we live to represent pleasure as [30] a bad thing, even if it is not. For they think that the masses are inclined towards it and are slaves to their pleasures, and that we ought therefore to lead them in the opposite direction, since in this way they might arrive at the mean point. But surely this view is incorrect. For in matters to do with feelings and actions, arguments are less reliable than the facts; so [35] when they conflict with the facts of perception, they are scorned, and undermine the truth as well. For if a person who criticizes pleasure is once [ 1172b ] seen aiming at it, the reason for his inclining towards it is thought to be that he regards all pleasure as worth pursuing, because it is not characteristic of the masses to draw distinctions. True arguments, then, seem to be [5] the most useful, not only in the acquisition of knowledge, but in how we live. For since they are in harmony with the facts, they are believed, and for that reason they spur those who understand them to live in accordance with them.

Enough of such matters, then; let us consider the views that have been expressed about pleasure.

## Chapter 2

[10] Eudoxus thought pleasure was the good because he saw that all things, whether rational or not, aim at it. And in everything, he says, what is worthy of choice is good, and what is most worthy of choice is best; thus the fact that everything is borne towards the same thing shows that this is what is best for all, since each thing finds its own good, as it finds its own food; and that which is good for all things and at which all aim is the good.

[15] His arguments were accepted more because of the virtue of his character than on their own account. For since he seemed remarkably temperate, it seemed that he was not saying these things because he was a friend of pleasure, but that this was really how things were. He thought that the matter was just as clear if one considered it from the opposite point [20] of view. Pain, he thought, is in itself something to be avoided by all, and therefore, similarly, its contrary is something to be chosen by all. What is the most worth choosing is what we choose neither because of nor for the sake of something else. And everyone agrees that pleasure is like this, since no one asks for justification of anyone’s being pleased, on the assumption that pleasure is worthy of choice in itself. He said too that [25] pleasure, when it is added to any other good, such as acting in a just or temperate manner, makes the other good more worthy of choice; and that the good is increased by the addition of itself.

This last argument, at least, seems to represent it as one good among others, and no more a good than any other, because any good thing is more worthy of choice when another good is added to it than it is on its own. Indeed, it is with an argument like this that Plato destroys the claim of pleasure to be the good: 77 the life of pleasure is more worthy of choice [30] with the addition of intelligence than without it, and if the mixture is better, pleasure is not the good, because the good cannot become more worthy of choice by anything’s being added to it. And clearly nothing else can be the good either, if it becomes more worthy of choice with the addition of anything that is good in itself. What, then, is there that is like this, and that we share in? This is what we are looking for. [35]

People who object that what all things aim at is not good are talking nonsense: whatever seems to all to be the case, we say is the case. And the [ 1173a ] person who attacks this belief will not generally have anything more convincing to say. If it were creatures without intellect that desired pleasures , there might be something in what they said; but if intelligent beings do so as well, what sense can be made of it? Presumably even in the lower animals there is some element better than themselves that aims at [5] their proper good.

Nor does the argument about the contrary of pleasure seem plausible. They say that if pain is an evil, it does not follow that pleasure is a good, because evil is also opposed to evil, and both are opposed to what is neither good nor evil. This is fair enough, but is not true in the case we are discussing. For if both were evils, they ought both to be things to be [10] avoided, and if neither is an evil, neither ought to be something to be avoided, or they should be so to the same extent. But people manifestly avoid the one as an evil, and choose the other as a good; so this is the way they are opposed to one another.

## Chapter 3

Again, if pleasure is not a quality, this does not prevent its being a good, because the activities of virtue are not qualities either; nor is happiness. [15]

But they say that the good is determinate, whereas pleasure is indeterminate, since it admits of degrees. If they make this judgement on the basis of the experience of pleasure, the same will apply in the cases of justice and the other virtues. In respect of these, people are plainly said to have a certain character, and to act in accordance with the virtues , to [20] a greater or lesser degree, since people can be more just or more courageous, and one can act in a just or temperate way to a greater or lesser degree.

But if their judgement is based on the pleasures, surely they are not giving us the real reason, if some pleasures are in fact unmixed and others mixed? And why should pleasure not be like health, which is determinate [25] despite admitting of degrees? For it does not consist in the same proportion in everyone, nor is it even always the same one proportion in the same person, but even when it is fading it remains up to a point, and differs in degree. So the same may go for pleasure as well.

And they assume the good to be complete, and processes and comings- [30] to-be to be incomplete, and try to represent pleasure as a process and a coming-to-be. But it would seem that they are wrong, and that pleasure is not a process, since quickness and slowness seem to be proper to every process, if not in itself – as, for example, with the cosmos – then in relation to something else. But neither of these is true of pleasure. For though one can become pleased quickly, as [ 1173b ] one can become angry quickly, one cannot be pleased quickly, not even in relation to another person; we can, however, walk, grow and so on quickly. So, while one can change quickly or slowly into a state of pleasure, one cannot quickly engage in the activity in accordance with it, that is, be pleased quickly.

[5] And how could it be a coming-to-be? For, it seems, not any chance thing comes to be from any other chance thing, but things are resolved into that from which they came to be; and where pleasure is the coming to be of something, pain would be the destruction of it.

They say as well that pain is a deficiency in our natural being, and that pleasure is replenishment. But these experiences are bodily; so if [10] pleasure is replenishment of our natural being, that in which the replenishment takes place will experience pleasure. It will therefore be the body that does so. But this does not seem to be true. The replenishment, then, is not pleasure, though one would be pleased when the replenishment was taking place, as one would be pained if one were being cut. This belief seems to have arisen from consideration of the pains and pleasures [15] connected with eating: because we have developed a need and experienced pain beforehand, we take pleasure in the replenishment. But this does not happen in the case of all pleasures: those of learning are painless, as are, among those involved in perception, the pleasures of smell, and many sounds, sights, memories and hopes as well. Of what, then, will they [20] be the comings-to-be? For no deficiency of anything has arisen, of which there might come to be a replenishment.

Against those who bring up disgraceful pleasures , we could argue that these are not pleasant. For if they are pleasant to people in a bad condition, we should not think that they are also pleasant, except to these people, just as we should not think that things that are healthy, sweet or bitter to sick people are such, except to them, or that things that appear white to those with diseased eyes are such, except to them. [25]

Or we might argue in the following way: that the pleasures are worthy of choice, but not when they come from these sources, as wealth , for example, is worth choosing, but not at the price of being a traitor, or health, but not at the price of eating anything whatsoever. Or perhaps pleasures differ in species; those from noble sources are different from those from bad ones, and we cannot experience the pleasure of the just [30] person without being just, nor that of the musical person without being musical, and similarly in the other cases.

The difference between a friend and a flatterer seems to make it plain that pleasure is not good, or that pleasures differ in species. For in associating with us the friend seems to have his eye on the good, the flatterer on what is pleasant; and the flatterer is criticized, while the friend is praised, on the ground that he is associating with us for different reasons . [ 1174a ]

And no one would choose to live the whole of his life with the mind of a child, even if he were to take the utmost pleasure in what pleases children, or choose to enjoy doing some terribly disgraceful deed, even if he would never suffer any pain as a consequence.

And there are many things we should be concerned to have even if they brought no pleasure with them, such as seeing, remembering, knowing, [5] possessing the virtues. Even if pleasures necessarily accompany these, it makes no difference, since we should choose them even if no pleasure arose from them.

It seems to be clear, then, that pleasure is not the good, that not every pleasure is worthy of choice, and that some pleasures are worthy of choice [10] in themselves, differing from others in species or in their sources.

Enough said, then, about pleasure and pain.

## Chapter 4

What pleasure is, or what sort of thing it is, will become clearer if we take up the question again from the beginning.

Seeing seems at any moment to be complete, because it does not lack [15] anything that will come to be later and complete its form. And pleasure seems to be like this as well, since it is a whole, and at no time can one find a pleasure such that, if it comes to be for a longer time, its form will become complete.

[20] For this reason it is not a process either, since every process – building, for example – takes time and has an end, and is complete when it has produced what it aims at; it is complete, therefore, in the whole time it takes, or at the final moment. And each process is incomplete during those processes that constitute its parts – the time it takes, in other words – and these parts differ in form from the whole and from each other. For there is a difference between placing stones together and fluting a column, [25] and these are both different from the production of the temple. The production of the temple is complete, since it needs nothing further to achieve what was proposed, while that of the foundation and the triglyph is incomplete, since each is the production of a part. They differ in form, then, and one cannot find at any particular moment a process complete in form, but, if at all, only in the whole time. The same goes for walking [30] and the other processes. For if locomotion is a process from one place to another, there are differences of form here as well – flying, walking, jumping, and so on. And not only this, but even in walking itself there are differences: the starting-point and the finishing-point are not the same in the whole racecourse as they are in a part of it, or in one part as in another; nor is traversing the length of this line the same as traversing the [ 1174b ] length of that, since one does not merely travel along a line, but a line in a certain place, and this line is in a different place from that.

We have discussed process in detail in another work, but it does seem that it is not complete at every moment, and that the many movements [5] are incomplete and different in form, since the points from where they begin and where they end give them their form. But the form of pleasure is complete at any given moment, so it is clear that it is different from a process, and that pleasure is something whole and complete. This would seem true also from the fact that a process must take time, whereas being pleased does not, since what takes place at the present moment is a kind of whole.

[10] It is also clear from these considerations that it is wrong to say that there is a process or a coming-to-be of pleasure. For not everything can be so described, but only what has parts and is not a whole; for there is no coming-to-be of seeing, or a point, or a unit, and none of these is either a process or a coming-to-be. Thus, since it is a whole, there is no coming-to-be of pleasure either.

Every sense engages in activity in relation to its object, and its activity [15] is complete when it is in good condition in relation to the noblest of its objects. For this seems in particular to be the nature of complete activity, and we can assume it to be irrelevant whether one says that it is the sense that engages in activity or the subject in which it exists. In the case of each sense, then, the best activity will be that of the subject in the best condition in relation to the best of that sense’s objects.

And this activity will be the most complete and the most pleasant. For [20] there is a pleasure corresponding to every sense, just as there is to thought and contemplation; and it is most pleasant when it is most complete, and most complete when the subject is in good condition and it occurs in relation to the best of its objects. Pleasure completes the activity, but not in the same way as the object of the sense and the sense complete it when they are both good, just as health and the doctor are not responsible in [25] the same way for one’s being healthy. For it is obvious that a pleasure comes about corresponding to each of the senses, since we speak of sights and sounds as pleasant; and it is obvious too that it comes about most of all whenever the sense is at its best and engaged in activity in relation to the best sort of object. When both object and subject of perception are [30] at their best, there will always be pleasure, since what will produce it and what will experience it are both present. Pleasure completes the activity not as the inherent state does, but as a sort of supervenient end, like the bloom on the faces of young men. So long, then, as the objects of intellect or perception, and the faculties of judgement or contemplation, are as they should be, there will be pleasure in the activity. For when that which [ 1175a ] experiences and that which produces the experience remain similar, and are in the same relation to one another, the same thing naturally comes about.

How is it, then, that no one is continuously pleased? Is it that one grows weary? For nothing human is capable of continuous activity, and [5] so no continuous pleasure comes about, since pleasure follows upon the activity. And some things delight us when they are new, but less later, for the same reason. For at first our thought is stimulated and engages vigorously in activity in relation to them, as happens with people’s sense of sight when they are looking closely at something; but afterwards our activity is not like this and we lose interest, and for this reason the [10] pleasure is dimmed as well.

Because everyone aims at life, we might think that everyone desires pleasure. Life is a kind of activity, and each person engages in activity in relation to those objects and with those faculties that he likes best; the musician, for example, engages in activity with his hearing in relation to [15] songs, the student with his thought in relation to what he studies, and so on in each case. Pleasure completes the activities, and therefore also life, which they desire. It is reasonable, then, for them to aim at pleasure as well, since for each person it completes life, and life is something worth choosing.

But whether we choose life for the sake of pleasure or pleasure for the [20] sake of life is a question we may dismiss for the present. For they appear to be bound closely together and not to admit of separation, since pleasure does not occur without activity, and it completes every activity as well.

## Chapter 5

For this reason, pleasures also seem to differ in species, because we assume that things of different species are completed by different things. [25] This is apparently what happens with natural and artificial objects, such as animals, trees, a picture, a statue, a house, or a tool. Similarly, we assume that activities that differ in species are also completed by things differing in species. The activities of thought differ in species from those of the senses, and both differ among themselves; so therefore do the pleasures that complete them.

This is evident also from the fact that each of the pleasures is closely [30] related to the activity it completes. For the pleasure proper to an activity enhances it, because those who engage in activity with pleasure show better and more accurate judgement. It is people who enjoy geometry, for example, who become geometricians and understand each aspect of it [35] better, and similarly lovers of music, building and so on improve in their own proper sphere by finding enjoyment in it. And the pleasures enhance [ 1175b ] the activities, and what enhances an activity is proper to it; and what are proper to things different in species are themselves different in species.

This is even more evident from the fact that activities are hindered by pleasures arising from different activities. Lovers of the flute are incapable of paying attention to a discussion once they overhear someone playing the flute, since they find more enjoyment in flute-playing than in their [5] present activity; so the pleasure connected with the flute ruins the activity of discussion. This same thing happens in other cases as well, when a person engages in activity in two spheres at the same time; the more pleasant activity pushes aside the other, the more so if the difference in pleasure is a large one, even to the point where the other activity ceases. This is why, when we enjoy something a great deal, we do not really do [10] anything else, and when we are only mildly pleased by something, we do other things; people who eat sweets in the theatre, for example, do it most when the acting is bad.

And since activities are made more rigorous, longer lasting and better by their proper pleasure, and impaired by foreign pleasures, it is clear [15] that the two kinds of pleasure are very different. For foreign pleasures do almost what the pains proper to an activity do; the pains proper to activities ruin them, so that if, for example, someone finds writing or calculating unpleasant and painful, he does not write or calculate, since the activity is painful. So an activity is affected in contrary ways by the [20] pleasures and pains proper to it, those occurring in relation to the activity in itself. And, as we have said, foreign pleasures produce much the same result as pain, since they ruin the activity, though not in the same way.

Since activities differ in their goodness and badness, and some are [25] worthy of choice, some to be avoided, others neither, the same goes for pleasures, each activity’s having its own proper pleasure. Thus the pleasure proper to a virtuous activity is good, and that proper to a wicked one bad, because appetites for noble objects are to be praised, those for disgraceful things blamed. And the pleasures in activities are more [30] proper to them than the desires for them, since the desires are distinct both in time and in nature, while the pleasures are closely related to the activities, and are so difficult to distinguish that there is a question whether the activity and the pleasure are the same. Nevertheless, pleasure does not seem to be thought or perception, since that would be odd. But because they are not found separately they appear to some people to [35] be the same.

As activities differ, then, so do pleasures. Sight differs from touch in [ 1176a ] purity, as do hearing and smell from taste, and so their pleasures also differ in the same way. The pleasures of thought differ in turn from these, and within each class some differ from others.

Each animal seems to have its own proper pleasure , as it has its own characteristic activity, since its proper pleasure will be that in line with the activity it engages in. This will be evident if we consider each kind [5] as well. A horse, a dog and a human being have different pleasures; and, as Heraclitus says, a donkey would choose sweepings over gold, since donkeys find food more pleasant than gold. 78 So the pleasures of animals that differ in species themselves differ in species, and it is plausible that those of a single species do not differ.

[10] But, in the case of human beings at any rate, they do vary a great deal, since the same things delight some people and pain others, and while to some they are painful and hateful, to others they are pleasant and worthy of love. This happens too with sweet things. For the same things do not [15] seem sweet to a feverish as to a healthy person, or hot to a sick as to a fit person; and the same thing happens in other cases. But in all such things, it seems that what is so is what appears so to the good person. If this view is right, as it seems to be, and virtue – that is, the good person in so far as he is good – is the measure of each thing, then pleasures will be [20] what appear so to him, and pleasant things will be what he enjoys. And if things that he finds disagreeable appear pleasant to someone, that is not surprising, since there are many ways for people to become ruined and perverted. The things are not pleasant, except to these people, with this disposition.

Clearly, then, we should say that those that everyone agrees to be disgraceful are not pleasures, except to people who have been ruined. But of those that seem good, what kind of pleasure, or what particular [25] pleasure, should we say is the pleasure characteristic of a human being? Or, since the pleasures follow upon the activities, will it not be clear from the activities? So whether the complete and blessed person has one activity or several, the pleasures that complete these will be said to be the pleasures really characteristic of a human being, and the rest will be so in a secondary and less real sense, as are the activities.

## Chapter 6

[30] Now that we have discussed the virtues, friendships and pleasures, it remains for us to offer an outline account of happiness, since we assume it to be the end in human affairs. Our argument will be more concise if we first sum up what has been said already.

We said, then, that it is not a state, since if it were it might be possessed [35] by someone asleep all his life, living a vegetable existence, or someone [ 1176b ] suffering the greatest misfortunes. So if this is implausible, we should put it rather in the class of activities , as we said above. And some activities are necessary, that is, worth choosing for the sake of something else, while others are worthy of choice in themselves; clearly, happiness must be classed as one of those worthy of choice in themselves and not as one of those worth choosing for the sake of something else. For happiness lacks [5] nothing, but is self-sufficient; and an activity is worthy of choice in itself when nothing is sought from it beyond the activity. Actions in accordance with virtue seem like this, since doing noble and good actions is worthy of choice in itself.

But pleasurable amusements also seem to be in this class; for people do not choose them for the sake of other things, since they are more harmed [10] than benefited by them, through failing to take care of their bodies and their property. And most of those called happy have recourse to pastimes like this, which is why those who are adroit in them are highly esteemed at the courts of tyrants; they offer themselves as pleasant purveyors of what the tyrants are after, and the tyrants want people like this. And so [15] these amusements seem to be connected with happiness, because those in positions of power spend their leisure time on them.

But presumably people like this prove nothing, since virtue and intellect, from which come good activities, do not depend on positions of power. And if these people, never having tasted pure and gracious pleasure, have [20] recourse to bodily pleasures , that is no reason to believe these pleasures to be more worthy of choice, since children also believe that what they give honour to is best. So it is to be expected that, just as different things appear honourable to children and adults, so it will be with good people and bad.

As we have often said, then, what is honourable and pleasant is what is [25] so for the good person. And for each person the activity that accords with his own proper state is the most worthy of choice, and therefore for the good person it is that which accords with virtue.

Happiness, then, does not consist in amusement, because it would be absurd if our end were amusement, and we laboured and suffered all of our lives for the sake of amusing ourselves. For we choose virtually [30] everything for the sake of something else, except happiness, since it is the end; but serious work and exertion for the sake of amusement is manifestly foolish and extremely childish. Rather, as Anacharsis 79 puts it, what seems correct is amusing ourselves so that we can engage in some [35] serious work, since amusement is like relaxation, and we need relaxation [ 1177a ] because we cannot continuously exert ourselves. Relaxation, then, is not an end, since it occurs for the sake of activity.

And the happy life seems to be one in accordance with virtue, and this implies a level of seriousness, and is not spent in amusement. And we say [5] that serious things are better than funny or amusing ones, and that in every case the activity of the better person, or the better part of a person, is more serious, more virtuous; and the activity of what is better is superior, and for this very reason more conducive to happiness . And absolutely anyone, a slave no less than the best of people, can enjoy the bodily pleasures; but no one attributes a share in happiness to a slave, unless he [10] also attributes to him a share in the life we live. For happiness does not consist in occupations like this, but in activities in accordance with virtue, as we have also said before.

## Chapter 7

If happiness is activity in accordance with virtue, it is reasonable to expect that it is in accordance with the highest virtue, and this will be the virtue [15] of the best element. Whether this best element is intellect or something else we think naturally rules and guides us and has insight into matters noble and divine, and whether it is divine or just the most divine element within us, its activity, in accordance with its own proper virtue, will be complete happiness .

That this activity is that of contemplation we have already said. This would seem to agree both with our earlier discussion and with the truth. [20] For this is the highest activity, intellect being the highest element in us, and its objects are the highest objects of knowledge. And it is also the most continuous, since we can contemplate more continuously than we can do anything. And we think that happiness must have pleasure mixed in with it; and the most pleasant of activities in accordance with virtue [25] is agreed to be that in accordance with wisdom. At any rate, philosophy seems to involve pleasures remarkable for their purity and stability, and it is reasonable to expect that those who have knowledge will pass their time more pleasantly than those who are still in search of it. And the self-sufficiency that is spoken of will belong to the activity of contemplation most of all. For though a wise person, a just person, and anyone with any other virtue, all require the necessities of life, nevertheless, when they are adequately provided with such things, the just person will need people [30] as associates in and objects of his just actions, and the same is true of the temperate person, the courageous person and each of the others; but the wise person can contemplate even when he is by himself, the more so the wiser he is. Maybe he can do it better with collaborators, but he is nevertheless the most self-sufficient. [ 1177b ]

Again, contemplation alone seems to be liked for its own sake, since nothing results from it apart from the fact that one has contemplated, whereas from the practical virtues, to a greater or lesser extent, we gain something beyond the action. Again, happiness seems to depend on leisure, because we work to have leisure, and wage war to live in peace. The activity [5] of the practical virtues occurs in politics or war, and actions in these spheres seem to involve exertion. This seems entirely so as regards those in war, since no one chooses to make war, or even starts a war, for the sake of making war; for if someone turned his friends into enemies to bring about [10] battles and killings he would seem utterly murderous. But the activity of a politician also involves exertion, and, apart from the business of politics itself, it is designed to secure power and honours, or at least happiness for himself and the citizens, which is different from politics and which we clearly pursue as something different. [15]

So, among actions performed in accordance with virtue, those in politics and war are distinguished by their nobility and extent, but they involve exertion, aim at some end, and are not worthy of choice for their own sake. The activity of intellect, on the other hand, in so far as it involves contemplation, seems superior in its seriousness, to aim at no end beyond itself, and to have its own proper pleasure, which augments [20] the activity; it seems also to possess self-sufficiency, time for leisure, and freedom from fatigue, as far as these are humanly possible. And clearly this activity also involves whatever else is attributed to the blessed person. Thus it will be complete happiness for a human being – if it consumes a [25] complete span of life, because there is nothing incomplete in matters of happiness.

Such a life is superior to one that is simply human, because someone lives thus, not in so far as he is a human being, but in so far as there is some divine element within him. And the activity of this divine element is as much superior to that in accordance with the other kind of virtue as the [30] element is superior to the compound. If the intellect, then, is something divine compared with the human being, the life in accordance with it will also be divine compared with human life. But we ought not to listen to those who exhort us, because we are human, to think of human things, or because we are mortal, to think of mortal things. We ought rather to take on immortality as much as possible, and do all that we can to live in [ 1178a ] accordance with the highest element within us; for even if its bulk is small, in its power and value it far exceeds everything.

It would seem, too, to constitute each person, since it is his authoritative and better element; it would be odd, then, if he were to choose not his own life, but something else’s.

[5] And what we said above will apply here as well: what is proper to each thing is by nature best and pleasantest for it; for a human being, therefore, the life in accordance with intellect is best and pleasantest, since this, more than anything else, constitutes humanity. So this life will also be the happiest.

## Chapter 8

The life in accordance with the other kind of virtue is happy in a [10] secondary way, since the activities in accordance with it are human. For we do just actions, courageous actions, and the other actions in accordance with the virtues, in relation to each other, observing what is proper to each in contracts, services and actions of all kinds, and in feelings as [15] well; and all of these are manifestly human. Some feelings seem in fact to have their origin in the body, and virtue of character in many ways to be closely bound up with the feelings.

Practical wisdom, too, is tied up with virtue of character, and this with practical wisdom, since the first principles of practical wisdom are in accordance with the virtues of character, and correctness in the virtues of character is in accordance with practical wisdom. And since they are [20] also united with the feelings, the virtues of character must be concerned with the compound. Because the virtues of the compound are human, so are the life and happiness in accordance with them. The virtue of intellect, however, is separate. Let us leave it at that, since a detailed account would be beyond the scope of our project.

It would seem also to require external means to a small extent, or to a [25] smaller extent than virtue of character. Let us accept that they both require the necessities of life, and to an equal extent, since even though the politician expends more effort on matters of the body and suchlike, any difference here would be a small one; nevertheless, in what they need for their activities, there will be a big difference. For the generous person will need money for doing generous actions; and the just person will [30] need it for repaying debts, since wishes are uncertain, and even those who are not just pretend that they wish to act justly. And the courageous person will need power, and the temperate person opportunity, if they are to accomplish any of the actions that accord with their virtue. For how else will he, or any of the others, make manifest what he is?

It is debated as well whether it is the rational choice or the actions that [35] are more really characteristic of virtue, on the assumption that it depends [ 1178b ] on both. Its being complete would clearly involve both, but for actions many things are needed, and the greater and nobler the actions, the greater the number of things needed. But a person who is contemplating needs none of these, for that activity at any rate; indeed, one might say that they are even obstacles, to contemplation at least. But in so far as he [5] is a human being and lives together with a number of others, he chooses to do actions in accordance with virtue; he will therefore need such things for the living of a human life.

That complete happiness consists in some contemplative activity is also apparent from the following. We assume the gods to be supremely blessed and happy; but what sorts of actions should we attribute to them? Just [10] actions? But will they not obviously be ridiculous if they make contracts, return deposits and so on? Courageous acts, then, enduring what is fearful and facing dangers because it is noble to do so? Or generous acts? To whom will they give? And it will be absurd if they have money or anything [15] like it. And what would their temperate acts consist in? Is such praise not cheap, since they have no bad appetites? If we were to run through them all, anything to do with actions would appear petty and unworthy of the gods.

Nevertheless, everyone assumes that they are at least alive and therefore engage in activity, since we do not take them to sleep like Endymion . 80 So if we remove from a living being the possibility of action, [20] and furthermore the very possibility of producing anything, what is left apart from contemplation? So the god’s activity, which is superior in blessedness, will be contemplative; and therefore the human activity most akin to this is the most conducive to happiness.

[25] There is an indication of this in the fact that the other animals have no share in happiness , being completely deprived of the activity in question. For while the life of the gods is entirely blessed, and that of human beings is so to the extent that it contains something like this sort of activity, none of the other animals is happy, because they have no share [30] at all in contemplation. Happiness , then, extends as far as contemplation, and the more contemplation there is in one’s life, the happier one is, not incidentally, but in virtue of the contemplation, since this is honourable in itself. Happiness, therefore, will be some form of contemplation.

But because the happy person is human, he will also need external prosperity; for human nature is not self-sufficient for contemplation, [35] but the body must be healthy and provided with food and other care. [ 1179a ] Nevertheless, we should not think that someone who is going to be happy will need many substantial things, just because one cannot be blessed without external goods. For neither self-sufficiency nor action depends [5] on excess, and we can do noble actions without ruling over land and sea, because we can act in accordance with virtue even from modest resources. This can be seen quite clearly, since private individuals seem to do good actions no less – indeed more – than those in positions of power. And it is enough to have moderate resources, since the life of a person whose [10] activity conforms with virtue will be happy. Solon , too, was presumably right in his portrayal of happy people, when he said that they had been modestly furnished with external goods, but had done what he regarded as the noblest actions and had lived temperately. For people can do what they ought even when their possessions are modest. Anaxagoras also seems to have assumed the happy person to be neither rich nor powerful, [15] since he said that he would not be surprised if the happy person appeared an absurd sort of person to the masses; 81 for since they perceive only externals, it is by these that they judge. The beliefs of the wise, then, seem to harmonize with our arguments.

But while such things do carry some conviction, the truth in practical [20] issues is judged from the facts of our life, these being what really matter. We must therefore examine what has been said in the light of the facts of our life, and if it agrees with the facts, then we should accept it, while if it conflicts, we must assume it to be no more than theory.

The person whose activity is in accordance with intellect and who cultivates it seems to be in the best condition and dearest to the gods. For if the gods feel any concern for human affairs, as they seem to, it [25] would be reasonable for them to find enjoyment in what is best and most closely related to them – namely, intellect – and to reward those who like and honour this most, on the assumption that these people care for what is loved by the gods, and act rightly and nobly. And it is quite clear that all of these qualities belong most of all to the wise person; he, therefore, is [30] dearest to the gods. And it is likely that this same person is also the happiest; so in this way too the wise person will be more happy than anyone else.

## Chapter 9

We have now said enough in outline about the above questions and the virtues, and about friendship and pleasure as well, so should we think that our project has been achieved? Or is it not true that, as we say, in practical [35] studies the end consists not in contemplating and knowing about [ 1179b ] particular points, but rather in acting upon them? So knowing about virtue is not enough, but we must also try to attain and exercise it, or become good by any other available route.

If arguments were sufficient by themselves to make people good, then [5] they would have won many great rewards, and justly so, as Theognis says, 82 – in other words, it would have been right to award them. But as things are, though they appear to have the power to influence and encourage those young people who possess generosity of spirit, and perhaps to make susceptible to virtue a character that is well bred and truly loves what [10] is noble, they seem unable to influence the masses in the direction of what is noble and good. For the masses naturally obey fear, not shame, and abstain from shameful acts because of the punishments associated with them, not because they are disgraceful. For, living by their feelings as they do, they pursue their own personal pleasures and the means to them, and avoid the opposed pains; and they do not have even an idea of what is noble [15] and truly pleasant, since they have never tasted it. What argument, then, could reform people like this? For displacing by argument what has been long entrenched in people’s characters is difficult if not impossible. And presumably we should be content if, when we have everything that seems [20] required for becoming good, we attain some share of virtue.

Some think we become good by nature, some by habit , and others by teaching. Nature’s contribution is clearly not in our power, but it can be found in those who are truly fortunate as the result of some divine dispensation. Argument and teaching, presumably, are not powerful in [25] every case, but the soul of the student must be prepared beforehand in its habits, with a view to its enjoying and hating in a noble way, like soil that is to nourish seed. For if someone were to live by his feelings he would not listen to an argument to dissuade him, nor could he even understand it. How can we persuade a person in a state like this to change his ways? And, in general, feelings seem to yield not to argument but to [30] force. There must, therefore, somehow be a pre-existing character with some affinity for virtue through its fondness for what is noble and dislike of what is disgraceful.

But if one has not been reared under the right laws it is difficult to obtain from one’s earliest years the correct upbringing for virtue, because the masses, especially the young, do not find it pleasant to live temperately and with endurance. For this reason, their upbringing and [35] pursuits should be regulated by laws, because they will not find them painful once they have become accustomed to them.

[ 1180a ] Perhaps it is not enough, however, that when they are young they get the right upbringing and care; rather, because they must continue to practise and develop their habits when they are grown up, we shall need laws for this as well, and generally for the whole of life. For the masses heed [5] necessity rather than argument, punishments rather than what is noble.

This, some people think, is why legislators ought to urge people to virtue and encourage them to act for the sake of what is noble – on the assumption that those who have been trained well in their habits will respond – but ought also to impose punishments and penalties on those who disobey or whose nature is more deficient, and completely banish [10] the incorrigible. For, they think, the good person, since he lives with a view to what is noble, will listen to reason, while the bad person, since he desires pleasure, is chastened by pain, like a beast of burden; this is also why they say the pains inflicted should be those most opposed to the pleasures they like.

[15] As we have said, then, the person who is to be good must be nobly brought up and habituated, and then spend his life engaged in good pursuits and do nothing bad whether involuntarily or voluntarily. And this would happen when people lived in accordance with a kind of intellect and a correct system with power over them.

Now the command of a father has no strength or compulsive power, nor in general does that of a single person, unless he is a king or something [20] like that; but law does have compulsive power, and it is reason proceeding from a kind of practical wisdom and from intellect. And people hate a human being who stands in opposition to their impulses, even if he is right to do so; but there is no oppressiveness in the law’s prescribing what is good.

But it is in the city of Sparta alone, or almost alone, that the legislator [25] seems to have been careful about people’s upbringing and pursuits. In most cities, such matters have been neglected, and each person lives as he wishes, ‘laying down the law for children and wife’, like a Cyclops . 83 The best thing, then, is for there to be correct public concern with such [30] things. But if they are neglected in the public sphere, it would seem appropriate for each person to help his own children and friends on the way to virtue, and for him to be able to do this, or at least rationally choose to do so. From what we have said, however, it would seem that he will be better able to do this if he has the chance of legislating, because care at the public level is evidently demonstrated through laws, and good care through good laws. And whether they are written or [35] unwritten, whether they are to educate one or many, seems not to matter, any [ 1180b ] more than it matters in the case of music, gymnastics and other pursuits. For just as in cities laws and people’s characters are powerful, so in [5] households are the words and character of fathers, all the more because of the relation of kinship and the benefits he confers; for from the start the children are naturally fond of him and inclined to obey.

Again, education on an individual basis is superior to education in common, as in the case of medical care. For though in general rest and abstinence from food are beneficial for a person in a fever, presumably they may not be for a particular person; and a boxer, presumably, will not [10] prescribe the same style of fighting for all his pupils. It would seem, then, that particular cases are treated with greater subtlety if there is attention to individuals, since each person is more likely to obtain what suits him.

But the best at providing individual attention will be the doctor, the gymnastic instructor or anyone else who has the universal knowledge of [15] what is good for everyone or for specific people, since the sciences are said to be, and indeed are, concerned with what is common. Nevertheless, there is perhaps nothing to prevent someone’s taking care of an individual person well, even lacking any scientific knowledge , if he has considered precisely, in the light of experience, what happens in each case, just as some [20] people seem to be their own best doctors, though incapable of helping anyone else. None the less, presumably it does seem that if a person does wish to become practised in a skill or in something theoretical, he must go to the universal, and come to know it as well as he can; for, as we have said, it is with this that the sciences are concerned.

Then perhaps as well a person who wishes to improve people, whether [25] many or few, through his concern for them should try to develop a capacity for legislating, if it is through laws that we will become good. For producing a noble disposition in just anyone, whoever is put before one, is not a task that just anyone can perform; if it is anyone’s task, it is that of the person who knows, just as in the case of medicine and the other sciences that require some kind of care and practical wisdom.

Should we not move on, then, to consider where or how one might [30] acquire a capacity for legislation? Is it, as in other cases, from politicians? For we did think that it was part of political science. Or is there not an apparent difference between political science and the other sciences and capacities? For in the others, we find the same people – doctors and painters for example – both imparting their capacities to others, and [35] exercising them too. The sophists, however, profess to teach politics, [ 1181a ] though none of them practises it; that is done by the politicians, and they seem to act with some kind of capacity and experience rather than with thought. For we do not find them writing or speaking about such matters, though it would presumably be nobler than speaking in legal cases or the [5] assembly; nor do we find that they have made their sons or any other of their friends into politicians. And yet one would have expected them to do so if they were able, since there is nothing better than such a capacity that they could have bequeathed to their cities, or could rationally choose to have for themselves, or therefore for those dearest to them. Nevertheless, [10] experience has much to contribute, for otherwise people would not have become politicians through familiarity with politics. So it seems that those who seek to know about political science also need experience.

But those of the sophists who profess to teach appear very far from actually doing so, being completely ignorant about what kind of thing it is and what its sphere of concern is. Otherwise, they would not have classed it with rhetoric or even as inferior to it, nor would they have thought [15] it easy to legislate by collecting those laws of which people think well. For they think it is possible to pick out the best laws, as if the very act of picking out did not call for judgement and as if correct judgement were not the most important factor, as in music. For it is people experienced in any area who judge its products correctly, and understand by what [20] means and how they are accomplished, and what is in harmony with what; the inexperienced must be content if it does not escape them whether the product has been well or badly made, as in painting. Laws seem to be the products of political science; how, therefore, could one develop a capacity for legislation, or judge which are best, from laws alone? For neither do [ 1181b ] doctors appear to acquire their skill from books.

And yet doctors try to describe not only the treatments, but also how particular groups could be cured and ought to be treated, distinguishing the various states. This seems beneficial to those with experience, but [5] useless to the ignorant. So presumably collections of laws and political systems might be very useful to people who can study them and judge which are noble, or the contrary, and which suit particular circumstances. [10] But those who go through them without being in this state will not be able to judge well, unless by instinct, though they may perhaps become more discriminating in such matters.

Since, then, our predecessors have left the question of legislation unexamined, it is presumably better that we study it, and the question of political systems in general, so that our philosophy of humanity might [15] be as complete as possible. First, then, if any part of what has been said by those before us is plausible, let us try to go through it. Then, in the light of the political systems we have collected, let us try to consider what sorts of things preserve and destroy cities and each type of political system, [20] and what causes some cities to be well run, and others badly run. For when these issues have been considered, we shall perhaps be more likely to see which political system is best, how each must be arranged, and what laws and habits it should employ. Let us, then, discuss these matters from the beginning .

items.text: The central problem is to identify the highest attainable human good that orders the plurality of practical ends.
The argument is architectonic, dialectical, functional, and practical, with a polemical exclusion of a separate universal Good.
The argument moves from purposive action through the hierarchy of ends to political science as the governing inquiry into the human good.
Received conceptions of happiness are filtered through actionability, completeness, self-sufficiency, and independence from merely instrumental goods.
The human function converts the formal criteria of the chief good into rational activity of the soul performed according to virtue.
The activity account integrates pleasure while subordinating external goods and fortune to enabling or obstructive roles.
The definition of happiness generates the inquiry into the rational structure of the soul and the corresponding division of virtue.
Every skill, inquiry, action, and rational choice aims at a good as its end.
When one pursuit is subordinate to another, the end of the superordinate pursuit is more choiceworthy.
A non-vain order of practical desire must terminate in an end wanted for itself.
The human good relevant to political inquiry must be attainable through action.
Political science is architectonic because it orders practical capacities, prescriptions, and their ends toward the common human good.
The proper exactness of an ethical account is limited by the variability of its subject matter.
Competent ethical inquiry begins from habituated practical experience and tests its principles against credible appearances.
Happiness is the commonly recognized name of the highest human end and signifies living and acting well.
A complete end is always chosen for itself and never merely for another end.
A self-sufficient end makes a socially situated life choiceworthy and lacking in nothing essential.
The distinctive human function is rational activity of the soul.
A function is performed well when its activity accords with the virtue appropriate to it.
Human happiness must characterize a complete life rather than an isolated moment or undeveloped potential.
Realized human good consists in virtuous activity rather than the inactive possession of a state.
Activity in accordance with virtue is intrinsically good, noble, and pleasant to the virtuous agent.
External goods are necessary instruments and conditions of many noble activities without being the highest end.
Virtuous activity supplies relative stability, although grave misfortunes can obstruct or diminish a fully blessed human life.
The ethically relevant soul contains reason proper and appetite capable of obeying or resisting reason.
Practical ends cannot all be chosen solely for the sake of further ends.
Ethical inquiry cannot properly demand mathematical precision from variable practical matters.
Ethical knowledge is not practically effective in an agent governed by untrained feeling.
Pleasure detached from virtuous activity is not the chief human good.
Honour is not the chief good because it depends primarily on those who confer it.
Wealth is not the chief good because it is useful only as a means.
Mere possession of virtue is not happiness when it remains inactive or accompanies a ruined life.
Good does not possess one common definition across all categories and practical sciences.
A separate universal Good is not an attainable object of action and supplies no necessary guidance to particular skills.
Self-sufficiency does not mean solitary independence from family, friends, or fellow citizens.
Happiness is not a capacity, a dormant state, or a brief episode of success.
Happiness is not properly constituted or distributed by chance.
Happiness is not merely praised as a relational excellence but honoured as a governing first principle.
Neither nutritive life nor shared sentience defines the distinctive human function or human virtue.
A hierarchy of practices entails a hierarchy of goods ordered by their governing ends.
The terminal end of practical desire is the chief good.
Inquiry into the chief attainable human good belongs to political science.
The common good of the city is more architectonically complete than the isolated good of an individual.
Ethical adequacy requires an action-guiding outline grounded in experienced judgment rather than universal demonstrative exactness.
Happiness satisfies the formal criteria of the chief good because it is chosen for itself and renders life self-sufficient.
Human happiness is rational activity of the soul performed in accordance with complete virtue across a complete life.
Virtue contributes to happiness only through sustained exercise rather than mere possession.
The pleasure proper to happiness is internal to virtuous activity rather than externally added to it.
Political science must cultivate citizens capable of performing noble actions.
External prosperity affects happiness by furnishing or withholding the means and opportunities for virtuous activity.
Happiness is more stable than fortune but remains qualified by the temporal and material conditions of human life.
Virtue divides into excellences of reasoning and excellences of character formed through appetite’s relation to reason.
Happiness is principally cultivated through education, habituation, and action rather than allotted by chance.
Political order and ethical formation constitute a circuit in which institutions shape the character required to realize the human good.
Happiness has an active formal core and externally conditioned material realization.
The criterion of human goodness is immanent to characteristic human activity rather than imposed by a separate universal object.
Practical reason becomes ethically effective only when desire has been educated into responsiveness to it.
Happiness is temporally cumulative because its identity depends on the durable organization of a life rather than episodic achievement.
Happiness organizes intrinsic goods, pleasure, social relations, and material resources without becoming one additive good among them.
Rational choice does not create its final standards ex nihilo but operates within an antecedent order of goods and ends.
Human flourishing cannot be constituted as a wholly private achievement independent of political and social relations.
Correct propositions cannot substitute for the formation of desires capable of receiving practical reason.
Human virtue cannot abolish contingency or render embodied action independent of external conditions.
Practical coordination among goods does not require their reduction to one univocal metaphysical essence.
Human excellence cannot be reduced either to biological functioning or to disembodied intellectual possession.
Virtue does not eliminate appetite but requires its education into obedience and harmony.
An unconditionally invulnerable human good is unavailable because self-sufficient activity remains materially and temporally conditioned.
Neither virtue nor fortune is granted complete sovereignty over happiness, and their exact boundary remains unformalized.
A value-neutral political order is inadmissible because political authority necessarily organizes the formation and exercise of character.
A purely theoretical route to ethical competence is foreclosed by the prior necessity of habituated desire.
A final metaphysical explanation of the unity among heterogeneous goods remains absent after the universal Form is rejected.
The initial operation is purposive practices → plural ends → relations of subordination → ranked goods.
The closure operation is avoidance of infinite regress → terminal end → chief good.
The architectonic operation is ranked practical ends → governing political science → common human good.
The critical operation is received candidates → actionability test → completeness test → self-sufficiency test → rejection or subordination.
The specifying operation is distinctive human capacity → rational activity → excellent performance → activity according to virtue.
The temporal operation is virtuous activity → sustained complete life → relative stability of happiness.
The conditioning operation is external resources and fortune → enabled or obstructed action → qualified human blessedness.
The recursive operation is happiness as virtuous activity → inquiry into virtue → analysis of reason and appetite → division of intellectual and character virtue.

Universal purposiveness → hierarchy of ends → architectonic politics → nominal happiness → elimination of rival goods and the universal Form → completeness and self-sufficiency → rational function → virtuous activity over a complete life → qualification by external goods and fortune → analysis of soul and virtue.
Variable practical subject matter → calibrated precision → habituated starting points → dialectical testing against accepted beliefs → actionable ethical outline.
A flat plurality of goods becomes a hierarchy structured by relations of means, subordinate ends, and governing ends.
Ethics is relocated within political science as the architectonic practice of forming and coordinating human action.
The good is reclassified from a common transcendent substance into the role of an end across heterogeneous practices.
Happiness is reclassified from feeling, possession, reputation, or resource into sustained excellent activity.
Pleasure ceases to be a rival to virtue and becomes an internal completion of rightly formed activity.
Fortune ceases to constitute happiness and becomes a variable condition affecting its exercise and fullness.
Self-sufficiency is redrawn as relational completeness within human association rather than solitary independence.
Happiness is elevated from a praiseworthy quality to an honourable first principle by reference to which other goods are assessed.
The opposition between reason and non-reason becomes a graded structure in which appetite can participate in reason through obedience.
Surface: The inquiry determines what happiness is and distinguishes it from prominent rival candidates.
Structural: The argument coordinates hierarchies of ends, political authority, external conditions, and divisions of the soul.
Metastrategic: Ethical inquiry is reframed from selecting a desirable object into forming agents and institutions capable of sustained virtuous activity.
Ontological/Temporal: The human being is presupposed to be a social and rationally active being whose good exists only across an embodied, contingent, and complete life.
Epistemic: Practical first principles arise from habituated experience, permit only subject-relative precision, and are tested against credible appearances.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the movement from universal purposiveness through the function argument to the division of virtue.
The negative architecture preserves the eliminations required to distinguish happiness from instruments, passive states, chance, and a separate universal Good.
The structure is strongest in distinguishing final ends from instrumental goods and active excellence from mere possession.
The content of the best and most complete virtue remains underdetermined because the final status of contemplation is deferred.
The required quantity of external goods and the significance of posthumous relational effects remain without a determinate threshold.
Self-sufficiency remains in tension with dependence on prosperity, while permanence remains in tension with grave reversals of fortune.
The function analogy, the superiority of the civic good, and the unity of heterogeneous goods depend on compression or deferred justification.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only as a provisional outline whose completion requires the subsequent analyses of virtue, action, and contemplation.
The inquiry seeks a practical account of how virtue of character is acquired, constituted, and enacted.
Virtue of character is an acquired disposition produced by habituated activity and completed in rationally chosen action.
The argument is reconstructive, classificatory, and strategic rather than purely theoretical.
The analysis moves from natural capacity to habituation and then to the reciprocal production of activities and states.
Pleasure and pain expose the affective mechanism by which conduct forms and reveals character.
The classification of psychic conditions culminates in virtue as a reason-determined mean relative to the agent and situation.
The doctrine terminates in asymmetrical correction of bias under irreducibly perceptual judgment.
Human nature supplies the capacity for virtue of character, but habituation completes that capacity.
Repeated activities produce corresponding stable states of character.
Differences in how activities are performed determine whether the resulting states are virtuous or vicious.
Formed states increase an agent’s ability to perform the kinds of activities that produced them.
Ethical inquiry and legislation are practical enterprises ordered to forming good agents rather than merely producing knowledge.
Ethical action concerns variable particulars, so general accounts are necessarily rough and final judgment depends on perception.
Pleasure and pain are motivational media through which actions form, strengthen, or corrupt character.
The pleasure or pain accompanying action indicates the quality of the agent’s state.
Virtues and vices are stable states that dispose agents well or badly toward feelings and actions.
An agent acts virtuously only by acting knowingly, choosing the action for its own sake, and acting from firm character.
Human virtue makes its possessor good and enables characteristic human activity to be performed well.
Where feelings and actions admit degrees, excess and deficiency miss the target while the context-relative mean hits it.
Virtue of character is a state involving rational choice of the mean relative to the agent as right reason embodied in practical wisdom determines it.
Correct feeling and action require simultaneous fit across object, amount, time, end, and manner.
Some feelings and actions are bad without qualification and therefore admit no virtuous mean.
The mean stands between two opposed extremes, and each disposition is perceived relationally against the other two.
An extreme appears especially contrary to the mean when it is objectively farther from or less like the mean.
Agents are naturally and individually biased toward some extremes, especially toward excessive pleasure.
Virtue of character is neither a natural possession nor a condition imposed against nature.
Possessing a natural capacity for feelings does not make its possessor morally good or bad.
Ethical inquiry is not justified by knowledge detached from moral formation.
Argument and instruction without enacted practice do not make a person good.
General ethical accounts cannot function as exact rules for every particular action.
Virtue and vice are not feelings.
Virtue and vice are not natural capacities for experiencing feelings.
Outward conformity to a virtuous action is not sufficient for acting virtuously.
Virtue is not insensibility, affective rest, or the elimination of pleasure and pain.
The ethical mean is not an arithmetical midpoint identical for every agent.
The doctrine of the mean does not license moderated forms of actions that are bad without qualification.
Minor deviation from the mean is not automatically blameworthy, and no exact threshold of blame can be fixed.
Early education and legislation are constitutive causes of character rather than supplements to an already formed moral agent.
Political systems differ ethically according to how effectively their laws habituate citizens into good states.
Habituation creates a feedback loop in which activity forms character and character subsequently stabilizes corresponding activity.
A virtue-conforming action can precede virtuous character, but it becomes fully virtuous only when the agent satisfies the internal conditions of virtuous agency.
Knowledge of virtue without repeated practice cannot produce a virtuous agent.
Moral education must train agents to enjoy and suffer in relation to the right objects rather than merely restrain outward conduct.
The mean is a dynamic contextual target rather than a fixed quantity transferable unchanged across persons and situations.
Excellence is rare and difficult because success requires coordinated correctness across several dimensions while failure can occur along any one of them.
Agents positioned at opposed extremes systematically misclassify the mean as the contrary vice.
Practical correction should steer away from the greater danger and accept lesser error as a second-best route toward the mean.
Individual self-correction requires diagnosing one’s affective bias and pulling in the opposite direction, with special distrust of pleasure.
Ethical agency is temporally recursive because present actions produce the character from which future choices will proceed.
Political and educational institutions shape the pre-reflective affective field within which mature rational choice later operates.
Moral formation is reducible neither to natural determinism nor to unconditioned voluntarism.
The formal doctrine of the mean cannot independently select determinate actions because its application delegates final authority to practical wisdom and perception.
Virtue is intermediate relative to opposed vices while remaining maximal relative to functional goodness.
Intrinsically bad actions establish an absolute boundary within an otherwise context-sensitive model of ethical judgment.
Stable character is not behavioral invariance but reliable context-sensitive selection of fitting feelings and actions.
The same habituating apparatus can generate virtue or vice, making ethical formation structurally reversible.
Moral identity cannot be an immutable substance antecedent to repeated practice.
The ethical quality of an action cannot be exhausted by its outward form or product.
Stable character cannot mean rigid repetition of identical behavior across changing circumstances.
Practical reason cannot operate independently of the agent’s habituated desires and aversions.
Pleasure and pain cannot be treated as normatively neutral accompaniments to action.
Ethical fitness cannot be universally commensurated by a single quantity applying equally to every person.
The continuum of excess, deficiency, and mean cannot totalize the entire moral field.
Practical danger cannot be inferred from formal symmetry because human biases make one extreme more threatening than another.
The system excludes an already virtuous origin of virtue, so moral formation must begin with actions whose full virtue the learner does not yet possess.
A neutral standpoint outside habituated pleasure and pain is unavailable to the acting subject.
A wholly self-authored ethical subject is unavailable because early educational and political formation precedes mature choice.
A complete formal procedure for deriving right action in particulars is unavailable because practical wisdom and perception occupy the irreducible remainder.
An independent criterion for identifying the practically wise determiner is not supplied within this book.
A precise point at which deviation becomes blameworthy remains unavailable.
Character genesis follows the sequence natural receptivity → repeated activity → acquired state.
Character reproduction follows the sequence acquired state → increased practical capacity → corresponding activity → strengthened state.
Affective formation follows the sequence pleasure or pain → pursuit or avoidance → repeated conduct → virtue or vice.
Generic classification proceeds through moral attribution → exclusion of feelings and capacities → identification of virtue as a state.
Functional determination proceeds through human activity → criterion of good performance → virtue as the state enabling excellence.
Normative determination proceeds through scalar field → excess and deficiency → context-relative mean → rational choice under practical wisdom.
The intrinsic-wrongness filter removes some actions from mean-calculation before contextual evaluation begins.
Practical correction proceeds through objective asymmetry plus personal bias → contrary steering → feasible approximation → perceptual judgment.
The argument moves from natural capacity → habituated practice → stable character → reinforced practice.
The argument moves from affective evidence → classification of psychic conditions → virtue as a dispositional state → functional excellence.
The argument moves from scalar variation → relative mean → determination by practical wisdom → exclusion of intrinsically bad actions.
The argument moves from triadic opposition → asymmetrical practical risk → compensatory correction → perceptual closure.
The opposition between nature and acquisition is redrawn as natural receptivity completed through habituation.
Action is reclassified as both the product of character and the mechanism that produces character.
Moral evaluation shifts from the observable deed alone to the knowledge, choice, and stability of the agent.
Pleasure and pain become the formative infrastructure and diagnostic evidence of moral character.
The mean is relocated from numerical centrality to context-sensitive practical fit.
Moderation ceases to be a universal formula because some actions are excluded from scalar evaluation.
Ethical knowledge is redrawn from rule application to rough orientation completed by situated perception.
Political order becomes visible as an apparatus for producing character through organized habituation.
Moral opposition becomes asymmetric because objective distance, social perspective, and personal bias alter which extreme presents the greater danger.
Surface: The inquiry specifies how feelings and actions can be performed at the right time, toward the right objects, for the right ends, and in the right manner.
Structural: Repeated activity, affective reinforcement, stable disposition, and renewed activity form a recursive mechanism of character production.
Metastrategic: Ethical reasoning becomes a practice of diagnosing bias, steering against dominant error, and approximating a context-sensitive target.
Ontological/Temporal: Human character is a sedimented actuality produced over time from natural capacities through repeated practice.
The chapter’s axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the genesis of character through its definition to its practical correction.
The content of right reason and the full account of practical wisdom remain underdetermined because their explanation is deferred.
The transition from merely virtue-conforming action to choice from firm character remains partly bootstrapped by prior habituation.
The system is internally coherent where it distinguishes formative actions from fully virtuous actions and contextual means from intrinsically bad acts.
The architecture is strongest in its reciprocal model of activity, affect, and stable character.
The account depends on compressed transfers from analogies with skills, health, strength, and functional excellence.
The claim that correctness forms a determinate target remains in tension with the absence of exact rules and blameworthy thresholds.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the argument’s real movement from formation through classification and definition to situated strategy.
The argument seeks the causal boundary that makes feelings, actions, and character eligible for praise, blame, pardon, pity, honour, and punishment.
Its core thesis is that conduct is voluntary when its moving principle is in the agent and the agent knows the relevant particulars.
It narrows voluntary agency into rational choice by connecting wished ends, deliberated means, and executable action.
It extends responsibility diachronically from chosen actions to the character states those actions generate.
It reconstructs courage as rationally ordered endurance of fearful pain for the noble rather than behavioral fearlessness.
It reconstructs temperance as rational harmony of appetite in bodily pleasure rather than indiscriminate deprivation.
The argument is a reconstructive taxonomy moving from causal attribution through practical reasoning and habituation to differentiated virtue.
Praise, blame, pardon, and pity track whether feelings and actions are voluntary or involuntary.
An action is forced when its moving principle is external and the agent contributes nothing.
Ignorance makes an action involuntary only when it concerns relevant particulars and produces pain and regret.
An action is voluntary when its moving principle is in the agent and the agent knows its relevant particular circumstances.
An action unwanted in itself but chosen under pressure is voluntary at the time of performance when its moving principle remains in the agent.
Spirit and appetite are internal human sources of voluntary action even though they are non-rational.
Rational choice is deliberative desire for an achievable means within the agent’s power and is narrower than voluntary action.
Deliberation concerns contingent and uncertain means that the agent can bring about.
Deliberation analyzes backward from an established end until it reaches the first executable cause of forward action.
Wish takes the end as its object: the good in truth without qualification and the apparent good for a particular agent.
Character conditions how ends appear, while good character functions as the measure that discloses what is genuinely noble and pleasant.
Repeated activities generate corresponding states of character.
Responsibility for controllable formative actions extends to the resulting character even when that character can no longer be immediately reversed.
A virtue is a mean state whose activity is selected and governed by correct reason.
Courage is the mean that orders fear and confidence to the right objects, degree, time, manner, and reason for the sake of the noble.
Courage is tested primarily by painful risks of immediate death in which resistance or death can be noble.
Temperance is the mean that orders appetites for bodily pleasures, principally appetitive pleasures of touch shared with animals, as correct reason prescribes.
Appetite is strengthened by enactment and must be habituated into obedience and harmony with reason.
External pressure does not make an action forced when the agent remains its moving principle.
Pleasant and noble objects do not coerce from outside, since treating attraction as force would make every purposive action forced.
Ignorance of universal good, beneficial ends, or correct rational choice does not establish involuntariness.
An unregretted action performed through ignorance is non-voluntary rather than involuntary.
Ignorance induced by intoxication, anger, negligence, or culpable legal ignorance does not remove responsibility when its cause was avoidable.
Action from appetite or spirit is not involuntary merely because its source is non-rational.
Rational choice is not identical with appetite, spirit, wish, or belief.
Deliberation does not concern ends, necessary events, natural regularities, chance occurrences, exact procedures, perceptual particulars, or affairs beyond the agent’s power.
