Wish cannot be reduced either to whatever appears good to each person or to only those objects that are genuinely good.
Present inability to reverse an entrenched state does not erase responsibility for its controllable formation.
Courage is not generalized fearlessness, rash confidence, escape through death, or endurance imposed solely by threatened pain.
Legal compulsion, military expertise, spirit, optimism, and ignorance can imitate courageous behavior without constituting courage.
Temperance does not regulate every pleasure or every bodily sensation; its proper field is appetitive gratification through touch.
Temperance is not insensibility to pleasure, and virtue does not require the elimination of appetite.
Institutional reward and punishment are justified only where action originates in the agent or where the agent culpably produced the ignorance behind it.
Mixed actions remain attributable at the moment of choice even though their objects are unwanted without qualification.
Regret distinguishes involuntary action from action that merely lacks voluntariness because it was performed unknowingly.
Avoidable intoxication, negligence, and character-formed ignorance inherit voluntariness from prior controllable acts.
A wished end fixes deliberation’s target, backward analysis identifies an executable means, rational choice desires it, and action realizes it.
Rational choice reveals character more reliably than isolated action because it expresses a deliberatively endorsed relation to good and bad.
Practical error can arise from character-shaped appearance rather than from simple false belief.
Virtue and vice are equally attributable insofar as each is formed by repeated voluntary conduct, although neither state remains wholly reversible at every later moment.
The extremes around courage concern the same fearful objects but misorder fear and confidence through excess, deficiency, timing, manner, or end.
Behavioral resemblance cannot establish courage because exposure to danger can arise without noble rational choice.
The more goods a courageous person stands to lose, the more painful exposure to death becomes and the more clearly courage consists in chosen endurance rather than numbness.
Temperance preserves natural appetite while limiting its objects, intensity, timing, and cost by health, resources, nobility, and reason.
Intemperance is more voluntary and reprehensible than cowardice because it actively pursues pleasure through appetite, whereas painful fear can disrupt agency in particular situations.
Cowardice is more attributable as a formed disposition than in panic-driven episodes, whereas intemperate episodes are more directly voluntary than the disposition desired by no one as such.
The model of agency is recursively temporal: character shapes apparent ends, choices generate actions, actions consolidate character, and consolidated character reshapes future appearances.
Freedom is located in attributable causal origins rather than in a permanent capacity for immediate self-reversal.
Practical truth is ethically conditioned because seeing the good correctly depends on a character state that is itself formed through action.
Moral assessment must classify outwardly similar conduct differently when its internal principle, knowledge, chosen end, or temporal origin differs.
Virtue governs non-rational nature by ordering it toward the noble rather than removing fear, pain, pleasure, or appetite.
The mean is multidimensional fitness to particulars rather than an arithmetic midpoint because rightness varies by object, degree, time, manner, reason, and end.
Fear and pleasure threaten rational agency differently: fear can overwhelm action episodically, while repeated pleasure can train appetite to displace calculation.
Attribution is simultaneously contextual and diachronic because immediate circumstances determine present voluntariness while prior conduct determines responsibility for current incapacity.
The system requires that human action not be exhaustively reducible to nature, necessity, chance, social pressure, or affective impulse.
The system requires that attractive ends not count as external coercers even when they powerfully move desire.
The system requires that character-shaped perception of the good not be wholly fixed by birth or nature.
The system requires that causal history remain normatively attributable after direct control has diminished.
The system requires that non-rational feeling be educable by reason rather than intrinsically rebellious or morally alien.
The system requires that objective goodness survive individual variation in apparent good despite using good character as its epistemic measure.
The system requires that noble purpose be irreducible to behavioral success, social appearance, pleasure, safety, or confidence.
A fully naturalized genesis of character is foreclosed because it would make the appearance of ends involuntary and place virtue and vice beyond responsibility.

An infinite regress behind the agent’s formative dispositions is halted rather than resolved because the person must remain an originating principle even though the origin of that capacity is underdetermined.
A threshold at which pressure, fear, or pain eliminates agent contribution is presupposed but left unformalized because mixed action must remain separable from genuine force.
The possibility that entrenched vice destroys the agency required to have formed it is excluded, although the transition from voluntary acts to diminished control is explained only retrospectively.
A non-circular criterion of the true good remains absent because correct character measures correct appearance while correct character is identified by its orientation toward the good.
The terminally excluded figure is an ethically passive subject whose desires, perceptions, actions, and states occur without attributable participation.
Normative appraisal generates a demand for causal classification, which generates the voluntary–involuntary boundary.
An external first principle combined with zero agent contribution generates force, involuntariness, and eligibility for pardon or pity.
Relevant particular ignorance combined with regret generates involuntariness, while such ignorance without regret generates non-voluntariness.
An internal first principle combined with knowledge of particulars generates voluntariness, while pressure combined with retained internal control generates contextual voluntariness.
Apparent good → wish for an end → backward analysis of means → decision → deliberative desire → action.
Repeated action → character state → perception of apparent good → renewed wish and choice → reinforcement or correction of character.
Controllable initiation combined with gradual, unnoticed consolidation generates indirect voluntariness of character alongside diminished later reversibility.
Fearful object → rational calibration of fear and confidence → noble end → painful endurance → courage.
Danger without noble rational calibration → compulsion, expertise, passion, optimism, or delusion → resemblance to courage without courage.
Bodily appetite → rational limitation and habituated harmony → temperance, whereas repeated excessive gratification → strengthened appetite → displacement of calculation → intemperance.
The first movement runs from moral appraisal through the exclusions of force and ignorance to an internal-principle account of voluntary action.
The second movement runs from voluntary action through wish, deliberation, and rational choice to action, habituated character, and diachronic responsibility.
The final movement runs from the general structure of voluntary mean states to courage under fearful pain and temperance under bodily pleasure.
Voluntariness is reclassified from absence of constraint to the conjunction of internal causal origin and knowledge of particulars.
The voluntary–involuntary binary is made contextual by mixed actions and internally differentiated by the category of the non-voluntary.
Rational choice is separated from spontaneous action, affective impulse, wish, and belief and becomes a distinct index of character.
Deliberation is confined to contingent means within agency, separating practical inquiry from speculation, perception, and wish for ends.
Character is redrawn as both the product of action and the perceptual condition of future action.
Moral truth is relocated from abstract belief alone to the character-dependent ability to perceive the genuinely good.
Courage is reclassified from visible boldness to the motive, end, and rational ordering that produce endurance.
Outwardly identical confrontations with danger become distinguishable as courage, compulsion, expertise, passion, optimism, or ignorance.
Temperance is reclassified from abstention to the disciplined agreement of appetite and reason within a restricted sensory field.
Surface — The text defines voluntary action, rational choice, deliberation, courage, and temperance while distinguishing their neighboring counterfeits.
Structural — Internal causation, knowledge of particulars, means-end reasoning, habituation, and character formation constitute the mechanism of moral attribution.
Metastrategic — Ethical classification shifts from visible behavior to causal origin, motive, temporal formation, rational order, and noble end.
Ontological/Temporal — The human being is treated as a contingent first principle whose present agency both inherits prior self-formation and produces future constraints on perception and action.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the transition from moral attribution to voluntary agency, rational choice, character formation, courage, and temperance.
The extracted system is sufficient to recover the distinction between direct voluntariness of actions and indirect voluntariness of states.
The thresholds separating coercive pressure from retained agency and excusing ignorance from culpable ignorance remain underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent where internal origin, particular knowledge, deliberated means, and habituated consequence are linked.
The system is strongest in distinguishing rational choice from adjacent psychological states and genuine virtue from behavioral resemblance.
The account depends on compression where the good person is made the measure of the true good without an independent criterion of correctness.
The responsibility argument leaves unresolved how much control precedes the earliest formation of character and how nature conditions the appearance of ends.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement of the text by proceeding from attribution through practical agency and habituation to the rational ordering of fear and appetite.
The inquiry determines which stable dispositions make action and feeling correct in wealth, honor, anger, social interaction, and responses to disgrace.
Its central thesis is that virtue realizes a context-relative mean bounded by excess and deficiency.
The argument is diagnostic, taxonomic, and reconstructive, testing each candidate disposition against the formal structure of virtue.
Each analysis moves from delimiting a domain to specifying its parameters of correctness, identifying its mean, and differentiating its deviations.
The argument introduces scalar refinements where ordinary virtue divides into moderate and great forms.
The same calibrating structure is extended from external goods to passions, interpersonal conduct, self-presentation, and amusement.
The inquiry terminates by excluding shame from virtue because it is a remedial feeling rather than a stable state of good character.
A character virtue is a stable disposition that realizes a relative mean in action or feeling.
The mean is fixed by the right object, person, amount, time, manner, source, and end as relevant to the case.
Virtuous action is rationally chosen for the sake of the noble and accompanied by fitting pleasure or pain.
Exact practical correctness depends on perception of particulars rather than a universally stated quantitative rule.
Generosity uses wealth well by coordinating right giving with right taking while assigning ethical priority to giving.
Generous giving is proportionate to the giver’s resources and directed toward worthy recipients at fitting times.
Wastefulness miscalibrates toward excessive giving and deficient taking, whereas stinginess miscalibrates toward deficient giving and excessive taking.
Magnificence produces a fitting great result through large expenditure relative to the agent, resources, object, and circumstances.
Magnificent expenditure takes the noble fitness of the result, rather than display or minimum cost, as its governing end.
Greatness of soul is extreme in the scale of deserved claims but intermediate in the accuracy of self-estimation.
True greatness of soul requires total virtue and enlarges the virtues as their crown.
Goods of fortune affect recognition and opportunity, but virtue alone grounds true worth.
A right mean governs the desire for ordinary honor even though ordinary language leaves that mean unnamed.
Even temper makes anger follow reason in its object, target, intensity, timing, and duration.
Right social accommodation distributes pleasure and pain according to the noble and useful rather than affection or appeasement.
Social truthfulness acknowledges one’s qualities without inflation or concealment.
Tasteful wit regulates the production and reception of humor by seemliness, audience, and the legitimate need for relaxation.
Shame is a fear-like bodily feeling occasioned by disgrace rather than a stable state that prevents voluntary wrongdoing.
Wastefulness is not every form of intemperate expenditure but specifically the ruinous misuse of property through monetary excess.
Generosity is not measured by the absolute amount transferred.
Giving to wrong recipients or for non-noble ends is not generosity regardless of its scale.
Mere abstention from taking does not constitute generosity.
Magnificence is not sheer numerical expenditure or generosity indiscriminately enlarged.
Expenditure beyond an agent’s fitting resources is not magnificent merely because it is large.
Unsupported belief in one’s greatness is not greatness of soul but vanity.
Wealth, power, birth, and reputation do not confer magnanimity without virtue.
The mean in seeking honor is not eliminated by its lack of a conventional name.
Even temper is not angerlessness, emotional insensibility, or passive acceptance of insult.
Right social accommodation is not friendship because it does not require affection.
Right social accommodation is neither indiscriminate pleasing nor indiscriminate opposition.
Social truthfulness is not the contractual truthfulness governed by justice.
Tasteful wit is neither the pursuit of laughter at any cost nor the refusal of all amusement.
Shame is not virtue merely because shameless wrongdoing is vicious.
Continence is not virtue without qualification, although its mixed character is deferred for later analysis.
Generosity is displayed more fully in active benefaction than in merely refusing wrongful acquisition.
A poorer giver can be more generous than a richer giver when the gift expresses a better proportion of resources and worthier direction.
The generous person tends not to remain rich because wealth is retained principally as an instrument of future noble giving.
Pure wastefulness is structurally nearer generosity than stinginess because it preserves giving and non-acquisition while lacking correct calibration.
Resource exhaustion can turn wasteful spending into acquisition from wrongful sources, producing a mixed vice rather than a pure opposite.
The two dimensions of stinginess can separate into withholding without predation or acquisitiveness without complete withholding.
Stinginess is functionally farther from generosity because it blocks benefaction and can add wrongful taking, whereas pure wastefulness retains a beneficent tendency.
Magnificence is a restricted, large-scale realization of generosity rather than an independent alternative to it.
Vulgarity and niggardliness corrupt the relation among cost, object, agent, and result rather than merely spending too much or too little in absolute terms.
The great-souled person accepts deserved honor without depending on it because no external reward is adequate to total virtue.
Fortune without virtue produces counterfeit magnanimity expressed as arbitrary superiority, display, and violence.
Smallness of soul obstructs noble action because underestimated worth contracts the field of goods and projects a person will pursue.
A nameless mean can resemble either extreme when viewed from the position of the other, so lexical opposition conceals a three-part moral structure.
Blame for anger must be graded by the seriousness and multiplicity of deviations rather than triggered by every departure from exactness.
Right sociability can require causing immediate pain when acquiescence would produce disgrace, harm, or the loss of greater future benefit.
Truthfulness when nothing is at stake indicates a stable disposition likely to remain truthful when advantage or danger is present.
The tasteful person becomes a practical law to himself because no fixed rule can determine which jokes suit every audience and circumstance.
Shame is conditionally useful for the error-prone young but becomes inappropriate as a defining feature of completed adult virtue.
Heterogeneous domains are unified by one practical calibration model without reducing the mean to an arithmetic midpoint.
The virtues form a nested hierarchy in which generosity enables magnificence and total virtue enables greatness of soul.
Moral worth cannot be inferred from magnitude, reputation, emotional intensity, or surface pleasantness because intention and relational fitness govern classification.
Nameless means and asymmetrical blame reveal that the topology of virtue is neither a simple binary nor a geometrically symmetrical scale.
Full virtue coordinates judgment, desire, choice, affect, resources, and action, making isolated capacity or outward conformity insufficient.
The highest social excellences combine inward virtue with external enabling conditions, creating dependence on goods that cannot themselves confer worth.
Mature goodness tends to remove occasions for shame because stable noble choice prevents the voluntary actions that would warrant it.
No arithmetic midpoint can determine the mean independently of practical circumstances.
No outwardly identical action has the same ethical value independently of the agent’s resources, motive, and object.
Possession of an external good cannot establish the virtue required to use that good well.
Absence or repression of passion cannot substitute for rationally calibrated feeling.
Immediate interpersonal harmony cannot be the sovereign criterion of right social conduct.
Ordinary vocabulary cannot delimit the structure of virtue because ethically real means can remain unnamed.
Higher excellences cannot be instantiated independently of lower virtues, total character, or enabling resources.
A single correct deed cannot establish virtue without a stable disposition, noble choice, and fitting affect.
The noble, worthy, and fitting remain terminal evaluative terms for which the system supplies no independent formal criterion.
Universal accessibility to the highest forms of excellence is foreclosed because magnificence requires wealth and greatness of soul remains entangled with honor and social standing.
The boundary between justified superiority and vicious arrogance rests on antecedent total virtue without an independent social test of that virtue.
Greatness of soul is organized around honor as the greatest external good while treating every available honor as inadequate and ultimately of limited importance.
Completed adult virtue leaves shame no positive field except a hypothetical lapse that completed virtue itself excludes.
The movement from vice to the mean is attributed to habituation, guidance, age, or changed circumstances without a developed mechanism of moral transformation.
The classifier begins with a practical domain, isolates its characteristic objects and operations, and identifies the dimensions along which fit can succeed or fail.
Rational perception of particulars joined to a noble end, correct action, and fitting affect generates a stable mean-state.
Parameter excess or deficiency generates vice, subtype differentiation, and an asymmetrical determination of the primary contrary.
Wealth as instrument produces the giving-and-taking matrix, which yields generosity and then magnificence under a large-scale result condition.
External honor is processed through actual-merit calibration, yielding greatness of soul at great scale and an unnamed mean at ordinary scale.
Anger, interpersonal pleasure and pain, self-presentation, and amusement each undergo the same mean–excess–deficiency test.
A candidate disposition undergoes a state-or-feeling test and an age-and-voluntariness test before inclusion among the virtues.
Use of wealth → proportional generosity → monetary extremes → fitting large expenditure → magnificence.
Large-scale expenditure → large-scale worth → honor → greatness of soul → moderation in ordinary honor-seeking.
Honor relations → anger → interpersonal pleasure and pain → social truth → amusement → differentiated modes of social virtue.
Catalogued means → categorical audit of shame → reclassification as youthful remedial feeling → transition toward justice.
Wealth is reclassified from a possession valued in itself into an instrument whose ethical meaning lies primarily in noble use.
Expenditure is reclassified from absolute quantity into a relation among agent, resources, object, circumstance, and result.
Honor is reclassified from public recognition alone into a test of whether self-valuation corresponds to actual virtue.
Emotional excellence is reclassified from suppression into reason-governed responsiveness.
Sociability divides into distinct regulation of pleasure and pain, truthful self-presentation, and amusement.
Namelessness becomes evidence of lexical deficiency rather than evidence that a moral mean is absent.
Excess and deficiency become combinable and asymmetrical structures rather than fixed, equally distant opposites.
Shame is removed from the catalog of virtues and relocated within bodily feeling, youth, correction, and hypothetical remorse.
Surface: The inquiry classifies virtues and opposed defects concerning wealth, honor, anger, social intercourse, truth, humor, and shame.
Structural: A recurring relational matrix calibrates agent, object, scale, circumstance, motive, action, and affect.
Metastrategic: The analysis corrects ordinary moral language by recovering unnamed means, narrowing overbroad vice terms, and distinguishing apparent from genuine excellence.
Ontological/Temporal: Character is treated as a stable, habituated organization of perception and desire, while feelings such as anger and shame unfold through duration, age, memory, and correction.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the recurrent mean-based classifier and its extension across all principal domains.
The domain-specific axioms are sufficient to recover the distinctions among generosity, magnificence, greatness of soul, social virtues, and shame.
The structure is internally coherent in linking stable character, noble choice, particular judgment, action, and affect.
The system is strongest in its recursive classification of outwardly similar conduct by motive, proportion, object, and circumstance.
The substantive content of the noble, worthy, fitting, and deserved remains underdetermined.
Exact thresholds are deliberately elided into perceptual judgment, preventing complete formal specification of the mean.
Greatness of soul remains tense because honor defines its domain while the fully virtuous person treats honor as inadequate and relatively unimportant.
Magnificence and greatness of soul remain structurally dependent on external resources and recognition that the system denies can ground virtue.
Rankings of the worse or more contrary extreme sometimes depend on asserted moral psychology and common opinion rather than strict derivation.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from domain analysis through scalar refinement and social extension to categorical exclusion, while compressing examples, subtypes, and behavioral imagery.
The inquiry determines the senses, objects, mean, and extremes of justice and injustice.
The argument is diagnostic, taxonomic, formal, and reconstructive.
Justice divides into universal lawfulness and particular fairness because its apparently unified usage conceals distinct operations.
Universal justice is complete virtue insofar as virtue is exercised toward others under law.
Particular justice regulates divisible goods through equality, distribution, rectification, and proportionate exchange.
Political justice exists within law-governed association among persons capable of reciprocal equality.
Just agency requires voluntary action, while just law requires equitable correction when universal rules misfit particulars.
The movement proceeds from semantic division through mathematical formalization and political delimitation to responsibility, equity, and the exclusion of self-injustice.
A state of character disposes its possessor toward corresponding actions and wishes rather than contrary ones.
Justice and injustice each have a universal sense ordered by lawfulness and a particular sense ordered by fairness.
Universal justice is complete virtue in relation to others because law orders the virtues toward political happiness.
Particular injustice seeks disproportionate gain or avoidance of loss in divisible goods, and particular justice opposes this inequality.
The object of particular justice is relational equality between excess and deficiency for persons and shares.
Distributive justice joins persons to common shares according to geometric proportion.
A distributive proportion cannot be fixed without a politically specified criterion of merit.
Rectificatory justice restores arithmetic equality between injurer and injured without regard to their comparative moral status.
Exchange sustains association only when unequal producers and products are made proportionately reciprocal.
Demand makes heterogeneous goods sufficiently commensurable, while conventionally instituted money represents demand as a common measure and guarantee of future exchange.
Political justice exists among free and self-sufficient associates capable of proportionate or arithmetic equality whose relations are governed by law and reciprocal rule.
Political justice includes natural standards independent of opinion and legal standards binding through adoption, although both remain changeable in human affairs.
Law necessarily speaks universally about practical matters whose particular instances remain indeterminate.
A deed counts non-incidentally as a just or unjust act only when it lies within the agent’s control and is done knowingly and without compulsion.
Voluntary injustice manifests an unjust character only when rational choice is its governing principle.
A person is treated unjustly only when harmed against that person’s wish through another’s unjust agency.
Responsibility for injustice belongs to the voluntary initiating source of an unequal allocation or harm rather than merely to its recipient or instrument.
Equity is the rational correction of a universal legal rule when its unqualified form misfits a particular case.
Justice is not a univocal state with only one object or operation.
A character state cannot generate contrary actions in the way a single capacity can concern contraries.
Particular unfairness is not identical with universal lawlessness, even though it is treated as part of universal injustice.
Distributive equality is not the assignment of identical shares irrespective of differences between persons.
Rectificatory equality does not vary according to the virtue, rank, or desert of the parties.
Reciprocity understood as identical retaliation is not justice without qualification.
Heterogeneous goods are not naturally or exactly commensurable, and money is not a natural standard.
Political justice does not apply without qualification to relations with property, dependent children, household subordinates, or oneself.
Performing something materially unjust is not sufficient for acting unjustly or possessing an unjust character.
Natural justice among human beings is not absolutely immutable.
Equity is neither a separate genus from justice nor superior to justice without qualification.
Good citizenship is not established as identical with goodness without qualification.
Correctly established law converts the requirements of each virtue into obligations toward others and thereby coordinates character with civic happiness.
Gain-directed wrongdoing is attributable specifically to particular injustice when it is not explained by another vice.
Distributive conflict arises when the ratio between persons is not reproduced in the ratio between their shares.
The judge functions as an intermediary who removes excess, repairs deficiency, and restores the arithmetic mean.
Civic association through exchange requires the sequence commensurability, equality, reciprocity, and transfer.
Justice differs from the other virtues as a mean because it is concerned with an equal mean while injustice occupies both excess and deficiency.
Political authority must be subordinated to law because personal rule can convert guardianship of equality into self-allocation.
The changeability of human norms does not eliminate the distinction between standards grounded in nature and standards grounded in adoption.
Injury is graded as misadventure, error, unpremeditated injustice, or character-expressing injustice according to expectation, knowledge, control, and rational choice.
Knowingly receiving an excessive share does not by itself make the recipient the responsible unjust agent when the distributor initiates the allocation.
Voluntary self-harm cannot constitute injustice suffered by the self, although illegal self-destruction can constitute injustice against the city.
An equitable judgement preserves the law’s just purpose by departing from its defective universal wording.
Committing injustice is worse in itself than suffering it because the former is blameworthy and may express vice, whereas the latter does not itself imply vice.
Justice is a human affair because human associates possess divisible goods whose benefits admit proportionate excess and deficiency.
Justice forms an integrated architecture connecting character, law, allocation, exchange, political membership, agency, and equitable judgement.
Equality is a family of formally distinct operations comprising geometric proportion, arithmetic restoration, and proportionate commensuration.
Political community is reproduced normatively through lawful virtue and materially through commensurable exchange.
Legal normativity is internally corrigible because law’s necessary universality cannot exhaust the contingent particulars it governs.
Moral attribution forms a layered sequence from the normative form of a deed through voluntary agency and rational choice to stable character.
Human political justice is contingent without being wholly conventional because mutable institutions remain answerable to natural, proportional, and equitable standards.
Justice cannot be reduced to private self-perfection because relation to another is constitutive of its operation.
Persons and shares cannot be treated as naturally interchangeable because distributive justice depends on differentiated ratios.
No exact natural metric unifies heterogeneous products because economic equality requires conventional mediation.
No universal practical rule can determine every particular case without remainder.
No outward description of a deed can exhaust its moral status because agency depends on knowledge, control, deliberation, and character.
Full political justice is unavailable wherever law and reciprocal equality between associates are absent.
Voluntary suffering cannot count as being treated unjustly without dissolving the relational distinction between perpetrator and victim.
A universally accepted criterion of distributive merit is absent, leaving rival constitutions to specify incompatible ratios.
An intrinsic measure of heterogeneous value is absent, and money manages rather than eliminates this incommensurability.
Political personhood is withheld from dependent household relations, so the jurisdiction of justice presupposes a prior boundary of membership.
A complete legal code adequate to every possible circumstance is unavailable because action remains irreducibly indeterminate.
Full intrapersonal justice is foreclosed because justice requires numerically distinct parties, leaving psychic justice only analogical.
The naturally best political order is invoked as a universal standard but left substantively unspecified.
The semantic diagnostic proceeds from common attribution through contrary-state analysis to concealed homonymy and the division between lawfulness and fairness.
The universal branch proceeds from lawfulness through legally ordered virtues to complete virtue exercised toward others.
The particular branch proceeds from unfair gain through equality as mean to geometric distribution and arithmetic rectification.
The associative branch proceeds from unequal producers through demand and monetary commensuration to proportionate reciprocity, exchange, and civic cohesion.
The jurisdictional branch proceeds from free reciprocal association through law to the distinction between natural and adopted political standards.
The agency branch proceeds from a normatively unjust deed through knowledge, control, voluntariness, and rational choice to blame and character attribution.
The corrective branch proceeds from universal legislation through exceptional particulars to equitable restoration of legislative intent.
The terminal boundary proceeds from unwilling suffering and relational plurality to the denial of voluntary victimhood and full self-injustice.
Ordinary usage → concealed plurality → lawfulness and fairness → universal and particular justice.
Particular injustice → inequality → equality as mean → geometric distribution → arithmetic rectification → proportionate exchange.
Civic association → political jurisdiction → natural and legal norms → voluntary attribution → equitable correction → exclusion of self-injustice.
Justice is reclassified from a single virtue into both complete relational virtue and a distinct virtue governing fair shares.
Equality is reclassified from numerical sameness into several relation-specific forms of proportion and restoration.
The terrain of responsibility is divided among unjust objects, unjust deeds, unjust acts, and unjust characters.
Exchange is reclassified from private transfer into a constitutive mechanism of civic association.
Legality is reclassified from final normative closure into a universal form requiring immanent equitable correction.
Nature and convention cease to be mutually exclusive alternatives because natural justice can change and conventional justice can bind.
The political, household, and intrapersonal domains are separated according to the presence or absence of reciprocal legal equality.
Surface — Justice regulates allocations, injuries, transactions, exchanges, judgements, and responses to law.
Structural — Laws, courts, political offices, distributive institutions, demand, and money mediate relational equality.
Metastrategic — Semantic division, mathematical proportion, and agency distinctions prevent lawfulness, fairness, outcome, action, and character from collapsing into one another.
Ontological/Temporal — Justice presupposes plural agents, contingent action, finite divisible goods, mutable norms, and future need secured through exchange.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the division of justice, its proportional forms, its political jurisdiction, its agency conditions, and its equitable correction.
The criterion of distributive merit and the content of the naturally best constitution remain underdetermined.
The relation between education for good citizenship and formation of the good person remains unresolved.
The system is coherent around relational equality, but the part–whole relation between lawlessness and unfairness is not fully stabilized by its extensional wording.
The structure is strongest where distributive, rectificatory, and agent-responsibility distinctions receive explicit formal criteria.
Compression is greatest where legality is linked to communal happiness and where demand is made to ground sufficient commensurability.
Structural tensions remain between mutable natural justice and universal force, legal justice and equity, and universal other-regard and restricted political membership.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the movement from semantic diagnosis through formal equality and political scope to agency, correction, and relational closure.
The central problem is that defining the ethical mean by correct reason leaves the governing standard indeterminate.
Correct reason in action is practical wisdom, a truth-attaining rational state inseparable from rightly formed desire and character.
The argument is classificatory, differential, dialectical, and reconstructive.
The argument moves from an indeterminate ethical prescription through a division of rational capacities and a taxonomy of truth-attaining states.
The taxonomy culminates in the distinction between theoretical wisdom, productive skill, and practical wisdom.
The final movement integrates practical wisdom with virtue of character while preserving the superiority and independence of theoretical wisdom.
The ethical mean is determinable only through a determinate account of correct reason.
Rational capacities are differentiated by whether their objects can or cannot be otherwise.
The virtue of each rational capacity is the state that best realizes truth in its proper activity.
Good rational choice requires true practical reason and correct desire to affirm and pursue the same object.
Rational choice is deliberative desire directed by goal-oriented reason toward achievable contingents.
Scientific knowledge demonstrates necessary and universal conclusions from principles it cannot itself demonstrate.
Intellect directly apprehends termini unavailable to rational account, including theoretical first principles and practical last particulars.
Skill is true productive reason concerning contingent products whose originating principle lies in the producer.
Production has an end distinct from its activity, whereas action has acting well as its end.
Practical wisdom is true practical reason concerning action and human good as a whole.
Practical wisdom requires universal understanding joined to experience-based apprehension of actionable particulars.
Individual practical good is structurally dependent on household and political order.
Wisdom is intellect combined with scientific knowledge of the most honourable necessary realities.
Good deliberation is correct reasoning toward a genuinely good end through the right means, manner, and time.
Virtue of character makes the practical end right, while practical wisdom determines what realizes it.
Cleverness is an ethically indeterminate capacity to secure a posited end.
Developed practical wisdom and complete virtue of character are reciprocally dependent.
Possession and exercise of rational virtue are intrinsically choiceworthy and contribute constitutively to happiness.
Correct reason is not adequately specified by the injunction to avoid excess and deficiency.
Perception alone does not constitute the principle of rational action.
Scientific knowledge does not concern objects that can be otherwise.
Skill does not concern action, necessary being, or natural generation.
Practical wisdom is neither scientific knowledge nor productive skill.
Wisdom is not political or practical science, and human goods are not the highest objects in the cosmos.
Good deliberation is not knowledge, belief, guesswork, speed, successful false inference, or correct calculation toward an evil end.
Judgment is not practical wisdom because judgment assesses while practical wisdom commands.
External conformity to just or noble conduct does not by itself constitute virtuous action.
Cleverness is not practical wisdom because successful means-end calculation is ethically neutral.
Natural virtue without practical intellect is not real virtue and can become harmful.
Practical wisdom does not govern theoretical wisdom merely because it issues prescriptions for action.
Intellectual virtues form a matrix determined by the modality of their objects and the ends of their activities.
Theoretical cognition depends on intellect for principles, scientific knowledge for demonstrations, and wisdom for their integration at the highest objects.
Practical truth consists in the agreement of cognition with ethically formed desire rather than in truth detached from motivation.
Production and action require different rational excellences because their ends have different structures.
Practical wisdom cannot be scientific knowledge because action is contingent, and it cannot be skill because acting well has no external product.
Experience is a condition of practical wisdom because action terminates in particulars that universal demonstration cannot supply.
Personal, household, legislative, deliberative, and judicial prudence differentiate one practical capacity by scale and function.
Good deliberation requires both a morally valid destination and a valid inferential path, so successful calculation can remain practically bad.
Natural dispositions become real virtues only when practical wisdom directs their operation.
The developed virtues form a unity because complete character excellence depends on a shared practical wisdom.
Temperance preserves practical wisdom by preventing pleasure and pain from corrupting the practical end.
Correct reason is an embodied integration of true judgment, right desire, experience, and virtuous character rather than a detachable ethical formula.
Truth is distributed across demonstrative, intuitive, productive, and practical modes according to differences among objects and activities.
Ethical rationality cannot be reduced to formal validity because its success depends on the goodness of both its end and its path.
Practical normativity is co-constituted by character and cognition, so neither independently grounds complete practical correctness.
The plurality of natural dispositions is unified at the developed level by a single integrated capacity for practical truth.
Human fulfilment has a non-sovereign practical architecture in which practical wisdom is indispensable for good action but subordinate in object to theoretical wisdom.
Individual prudence is structurally political because an agent’s good cannot be realized independently of household and civic order.
A homogeneous rational faculty cannot govern necessary and contingent objects without internal differentiation.
Universal propositions cannot determine action without irreducible apprehension of the particular situation.
Formally successful means-end reasoning cannot generate the moral validity of its end.
Cognitive truth alone cannot move action or constitute rational choice.
Virtuous action cannot be identified solely by external outcome or conformity.
Practical reason cannot remain ethically neutral and still qualify as practical wisdom.
Human advantage cannot determine the cosmic rank of objects of knowledge.
Complete practical agency cannot be atomistically self-sufficient.
No rule-governed algorithm can replace experienced virtuous perception at the endpoint of deliberation.
No discursive proof can ground either ultimate theoretical principles or ultimate practical particulars.
No morally unformed chooser can acquire practical wisdom through clever calculation alone.
No external product can serve as the final measure of praxis because acting well closes the practical sequence.
No criterion external to the developed good agent is supplied for independently validating the right practical end.
Neither fully formed virtue prior to practical wisdom nor developed practical wisdom prior to formed character is admitted as complete.
No authority relation permits practical wisdom to command theoretical wisdom as though the higher contemplative good were its instrument.
An indeterminate mean-formula generates the demand for a determinate standard of correct reason.
Object modality determines rational subpart, characteristic truth, and corresponding intellectual virtue.
For necessary objects, intellect supplies first principles, scientific knowledge demonstrates consequences, and their union concerning the highest objects yields wisdom.
For contingent products, productive reason proceeds from the producer toward an external product and yields skill.
For contingent actions, right desire and true goal-directed reason generate rational choice and practical wisdom directed toward acting well.
Universal understanding joins experienced apprehension of particulars, after which deliberation searches, judgment assesses, discernment applies equity, and practical wisdom commands.
Human good extends practical wisdom across personal, household, legislative, deliberative, and judicial scales.
Practical wisdom converts natural dispositions into real virtues, while a right end converts cleverness into an operative component of good action.
Virtue sets the end and practical wisdom specifies its realization, producing correct choice, good action, characteristic activity, and constitutive happiness.
The first movement is indeterminate correct reason → division of rational capacities → truth as their characteristic activity → taxonomy of intellectual virtues.
The second movement is necessary versus contingent objects → demonstration versus deliberation → production versus action → scientific knowledge, skill, practical wisdom, and wisdom.

The third movement is practical particulars → deliberation, judgment, and discernment → utility puzzles → cleverness and natural virtue → reciprocal dependence of practical wisdom and complete character.
The terminal movement is integrated practical virtue → correct rational choice → good action and happiness → practical service to rather than governance of theoretical wisdom.
The ethical mean is remapped from a formally stated midpoint into an achievement of developed practical judgment.
Reason is reclassified as a plurality of capacities indexed to the modal status of their objects.
Truth in action is reclassified as agreement between reason and desire rather than cognition considered in isolation.
Action and production become categorically distinct through the contrast between an internal end and an external product.
Practical cognition is subdivided by function into inquiry, deliberation, judgment, equitable discernment, and command.
Universal knowledge and particular perception cease to be rivals and become jointly necessary components of practical wisdom.
Private prudence is relocated within household and political structures rather than treated as isolated self-management.
Moral virtue is reclassified from natural disposition or compliant conduct into a state constituted by practical reason.
The hierarchy of intellectual virtues is redrawn so that superiority of object does not eliminate practical indispensability.
Surface: The explicit inquiry determines correct reason by defining the virtues of thought.
Structural: The rational soul is organized by object modality, activity type, causal origin, and end structure.
Metastrategic: Ethical instruction shifts from stating a general rule to forming an agent capable of perceiving, desiring, deliberating, and choosing correctly.
Ontological/Temporal: Necessary and eternal realities ground demonstration, while contingent future particulars delimit deliberation and the fixed past remains outside rational choice.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the passage from an indeterminate appeal to correct reason to a differentiated account of intellectual virtue.
The extracted system is sufficient to recover the distinctions among scientific knowledge, intellect, skill, practical wisdom, and wisdom.
The relation between induction, experience, and intellect in acquiring first principles remains underdetermined.
The system is internally coherent where differences among objects, activities, and ends generate corresponding differences among rational virtues.
The structure is strongest in distinguishing action from production and practical wisdom from cleverness.
The account depends on compression where the developed good agent’s perception validates the practical end without an independent criterion.
The reciprocal dependence of practical wisdom and virtue preserves ethical integration but leaves their developmental sequence partially circular.
The hierarchy between theoretical and practical wisdom remains tense because practical wisdom is indispensable to human fulfilment while denied authority over the superior contemplative object.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement while omitting examples, terminological etymologies, and local dialectical supports.
The central problem is how a person can knowingly act against better judgment without reducing incontinence either to ignorance or to vice.
Ethical adequacy is established by preserving authoritative appearances after their internal puzzles have been resolved.
Incontinence is an episodic defeat of correct practical commitment by affect, not a corruption of the practical first principle.
Unqualified incontinence is delimited by the natural bodily pleasures and pains that also define temperance and intemperance.
Defective states are ordered by whether the rational principle is absent, corrupted, preserved but ineffective, or effectively enacted.
Political inquiry must examine pleasure because character and happiness are organized through pleasure and pain.
Pleasure is reconstructed as unimpeded natural activity rather than as a process of restoration.
The argument is dialectical and reconstructive, moving from received opinions through puzzles and causal distinctions to ethical taxonomy, pleasure, and happiness.
An ethical state is classified jointly by its object and by the ordering of reason, appetite, rational choice, and action.
Vice is a settled condition that corrupts the practical first principle.
Brutishness lies beyond vice because the superior rational principle is absent rather than corrupted.
Incontinence preserves correct rational judgment and choice but acts against them under the influence of affect.
Practical knowledge can be possessed either actively or without being exercised.
Practical action depends on the conjunction of a universal judgment with an action-governing perceptual particular.
Affect can prevent correct particular cognition from being exercised while universal formulations remain verbally available.
Unqualified incontinence concerns the natural human bodily pleasures and pains associated with touch, taste, nourishment, and sex.
Failures concerning spirit, honour, gain, brutish appetite, or diseased appetite count as incontinence only with qualification or by resemblance.
Intemperance chooses excessive bodily pleasure as right and therefore lacks regret.
Practical wisdom entails good character and a disposition to act, so it cannot coexist with incontinence.
Self-control maintains correct reason against bad appetites, whereas temperance has no appetites contrary to reason.
Endurance and softness concern resistance or surrender to bodily pains, whereas self-control and incontinence concern overcoming or yielding to bodily pleasures.
Goods and pleasures can be good without qualification or only relative to a particular person and condition.
Pleasure is the unimpeded activity of a natural state rather than a perceived process of coming-to-be.
Pleasure belonging to an activity strengthens its exercise, whereas an extraneous pleasure impedes it.
Restorative bodily pleasures are pleasant only incidentally and are bounded by need, whereas pleasures of an unimpaired nature do not arise from deficiency.
Happiness is complete unimpeded activity, so its life is pleasant and requires bodily and external goods insofar as their absence would impede it.
Incontinence is not vice or intemperance merely because it can produce similar actions.
The possibility of incontinence is not eliminated by asserting that knowledge must always master appetite.
The distinction between knowledge and belief does not explain incontinence, because belief can be held as firmly as knowledge.
Possessing knowledge is not identical with attending to and exercising it.
Standing by every belief is not self-control, because steadfastness in false judgment can be bad.
Obstinacy is not self-control, because it resists reason rather than appetite.
Unqualified incontinence is not concerned indiscriminately with every pleasure, pain, or object of desire.
Brutish and diseased appetites are not ordinary human wickedness.
Animals are not continent, incontinent, temperate, or intemperate except by metaphorical extension.
Cleverness is not practical wisdom, and its coexistence with incontinence does not establish that practical wisdom can be incontinent.
Pleasure is not essentially a perceived restoration toward a natural state.
The existence of shameful, harmful, or unhealthy pleasures does not make pleasure as such bad.
Temperance does not avoid every pleasure, but only pleasures and excesses contrary to correct reason.
Good fortune is not happiness, because fortune is only enabling and can become an impediment in excess.
A person can act knowingly in a dispositional sense while lacking active command of the knowledge required for the particular action.
Verbal availability of a practical proposition does not establish its active possession.
Incontinence occurs when appetite activates a pleasure-directed particular cognition before correct universal judgment governs bodily action.
Animals cannot be incontinent because they lack the universal practical cognition against which a particular appetite could rebel.
Similar actions can express radically different characters because ethical identity depends on choice and first principle rather than outcome alone.
Incontinence is curable through persuasion because its correct practical principle survives, whereas intemperance resists cure because its principle is corrupted.
The incontinent agent acts voluntarily and may perform unjust acts without being unjust without qualification, because the acts are not planned from a corrupt principle.
Weak incontinence is structurally worse than impetuous incontinence because it overturns completed deliberation under a weaker affect, while impetuosity pre-empts deliberation.
Self-control is more choiceworthy than endurance because overcoming appetite is a stronger achievement than merely resisting pain.
Spirited incontinence is less shameful than appetitive incontinence because spirit follows a premature rational appearance, whereas appetite is moved directly by pleasure.
Brutishness is less morally bad than vice because it lacks rather than corrupts rational principle, but it is more fearsome because no superior principle governs it.
Self-control and incontinence are defined without qualification by adherence to or departure from true reason, not by constancy or change as such.
The qualified badness of some pleasures does not preclude a natural unimpeded pleasure from being good or even the chief good.
Contemplative pleasure demonstrates that pleasure can arise without appetite, pain, deficiency, or restoration and can intensify rather than impede thought.
A happy life must be pleasant because complete activity cannot remain complete while impeded by pain.
Bodily pleasures appear paradigmatic because their remedial intensity displaces pain and attracts those unable to enjoy non-remedial activities.
Good fortune contributes to happiness only as a bounded condition preventing impediment rather than as happiness itself.
Incontinence is a temporary interface failure between rational principle, perceptual particular, and bodily movement rather than a loss of the governing norm.
The ethical taxonomy differentiates absence of reason, corruption of reason, episodic failure to enact reason, resistance under conflict, and appetitive harmony with reason.
Culpability tracks the source and settled choice of an action more fundamentally than its external result or the intensity of its appetite.
Curability decreases as disorder moves from impetuous interruption through habituated weakness and natural disposition to corruption of the practical first principle.
The distinction between unqualified and qualified incontinence constructs ordinary human bodily appetite as the normative centre of the character taxonomy.
The rehabilitation of pleasure separates the formal condition of pleasantness from the worth of its object, allowing pleasure to be good while particular pleasures remain bad.
Happiness is embodied and vulnerable to fortune because complete activity depends on the removal of bodily and external impediments.
Mutable human pleasure reflects composite and deficient nature, whereas invariant divine pleasure represents the limiting case of simple unimpeded activity.
True practical knowledge does not guarantee uninterrupted governance of perception and bodily movement.
Practical error cannot be reduced to false universal judgment.
The acting subject is not functionally unitary at the moment when affect, perception, reason, and motion diverge.
External action does not disclose settled character independently of rational choice, regret, and practical principle.
Natural, excessive, diseased, brutish, and non-bodily desires cannot be placed within a single undifferentiated class.
Rational persistence has no intrinsic ethical value independently of the truth of what is maintained.
Pleasure cannot be evaluated solely by its intensity, genesis, bodily manifestation, or popularity.
Happiness cannot be reduced to disembodied virtue insulated from pain, material deprivation, and fortune.
A fully sovereign and self-transparent rational agent whose knowledge automatically becomes action is unavailable.
A flat continuum of bad character is excluded by the irreducible differences among absent, corrupted, preserved, and effective rational principle.
There is no evaluatively neutral substance called pleasure whose moral status remains constant across activities and natures.
Human happiness cannot be invulnerable, self-sufficient actuality entirely independent of embodiment and circumstance.
Simple, invariant human satisfaction is foreclosed; unchanging pleasure belongs only to the divine limiting case.
Received appearances generate puzzles, puzzles force distinctions, and distinctions preserve the authoritative appearances that survive contradiction.
Object of desire plus mode of affect plus relation to reason plus rational choice generates the classification of the ethical state.
Universal practical judgment plus perceptual particular normally generates action, while affective capture of the particular generates action contrary to preserved judgment.
Preserved first principle generates regret and persuadability, while corrupted first principle generates conviction, absence of regret, and resistance to cure.

Natural human bodily appetite generates unqualified classification, non-bodily appetite generates qualified classification, and brutish or diseased appetite generates analogical classification beyond ordinary vice.
Misgeneralization from restorative bodily pleasure generates the false process model, while separation of remedial and natural activity generates the unimpeded-activity model.
Unimpeded worthy activity plus its proper pleasure plus enabling bodily and external goods generates complete happiness.

The inquiry into incontinence moves from received classifications → paradoxes of knowledgeable wrongdoing → distinctions within knowledge → action through the perceptual particular → delimitation of proper objects → differentiation from vice, brutishness, and practical wisdom → graded curability.

The inquiry into pleasure moves from anti-pleasure arguments → distinction between qualified and unqualified goods → separation of restoration from activity → definition of pleasure as unimpeded natural activity → integration of pleasure into happiness → contrast between mutable human and invariant divine pleasure.
The knowledge-versus-ignorance opposition is replaced by a distinction between possessed, attended, universal, particular, and affectively disabled cognition.
Wrongdoing is reclassified according to its relation to rational choice and first principle rather than by action type alone.
Moral defect is divided into absence of rational principle, corruption of principle, and episodic failure of execution.
The distinction between unqualified and qualified attribution separates central human character states from analogous failures involving other objects or abnormal natures.
Self-control becomes a conflictual achievement distinct from temperance rather than a complete virtue identical with it.
Pleasure is relocated from the category of transition and replenishment to the category of activity and actuality.
Bodily pleasure ceases to define pleasure as such and becomes a limited, often remedial, subset of a wider field.
Happiness becomes visibly dependent on proper pleasure and on the bodily and external conditions that prevent complete activity from being impeded.
Surface: The inquiry distinguishes incontinence, self-control, softness, endurance, temperance, intemperance, and varieties of pleasure.
Structural: The argument models action through rational choice, universal judgment, perceptual particular, affective activation, and bodily motion.
Metastrategic: Dialectical resolution reorganizes ordinary ethical language into a hierarchy of unqualified, qualified, analogous, curable, and incurable states.

Ontological/Temporal: The system contrasts states with activities, restoration with actuality, episodic affect with chronic vice, habituation with nature, and composite human mutability with divine simplicity.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct both the analysis of incontinence and the argument concerning pleasure with sufficient conceptual scope.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if the progression from received opinions through puzzles to causal and classificatory distinctions is retained.
The system is internally coherent at the level of its distinctions among practical principle, rational choice, active cognition, and action.
The strongest reconstructive mechanism is the explanation of knowledgeable wrongdoing through inactive universal knowledge and affective disruption of the perceptual particular.
The physiological process by which affect disables or reactivates particular knowledge remains delegated to natural science and is therefore underdetermined.
The claim that incontinent action is voluntary remains in tension with the claim that its decisive knowledge is present only in a compromised or inactive form.
The pleasure analysis oscillates between identifying pleasure with unimpeded activity and treating pleasure as something arising from and strengthening activity.
The restriction of unqualified incontinence to bodily appetite depends partly on ordinary naming practices, leaving its normative privilege compressed.
The dependence of complete happiness on external goods and the derivation of invariant divine pleasure from simplicity are structurally consequential but only briefly established.
The inquiry determines the conditions, species, hierarchy, and proper reciprocity of friendship.
Friendship is recognized reciprocal goodwill ordered by the good, the pleasant, or the useful.
Complete friendship exists between virtuous people who love one another for who they are.
Utility and pleasure friendships are conditional approximations to complete friendship.
Friendship and justice articulate the same communal field and vary with its structure.
Equality preserves friendship through equal reciprocity among equals and proportional reciprocity among unequals.
The argument is classificatory and ethical-political, moving from lovable objects through relational forms to communal order and the regulation of disputes.
Friendship is a virtue-involving relation that is necessary and noble in human life.
An object is loved only as actually or apparently good, pleasant, or useful to the lover.
Friendship requires mutually recognized goodwill in which each party wishes goods to the other under the reason grounding the affection.
Differences among the grounds of love generate differences among the species of friendship.
Utility- and pleasure-based friends love one another incidentally rather than for who the other is.
An incidental friendship lasts only while its utility or pleasure remains.
Complete friendship exists between people alike in virtue who love one another as good and for the other’s own sake.
Complete friendship integrates goodness, pleasure, usefulness, trust, and durability because it is grounded in virtuous character.
Friendship is a chosen state of character rather than a mere feeling of affection.
The activity of friendship consists in shared life, reciprocal beneficence, and common enjoyment.
Friendship is constituted more by loving than by being loved.
Every friendship is ordered either between equals or across a relation of superiority.
Equality is preserved through equal reciprocity among equals and proportional affection and return among unequals.
Friendship and justice extend only as far as shared community extends, and their claims intensify with communal closeness.
The political community contains partial communities because it orders common utility across the whole of life.
Rule remains correct by serving common benefit according to merit and becomes deviant by serving the ruler’s private advantage.
Familial friendships arise from natural generation, shared origin, common life, and complementary household contribution.
The proper measure of return is determined by the friendship’s end, terms, and proportional structure.
Human friendship is not explained by cosmological theories of attraction between likenesses or opposites.
Affection toward a soulless object is not friendship because reciprocity and goodwill are absent.
Unreciprocated or unrecognized goodwill is not friendship.
Variation by degree does not establish that friendship has only one species.
Utility and pleasure do not ground love of the other as the person he is.
Quick signs of affection and a wish to become friends do not constitute complete friendship before tested knowledge and confidence.
Wicked people cannot be complete friends merely through shared wickedness.
Affection as a feeling is not identical with friendship as a chosen state.
Quantitative sameness is not an adequate standard for friendships involving superiority.
Friendship cannot survive an unlimited disparity between the parties.
Justice is not sufficient for shared life because just people still require friendship.
Instrumental status cannot ground friendship, although common humanity can restore its possibility.
External prosperity cannot replace friendship because its noble use, protection, and preservation depend on shared action and beneficence.
The three grounds of love generate exactly three species of friendship: virtue, pleasure, and utility.
Utility and pleasure friendships dissolve when changing circumstances remove the quality for which the parties were loved.
Virtue friendship is friendship without qualification, while utility and pleasure friendships count as friendships by resemblance to it.
Complete friendship is rare and cannot be widely multiplied because it requires virtuous character and sustained shared experience.
Separation can suspend friendship’s activity without immediately eliminating its dispositional state, although prolonged absence can erode that state.
Bad people can sustain utility or pleasure friendships but cannot sustain friendship grounded in the other’s intrinsic goodness.
A self-sufficiently happy person does not need useful friends as remedies for deficiency but still needs good and pleasant companions for shared life.
Loving according to merit converts unequal affection into proportional equality.
Distinct forms of community generate corresponding forms and degrees of friendship and justice.
Tyrannical relations contain little friendship or justice, while more equal political relations contain more of both.
A slave considered only as an instrument falls outside friendship and justice, but the same person considered as a human capable of law and agreement re-enters both.
Degrees of kinship generate proportional degrees of affection, common identity, and obligation.
Utility friendship produces complaints because each party evaluates the exchange by personal advantage and suspects an unequal return.
Fixed-term utility is measured by agreement, character-based utility by advantage to the recipient, and virtue friendship by the benefactor’s rational choice.
Unequal friendship is preserved when the superior party receives more honour and the needy party receives more material benefit.
When exact repayment is impossible, friendship requires the best practicable return rather than strict equivalence.
Complete friendship functions as the normative model that permits lesser relations to be recognized as friendships while ranking them as deficient.
Complete friendship makes self-concern and concern for another converge because the intrinsically loved friend also becomes a good for the lover.
Durable friendship is a temporal achievement produced by stable character, repeated activity, familiarity, and tested confidence.
Political corruption simultaneously erodes justice and friendship because private rule destroys the common field supporting both.
Equality in friendship is relational rather than homogeneous because proportion can equalize unlike contributions without making them identical.
Kinship converts shared origin and common life into graded moral claims whose strength decreases with relational distance.
Human capacity for law and agreement places an internal limit on social relations that reduce persons to instruments.
Civic friendship must remain broader than complete friendship, leaving most political bonds dependent on analogical or partial forms of friendship.
A single undifferentiated essence cannot explain relations grounded in distinct lovable ends.
Mutual affection cannot be morally classified independently of its object, purpose, and mode of reciprocity.
Complete friendship cannot rest on qualities whose identity is determined by rapidly changing circumstances.
Political association cannot be reduced to legal coordination because law alone does not generate concord.
Coercion and private advantage cannot produce the common participation required for substantial friendship.
Formal equality cannot resolve unequal relations without a prior conception of merit and proportion.
A human person cannot be exhaustively identified with instrumental social status while retaining the capacity for community.
The good of the agent and the good of the friend are not assumed to form a zero-sum opposition.
Immediate attraction cannot substitute for the temporal testing required by complete friendship.
No friendship is available where the parties share no common activity, good, law, agreement, or form of life.
Absolute superiority abolishes friendship by removing the common measure through which reciprocity could occur.
No universal currency can commensurate every contribution, since honour, gain, virtue, benefit, and inherited debt require different returns.
No political order is treated as secure through justice alone when concord and reciprocal concern are absent.
The system admits no greatest good for a friend that abolishes the friend’s human identity and thereby destroys the friendship itself.
A fully symmetrical household relation independent of naturalized paternal and sex-specific roles remains unavailable within the framework.
The entry sequence is: human necessity and noble agency → analysis of lovable objects → criterion of recognized reciprocal goodwill.
The classificatory sequence is: good, pleasure, or utility → distinct reason for loving → distinct species of friendship.
The incidental sequence is: conditional valuation → alteration of the valued quality → withdrawal of affection → dissolution.
The complete-friendship sequence is: virtuous character → love of the person as good → convergence of goodness, pleasure, and utility → trust and duration.
The enactment sequence is: chosen disposition → shared life and beneficence → reciprocal loving → maintained equality.
The political sequence is: common participation → coextensive friendship and justice → political incorporation of partial communities → constitutional differentiation by common or private advantage.
The familial sequence is: origin and common life → graded identity and superiority → differentiated obligations → proportional affection and return.
The conflict sequence is: divergent expectations → incompatible valuation → complaint → form-specific measurement → proportional restoration or dissolution.

Necessity and nobility → lovable-object criterion → reciprocal goodwill → three species → primary virtue friendship → state and activity → equality and superiority → community and justice → polity and household → complaint and proportional repair.
Friendship is reclassified from subjective affection into a recognized reciprocal state expressed through shared activity.
A seemingly unitary relation is reorganized into three species and ranked by whether the person or an incidental quality is loved.
Goodness, pleasure, and usefulness cease to be exclusive alternatives because complete friendship integrates all three.
Equality is redefined from identical shares into a variable structure of equal or proportional reciprocity.
Justice is relocated inside communal relations rather than treated as an autonomous legal domain.
Political constitutions become diagnosable as relational orders that expand or contract friendship through their degree of commonality.
Kinship and household relations become graded structures of common identity, benefit, authority, and obligation.
Complaints are reclassified as failures to share a measure of benefit rather than merely failures of goodwill.
The distinction between human capacity and instrumental status exposes a limit within relations of domination.

Structural: Friendship operates through chosen states, shared activity, equality, hierarchy, commonality, and differentiated measures of reciprocity.
Metastrategic: The hierarchy of friendship species supplies standards for diagnosing personal disputes, household relations, and political constitutions.
Ontological/Temporal: Complete friendship presupposes relatively stable character, finite relational capacity, embodied shared life, and time sufficient for mutual testing.

The exact thresholds at which disparity, distance, or moral deficiency terminate friendship remain underdetermined.

The system is strongest in its distinction between loving a person and loving an incidental benefit, and in its linkage of friendship, justice, and community.
The conjunction of loving another for the other’s sake with each person’s primary wish for his own good remains incompletely resolved.
Proportional equality stabilizes hierarchy only by presupposing contestable standards of merit, superiority, and appropriate return.
The political and household applications depend on compressed analogies and unargued assumptions concerning paternal, marital, and social superiority.
Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the real movement from definition and classification through communal extension to conflict regulation.
The central problem is how friendship can sustain just claims and virtuous attachment amid inequality, divergent expectations, character change, competing duties, and human self-sufficiency.
The governing thesis is that friendship’s form is fixed by its object: transient advantage supports conditional bonds, while rationally unified character supports durable shared activity.
Proportionality and contextual fittingness regulate asymmetrical relations without reducing every obligation to a single metric.
The argument is reconstructive and diagnostic because disputes are traced from failed reciprocity to mistaken friendship-types and disordered character.
The inquiry moves from external exchange and dissolution to the self-relation that generates friendship, goodwill, concord, and benefaction.
The opposition between self-love and sacrifice is resolved by distinguishing appetitive appropriation from rational possession of the noble.
The final movement redefines happiness as socially actualized life whose finite shared activity requires virtuous friends and reproduces character.
Utility and pleasure friendships take transient qualities as their objects, whereas virtue friendship takes character itself as its object.
Proportional reciprocity establishes equality between dissimilar friends.
Conditional exchange requires mutually fair valuation, whereas an uncontracted benefit given for another’s sake requires a return governed by rational choice.
Practical obligations are role-specific claims whose priority varies with relationship, virtue, usefulness, nobility, and necessity.
Continuing friendship requires lovable character and sufficient evaluative similarity for shared life.
Relations of friendship toward others originate in the agent’s relation toward himself.
The person is primarily the rational element whose authoritative activity constitutes voluntary agency.
Virtue makes the agent concordant with himself by stabilizing desire, choice, pleasure, pain, memory, and hope around rational good.
Vice divides the agent against himself and thereby destroys self-friendship.
Goodwill is a necessary but insufficient inception of friendship and becomes friendship only through intimacy and active concern.
Political concord consists in shared practical judgment, common choice, and coordinated action concerning common benefit.
An agent loves a beneficiary or product as a persisting actuality of his own activity, with nobility and effort intensifying the attachment.
Proper self-love assigns noble activity to the rational self, whereas corrupt self-love assigns excessive competitive goods to appetite.
The rational self-lover can surrender external goods for another because noble action is the greater good he thereby assigns to himself.
Human happiness is continuous, reflexively pleasant virtuous activity within a naturally social life rather than a self-contained possession.
A virtuous friend is another self whose good being and activity become perceptible and choiceworthy through shared life.
Close friendship is bounded by the finite capacity for reciprocal co-living and sustained participation in one another’s joys and sorrows.
Living together around chosen ends assimilates the characters of friends, improving the good and worsening the bad.
Equality between dissimilar friends is not identity of status or equality of numerical return.
