Utility and pleasure friendships are not attachments to the other’s character and do not possess intrinsic permanence.
Just valuation is not the giver’s unilateral estimate or the recipient’s depreciated estimate after receiving the benefit.
A freely given benefit within virtue friendship is not an enforceable contract governed by exact financial equivalence.
Obligation does not require giving every good or the same return to the same person.
Honour and assistance are not undifferentiated goods but must be fitted to the recipient’s role and claim.
Friendship does not require preserving intimacy with an incurably vicious or radically incompatible person.
Stable friendship toward another does not arise independently of the agent’s capacity for self-friendship.
Goodwill is neither friendship nor affection because it can lack intimacy, intensity, cooperation, and sustained concern.
Concord is neither agreement about theoretical belief nor rival desire for the same private possession.
A benefactor’s love is not reducible to a creditor’s interest in repayment.
Proper self-love is not appetitive acquisition of money, honour, or bodily pleasure.
Self-sufficient happiness is not solitude, freedom from virtuous companions, or the absence of recipients for beneficence.
Close friendship is not indefinitely scalable and is not equivalent to generalized civic friendliness.
Living together is not mere spatial proximity but shared perception, speech, thought, and activity.
Unacknowledged divergence about the good being exchanged generates complaint because no return can satisfy both parties’ expectations.
The disappearance of utility or pleasure rationally dissolves an instrumental friendship, while falsely presenting such a bond as character friendship makes complaint just.
When no common estimate of a conditional benefit is available, the recipient should assess it by prior valuation rather than by its diminished value after possession.
Repayment is normally prior to voluntary favour, but an act of overriding nobility or necessity can supersede the debt.
Reformable vice calls for an attempt to rescue the friend’s character, whereas incurable vice permits dissolution and former friendship leaves a residual claim to consideration.
Rational self-concord enables stable concern for another, whereas psychic division deprives the agent of the structure required for complete friendship.
Goodwill is latent virtue friendship only when admiration of excellence develops into sustained intimacy and cooperative action.
Good citizens can maintain concord because their stable wishes converge on just common action, whereas vicious overreaching converts nominal agreement into civil strife.
Benefactor-beneficiary affection is predictably unequal because the benefactor contemplates an enduring noble actuality while the beneficiary primarily receives passing utility.
General pursuit of noble rational self-love aligns individual perfection with the common interest.
Sacrificing wealth, honour, office, action, or life can express intensified self-preference when the agent chooses the greater good of nobility.
The happy person needs virtuous friends not to repair material deficiency but to exercise beneficence, sustain virtuous activity, and perceive another good life as his own.
The number of close friends must remain small because complete friendship requires reciprocal intimacy, mutual compatibility, and continuous shared activity.
Friends should be welcomed into good fortune, spared avoidable burdens in bad fortune, and assisted without waiting to be asked when they are in need.
Friendship functions as a recursive mechanism of moral formation because friends repeatedly confirm and imitate what each approves in the other.
Friendship forms a graded architecture in which proportional exchange regulates asymmetrical bonds, rational choice governs virtue-giving, and shared activity realizes complete friendship.
Virtue is simultaneously a condition of coherent selfhood and a condition of stable relationality.
Political concord externalizes psychic concord, while civil strife externalizes the vicious agent’s internal division.
The relation to another self extends reflexive awareness beyond the isolated agent without eliminating personal distinction.
Human self-sufficiency is relational completeness rather than independence from external persons.
Ethical community is necessarily finite and recursively formative because sustained association both presupposes and reproduces character.
Justice bounds friendship through proportion and fittingness, but complete friendship exceeds equivalence through unpriced rational choice and noble self-expenditure.
Friendship is temporally path-dependent because expectations, remembered activity, character change, and repeated association alter both present claims and future durability.
No universal quantitative procedure can replace practical judgment in conflicts among heterogeneous obligations.
Persons cannot be reduced to bundles of satisfactions because stable friendship requires character as an enduring object of attachment.
The self cannot be treated as a flat aggregate of desires because normative identity requires rational hierarchy and psychic concord.
Common benefit cannot arise from the coincidence of private acquisitive aims because concord requires shared choice and willingness to bear common burdens.
Virtuous activity cannot be fully actualized in isolation because beneficence, mutual perception, and shared action require others.
Association cannot be morally neutral because repeated common activity assimilates character.
Complete friendship cannot be instantaneous because goodwill requires temporal development into intimacy, tested character, and cooperative life.
Complete human autarky is unavailable because the isolated possessor of goods cannot realize socially actualized happiness.
Complete commensurability is unavailable at the level of virtue, parental debt, and formative benefit, so exact equivalence cannot close every relation.
Unconditional love independent of character is excluded because lovability and continued friendship remain indexed to goodness and shared evaluation.
Pure altruism without reflexive noble gain is unavailable because sacrifice is explained as the agent’s acquisition of the greater noble good.
Unlimited intimacy is impossible because finite attention, shared affect, and co-presence bound the circle of complete friends.
A final algorithm for weighing debt, kinship, virtue, usefulness, nobility, and necessity is absent from the system.
Otherness not assimilable to likeness remains unformalized because complete friendship is generated through the friend’s status as another self.
No determinate criterion establishes when vice is incurable, when evaluative inequality becomes excessive, or when residual obligation to a former friend expires.
The exchange module runs as friendship-object → expected good → valuation standard → proportional or choice-governed return → preservation or complaint.
The obligation module runs as competing claims → classification by role → comparison of closeness, virtue, usefulness, nobility, and necessity → contextually fitting action.
The continuity module runs as character change → test of lovability and shared life → attempted reform where possible → dissolution with residual consideration where reform fails.
The constitutive module runs as rational self-rule → psychic concord → extension of self-relation toward another self → complete virtue friendship.
The relational differentiation module separates goodwill as inception, concord as political coordination, and benefaction as productive asymmetry.
The self-love module runs as apparent egoism–altruism contradiction → division between appetite and reason → reclassification of noble sacrifice as rational self-preference.
The happiness module runs as activity rather than possession → social and reflexive actualization → perception of the friend’s good being → necessity of virtuous friendship.
The terminal module runs as finite capacity for co-living → limitation of close friends → fortune-sensitive conduct → shared activity → reciprocal moral assimilation.

The argument moves through exchange asymmetry and quarrel → contextual allocation of obligations → temporal testing and dissolution → self-relation as friendship’s source → differentiation of goodwill, concord, and benefaction → reconstruction of self-love → relational necessity and finite scale of happiness → co-living as moral reproduction.
Equality is remapped from identical treatment to proportional reciprocity among dissimilar persons.
Obligation is remapped from universal repayment to practical adjudication among heterogeneous role-specific claims.
Dissolution is reclassified from simple disloyalty into a differentiated response to vanished benefit, deception, reformable vice, incurable vice, or radical divergence.
Friendship is relocated from an external social bond to an extension of rational self-relation.
Goodwill, concord, and benefaction become distinct relational forms rather than interchangeable names for friendship.
The opposition between egoism and altruism collapses once self-love is divided into appetitive acquisition and rational pursuit of nobility.
Self-sufficiency is reclassified as the completeness of social activity rather than independence from friends.
Living together is reclassified from proximity into the perceptual and formative actuality through which friendship reproduces character.
Surface — The inquiry adjudicates repayment, conflicting duties, broken friendships, self-love, the need for friends, their proper number, and conduct across changing fortune.
Structural — Friendship is organized by its object, mode of reciprocity, quality of character, degree of shared life, and capacity for sustained mutual activity.
Metastrategic — Apparent paradoxes are resolved by distinguishing kinds of friendship, valuation, self-love, need, concord, and companionship before practical judgment is applied.

Ontological/Temporal — Rational activity constitutes the person, reflexive perception makes good being choiceworthy, the friend extends that perception as another self, and repeated co-living forms character through time.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the full movement from exchange disputes to co-living as the actuality and formative end of friendship.
The system is sufficient because it preserves the governing transitions among reciprocity, character, self-relation, virtuous activity, sociality, and moral formation.
The ranking of heterogeneous obligations remains underdetermined because no fixed weights govern closeness, virtue, usefulness, nobility, and necessity.
The structure is internally coherent where rational self-concord, proper self-love, virtue friendship, and political concord instantiate the same ordering principle.
The reconstruction is strongest where friendship is derived from virtuous activity rather than treated as a merely external possession.
The claim that determinate life is naturally pleasant and the transition from self-awareness to choice of a friend’s being depend on compressed metaphysical premises.

Tension remains between self-sufficient happiness and dependence on external friends, between love of the person and conditional love of good character, and between sacrifice and its reinterpretation as noble self-gain.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement because practical puzzles progressively expose the psychic, political, and ontological conditions of complete friendship.
The governing problem is how pleasure can pervade choice, character, and happiness without being either the unqualified good or an undifferentiated evil.
Pleasure is a temporally complete, supervenient completion of activity whose species and value follow the activity it completes.
Happiness is self-sufficient virtuous activity chosen for itself rather than a passive state, bodily enjoyment, or amusement.
Complete happiness is contemplation, while practical virtue constitutes secondary happiness tied to embodied and social life.
Practical ethics succeeds only when true argument is converted into habituated desire, action, and law-governed formation.
The argument is dialectical in its treatment of pleasure, teleological in its ranking of activities, and institutional in its practical closure.
Disputed pleasure → activity ontology → pleasure hierarchy → contemplative happiness → habituation → legislation → political science.
Practical claims are acceptable only when they accord with the facts of life.
Pleasure is a whole whose form is complete at every present moment.
Pleasure supervenes upon and completes an activity without being identical to it.
Pleasures differ in species according to the activities they complete.
Pleasure modulates activity according to fit: proper pleasure strengthens activity, while foreign pleasure displaces it.
The moral value of a pleasure derives from the moral value of its activity and source.
The virtuous person is the normative measure of what is genuinely pleasant.
Happiness is self-sufficient activity chosen solely for itself.
Complete happiness realizes the virtue of the highest element in a person.
Intellect is the highest and authoritative element in a human being.
Contemplation is the activity proper to intellect.
Contemplation most fully combines continuity, proper pleasure, self-sufficiency, leisure, and intrinsic finality.
Activities of character virtue constitute secondary happiness because they belong to the embodied social compound and depend upon other persons and external means.
Human contemplation requires moderate bodily and external support despite its relative self-sufficiency.
Practical inquiry terminates in the formation and exercise of good action rather than in knowledge alone.
Rational teaching becomes effective only in a character habituated to love the noble and hate the disgraceful.
Law joins reason derived from practical wisdom to coercive power across the whole of life.
Legislative expertise requires universal knowledge, experience of particulars, and correct situational judgment.
Pleasure is not the unqualified good, because a life of pleasure can be improved by the addition of intelligence.
Pleasure is not evil simply in virtue of being pleasure.
Deliberately misrepresenting pleasure as evil cannot provide sound moral education because conflict with experience discredits the argument.
Universal pursuit cannot by itself establish pleasure as the complete good.
Pleasure is not a process, coming-to-be, or temporally incomplete movement.
Admitting degrees does not make pleasure indeterminate.
Bodily replenishment cannot provide a general account of pleasure.
Pleasure experienced by a corrupted agent does not establish genuine pleasantness.
Pleasure is not identical with perception, thought, or the activity it completes.
Happiness is not a passive state, amusement, or the accumulation of bodily pleasures.
Political and military action cannot constitute primary happiness because they are exertive and ordered beyond themselves.
Ethical argument alone cannot produce virtue in an unprepared character.
Private paternal authority cannot fully substitute for public legal power.
Legislative science cannot be reduced to collecting statutes, sophistic instruction, or unreflective political experience.
Pleasure is conditionally good when it completes good activity, but it has no unconditional value independent of activity and character.
Pleasures cannot be ranked by intensity alone because the rank of the activity and the condition of the enjoyer precede quantitative comparison.
Enjoyment of an activity improves attention, accuracy, and persistence when the pleasure is proper to that activity.
The highest characteristically human pleasure is the proper completion of contemplation rather than an independent sensation.
Practical virtue yields genuine but secondary happiness because its activities remain relational, embodied, and externally dependent.
Contemplative self-sufficiency is relative rather than absolute because its human exercise still depends upon material maintenance.
Leisure is the condition for intrinsically final activity rather than a synonym for amusement.
Pleasure and pain function as formative conditions of rational receptivity rather than merely as consequences of moral judgment.
Legal coercion provides the pedagogical bridge from affective obedience to reason-responsive noble action.
Public legal education has priority over private formation, while individualized care remains a fallback under defective institutions.
Competent legislative inquiry must move reciprocally between universal principles and experienced particular cases.
Ethics requires continuation as comparative political inquiry because laws produce character and legislative judgment requires tested experience.
Ethical formation operates as a feedback circuit in which activity elicits pleasure, proper pleasure strengthens activity, repetition stabilizes disposition, and law organizes repetition.
Normative hierarchy is indexed to the excellence of activities rather than to the intensity of desire or pleasure.
Complete happiness is simultaneously the activity of humanity’s authoritative self and a life superior to the merely embodied human compound.
The good agent judges pleasures correctly, while law produces the habits that make such judgment possible, so normative authority is recursively reproduced.
External goods are demoted from final constituents of happiness to enabling conditions for activities whose value lies in themselves.
Political science completes ethics by converting knowledge of the human end into institutions capable of producing agents fitted to pursue it.
Pleasures cannot occupy a single homogeneous normative scale independent of their activities.
Immediate preference cannot function as moral self-evidence.
A human person cannot be reduced without remainder to the embodied social compound.
The highest end cannot depend for its value upon an external product.
Reason cannot create its own receptive moral subject without prior affective formation.
Private choice cannot by itself sustain the production of virtuous character across a community.
Universal theory and accumulated experience cannot substitute for one another in practical science.
A transient achievement cannot constitute complete happiness without sustained activity across a complete life.
An egalitarian plurality of human ends is foreclosed by the hierarchy culminating in contemplation.
A fully immanent account of human flourishing is unavailable because complete happiness is modeled on divine activity.
A noncoercive path from mass appetite to stable virtue is treated as unavailable.
No neutral standard independent of virtuous character is supplied for identifying the virtuous person’s judgments as authoritative.
Absolute contemplative autarky is denied by the continuing dependence of human activity upon body, resources, and social order.
The legitimacy threshold separating rational legal formation from oppressive coercion remains unnamed.
Practical salience of pleasure + disputed extremes → test by lived facts → rejection of strategic falsehood.
Temporal completeness → exclusion of process and replenishment → location of pleasure in completed activity.
Activity–pleasure correspondence → species differentiation → enhancement or interference → valuation through activity.
Variation among agents → distinction between apparent and genuine pleasure → virtuous-agent measure.
Happiness as self-sufficient final activity → exclusion of amusement and passive states → selection of virtuous activity.
Highest element → intellect → contemplation → primary happiness.
Embodied social dependence → practical virtue and moderate external goods → secondary happiness and qualified self-sufficiency.
Knowledge–action gap → prior habituation of desire → lifelong legal discipline.
Public formation through law → demand for legislative expertise → synthesis of universals, particulars, and experience.
Comparative constitutions and laws → causes of preservation and destruction → best regime, laws, and habits → completion of practical philosophy.
Dispute over pleasure → correction by facts → ontological reclassification → activity-indexed plurality → ethical ranking.
Happiness as final activity → amusement excluded → highest virtue selected → contemplation primary → practical virtue secondary → external qualification.
Ethical knowledge insufficient → character habituation → legal coercion → legislative expertise → comparative constitutional inquiry.
Pleasure ethics → hierarchy of activities → contemplative end → institutional production of agents capable of pursuing that end.
Pleasure is reclassified from a homogeneous feeling or restorative process into the species-specific completion of activity.
The opposition between pleasure and virtue collapses because pleasure can either perfect or corrupt activity according to its object and source.
Competition among pleasures becomes visible as competition among activities for attention and persistence.
Happiness is relocated from possession, feeling, and entertainment to sustained excellent activity.
Leisure is separated from amusement and reclassified as the temporal condition of intrinsically final activity.
Human identity is divided between the embodied social compound and the authoritative intellect that most fully constitutes the person.
Ethics and politics cease to be separable domains because institutional habituation becomes a condition of practical virtue.
Political expertise is reclassified from command, statute collection, or routine experience into judgment integrating universals and particulars.
Surface: Pleasure, happiness, amusement, contemplation, and ethical education are explicitly classified and ranked.
Structural: Activities generate corresponding pleasures, habituation stabilizes dispositions, and law organizes the reproduction of character.
Metastrategic: Ethical inquiry is redirected from knowing the good to constructing the institutional conditions under which agents can enact it.
Ontological/Temporal: Pleasure is complete in the present, happiness requires sustained activity across a life, and contemplation activates a divine-like element within embodied human existence.
The chapter’s axioms reconstruct the real movement from pleasure through activity to happiness and from happiness to legal-political formation.
The system is sufficient to recover the distinctions between process and activity, proper and foreign pleasures, primary and secondary happiness, and argument and habituation.
The relation between pleasure and activity remains underdetermined because supervenient completion names their conjunction without fully explaining its causal form.
The virtuous-person criterion remains partly circular because virtue determines proper pleasure while habituated pleasures help produce virtue.
The hierarchy is internally coherent only if intellect is accepted as both the highest human element and the person’s authoritative self.
Self-sufficiency is coherently qualified by external necessity, but no exact threshold of sufficient material support is supplied.
The strongest generative sequence is the transition from the insufficiency of argument through habituation to law, though it compresses the anthropology of affective resistance.
The account of legislative science identifies universal knowledge, experience, and judgment but postpones their systematic integration.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s actual movement, while the divine analogy, coercive legitimacy, and relation between contemplative and political life remain dependent on elision.
The central problem is to connect the highest attainable human good to the formation, causal structure, and concrete exercise of the agency required to realize it.

The core thesis is that happiness consists in rationally excellent activity across a complete life, while the virtue enabling that activity is acquired through habituation and enacted through attributable choice.
At this scale, the argument becomes an architectonic practical theory joining teleology, character production, causal attribution, and differentiated virtue.
Its movement runs from ordered ends to the human function, from function to virtue, from virtue to habituated character, and from character to choice, responsibility, courage, and temperance.
Action is the central relay: it realizes happiness, produces and reproduces character, and supplies the causal basis for praise and blame.
Political order is therefore internal to ethics: institutions organize habituation and accountability rather than merely protecting independently formed agents.

The directional form is recursive and path-dependent: prior activity sediments into character, character shapes future appearances and choices, and later activity either reinforces or corrects the inherited state.

Closure is practical rather than demonstrative: general structure terminates in formed perception and situated judgment, leaving the ultimate measures of right reason and true appearance only partially specified.
[Persistent] Practical movement is end-ordered: means derive their worth from governing ends, and a non-vain hierarchy of pursuit terminates in happiness as the chief human good.
[Attractor] Human flourishing consists principally in rational activity performed excellently across a complete life, not in possession, reputation, resource, or episodic success.
[Persistent] Virtue has ethical reality only in properly motivated activity; neither a dormant state nor outward conformity is sufficient.
[Emergent] Character is recursively produced: repeated activities generate stable dispositions, and those dispositions increase the capacity and tendency to repeat corresponding activities.
[Mutating] Practical reason governs through the education and ordering of appetite rather than through the elimination of non-rational feeling.
[Emergent] Fully assessable virtuous action requires an internal moving principle, knowledge of relevant particulars, deliberative choice, and action from a formed state.
[Emergent] Character is both a consequence of action and an epistemic condition of action because it shapes how ends appear as good, noble, or pleasant.
[Attractor] Action is the system’s generative nexus: it instantiates the good, forms the agent, discloses character, and transmits responsibility across time.
[Emergent] Political and educational institutions produce the affective and dispositional field within which mature deliberation and responsibility operate.
[Terminal] General ethical accounts terminate in context-sensitive perception because right action requires simultaneous fit across variable particulars that no exact formula can exhaust.
[Mutating] Ethical time is cumulative and asymmetrical: complete-life flourishing depends on sustained activity, while formative actions sediment into states that later become difficult to reverse.
[Persistent] Human excellence is neither sovereign over contingency nor constituted by it; external conditions enable, obstruct, and pressure action without replacing its formal source.
[Mutating] Pleasure is neither the chief good nor a neutral accompaniment: it may complete virtuous activity, train desire, diagnose character, or strengthen appetite against reason.
[Attractor] The noble functions as the orienting end that distinguishes excellent action from behavior motivated merely by pleasure, safety, confidence, conformity, or external compulsion.

[Stable identity → expansion] The good persists as the end of action but expands from the terminal object of an architectonic hierarchy into the apparent end that organizes wish, deliberation, and character-shaped choice.
[Mutation] Virtue moves from functional excellence specifying happiness to an acquired mean disposition and then to the rational ordering of determinate fields such as fear and bodily appetite.
[Functional recurrence → escalation] Activity first realizes happiness, then produces character, and finally becomes the attributable cause through which responsibility reaches later states.

[Reversal and displacement] Pleasure shifts from a rejected rival conception of happiness to an internal completion of virtuous activity, then to the formative and diagnostic medium of character, and finally to an appetitive force requiring rational discipline.

[Functional recurrence] The reason–appetite distinction persists while changing function: it begins as a division of the soul, becomes the mechanism of habituation, and terminates as the field in which voluntary affect is harmonized with correct reason.

[Domain migration] Politics moves from architectonic coordination of ends into the institutional production of affective character and then into the administration of praise, punishment, pardon, and accountability.

[Escalation] Variability begins as a limit on ethical exactness, becomes the reason the mean is context-relative, and culminates in underdetermined thresholds separating retained agency from force or excuse.
[Displacement] The rejected separate Good is replaced not by relativism but by an immanent standard located in characteristic activity and disclosed through well-formed character.
[Absorption] The mean is absorbed into a broader theory of agency: contextual fitness becomes virtuous only when knowingly chosen from firm character for the correct end.

[Disappearance after structural work] Completeness and self-sufficiency recede from the operative foreground after identifying happiness; subsequent analysis shifts to producing and attributing the activity capable of satisfying those criteria.

[Local] The polemic against the separate universal Good and the unresolved thresholds of fortune remain local framing problems; what scales upward is the immanent and materially conditioned character of human excellence.

[Local] The triadic geometry of opposed extremes and the specific heuristic of steering away from personal bias remain lower-layer correction techniques; their scalable residue is the need for asymmetrical, perceptual judgment.

[Local] The detailed classifications of force, ignorance, courage, and temperance remain domain-specific; their scalable structures are internal causal origin, knowledge of particulars, rationally selected means, and ordered affect.
[Scaled] The function argument scales upward because it supplies the standard by which habituated states and voluntary actions count as excellent rather than merely stable or attributable.
[Bridge] The participatory relation of appetite to reason bridges the definition of happiness, the mechanism of character formation, and the differentiated virtues governing fear and pleasure.
[Catalyst] Defining happiness as virtuous activity makes the genesis and structure of virtue a necessary next problem rather than an optional supplement.
[Catalyst] The reciprocal production of action and character generates the further problem of whether formed states remain attributable after immediate control diminishes.
[Superseded] Evaluation by outward deed is recoded into evaluation by knowledge, choice, motive, causal origin, character, and formative history.
Practical order cannot consist in an infinite succession of merely instrumental pursuits, nor can wealth or any other pure means occupy the position of the chief good.
Ethical normativity cannot depend on a separate universal Good detached from attainable action and heterogeneous practical domains.
Ethical competence cannot be produced by theoretical knowledge, exact rules, or verbal instruction without habituated desire and enacted practice.
Neither happiness nor virtue can be reduced to passive possession, undeveloped capacity, outward conformity, or isolated behavioral success.
Character can be neither a fixed natural substance nor the product of an unconditioned act of self-creation.
Virtue does not abolish pleasure, pain, fear, spirit, or appetite; it orders their objects, degrees, occasions, and ends.
The ethical mean is neither an arithmetic midpoint nor a license to moderate acts that are bad without qualification.
Human flourishing cannot be wholly private, solitary, or independent of political formation and social association.
Fortune, pressure, attraction, and affect cannot by themselves constitute happiness or erase agency when the agent remains a contributing internal principle.
The architecture excludes an atomistic model in which an already complete individual pursues flourishing independently of formative institutions and shared political order.
It excludes ethical intellectualism: correct propositions cannot substitute for a character whose desires and perceptions have been trained to receive practical reason.
It excludes both total determinism and unconditioned voluntarism because agency must be naturally receptive, socially formed, causally attributable, and never self-originating without conditions.
It excludes behavioralism: identical deeds may differ ethically because their knowledge, moving principle, motive, end, choice, and formative history differ.
It excludes a synchronic model of moral identity because flourishing, character, incapacity, and responsibility are intelligible only through cumulative temporal formation.
It excludes affective neutrality: pleasure and pain are constitutive motivational forces that shape pursuit, avoidance, perception, and character.
It excludes a universally commensurable decision procedure capable of replacing practical wisdom with metaphysical univocity, numerical calculation, or formal rule application.
The deepest absent object is an independent, non-circular measure of right reason and true appearance after the separate Good has been rejected.
A fully self-grounding origin of character is unavailable: formation must begin before mature virtue and choice, yet responsibility requires the regress of formative causes to stop at the agent.
An invulnerable human good is unavailable because excellent activity remains embodied, socially situated, temporally extended, and exposed to external obstruction.
A neutral standpoint outside habituated pleasure, pain, desire, and character-shaped appearance is unavailable to the acting subject.
The terminally inadmissible possibility is an ethically passive subject whose ends, affects, actions, and states occur without attributable participation.
Because happiness requires virtuous activity and virtue requires organized habituation, realization of the chief good is institutionally mediated rather than privately self-produced.
The same action can simultaneously instantiate flourishing, reproduce character, and transmit responsibility to a later state.
Rational agency is embodied affective organization: reason becomes practically effective only by habituating pleasure, pain, fear, and appetite into responsive participation.
Political order must both form agents before mature choice and preserve enough internal causal contribution to justify holding them responsible afterward.
Complete-life happiness and diachronic responsibility share one temporal architecture: present activity inherits sedimented character while producing the conditions of future activity.
Once the separate Good is rejected, practical truth becomes an enacted capacity to perceive ends correctly from within well-formed character.
Pleasure becomes the strategic hinge between flourishing and corruption because it can complete excellent activity while also reinforcing appetitive patterns that displace calculation.

External contingency conditions both flourishing and attribution without wholly determining either: fortune affects available activity, while pressure alters choice without necessarily removing internal agency.
Since neither exact rules nor a universal Form can determine particulars, ethical closure must be supplied by habituated perception, practical wisdom, and context-bound deliberation.
The formal mean acquires determinate ethical content only when a specific affective field, object, circumstance, motive, and noble end are supplied.
Human flourishing is the achievement of a self-reproducing practical organization in which excellent activity both expresses and regenerates the character capable of sustaining it.
The ethical subject is a socially formed yet causally attributable node: neither autonomous before formation nor reducible to the forces that formed it.
Practical epistemology is inseparable from ethics because correct recognition of ends depends on the character whose prior actions and institutions made such recognition possible.

Political authority becomes a dual apparatus of production and attribution: it habituates citizens into dispositions and later distributes honour, blame, pardon, and punishment according to causal participation.
Ethical time is path-dependent rather than reversible at will: early conduct changes later perception and capability, so freedom can decrease through the agent’s own prior activity.
Freedom is reconstructed as attributable causal origin within conditioned circumstances, not as independence from appetite, history, institutions, or external pressure.
Stable virtue is adaptive regularity rather than behavioral invariance: it preserves rational orientation by varying action and feeling with changing particulars.
Ethical intervention takes three coordinated forms: institutional habituation, self-correction of affective bias, and deliberative selection of executable means.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Happiness requires virtuous activity → virtue exists only through exercise → exercise forms and reinforces virtue → reinforced virtue sustains the activity constituting happiness.
Repeated action → acquired character → altered practical capacity → renewed corresponding action forms the primary character-reproduction loop.
Character → appearance of the good → wish → deliberation → rational choice → action → character forms the primary agency loop.
Pleasure or pain → pursuit or avoidance → repeated conduct → disposition → characteristic pleasure or pain forms the affective reinforcement loop.
Political law → habituated citizen → noble action → common good → renewed political formation forms the civic recursion joining ethics to architectonic politics.
Purposive action → ranked ends → happiness → human function → virtue → habituation → attributable choice marks the principal escalation from teleology to moral agency.
The noble is the conceptual attractor around which function, mean, pleasure, endurance, and appetite converge without being reduced to one behavioral form.
Bias → compensatory steering → approximate fit → renewed perception marks a corrective spiral rather than a linear application of rules.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Plural purposive practices → relations of subordination → terminal governing end → happiness.
Distinctive human function → rational activity → excellent performance → virtuous activity across a complete life.
Happiness as virtuous activity → need to explain virtue → natural receptivity without completed character.
Natural receptivity → repeated affectively reinforced activity → acquired disposition → increased capacity for corresponding activity.
Acquired disposition → characteristic appearance of the good → wish for an end.
Wished end → backward deliberation over contingent means → executable cause → rational choice → action.
Action → realization or obstruction of flourishing + reinforcement or correction of character + immediate or inherited attribution.
Political formation → organized habituation → mature agency → praise, blame, punishment, pardon, and renewed formation.
Variable particulars → rough general orientation → right reason and practical wisdom → perceptual closure in the case.
Sustained excellent activity + external enablement − grave obstruction → qualified, temporally cumulative happiness.
Purposive action → hierarchy of ends → terminal chief good → happiness.
Happiness → rational human function → excellent activity → need for an account of virtue.
Natural capacity → habituated activity → affective reinforcement → stable mean disposition.
Stable disposition → knowledge, choice, and firmness → fully virtuous action.
Moral appraisal → voluntary–involuntary boundary → wish and deliberation → rational choice → diachronic responsibility.
General mean state → rational ordering of fear and confidence → courage; rational ordering of bodily appetite → temperance.
Concrete virtue → sustained attributable activity → reinforced character → renewed pursuit of the human good under political and material conditions.
The good is reclassified from a detachable object or universal substance into the governing end immanent to organized human activity.
Action is reclassified from a transient deed into a threefold operator that realizes ends, manufactures character, and carries responsibility.
The subject is reclassified from an isolated chooser into a formed and forming causal history whose character shapes future perception.
Politics is reclassified from external administration into the architectonic organization of ends, habits, affect, agency, and accountability.
Freedom is reclassified from absence of influence into informed internal causal contribution under conditioned circumstances.
Practical truth is relocated from detached cognition to the character-dependent perception of genuinely good ends and fitting means.
Affect is reclassified from an irrational residue into an educable, voluntary, motivational infrastructure of virtue and vice.
Ethical time is redrawn from a sequence of independent decisions into sedimentation, reinforcement, entrenchment, and cumulative flourishing.
Stability is reclassified from sameness of conduct into reliable responsiveness to changing objects, occasions, motives, and ends.
[Surface] The system determines happiness, explains the acquisition and structure of character virtue, classifies voluntary choice, and specifies courage and temperance.

[Structural] Hierarchies of ends, recursive habituation, affective reinforcement, character-shaped appearance, deliberation, and political formation compose one distributed mechanism of practical agency.
[Metastrategic] Ethical intervention shifts from transmitting propositions to shaping institutions, diagnosing bias, training affect, and preserving attributable causal participation.
[Ontological / Temporal] The human being is a social, embodied, rationally active, path-dependent cause whose present conduct inherits prior formation and produces future capacities and constraints.

[Methodological / Performative] The argument performs its own doctrine by moving from rough formal outlines into habituation, causal distinctions, and concrete affective fields that require judgment beyond the outline.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Political and educational formation precedes mature choice, yet responsibility requires the formed agent to remain an originating principle rather than a product of institutions alone.
The true good is disclosed by good character, while good character is identified through correct orientation toward the true good, leaving the operative standard circular.
The mean is defined by right reason and practical wisdom, but the independent content and identifying criterion of that authority remain deferred.
Happiness is self-sufficient and relatively stable, yet its realization remains dependent on external goods and vulnerable to grave misfortune.
Responsibility extends to entrenched character even after immediate reversibility declines, but the degree of control present during earliest formation remains underdetermined.
Context-sensitive judgment resists universal rules, yet intrinsically bad acts and the objectively noble impose categorical boundaries within that variability.
Virtuous activity is said to be intrinsically pleasant, yet courage may become more painful as the courageous agent has more genuine goods to lose.
The good mutates from a rejected transcendent universal into functional excellence and then into the character-conditioned appearance governing wish.
Activity mutates from the actuality constituting happiness into the mechanism producing character and then into the causal origin of diachronic responsibility.
Pleasure mutates from a rival candidate into an internal completion, then into a formative diagnostic, and finally into a force capable of displacing calculation.
Non-rational appetite mutates from a soul-part capable of obeying reason into a voluntary source of action whose habits can either harmonize with or overpower rational order.
Reality appears as a civic-teleological feedback machine: nested ends orient action, action sediments character, and character recursively governs future access to ends.
The subject appears as an embodied, socially habituated, affectively organized causal node that is neither sovereign over its formation nor passive within it.
Time appears as cumulative sedimentation: activity builds dispositions, dispositions narrow or enlarge later possibility, and flourishing emerges only through durable organization across a life.

Possible navigation consists in political habituation, affective counter-steering, deliberative analysis, and perceptual calibration under conditions that can be ordered but never made fully invulnerable.

The global axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the cluster’s central machine: chief good → rational activity → habituated virtue → character-shaped choice → attributable action → recursive reinforcement.

The system remains underdetermined concerning the highest complete virtue, the substantive content of practical wisdom, the independent criterion of true appearance, and the thresholds of force and excuse.
Coherence is strongest where action is made simultaneously constitutive of flourishing, productive of character, and causally relevant to responsibility.

Reconstruction depends on sequencing and recursive return because happiness cannot be specified operationally without virtue, virtue cannot be explained without habituation, and habituation cannot be assessed without agency and attribution.
Situated perception remains resistant to axiomatic reduction: it is indispensable to correct action precisely because no extracted formula can determine every relevant particular.

The reconstruction preserves the actual movement of the cluster only if its unresolved tensions—social formation and responsibility, objective good and character-dependent appearance, self-sufficiency and contingency—remain operative rather than artificially resolved.

identity.title: Chapters 01–03
identity.context: Book I · Book II · Book III

items.text: The current-level problem is how context-sensitive virtue can possess a determinate rational standard, an interpersonal form, and a political field of operation without becoming an algorithm.
The governing thesis is that correct action arises from the convergence of stable character, relational proportion, right desire, voluntary choice, and truth-attaining practical judgment.
At this scale, the argument becomes a recursive calibration-and-correction architecture rather than a catalog of virtues, forms of justice, or intellectual states.
Its directional movement is qualitative mean-calibration → relational equality → institutional mediation → equitable correction → specification of practical wisdom.
The movement is spiral: every universal classification returns to particulars, while every particular judgment presupposes a formed disposition and a wider normative order.
Ethical scale expands from control of goods, passions, and social presentation to complete virtue toward others and then to household and political practical reason.
Practical closure occurs through the reciprocal dependence of virtue and practical wisdom operating inside law-governed association, not through an externally stated rule.
Closure remains incomplete because the right end, distributive merit, and best political order lack independent criteria, while theoretical wisdom retains superiority over practical completion.
[Persistent] Virtue is a stable state that organizes desire, choice, action, affect, and wish rather than an isolated deed or capacity.
[Mutating] The ethical mean begins as context-relative calibration, becomes relational equality within justice, and terminates as an achievement of developed practical judgment.
[Persistent] Practical universals remain incomplete until interpreted through perception of the relevant particular.
[Emergent] Complete practical correctness is jointly constituted by a right end supplied through character and a true means-to-end determination supplied through practical wisdom.
[Mutating] Relation to others develops from calibrated sociability into complete virtue under law and finally into the political conditions of individual prudence.
[Emergent] Equality is not one metric but a family of relation-specific operations whose appropriate form depends on the activity being regulated.
[Emergent] Law, courts, money, exchange, and political offices mediate ethical relations but cannot replace voluntary agency, equitable discernment, or formed character.
[Persistent] Outward magnitude, conformity, success, possession, or injury never suffices to determine moral status independently of motive, knowledge, control, choice, and end.
[Emergent] Ethical classification must differentiate domains by object, scale, relation, activity, causal source, and end instead of applying one homogeneous standard.
[Attractor] The noble, the just, and the human good as a whole function as end-selecting attractors that organize calibration without receiving a fully independent specification.
[Terminal] Practical wisdom completes the operational account of ethical action by integrating universals, particulars, desire, and command, while theoretical wisdom remains superior in object.
The mean retains its function as an anti-excess structure but changes form from multidimensional fit, to equality between persons and shares, to the judgment of the practically wise agent.
Particularity escalates from a limit on quantitative moral rules, through a source of legal exception, into the endpoint apprehended by practical intellect.
Stable character persists, but its function expands from regulating domains of conduct to grounding just agency and finally to supplying the right end of deliberation.
Other-regard migrates from social accommodation and truthful presentation into the constitutive definition of justice and then into the political embeddedness of prudence.
Scale shifts from moderate and great forms of individual virtue to distributive, civic, legislative, and judicial scales of practical reason.

Quantity reverses function: absolute amount is rejected as a moral measure, arithmetic and geometric proportion are admitted within restricted justice operations, and all formulas are reabsorbed into particular judgment.
External goods migrate from instruments and enabling conditions of individual excellence into objects of allocation and exchange, then into political conditions of personal practical good.
Truth changes function from accurate social self-presentation into the defining activity of differentiated rational capacities and the agreement of reason with desire in action.
Shame disappears after performing boundary work: its demotion from virtue helps stabilize the later distinction between reactive feeling, voluntary action, rational choice, and developed character.
[Local] Generosity, magnificence, magnanimity, anger, sociability, truthfulness, and wit remain domain-specific demonstrations of calibration rather than independent current-level foundations.
[Local] Geometric distribution, arithmetic rectification, and monetary commensuration remain specialized justice operators; none becomes a universal formula for virtue.
[Local] The labels scientific knowledge, intellect, skill, practical wisdom, and wisdom remain a rational taxonomy, while their generating differentiation by object and end scales upward.
[Scaling] Stable disposition, noble choice, particular perception, and fitting affect scale upward because they govern character virtue, just agency, and practical truth.
[Bridge] Universal justice bridges personal virtue and civic order by translating character excellence into law-governed conduct toward others.
[Catalyst] Equity converts the universal–particular conflict inside law into a demand for the discerning and commanding capacities later assigned to practical wisdom.
[Superseded] The initial appeal to “correct reason” as an unexplained standard is replaced by an embodied configuration of experience, right desire, deliberation, perception, and command.
No single arithmetic midpoint governs ethical correctness; numerical equality is legitimate only inside specifically delimited relations.
No outward act, result, or conformity independently determines virtue, justice, or practical wisdom.
Wealth, honor, power, shares, or civic position cannot themselves establish the excellence required to use or distribute them well.
Neither emotional suppression nor cognition detached from desire can constitute practical excellence.
Universal law cannot function as final normative closure because practical particulars necessarily generate remainder and correction.
Individual excellence cannot be atomistically self-sufficient because justice requires others and practical good depends on household and political order.
Moral vocabulary, equality, and reason cannot be treated as univocal because each divides into functionally distinct states and operations.
The architecture excludes ethical formalism: no rule can generate the right response independently of formed desire and perception of particulars.
It excludes surface consequentialism: magnitude, gain, harm, or successful completion cannot settle moral attribution without reference to agency and end.
It excludes an atomistic model of agency in which private character can be completed independently of reciprocal association, law, exchange, and political order.
It excludes sovereign legalism and pure conventionalism alike: adopted rules bind, but natural, proportional, and equitable standards remain capable of correcting them.
It excludes ethically neutral instrumental reason as the source of goodness because cleverness can optimize any end while practical wisdom requires a good end.
An independent criterion for the noble, the fitting, distributive merit, and the right practical end is unavailable; validation repeatedly returns to the developed good agent or political order.
A complete common metric of worth is absent: individual virtue, political merit, heterogeneous goods, and contemplative rank cannot be placed on one scale.
A perfectly exhaustive legal order is impossible because contingent action always preserves a zone unavailable to prior universal codification.

The origin of the already formed practical agent remains absent: habituation, education, law, experience, character, and practical wisdom presuppose one another without a complete developmental sequence.
Universal reciprocal personhood is not admitted; the full jurisdiction of justice depends on a prior political boundary that excludes dependent household relations.
A frictionless unity of practical and contemplative completion is unavailable because practical wisdom is indispensable to human action yet cannot govern the superior object of theoretical wisdom.

Justice is a specialized transformation of the mean: it externalizes calibration into relations among persons, shares, injuries, and institutions without turning all virtue into mathematical equality.
Equity is the juridical operation of practical wisdom because it joins a universal norm to an irreducible particular and commands the correction required by legislative intent.
Law and character form a recursive circuit: law coordinates virtues toward civic happiness, but only formed agents can deliberate, apply, and equitably correct law.

Moral attribution requires a layered passage from the material description of an act through knowledge, control, choice, desire, and character; no layer can be inferred directly from the preceding one.
Political institutions distribute the external conditions under which higher excellences can be exercised even though those conditions cannot confer virtue.

Ethical and political rationality seek sufficient relational determinacy rather than exact commensuration: proportional judgment, money, law, and practical wisdom each manage a remainder they cannot abolish.

“Complete virtue” is non-univocal: greatness of soul crowns character, justice completes virtue toward others, and practical wisdom completes action, while none displaces theoretical wisdom’s superiority of object.
Moral formation moves from reactive correction toward internally commanded choice: shame may restrain the unformed, but mature virtue requires voluntary action issuing from practical reason.
Ethical normativity is a distributed circuit in which character selects ends, practical wisdom specifies action, institutions structure relations, and equity repairs institutional universals.
The authority of a practical universal depends on its capacity for particular correction; corrigibility is therefore constitutive of practical normativity rather than an external concession.
Epistemic authority shifts from detached formula to the experienced and ethically formed perceiver, while that perceiver remains dependent on political and institutional formation.
Distribution and exchange indirectly shape the realizability of virtue by controlling resources, recognition, association, and future access without determining intrinsic worth.
Practical time is asymmetrical: settled character carries a formed past, deliberation addresses contingent futures, money secures future exchange, and equity responds to unforeseen cases.

Agency is neither wholly internal nor institutionally reducible: action originates in the chooser but receives its objects, opportunities, classifications, and consequences through relational structures.
Human fulfilment has a dual architecture: practical integration secures good action within a shared world, but contemplation preserves a superior object not subordinated to political usefulness.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Character–prudence loop: character makes the end right → practical wisdom determines realization → correct choice expresses and stabilizes complete virtue → complete virtue remains inseparable from practical wisdom.
Universal–particular loop: general norm → exceptional case → perceptual or equitable correction → restored normative purpose → renewed but still non-exhaustive universal.
Agent–polity loop: law coordinates virtue → formed agents deliberate and judge → prudent legislation and equity preserve law → political order sustains individual practical good.
Goods–association loop: resources enable benefaction and large action → allocation and exchange organize access → exchange reproduces association → association supplies the field for virtuous use.
End–choice loop: formed desire preserves the end → deliberation searches for realization → practical judgment commands choice → action expresses the end and the agent’s character.
Mean-escalation path: domain-relative fit → scalar differentiation → interpersonal equality → juridical correction → phronetic determination of the fitting particular.
The noble/right/fitting functions as the central attractor: it orders giving, anger, social conduct, law, deliberation, and choice while resisting reduction to a prior formula.

Taxonomic recurrence marks phase change: ordinary terms are divided into hidden senses, each sense receives a distinct operation, and the original term returns as a structured family rather than a unity.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Heterogeneous domains disclose multiple parameters of success and failure; excess and deficiency generate the initial need for relational calibration.
Relational calibration joined to noble choice, fitting affect, and stable disposition generates character virtue but leaves “correct reason” incompletely specified.
Extension toward others transforms calibrated character into justice, dividing complete lawfulness from particular fairness.
Particular fairness differentiates equality into distribution, rectification, and reciprocal exchange, thereby producing institutional rather than merely personal mediation.
The failure of universal law to exhaust particulars generates equity as an immanent corrective operation.
The unresolved demand for correct reason divides rational capacities by object and end, isolating practical wisdom as truth-attaining reason for contingent action.
Practical wisdom integrates experienced particulars, right desire, deliberation, judgment, and command, thereby operationally closing the mean and justice architectures.
The completed practical system remains nested beneath theoretical wisdom, producing a layered rather than unitary account of rational human fulfilment.
Heterogeneous conduct → parameter differentiation → context-relative mean → stable character virtue.
Character virtue → social relation → complete virtue toward others → universal justice.
Particular unfairness → relational inequality → differentiated equalities → distribution, rectification, and exchange.
Political association → universal law → misfitting particular → equitable restoration of legal purpose.
Indeterminate correct reason → differentiated rational capacities → practical truth → practical wisdom.
Right desire + experienced perception + deliberation + command → correct choice → good action → practical happiness → contemplative horizon.
The mean is redrawn from an apparent midpoint into a family of domain-sensitive, relation-sensitive, and judgment-dependent operations.
Virtue is redrawn from private self-command into a relational and politically embedded organization of action.
Equality ceases to mean sameness and becomes a selection among proportional distribution, arithmetic repair, reciprocal commensuration, and equitable judgment.
Law is reclassified from final command into a universal practical instrument whose legitimacy includes its correction by particulars.
Reason is reclassified from a homogeneous faculty or detachable rule into differentiated truth-attaining capacities indexed to objects, activities, and ends.
Moral reading shifts from classifying visible conduct to reconstructing the alignment among resources, motive, knowledge, control, desire, law, and character.

External goods become politically significant without becoming intrinsic measures of worth: they are instruments, distributable conditions, media of association, and constraints on practical possibility.
Surface level: the system classifies conduct concerning wealth, honor, passion, social interaction, allocation, injury, exchange, law, judgment, and rational activity.
Structural level: stable character, proportional relations, institutions, and differentiated rational capacities jointly mediate correct action.
Metastrategic level: ethical instruction shifts from naming virtues and rules to forming agents capable of semantic discrimination, proportional judgment, equitable correction, and practical command.

Ontological / Temporal level: reality divides between necessary objects of contemplation and contingent fields of action populated by plural agents, mutable norms, finite goods, formed histories, and open futures.

Methodological / Performative level: the system performs its thesis by repeatedly dividing an apparently unified term, testing its limits, returning to particulars, and rebuilding unity as a differentiated functional architecture.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: The substantive standards of nobility, merit, fittingness, and the right end remain underdetermined, forcing the architecture to rely on the very good agent and political order it seeks to explain.
Virtue is denied dependence on fortune for its worth yet higher excellences require wealth, recognition, institutional position, or favorable political conditions for their exercise.
Universal justice is defined through complete virtue toward others while full political justice is restricted to free reciprocal associates, leaving other-regard dependent on prior exclusion.
Natural justice must possess normative force yet remains changeable, while legal rules bind yet require equitable departure; neither stability nor mutability becomes sovereign.
Practical wisdom and developed virtue are mutually necessary, but their reciprocal dependence obscures how either first becomes complete.
Practical wisdom is indispensable to human fulfilment and political order but remains subordinate in object to a theoretical wisdom it neither governs nor fully integrates.
The mean mutates from qualitative fit into formal equality and then into the activity of an experienced practical judge.
Complete virtue mutates from a total character presupposed by greatness of soul, to complete virtue toward others, to the reciprocal unity of practical wisdom and character.
Correct reason mutates from an implicit criterion of the mean into a differentiated practical state integrating truth, desire, experience, and command.
Social relation mutates from a domain of interpersonal demeanor into the constitutive field of justice and then into the political infrastructure of individual good.

Reality appears as a multi-scale self-correcting calibrator: local actions are measured relationally, institutions stabilize those relations, and practical judgment repairs every universal at the point of application.
The subject is not an isolated will but a habituated, desiring, perceiving, deliberating node embedded in networks of law, exchange, household, and political association.
Time is a field of asymmetrical practical navigation: character condenses the past, deliberation addresses contingent futures, and equitable judgment responds to events no prior rule could exhaust.

Possible struggle consists neither in escaping mediation nor obeying it mechanically, but in preserving right ends while navigating excess, deficiency, unequal relations, institutional rules, and exceptional particulars.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the current-level engine: relational mean, differentiated equality, institutional mediation, particular correction, and integrated practical wisdom.
The architecture remains underdetermined concerning the content of the noble, distributive merit, the naturally best political order, and the independent validation of practical ends.
The system is coherent at this scale because its domain classifications, justice structures, and rational taxonomy converge on the same universal–particular and character–judgment architecture.

The architecture is strongest where it differentiates outwardly similar acts by relation, agency, end, and circumstance, and where it assigns distinct operations to distinct kinds of equality and reason.

Reconstruction depends on preserving the sequence from calibrated disposition through relational justice to practical wisdom, together with recursive returns from universals to particulars and from action to character.

The element most resistant to axiomatic reduction is the formed good agent whose perception supplies practical determinacy while the genesis and independent validation of that formation remain unavailable.

identity.title: Chapters 04–06
identity.context: Book IV · Book V · Book VI

items.text: The governing problem is how finite agents whose correct commitments do not automatically become action can nevertheless attain stable, shared, and politically supported flourishing.
Ethical order is reconstructed through two coupled coordinations: reason, affect, perception, and action within the agent; goodwill, recognition, activity, and reciprocity between agents.
The system moves from intrapersonal fracture through the revaluation of pleasure to interpersonal association and finally to communal-political organization.

Its argument is dialectical-classificatory: apparent sameness is decomposed by object, end, principle, activity, and measure, after which primary, qualified, and analogical forms are hierarchically reconstructed.
Stable ethical states become real only through activity; activity becomes complete only when neither internal affect nor external deprivation, isolation, or political disorder prevents enactment.
Pleasure changes from a possible captor of practical perception into an activity-specific amplifier and then into a test distinguishing incidental association from character-grounded shared life.

Individual ethics therefore expands rather than closes: preserved rational principle requires virtuous enactment, virtuous enactment requires suitable companions, and companionship requires a communal field of justice and common benefit.
The closure is recursive and conditional: flourishing is unimpeded virtuous activity continually maintained across psychic, relational, material, temporal, and political interfaces.
[Persistent] Ethical states and relations are classified by their governing object, end, principle, and mode of enactment rather than by surface behavior or affection alone.
[Persistent] Stable ethical identity resides in rational choice and character: vice corrupts the practical principle, while complete friendship is grounded in virtuous character.
[Mutating] A disposition is not identical with its exercise: knowledge may be possessed but inactive, and friendship may persist as a state while shared activity is suspended.
[Emergent] Human flourishing requires both intrapersonal coordination of practical cognition and interpersonal coordination through recognized reciprocal activity.

[Mutating] Pleasure has no fixed ethical valence: it can capture the practical particular, arise incidentally from deficiency, ground unstable association, or strengthen worthy activity and complete friendship.
[Persistent] Unqualified forms establish normative centres from which qualified and analogical forms derive their intelligibility without becoming identical to the primary form.
[Emergent] Disorder remains reparable only while a governing measure survives: correct practical principle permits persuasion, and a shared relational end permits proportional repair.
[Attractor] Unimpeded worthy activity shared with fitting companions is the point at which happiness, proper pleasure, virtue, and complete friendship converge.
[Persistent] Ethical coordination requires fitting relation rather than mechanical sameness: desire must answer to true reason, and unequal contributions must answer to proportion.
[Emergent] Virtue is simultaneously an internal ordering principle and the relational substrate of trust, durability, reciprocal benefit, and shared pleasure.

[Terminal] Politics enters the constitution of ethical life because communities distribute the common activities, justice, friendship, and external conditions through which character becomes effective.
[Attractor] The human agent is embodied, composite, temporally vulnerable, and relationally dependent rather than rationally sovereign or socially self-sufficient.
[Stable identity] The object or reason grounding a response continues to determine its ethical species, whether the response is appetite-directed action or love directed toward another.
[Functional recurrence] The state/activity distinction migrates from cognition and pleasure into friendship: possession establishes continuity, but exercise establishes ethical actuality.
[Reversal] Pleasure moves from affective disruption of correct action to the proper completion and strengthening of natural activity.
[Expansion] Pleasure then becomes relational: as an incidental reason for loving it produces conditional friendship, while in complete friendship it is integrated with goodness and shared activity.

[Absorption] The distinction between unqualified and qualified incontinence is absorbed into a broader architecture in which primary forms function as standards for deficient, conditional, and analogical relations.
[Functional displacement] Correct reason and proportional reciprocity perform parallel measuring functions: each converts heterogeneous impulses or contributions into an ordered relation.
[Terminal transformation] Self-sufficiency ceases to mean immunity from need and becomes freedom from remedial dependence compatible with constitutive dependence on companions and enabling goods.
[Escalation] Vulnerability expands from an episodic internal interruption of practical cognition to temporal erosion of friendship and political destruction of its communal basis.

[Disappearance after structural work] The universal-particular mechanism remains locally specific, but its result survives as the global proposition that a correct disposition never guarantees its own enactment.

[Productive reversal] Lack of rational capacity excludes animals from ethical attribution, whereas a human reduced to instrumental status can re-enter friendship and justice through retained capacities for law and agreement.

[Lower-layer local] The universal judgment–perceptual particular–bodily motion mechanism remains the specific explanation of incontinence; what scales upward is the nonidentity of disposition and enactment.

[Lower-layer local → Scales upward] The restriction of unqualified incontinence to bodily appetite remains local, while its primary/qualified/analogical taxonomy becomes a general classificatory operator.

[Lower-layer local → Scales upward] The three friendship species remain relational machinery, but their derivation from the reason for loving scales into a general rule that ethical value follows generative end.
[Bridge] The state/activity distinction links inactive practical knowledge, pleasure as activity, friendship as disposition, and shared life as enactment.
[Bridge] Proper pleasure joins the internal and relational architectures because it strengthens worthy activity and belongs intrinsically to complete shared life.
[Transition catalyst] The reconstruction of pleasure prevents the movement to friendship from reducing companions to remedies for deficiency.

[Transition catalyst] Preserved first principle becomes stable virtuous character at the relational threshold: the former makes correction possible, while the latter makes complete friendship durable.
[Superseded] Self-control is no longer an adequate terminal image of ethical success; conflictual adherence to reason must give way to virtuous activity capable of shared life.
[Current-level emergence] External goods are recoded from generic impediment-prevention into material, friendly, and political conditions of relational actuality.
Ethical identity is not inferable from an external action, an affective feeling, or an immediate sign of attachment.
Possessing correct knowledge or goodwill is not equivalent to actively governing conduct or sustaining shared life.
Pleasure is neither uniformly bad nor sufficient by itself to establish a good action, good life, or complete friendship.
Neither defective character nor friendship forms a single undifferentiated continuum; object, principle, end, and reciprocity produce irreducible species.
Happiness is not solitary rational possession insulated from embodiment, fortune, companionship, and common life.
Justice and formal agreement are not sufficient to produce concord where reciprocal concern and shared activity are absent.
Ethical equality is not identical quantity, indiscriminate constancy, or the erasure of difference.
A human being cannot be exhaustively reduced to present dysfunction or instrumental status when the relevant rational and communal capacities remain.
The system requires the falsity of automatic rational sovereignty: universal knowledge cannot be assumed to command perception, appetite, and movement without mediation.
It excludes atomistic flourishing because complete activity requires enabling goods, companions, shared life, and a viable communal field.
It disqualifies moral externalism: identical actions or exchanges can embody different principles, choices, ends, and relational forms.
It rejects hedonistic monism because pleasure varies with activity and nature, while pleasure-grounded love remains inferior to love grounded in character.
It excludes an atemporal model of ethical excellence: episodic affect, habituated character, tested confidence, distance, and changing circumstances alter what exists in activity.
It rejects ethical formalism because neither verbally available knowledge nor legal coordination can replace exercised cognition, common activity, and concord.
It excludes both flat equality and unlimited hierarchy: sameness cannot measure unequal relations, but absolute disparity destroys their common measure.
It disqualifies invulnerable human actuality: pain, deprivation, internal affective disruption, relational separation, and political corruption can impede otherwise correct states.
The unavailable centre is seamless conversion: neither knowledge into action nor goodwill into shared life occurs without vulnerable mediating interfaces.
No autarkic human subject is available whose good remains complete independently of body, fortune, friends, and political community.
No universal currency can reconcile every ethical difference; truth, honour, benefit, need, virtue, pleasure, and inherited obligation require heterogeneous measures.
Ethical relation becomes impossible where no common activity, law, agreement, good, or measure remains.
Invariant human satisfaction is unavailable: unimpededness remains contingent, mutable, and distributed, while unchanging pleasure is displaced to the divine limit.
Final identity between self-good and other-good remains unachieved; complete friendship coordinates them without fully deriving their nonconflict.
Fully symmetrical social reciprocity remains unavailable because proportional equality is articulated through naturalized structures of paternal, marital, political, and social superiority.
Dispositional correctness can survive interruption without constituting present ethical actuality: inactive knowledge and inactive friendship are real but incomplete states.
Proper pleasure is the relay between individual excellence and friendship because it strengthens worthy activity while making shared virtuous life intrinsically pleasant.

Relations grounded in deficiency or changing affect are structurally unstable, whereas activities and friendships grounded in unimpaired nature or stable character can persist through changing circumstances.
Corruption of the practical first principle disables complete friendship because the character unable to identify the good rightly cannot love another as good for the other’s sake.

The incontinent agent can preserve correct judgment yet cannot fully instantiate complete friendship qua incontinent, because complete friendship requires the practical wisdom and stable virtue that incontinence lacks.
Friendship specifies the relational content of happiness’s external dependence: good companions are required not as remedies for deficiency but as co-agents of excellent activity.
